Van Helsing 2 is ultimately an improvement over the first game, but not without it's own flaws.
PROS:
-A good aesthetic that lends itself to the story and place.
-Fun skills.
-3 classes. You MUST specialize in a few specific skills to be effective. I used the same 3-4 skills through the whole game.
-Better (more consistent) difficulty curve than the first game. Not without it's spikes though.
- More forgiving than the first game.
-Aside from a small complaint or two (See below) I never ran into any bugs or glitches.
-A lot of skills. This merits multiple playthroughs.
Cons:
-I started with keyboard and mouse. The problem with this is with this setup, you have to click on specific enemies to shoot them. If you don’t click on an enemy, your character just walks to that place instead. So i ended up walking into fight when I intended to fight from a distance. With a 360 controller, you press the skill and it finds the closest enemy, This seemed to be a better method in my experience.
-Occasionally I would get stuck on geometry on the ground that seemed like i should be able to walk through.
-Pressing up on the controller (D-PAD) teleports you to the base. The issue is i accidentally did this quite often and i became annoying.
-Could have been longer (was hoping for >15 hours)
Overall a good action RPG and easily an improvement over the first game. I will eventually go through it again with a different skill set.

Classic fighting game returns!
This is  also a surprisingly good fighting game, by virtue of being based mostly off of Mortal Kombat 2 (more juggling, less dial-a-combo) gameplay-wise, and then adding it's own super meter mechanics, and a slew of command moves to make the individual characters more varied while retaining the easy-to-learn basic 5 button setup the series started with.
Other improvements (some carried over from the earlier full 3D installments) are more unique models for characters that used to be straight pallette swaps, inclusion of tag-team matches, a few truckloads of unlockable assest (concept art, full soundtrack, alternate costumes), a basic tutorial, a Challenge Mode for more in-depth practice and weird twists, and a full-blown story mode that comprises of an alternate timeline to MK 1 - 3, which is delightfully cheesy and pretty cohesive.
Biggest issue I have is also with the story mode: While parts of them are rendered with the in-game engine, most of it is compression-artifact laden pre-rendered footage which was obviously recorded using the same in-game engine. So that seems kind of bone-headed. Also, far more annoying: the cutscenes can't be interrupted.
On the whole, this should be in any fighting games fan's collection.

Sanctum 2, the sequel to the popular FPS tower defense game Sanctum. Developed by Coffee Stain Studios.
Sanctum is an addicting tower defense game where you not only get to set up a maze for the lumes (the main enemies of the game) and set up towers to kill them off with, but also, being armed with weapons of your own, let's you partake in the defense. Like all TD games, you have to successfully defend a point without losing it, and in this case it is the Core. If you let the Core take too much damage from the lumes, then it explodes and you lose. Defend the core for a number of waves of lumes and you win (or keep going for as long as you can if you're playing on Survival mode). A rather unique concept for a game as you do not simply set up your towers and hope that they are able to kill the enemies in time, but you are also forced to plan out your maze first with the space provided in each level and help defend by also killing enemies alongside your towers.
Now, before you go ahead and start throwing your money, there are some things I would like to state my opinion on.
I found this game quite fun and addicting.
-Tower defense combined with FPS. Like I said, a unique concept. Can't just sit, stare, and hope for your towers to do all the work.
-You can now partially upgrade and overcharge towers. Partial upgrades increase tower power (Heehee. It rhymes.) slighty. If a tower is already at max level, you can overcharge it for more damage.
-Multiplayer is fun and balanced. The more players there are, the less damage each individual player does. (2 players= each does 50% damage. 3 players = 33% damage. 4 players= 25% damage.)
-New characters to play as! All have different abilities and gun play as well as different voice acting.
-Several new towers, weapons, and enemy types.
-New perk system which provides perks that help you in-game.
-An actual storyline presented in the game. As you play through the campaign, you get cutscenes before every level that are comics displaying the characters and their dialogue and actions.
-The lumes will actually attack you directly if you get too close to them.
-There are new boss type enemies that change up playstyle.
-Rank system. As you level up your rank, you unlock more towers, weapons, and perks.
-The new Feats of Strength system adds a new challenge perspective to the game. Instead of just more durable enemies, you can make them move faster, regenerate health over time, and more. The more Feats of Strength you add, the bigger exp bonus you get to level up your rank.
With all this aside, I, however, probably wouldn't recommend this for people who are fans of the first Sanctum.
Why? Well, compared to the first game, Sanctum 2 felt drastically different in a weird way.
-In Sanctum 1, you are able to upgrade your towers and weapons up by 5 levels for a total of 6 levels for each. In Sanctum 2, towers only have 3 levels and you cannot upgrade your firearms through spending resources at all.
-In 1, the resources you gain after waves increase in amount. In 2, you seemingly gain the the same/near the same amount of resources after every wave.
-In 1, everything required resources in-game (placing blocks, building towers, upgrading). In 2, tower blocks--- or should I say bases--- were separated from the resources. So now, You would need to spend tower bases instead of resources to lay out your maze. (In other words, tower bases= walls for your maze. Resources= towers and upgrades.)
-You can build no more than 15 towers in a level in 2 (unless you play on sandbox mode and remove the tower limit).
-Sanctum 2 seems to be tipping more towards gun play than tower play. You may start to feel so powerful with character abilities and the new perk system.
-You can pick a difficulty in 1. In 2, however, there is no definite scalable difficulty (except the Easymode game mode). With the Feats of Strength, it's just that enemies are faster, regenerating health over time, etc.
-There are no Televators in 2. The only way to teleport is to respawn at the core after dying (respawning typically has a 10 second wait time).
-DLC seems to be one of the main driving forces for 2 as not only are there DLC with many new maps, but also new storylines, weapons, perks, towers, and another new character.
-Even though Sanctum 2 does present some kind of story, it still feels a bit lacking. Not much explanation has gone into it.
-Sanctum 2, for some reason, felt just ...smaller... than the first game to me. The shorter tower base height, smaller resource gain, less tower upgrades, no weapon levels, and other factors contributed to this feeling.
Bottom line, I like it, but it's an awkward one to recommend to others. Sanctum 2 may be cool for people new to Sanctum and/or like FPS games, but fans of the first game and traditional TD games will and do have differing opinions. Whether you should buy it is up to you. As for me, I'll just click "Yes" and "Post Review".

This game is so lovely.
It beats the new Doom 4 game many times over and over again.
If you are standing for a choice between buying this,
or buying the new Doom 4, buy this instead.
You will enjoy it much more, I promise you.
This review applies to Doom 3 and RoE,
not the other doom games inside this package.
First, you get that nice peaceful playable intro
without action that almost every game have today.
Such intros always gives you a nice entrypoint
(where you come from and why) while it "starts up"
the story in a proper way, and also gives a exploration
opportunity to learn more about the
in-game world without being disturbed by enemies.
Then, you get pretty much thinking.
You must read PDA's, Emails, listen to audio logs,
figure out codes to proceed. Sometimes you need
to read Emails or listen to logs to figure out what to
do next, for example where specific mission-critical
objects are stored.
And you get no help, you need to figure out platforming
for yourself when that becomes applicable.
That makes it extra fun.
Another nice thing is that many ingame objects not
necessary for progressing, is also interactive,
so sometimes the object is just for fun/enjoyment,
sometimes the object is just a red herring to fool
you into thinking this is the next step to take, when
it turns out its not
(For example, a door that never can be unlocked,
eg requires a PDA or keycard not in game).
This interactivity also adds to realism and it
makes the game more fun to play.
Also, the really nice thing is that you sometimes
return to a central "hub" (so theres multiple "hubs")
that is specific for the chapter you played, after
having collected some keycard/PDA or done
some objective, which makes it extra fun as
you get to revisit old places and take new
paths from there. This gives you a more sense of the facility.
Also, theres a lot of puzzles that you need to figure out,
one notable example is the maintenace elevator/platform,
where you are given a slight hint and you have to figure
the rest out itself.
And the cryo storage bins puzzle is GREAT. First you
think its just a dead end but after a while you figure it out.
And that lovely crane minigame with the toxic leaking barrels
was just beutiful.
Also theres other cool minigames like the turkey punch-out too.
I could warmly recommend this instead of Doom 4.
Put Doom 4 in the garbage bin and buy this instead!
Why this should win the Steam Prize:
Because of the few, but excellent mix of minigames, both the crane game, the cryo game and the service platform minigame. Combine that with the hilarious turkey punch out arcade cabinet found in the canteen, and this is a prize winner!

Left 4 Dead or what we fans call 'L4D' is an action based horror FPS game developed by Valve in 2008. "Green Flu" a highly contagious virus causes extreme aggression, mutation to the body cells and loss of higher brain functions. Two weeks after the infection four immune survivors : Bill, a Vietnam veteran, Zoey, a college student; Louis, an IT analyst and Francis, an outlaw biker make their way through the city fighting infected, dangerous mutations. There are 2 types of infected, special infected like hunters, boomers, smokers and tanks and other type is common infected that aren't playable. There is one more special infected called 'witch', you can't choose her in Versus Mode. There are originally 20 maps and 10 weapons. Not all L4D1 achievements and maps are ported to L4D2. And not all of us play L4D2 as much as L4D1. So I recommend buying L4D Bundle, it better for you to decide which one is your type.
So there are 4 ways of playing this game :
● Single/Offline Mode : You and three AI bots play through campaigns battling against hordes of common infected & 5 special infected through many chapters divided into smaller maps.
● Multi/Co-op Mode : You and your 3 friends/online players play through campaigns battling against hordes of common infected & 5 special infected through many chapters divided into smaller maps. For the newbies, don't directly jump to expert servers as people there wouldn't care much to teach you what's right/wrong and will simply vote kick you. I'll cover this part at the end.
● Versus Mode lets you compete four-on-four with friends, either playing as a human trying to get rescued or as 4 playable special infected.
● Survival Mode : You survive in a closed area and hold out against the infected horde and special infected as long as possible and compare your stats with your friends. There are 3 medals : Gold, Silver and Bronze based on your survival time.
This game requires you to work with your teammates and help them and get help in return. When you get pounced on by a hunter or get dragged by smoker or generally incapped by an infected, only your friends can revive you so make sure you treat them nicely.
Only thing I see people complaining here is that they get vote kicked for not doing anything. Here is a list of things you should consider and follow to not get kicked by others.
● If you see an incapped survivor, based on situation if its possible and easy to revive them then help them, don't simply leave them there. I know its called Left 4 Dead :D
● Make sure you don't hurt your teammates. In case you hurt them, heal them with your kits or give them your pills [Pills Here!] Least you can do is apologize before they call a vote.

●
● In the Versus Mode, it is important to work as a team. Since it is 4v4 (or same level), all the players have to incap all the survivors at the same time. One survivor is enough to ruin others attempt. you will likely get kicked if you stay apart or just roam around as an infected.
● Don't change your team in Versus Mode, not just kicked, admin might ban you too. (Personal Experience :P)
Even after following all the rules and you might still get kicked. Don't get disappointed if someone kicks you, even players with 1k hours still get kicked. Sometimes, people just kick you to help their friend get a slot or if you have very high ping.

Honestly, I tried really hard to enjoy this game. I saw it on steam a few months ago and was really excited to get it and give it a try, as it had good reviews. I'm sure some of you will enjoy it, but personally I didn't. The controls are strange, which is fine, but the tutorial is very lack luster, and I was left confused for my play through wondering how dodges worked. I discovered combos were a thing right at the end of my playthrough. Combos didn't seem necessary when I could just as easily button mash and still kill the enemy just fine with no damage taken. The upgrades are also a little bit underwhelming. I would love to see the upgrades add more variation beyond pressing J and I repeatedly. OST is alright from what I heard, and the art is nice to look at.
My main problem, is the narration feels very forced at times. I understand where the inspiration for this game comes from, but it feels like the game was created purposely to try and push players not to listen to the narrator and to go out and find stuff, rather than surprising the player with the ability to ignore the narrator. I wish ignoring the narrator was just more subtle. Other than that, the fourth wall breaking is a nice touch, but it feels, again, very forced, as if the game "breaking" or "getting to an unfinished level" was so forced that the narrator, or game creator, tried so hard to force the player to experience that moment. I didn't feel like I was discovering things I wasnt supposed to, just because it was so easy to leave. Good moments involved the game going into some sort of console and toying with its own playability. I would've loved to see that expanded upon, as it instantly reminded me of games like Pony Island and SuperHot.
Aside from that, I'm sure some of you will enjoy the game. Give it a try if you've enjoyed The Stanley Parable and games of the like. Just for me personally, it wasnt a game I enjoyed.

Many eons ago, long-lived a futuristic cyberbot known as Proto Man. Proto Man was crafted from the ground-up through the utilization of determination while being that self-arrogant and prideful
character. While maintaining his cool apparatus with his awesome gear and accessories, he would eliminate all enemies standing in his way. The Battle Network series in
was known for its computer cyberspace world that transitioned well between computer terminals and other real-world locations. Is
another attempt at recovering
from Capcom’s losses entirely, or rather, is it a different game altogether?


centers around a beautiful protagonist looking creation that becomes very similar to Proto Man but with many better moves. Also, the genre is action, adventure with occasional platform elements to reinforce the main drive of its hack-and-slash roots. We are thrown into
within the main story as we first learn about a character named Judas. Whether this is the same Judas alluded to in biblical history, we will never know. However, we do know that Judas is the main antagonist that has sent robots and other strange creatures to do his own bidding against us. There is some talk about him attempting to become a god which is quite ambiguous, to say the least.

is told from the point-of-view of a separate narrator in traditional to simplified Chinese language. Likewise, of some languages, some can say more in fewer words while others say less in more words. It tends to be the latter when in comparison towards the audio dialogue by following along with English subtitles. One aspect that catches you off guard will be the procedure by which game difficulty is chosen. Instead of the standard layout in which difficulty can be changed and lowered through the main menu, it is rather determined through a short questionnaire throughout guided responses. These questions determine difficulty, enemy count, and story depth. Graphics, on the other hand, show some age and wear over time.

The art style is unique to the Chinese and Japanese culture. It takes place in a cyberpunk universe with dull scenery and a gloomy tint of color. I was expecting a brighter array of colors since the character is pretty translucent. It does make up some for it within its gameplay. The map layout could seldom be compared to
but without the addition of dazzling colors. I think it best alludes towards the earlier
graphics but more so the
series. It mirrors
perfectly almost even within its same shade. The bridges are a light sky blue color which prominently overtakes by a large margin the other environments.

Since
is hack-and-slash at heart, keyboard controls are exceptional, right? Wrong, the keyboard layout of controls is very uncomfortable. The original keybindings are not tied to the use of the mouse.
is best played through either a Xbox or PlayStation controller. One defect I found earlier on with the controls was a delay in time response frequency. Every time I would go to press A or B to interact with things tied to progression, sometimes, I would have to hit each button string of commands twice; the lack of response latency becomes more frustrating later on. Enemies are all patterned based; controls are combo based. It is a mash-up between the intersection of the intuitiveness of beat-em-up with low-budget
like actions to stun and disassemble enemies.
The story is meager and perplexing. It is sometimes classified as a dream within another dream. Remember the NetNavi’s in
? Yes, a similar mechanic is brought back front and center but completely remains out-of-place. The story’s pacing is ruined by messages that randomly pop-up in this NetNavi form, failure of system error’s in the computer terminal, and even the layout maps of places that block many messages from being read. This is the worse example of system implementation from navigating both in a logical order and outstanding balance between the two. Upgrades can be purchased which increase abilities, combo attacks, and new ways to slice-and-dice enemies. However, the lack of other allies to team up with together, options that are  not available nor can be accessed in-game without exiting to the main menu, and changing between controller, keyboard controls with a mediocre non-chronological storyline with poor use of locking into enemies once dashing makes for a mediocre experience. All in all, simply put,
adds a new flair of style but barely makes it over the mark to actually do what it tries to attempt, well.

I dislike this game as a tower defense game because it isn't.  A few maps are heavily dependent upon towers at easier difficulties but you quickly discover that the right combination of character and weapon can do more damage than all your towers combined, and hard mode is designed with this in mind.   There are some levels where you can do 90% of the total damage done and still lose the round.  And then the designers start trying to achieve greater difficulty by throwing in enemies that are 100% immune to towers, and then gimmicky enemies that towers stop targetting and then they return to 100% health if you don't kill them by yourself fast enough.
The worst part is that they have all the elements for perfection.  Their map design is really creative but then they only give you a  few walls and towers to work with, leaving you feeling like a kid drooling at the lego box for the Millenium Falcon but then looking down at your hand and realizing you only have a dozen blocks to work with. When you only have 2 towers going into round four and maybe 5 or 6 towers going into the final round, there's not much stategy. The game would be more more fun if you were given far more walls and towers and the outcome were determined more by your maze building and tower placement skills, rather than picking the right weapons and perks and then showing off on youtube by killing all the enemies without even bothering to build your token towers.
I thought this would be less of a problem in survival mode but there is no true survival mode.  Survival is just normal mode with the normal waves but it repeats after the last wave and just boosts the health, speed, and regen of enemies by a LOT.  So rather than being a mode where you can try to build the perfect setup and then see how many waves of every increasing monsters you can last through, you're instead just left with another form of hard mode that lasts maybe two or three times as long as normal.
I've never seen a game be SO close to perfection and then just ruin it with poor design choices.  But if you like PVE FPS then I do still recommend this game for you.  Just don't expect much tower strategy in hard mode or you'll be disappointed.

Aliens vs Predator returns and, while the game gets some elements right, it's too bogged down in ancient game mechanics to be a winner. With three short, flawed campaigns for single players and a variety of passable multiplayer games, it's a lopsided production that will disappoint even the most ardent fan.
The Pros
Excellent character models
Aliens are fun to use
Multiplayer is rather fun
The Cons
Looks like a 2010 game, plays like a 1999 one
Insanely frustrating control issues with targeting and kill moves.
Marine campaign is completely uninspired
Way back in 1999, developer Rebellion finally made the dreams of sci-fi-loving gamers everywhere come true. They managed to develop a game based on the Alien and Predator film franchises that lived up to expectations. The first-person shooter captured the elements of each race in an exceptional way, and provided PC gamers with a thrilling blend of horror and action. Sadly, what worked over a decade ago doesn’t necessarily work now, and after playing Rebellion’s Aliens vs Predator reboot, it appears that they’re still partying like it’s 1999.
Aliens vs. Predator

We’re Mincemeat, Man!

That’s not to say Aliens vs. Predator is without merit. It’s still fun to scamper across darkened ceilings as a Xenomorph (the technical name for the Aliens), drop down on unsuspecting, terrified Marines and eat their brains. As a Predator, there’s still a sense of menacing satisfaction when tracking prey through the jungle, then jumping down and ripping their spine and head out. Even the uninspired colonial marine campaign has its moments -- especially near the end when some epic firefights occur.

But all in all, it’s only in fleeting moments where the game really thrives. The story unfurls like a continuation of the god-awful movies, in which Lance Henrikson plays the head of the self-serving and vile Weyland-Yutani corporation. Weyland (now basically cloned over and over) is utterly obsessed with harnessing the Xenomorphs and using them as a bioweapon to make his corporation rich. To that end, he’s using an entire base as his personal science lab.

When Weyland discovers an ancient Predator ruin, a signal is inadvertently sent out to the hunters to come and do what they do best. Aliens escape and chaos ensues; there’s not a shred of originality in the set-up. The game’s dogged use of standards from the movies—right down to all the same sound effects--is partially understandable, yet, ultimately, it feels lazy in presentation.

Three Sides to Every Story

As in previous games, AvP is broken up into three chapters. The human campaign is easily the worst. It has every tired, overused shooter cliché from the late ‘90s. You wake up alone, with only a useless pistol, while some faceless entity keeps barking orders at you. Worse, you don’t even get a name or a voice. Your character is just called “Rookie” and never speaks. He can only carry two other weapons, and his progress is completely linear. Humans always did seem extraneous in a war between the two ultimate sci-fi predators, but the developers seem determined to prove how weak and ineffective humans are here.

The Predator campaign is hardly an improvement in game design, and suffers from the same sort of linear pacing. What’s worse is that Rebellion has actually made the Predator feel wimpy. Although it’s hard to imagine, your Predator is weak, goes on the hunt barely equipped, and only gets new weapons as the story dictates. He also has to find energy sources to suck up to power his gear, which is a suspect game mechanic at best.

The Aliens are the most interesting species to play by far. The sheer joy of blazing across any surface is enough to give the Xenomorph campaign a leg up. Combat is problematic, but once you learn to properly hang to surfaces (hint: hold the button down all the time and you can move from surface to surface without hesitation), they’re just fun bugs to play as. It’s a shame the Alien campaign is the shortest at just about three hours, compared to four or five for the others.  All three species go over common ground as well, so expect to the see the same sights a lot.
Aliens vs. Predator

Kill Your Friends

The controls for both extraterrestrials are the biggest problem. Targeting in the game is simply sloppy. Since you’ll spend a lot of time in melee combat, the game ideally should have a targeting system that makes focusing on prey simple. Instead, you suffer through an impossibly twitchy targeting control that usually leaves you overshooting your enemies with your back exposed and no idea where they are.

Another severe issue is the use of fatalities. Both aliens can perform grisly death moves, but doing so locks you into an uncontrollable canned action for several seconds—more than enough time for any nearby enemies to kill you. While these moves are cool at first, there’s only a few of them and you’ll tire of them quickly.

Thankfully, there is multiplayer, and it’s entertaining in spots, but it won’t force you off any online shooters you might be currently playing. Pitting the three races in a variety of deathmatch and species-based games is generally fun. Each species has their own special game, such as Predator Hunt, a Juggernaut variant in which one player takes the role of a Predator seeking to hunt down opponents. If he gets killed, he’s replaced by his assassin. The Xenomorph version tasks a player with infecting all of the Marines on a map. Most of the multiplayer maps, much like the single player levels, are merely serviceable. There are two excellent co-op survivor maps, in which up to four marines battle endless waves of Xenomorphs, not unlike Horde mode in other shooters. The multiplayer is fun, but not deep enough to draw much lasting power for many players.
Aliens vs. Predator
In Space, No One Can Hear You Sigh

Aliens vs. Predator isn’t an awful game, but it is incredibly disappointing since Rebellion appears to have done so little with the source material . It’s a hard sell when there are significantly better shooters available, both online and offline. While the game isn’t a total loss, there’s just not enough here to make the game recommendable. As it is now, AvP is mostly a visually updated version of an eleven year-old game, and that’s not what fans of the franchises or first-person shooters deserve.

In short:
This game has high potential. It's fun, and I'm looking forward to the full release and the campaign. As it is now the game isn't worth 20$, but once the campaign comes out along with more improvements it will be worth more than 20$. I was close to ask for a refund after 1 hour but decided to keep it and support the devs. There aren't enough games like this anymore and this one is promising. It's like a settlers style game but with much less buildings/resources/upgrades/research options, and on the other hand it has RTS elements and more action since you'll be playing a lot with your military units and fighting neutrals/AI. It's also a faster paced game.
Game play:
I had to restart a few times to get the resources right and not get destroyed in the first winter or storm. You have to manage resources/population/land correctly and save wood and food for winter and for hard times. It seems that after some point you stabilize and then don't have to worry that much anymore about food and wood. At that point you'll worry more about attack and defense. Random neutral attack or AI player attacking your land. The map consists of small areas that allow 2-5 structures each so the game is really pushing to expand, especially in the early-mid game. Most of the time you need fighting units to expand so the game will have you fighting early.
What i think needs to change or be improved (based only on 3-4 hours of play):
- Time should go by slightly slower, seasons are too short. Snow storms make it too hard to see, it's slightly annoying.
- The AI should be smarter.
- Add some diplomacy control options like agreements and pacts.
- Add more food production options.
- More research paths / options (the lore tree).
- Add a siege unit.
- Add special neutrals that give quests / can be recruited.
- Add more neutral structure types.
- Give the war-chief some hero-like aspects like levels.
- Give military units some kind of a slight experience bonus like "veteran".
- More buildings that produce things or give stuff. They should of course be available depending on geography/resources.
- Maybe allow another structure per area because i felt like I'm pushed to expand too quickly.
- More differences between the different clans.
I might sound too critical but that's because I think this game has high potential. I didn't list everything that's good about the game, you can read other reviews for that. Usually I don't leave reviews but this game deserved one.
conclusion:
This is a good game that you'll be able to enjoy for many hours even at this point in time. I think that it's a good investment.

It's a fun romp through Mars, with all the guns and baddies you might remember. Fun for fans, especially since it packs all three currently released titles in one package. Doom 3 itself is an OK title, good if you want to burn a few hours shooting hellspawn. The inclusion of the expansion is also a nice touch for those who want to get everything in one bundle.
It's not without its flaws, however.
The game relies too much on cheap tricks like jump scares and teleporting enemies right behind you, and the experience feels claustrophobic, with always that one route you're supposed to follow while everything else is locked out. The way said teleporting enemies tend to ram you out of nowhere and mess with your sight angle can get annoying, too.
The Brutal Doom mod is more faithful to the original spirit, if you just want to play Doom with a more modern touch up and features like actual aiming. One last personal peeve is the complete absence of subtitles, which can make it annoying to try to hear the keycode to a lock while fighting off random pests that pop up in between. That said, if you want something to pass the time while waiting to see if the new one is any good, this would be a good choice.

There are alot of gripes about this game, and alot of things that hold it back, but it's important to understand what you're getting into here.
First and foremost, I'll start with the bad.
The game had alot of features cut. I'm sure the developers would have liked to add advanced track editing, more songs, more characters, more anything, really. It's a game that aspired to be the best, and while it's good, it fell short of staying in the spotlight due to the aforementioned issues.
The good:
Kickbeat features something that most rhythm games don't have, especially among those that try to bend genres to include a wider audience (I'm looking at you, Audiosurf). At its heart, it's a competitive game. It's a hard game. It's one of the few rhythm games out there that has a scoring system which means something. If you can six-star a song on master, you can post a video on Youtube, and and proceed to feel good about it. This isn't a game that you zone out and play. At least not if you want to do well. At the same time, the game's not impossible, nor is it inaccessible. It incorporates a few ideas, but it doesn't make the gameplay awkward. It's simple, but different, and in this case, it works. The developers made sure that this game ran well, and of course felt good to play. What it skimmed on with features, it more than made up for with a good core.
Getting good at the game is hard, and for some people, just being able to play it is hard. Kickbeat's story mode does a great job of at least making you able to. It's cute. It's funny. It'll make you stop and ask yourself why most games try so hard with their stories.
Rating the value of a competitive rhythm game is hard, especially one that's well aged. I won't. If you play Kickbeat, from start to finish, you'll at least get 10 hours out of it, which isn't bad for the price. If you put it down because it's too hard after two, I guess I failed to warn you enough. The music selection is also one of the best I've heard in any rhythm game out there. They used good artists, and the tracks fit the gameplay well.
Lastly, I feel like I should touch on this, as it's the most important point of all. Do you like the concept of rhythm games, but feel like they're too pointless, are just for ♥♥♥♥♥♥y, and also like watching martial arts combat too intense for modern kung-fu movies? If you answered yes, I'm afraid you need to buy Kickbeat, because even with all of its flaws, this is the best rhythm game on the market for someone who doesn't want to either zone out and fall asleep, or play Osu! all the time.

Neon Drive is a sensational throwback to the 1980s culture cast upon a rhythm-based driving game.
You pilot one of various cars through seven levels, each with three unlockable difficulties. The soundtrack is the strongest part of the experience, featuring dizzying melodies and perfectly voiced harmonies, along with thumping bass.
First I will say that Neon Drive is arguably the most difficult game I have ever played, even at is easiest level. While I won't compare it to the obvious like Dark Souls, this is very much a game that requires concentration and strategy to play and succeed.
Prepare to fail a lot. If you are okay with restarting the same sequence over and over and over and over until you succeed, then this game will not fail you.
Neon Drive is rewarding in that the entire experience offers variety, the right amount of challenge, and a satisfying play session each time. After beating a level on "normal" it unlocks "hard" and "insane" difficulties, which are stupid fun and a true test of hand/eye coordination.
The level design is strong, with cyberpunk backdrops, neon vistas, and more 1980s pop culture references than you could shake your fist at. This game plays similar to Wipeout or Audiosurf and has many similarities to other rhythm games while uniquely defining its own identity.
My only gripes about the game are that it lacks true content. Neon Drive started its life as a mobile game and was ported over to the PC with improvements in graphics and gameplay, as well as adding controller support. If the game had more levels, I feel as though it would justify its current full-price cost of $10USD. However, I purchase it on sale and I would still recommend it. In the future, I would hope that the developers realize the potential of this game and award the fanbase with more levels or modes.
I won't give chew anybody's ears off about this game but I can strongly recommend it for fans of the 1980s, the "aesthetic" movement, or for people who enjoy challenging rhythm games. Neon Drive is a very well-made title.

Buildings have jobs attached to them and you can assign them to villagers and they will automatically do the work needed.
The game map is split into multiple tiles that require you to explore and pay food to expand to build more buildings since buildings are limited per tile.
Villigers can turn into combat units, which you can control to protect and prevent other settlements from taking your expanded areas.
Overally for an early access game, its very well worth the price, Pick it up!

This is one of those games that's look like a generic clone of some other series, but that's a huge disservice to Sleeping Dogs.
In a lot of ways, yes, it is GTA with chinese people, but everything about the world set up in this game is fantastic.
Sleeping Dogs has one of the most spectacular open worlds ever made. The graphics are amazing, even by PC standards. Everything feels alive and real, like it's a world that would continue to exist after you close the game. The main story in the game is executed surprisingly well, with characters you will actually care about and a story that makes sense, and is most importantly, interesting.
Instead of generic gunfights, the majority of the game uses a brawling system very similair to the Batman Arkham games, and it's much more satisfying taking down enemies this way than the standard "shoot the bad guys" approach. Gunplay does pop up occasionally and while it's not anything special, it works and feels decent enough.
If you want to be immersed in a game's world, and want to experience more than just a run of the mill story that's an excuse to shoot people, give Sleeping Dogs a try.

The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing is definitely a diamond in the rough! It is a quirky and humorous take on the traditional isometric RPG where every bit of fantasy media you have ever known and/or loved will be referenced, from a tandem reference to Drizzt Do'urden and Geralt of Rivia to Gandalf the Gray. Not even Terminator is safe from this game's scope with a comment made by Van Helsing that "He won't be back" upon finding an automaton near a foundry. Aside from the quirky aspects the gameplay is great. It has such a range of things to do, from the managment of generals and what jobs they go on, to tower defense, to a chimera named "Fluffy" that you send on hunts and call to your aid in battle. The dynamic between Van Helsing and Lady Katarina is amazing in both combat and story. The love/hate relationship is an instant classic, and the different ways you can level Katarina to either support you in combat, or tank the enemies damage, or sit on the back lines and throw curses, stuns, instakills, etc., is great. I have never seen an RPG with such an in-depth companion system. The only bad thing is that you have only three classes with two sub-classes for each. I may just be too used to the character system of Titan Quest, but I feel that 6 virtual classes is a bit restrictive. However, each class is so well done that I cannot say that the game is blemished much by the lack of other classes. A couple strange things is that some parameters on items display a variable name from the code and there are some typo's, I don't know if there is some sort of oversight involved there or if that's difficult to work out or what, but I can't dock points for mistakes that don't affect the game, so, Should you buy this? Yes. It is an ARPG that is on par with Titan Quest (Which I have spent a few hundred hours on, whether online or off), better than Diablo 2 (blasphemy I know, but there it is, I like D2, but I gotta be honest) and completely out of the sight of Path of Exile.

Neon Drive is a sensational throwback to the 1980s culture cast upon a rhythm-based driving game.
You pilot one of various cars through seven levels, each with three unlockable difficulties. The soundtrack is the strongest part of the experience, featuring dizzying melodies and perfectly voiced harmonies, along with thumping bass.
First I will say that Neon Drive is arguably the most difficult game I have ever played, even at is easiest level. While I won't compare it to the obvious like Dark Souls, this is very much a game that requires concentration and strategy to play and succeed.
Prepare to fail a lot. If you are okay with restarting the same sequence over and over and over and over until you succeed, then this game will not fail you.
Neon Drive is rewarding in that the entire experience offers variety, the right amount of challenge, and a satisfying play session each time. After beating a level on "normal" it unlocks "hard" and "insane" difficulties, which are stupid fun and a true test of hand/eye coordination.
The level design is strong, with cyberpunk backdrops, neon vistas, and more 1980s pop culture references than you could shake your fist at. This game plays similar to Wipeout or Audiosurf and has many similarities to other rhythm games while uniquely defining its own identity.
My only gripes about the game are that it lacks true content. Neon Drive started its life as a mobile game and was ported over to the PC with improvements in graphics and gameplay, as well as adding controller support. If the game had more levels, I feel as though it would justify its current full-price cost of $10USD. However, I purchase it on sale and I would still recommend it. In the future, I would hope that the developers realize the potential of this game and award the fanbase with more levels or modes.
I won't give chew anybody's ears off about this game but I can strongly recommend it for fans of the 1980s, the "aesthetic" movement, or for people who enjoy challenging rhythm games. Neon Drive is a very well-made title.

Playing through Doom 3 again will make you see the game in a whole different light.   It is no longer the game that Half Life 2 made look like a gaming relic upon its release.
Doom 3 BFG edition takes the original game and makes subtle tweaks to it.  Each of these tweaks combine to make the core game a whole different experience for the player.
The original game was a slow, methodical  shooter.   It was more of a first-person survival horror game than an action shooter. The game gave you just enough ammo to survive if you checked every nook and cranny and opened every locked cabinet.    Miss too many shots, and you had to rely on your fists.   You never felt safe.  You never felt in control of the situation.   It was a great game, but it never felt like "Doom".
Doom 3 BFG edition addresses this in various ways.
First, the game is brighter.   The original games' shadows were the centerpiece to its graphics engine.   It was like nothing you ever saw before.   Today, it's run of the mill stuff.   BFG edition reduces the shadows.   This changes the feel of the game immensely.
Second, they added ammo.   Playing through Doom 3 BFG edition, I don't believe I ever had a situation where I felt like I had to conserve ammo.   The ability to feel free to blow the crap out of enemies made Doom 3 BFG an absolute blast.
So, should you buy this game?
If you have never played Doom 3, I would suggest you play it first.
It's an game that every gamer should experience.   It's a masterwork of atmosphere.  The ammo deficit is also masterfully done.   It rewards firing accuracy and slow movement.    It's survival horror at its best.
But...after you have played the original doom, go back and play the BFG edition.   It will make you appreciate just how well Doom 3 did what it was designed to do, and how amazing the game was/is.
But, coincidentally, while playing the BFG edition, you may have a whole lot more fun being a demon killing machine instead of a hunted target.

Whew. Where to start.
First off, I give this game a recommendation only based on its uniqueness and potential to have been expanded upon. If anything, consider it a case study of rhythm games. In this case, we look upon what can be used to expand upon a simple concept like DDR/Stepmania and turn it into something with serious charm. I want as many people to see what this game has tried so that that future generations of indie/small-dev rhythm games can stand to benefit.
Consider Kickbeat to be like Stepmania. There are four directional button presses that have to be hit in time to the music. Where Kickbeat differs is assigning power-ups to directional double taps that are also assigned in accordance to the music. Adding to that, Kickbeat also throws in a Star Power element called Chi from the 'Hero' games, except it's built from regular successful note presses and reduced with damage. Power-ups can include things like bonus points, a Chi meter boost, health, invincibility, bombs, and even an extra multiplier. This is a bold change, since all these powerups are assigned with the music and not randomly, but they are entirely optional in the midst of actually completing a song or staying alive. It allows the ability to create serious high score challenges with countless accurately timed button presses without forcing insane clusters of missable (and thus, song-failing) notes that makes some Stepmania custom tracks infuriating. Kickbeat also enforces an honest penalty for button mashing. Making too many hits into air will cause your character to become fatigued, forcing them to be take a few hits of their own for a while on top of killing your score multiplier.
On top of all that, Kickbeat comes equipped with a simple story, a bit on the generic side, but not without its moments. but the core of the game overall is the visualizer. Kickbeat relays its otherwise simple core design by turning you into a lone man (or woman) beset by hordes of hostile enemies, all of whom need to be dispatched. This along with the dynamic camera movement, cinematic section finishers to fill lulls in the music, and the occasional boss fight makes a game that's as fun to watch as it is to play as opposed to certain other titles with colored arrows or dots.
Most of the above is a shining example of how to improve on existing rhythm game styles, but unfortunately Kickbeat suffers from a good share of problems that keep it from making a breakout into PC Rhythm Games. For one, the system requirements are a bit undersold. I run a computer with a bit over the recommended specs, but even on its lowest visuals, would get slowdowns and the occasional lockup. Adding on top of that is graphic tweaking is very minimal in Kickbeat's interface with no way of reducing particle effects or maximum size of the horde hovering around your character (new ones exceeding the maximum are phased in anyway, so it serves little purpose until you reach the closing moments where the numbers dwindle out). Crashes are also likely, which can cause SEVERE frustration when it comes to high-scoring songs for stars to unlock bonus characters and costumes, only for the game to crash. Next up is the fact that Kickbeat, even while labeled Steam Edition, does not play nice with the Steam overlay. Popups from friends entering games/coming online/IMs, groups hosting events, and even Kickbeat's own achievements can cause the game to grind to a halt or even crash it.
As for the key selling point of musically generated gameplay, heralded among the likes of Audiosurf, Beat Hazard, and Symphony, Kickbeat falls very short in this regard. The only parameters it seems to check in a song is BPM and when the initial beat starts, outside of an unusual tool that assists by having you tap out the beat yourself, making each added song a chore to make work, and even then, remains inconsistent in what beats it chooses to focus on as notes. There's no custom tracking, like one would have seen from Stepmania's track creator, so your level of enjoyment vs annoyance is entirely reliant on how well the tool works for you, never mind songs with variable or escalating BPM throughout that make that assigned number unreliable.
Lastly, the unfortunate truth is that the number of pre-programmed tracks only sits at 24 total songs, from 13 total artists. After a year of being released, it's disappointing that Zen Studios couldn't even bother with some DLC of track packs, maybe some extra stories, venues, or character costumes to go with it (perhaps even a larger library of cinematic takedowns). Perhaps they might be working on a sequel, given Kickbeat's awarded accolades, possibly even addressing all the issues I and others have listed here.
In conclusion, Kickbeat is worth picking up, but only if it's on sale. With the current problems it faces, there's just not that much replayability. Sure, the cosmetic unlockables add a nice flavor when unlocked, but after all the pre-programmed tracks are finished, the track generating tool is too tedious to bother with, compared to simple scan-and-play systems that other games deal with. The clear software issues push it over the edge, which becomes devastating in modes like Survival, that hinge on your methaphorical game ship holding together long enough for the respective Steam achievements, which alone will bear a threat when they slow your game upon being achieved.
Overall, I repeat: My recommendation comes as a case study. This game had a lot of potential that didn't get used, and I feel its contributions shouldn't be overlooked. Whatever serves as Kickbeat's spiritual successor doesn't necessarily have to be a kung-fu rhythm game visualizer, but should keep the spirit of optional notes, score building methods, subtle casual inclusion, and a visualizer that makes the game stylish and visually involved

However, Kickbeat has you pressing buttons along with the beat  and in-between the beat, which makes the game much more difficult, and is the reason most people do not like the game. At the highest difficulty level (Master) there are also button presses linked to the vocals, which turns the game into button mashing madness.
The game has 24 songs, a mix of hip-hop and rock, and 4 difficulty levels to choose from. You start out with one character in the story mode, but can unlock 6 more, and multiple costumes for each, thru game play.

The game does not automatically synch to the beat of the song, so you must use the included BPS (beats per second) counter to tap out the beat. This becomes tedious very quickly and no matter how much you tweak it the enemies and the beat always seems slightly out of synch.

This was relatively fun, with some incredibly frustrating issues of controller support.
For instance, one of your main attack buttons (X) is also used to teleport out of a tower defense mission at the end of a wave. Immediately. So pull your attacks off of X before playing tower defense missions.
Also, your healing and mana potions are right and left on the directional pad. Teleport back to the lair is up on the directional pad. No big deal, until you get into a gigantic SWARM of mobs (I love the swarms tbh) and frantically try to heal... and end up back at base. You don't have to start the mission over and there are no respawns, it's just a pain to run back.
Additionally, I couldn't for the life of me figure out how to use essences with a controller. There's no "Go. Create. Combine. WORK FFS." button.
Other than those couple of things, I had a pretty fun time. If you're willing to overlook those issues (and find this on sale), I'd recommend this.

I bought this way back when Chucklefish first released their site, which was many years ago. I have been spent a few days playing the unstable build, which will eventually be the 1.0 release in a few weeks.
There are three difficulty options: casual, survival, and hardcord. Casual does not have hunger, so I chose survival because I think hunger is an important part of the game. The problem with survival is that not only do you lose 30% of your pixels (money) when you die and you have to travel back to the location where you die, you also drop most of your items. To top that off, the game has no map or any visible coordinates so actually getting back there to get back my items is horrendous. This is supposed to be a game about exploration, but here I am, afraid of making any dumb mistake and traveling too far in case I die. Oh, and there is no pause option so you have to log out if you have to do something. I have spent a significant amount of time trying to find my last death location because I accidentally died.
Finally, the missions, which you have to do in order to progress through the story, consists of areas that you have to clear and whatnot with a boss at the end. If you die, then you have to start the entire thing over.
The game is fun, but I had waited years for this update and I'm just frustrated to the point where I will probably just stop playing. I want to emphasize that there are no maps that I know of so to get back out of the planet, you either have to dig your way up or you have to find the same spot where you dug down. And digging down hasn't been rewarding for me, even without death. Sigh.
Edit: This is my first time doing a review, but I don't like Steam having only either a yes or no for the ratings. This is a very good game. It's just that, it seems as if the ratings only consist of a perfect score (yes) or something less than perfect (no).

The game does run well in DX9 - you can crank up the detail and effects even on low-spec cards - but it all looks dreary and unimpressive due to an apparent lack of inspiration and polish, and clunky mechanics get in the way a lot. This is Bad for a supposed

Floating Point is a simple game where you swing from platform to platform as a little orange dot.
No, really, that's it.
There's a singular objective, and that's to swing your little dot through orange bars that grow taller (and become easier to touch) the faster you go.  Also, the faster you go, the more points you can accumulate for each randomly generated level.  It sounds easy!
Learning to swing effectively and exactly when to pull yourself in and when to just let yourself swing freely can be a little difficult, at first.  It's really the only learning curve there is.  It can lead to some frustrating moments, but one you get the hang of it, it's rather therapeudic to swing about in waves, compete circles, underwater, above water; all while snagging those orange bars and racking a higher score.  There's no "winning" to this game, really, and there's nothing really to distract you.
Of course, there could always be more.  The game could have other modes, more music, maybe a color mixer to choose the glow of your dot, your cable, the bars, and the general glow of the game; but I'm not going to complain about what there could be.  It's free, there's not really a reason for anyone not to try it at least once, and it's a fun little time waster.  I wouldn't play it for hours at a time, but it's always there when I need a break from something, and it's never stressful or boring.  Running into obstacles is a pain, but it's never the kind of thing you would throw your computer against a wall for.  You give a quick sigh, and you grab another block to swing off of, and the collision is but a thing of the past.
Give it a shot.  Like I said, there's not really a reason not to (It's free!).  It's just a pleasant game to play, nothing that anyone has lost sleep over, but continues to come to mind.

Bastion is a top down RPG/Hack and Slash game based around the so called "Bastion" which is the only hope of saving the world from the calamity. How does it work? You collect various cores around the world by venturing to different levels, and returning to the bastion as a kind of home base. As you traverse more of the world, more weapons become available to you, all of which are well balanced for any playstyle. This would be a fairly generic game if not for a single, vital piece of content in the game. The narrator. As you progress through your game, he will comment on things you do, how well you do them, and what weapons you're using. The entire game is an artistic wonder, using a more cartoony style for it's graphics. All of the game's asthetics come together wonderfully for a great experience. The only problem I have with this game is length. The game is extremely short, but the only thing that saves it is the prescence of New Game Plus after you complete the story once.

Don't let my "Not Recommended" rating dissuade you - Neon Drive is the most intense, addicting, visually arresting rhythm game that I sadly cannot recommend outright to everyone.  It's at times like these that I wish I had a different option other than a simple "Yes/No" answer.  This game is good - very good in fact - but it has problems that prevent it from being great.  If you love rhythm games, challenging difficulties, or the 80's aesthetic then you'll probably love this game as much as I do.  However, if not then don't let this game be your introduction.
In terms of gameplay, Neon Drive is similar to other rhythm games in that you move your vehicle left and right to dodge incoming obstacles.  The twist offered here is that instead of dodging around the musically generated obstacles, you drive to the music itself, shifting to the beat.
Herein is where the difficulty of the game relies - you need to move along the path in time to the music or else you'll hit the obstacles and have to restart.  Added difficulty comes in how the obstacles are laid out to form the path - sometimes multiple paths will be available with only one letting you through, other times the obstacles will move on the track to obscure the way forward.  With a little practice, though, you can find your way through.
And this is where the first big problem with the game.  Once you beat the level, you've seen everything it has to offer.  The higher difficulties are only "harder" because the song speeds up a little.  There are no additions to the levels and no new mechanics are thrown in to vary the gameplay.  Even when you transform into different vehicles like a hovercar or fighterjet, the mechanics remain the same: move left or right to dodge obstacles.
This kind of repetition is very dissappointing to me since there's so much potential for additions to each level.  If each higher difficulty added a new section and changed up existing sections in the level, then that would give the game significantly more depth of play.
That's not to say there isn't fun to be had.  Each level is unique and puts different twists on the game to create new and vastly different experiences.  The difficulty is fair and evenly ramps up throughout the game.  I mentioned the hovercar and fighter jet, but
level puts a spin on the base gameplay that keeps the game fresh as you progress.  And the soundtrack is absolutely phenomenal, expertly evoking the synth and rock of the 80's era.  If the OST could be bought by itself, I'd wholeheartedly recommend getting it.
The other big selling point for this game is how much it evokes the futuristic ideas of the 80's, and to that end it absolutely nails it.  Each level looks like it comes straight out of an 80's sci-fi movie or cartoon (some more literally than others).  The artists did their jobs with flying colors, especially given how diverse each art style is.
It's just a shame that it can't be fully appreciated when playing the game.
This game requires intense concentration  on the track, for to get distracted by the backgrouds and level design would mean almost certain failure.  As such there are details in the levels that will go entirely unnoticed unless you purposefully take your eyes of the track and admire the art for two seconds you have until you hit an obstacle.  The track and the surroundings are both screaming for your attention, and more often than not it's gonna be the surroundings that get neglected.  Had the game been designed in such a way as to let you take in the surroundings while still successfully navigating the level, weaving the two together in harmony rather than clashing with each other, then this could have been a great music & art game with the rhythm-action companants as a bonus.
With the latest update, Free Run Mode is now available which does allow to take in the artistic design without needing to worry about failure.  In fact, some of the levels have had redesigns to accomodate this mode - very considerate.  It also has a neat little "Hit The Targets" objective to it (though I don't think the scores count for anything).  While this does allow for observing the art of Neon Drive, the targets are still a little distracting in some areas.  They should be replaced with something more subdued, like bars on the track. I do really like the triangles in Level 3 though - they can most certainly stay.
What?  I like triangles.
Another update, another edit - this time a new level is added!  But sadly, it is a very lack-luster level that is more of a hodge-podge of ideas than a well-thought-out design. It does change the gameplay up in a way unseen, but it constantly changes the style, so you can't get used to any one variation.  Not to mention the art is significantly more minimalistic, almost to the point of being cheap.
Points for the addition of triangles, though.  Just enough to keep the current score.
As I said before, this is the greatest game so far that I won't recommend to everyone.  It's got interesting gameplay, awesome music and beautiful art design, but lacks the depth and cohesiveness to create something truly worth everyone's notice.  I wish I could give it a thumbs sideways because many people will enjoy it and many won't.  This really is a game dependant on your personal preferences (I know that's probably a useless statement but I feel it's apt for this situation).  A the very least this game accomplishes exactly what it set out to do so in that regard it's a success.  It's just a shame that it isn't taken further to achieve the greatness it absolutely deserves.

Great visuals and an awesome  soundtrack surround this bone crushingly hard game. Make no mistake about it, this game's simplistic setup is controller breaker for sure. With track progress measured and saved as a percentage, the feedback loop is strong, you will find your self deciding for one more play when ever you start to quit, just to finish a stage or eek out a higher percentage, as visible proof of your improving skill.
That by itself is a strong setup for an arcade style game, but Neon Drive  goes the extra mile, by introducing varied play based around the position changing mechanic. At the most basic level your a car who instantly change lanes with a tab of one of the controller bumpers, and must do so early and often in order to avoid obstacles in the road. This is expanded upon as you go deeper, with an overhead mode, an astroid defense mode and even an afterburner esque flying mode to name just a few.
Absolutely worth the price of admission, just know you may be budgeting for a new controller after some heavy play

This game is best described as melee heavy Asian GTA. Essentially, instead of having a gun most of the time, you'll be mostly fighting hand to hand combat with your enemies. I would definitely get it especially since it's a steal during flash sales or community sales.
This game's setting is beautiful. It's incredibly well done from the nitty gritty poor North Point (your first house) to the finer more beautiful area of Kennedy Town. The story as well is captivating and captures the lives of Triad gangsters well. You'll also see the heavier parts of how gangsters' lives can affect the people around them. It gives a different vibe from what we usually see shown by the media and game like Grand Theft Auto. Cutscenes in this game are done well. Character development is the best part of the story. As I mentioned earlier, you will see the transformation that Wei Shen, the character you play, goes through and it is magnificent. The hand to hand combat move choices are also pretty well done as well as the upgrades you can get. The idea of being able to get more bonuses by equipping sets of clothes (mmorpg style) is also great.
Problems with the game are mostly persistent with from combat. AI is incredibly stupid. There are times when they do not even hide when you can see their heads. The slowmo reel in this game makes shooting headshots and killing enemies way too damn easy. Melee weapons like a tire iron have durability and cannot be found easily. Hand to hand combat becomes a joke after you learn how to properly counter (mash the right click button). There are a few different AIs that try to change that (monks are the best to fight against but you literally fight them for one section, 1!!!), but only the fat models are the ones that cause you trouble. Also running from the police is almost a joke in this game cause it is incredibly easy to make them stop chasing you. Camera angles are very annoying as well at times.
There are a few weird bugs and features that make the game incredibly frustrating as well. There are boxes and objects you cannot jump to although it's literally 1 cm over you. There are times in the water where you cannot jump up to the dock for some odd reason although the dock is literally only 2 cm tall. You cannot also jump across the safety sections of ramps from the water or from land although your model jumps higher than them. There are some hilarious bugs like the lockbox flying bug, but generally most of them♥♥♥♥♥♥you off.
All in all, I would rate this game 7/10 and buy it especially if it's on sale (glorious $4 steam sale). The story DLCs are pretty great so you can pick them up if you'd like some humourous DLCs. I would advise against the DLC that gives you automatic LV 8 triad and police because the game is already pretty easy. The story will take you anywhere from 16-25 hours depending on how many side quests you complete.

I'll be up front right now, I like this game. It offers a unique experience and I find myself coming back again and again to play it. That being said I would not recommend it unless it was on at least a 75% sale as the game is not complete and pretty much never will be because the dev dropped it.
Now you can play the game, it isn't broken you can play and finish a scenario but this game was abandoned and a lot of promises that were made were broken by the dev so there is lack of content and after a few games you get the gist of how things will go and the prospect of losing goes out the window even on the hardest difficulty. The Blackbox mod can fix this a bit but overall it's a problem. In addition you will suffer a lot late game due to poor optimization that even a really powerful system can't power through. I put a lot of time into this game on my 3570k which was overclocked to 4.8Ghz and on the larger universe settings I still had significant slowdowns and juttering which can and will render the zoomed in direct fleet control unplayable. It basically leads to you sending massed fleets into enemy held systems and hoping that the AI can take care of things.
The best thing to do is the leave the universe size to normal and use the Blackbox mod to limit the number of ships the AI can have because if you don't you will quickly find that the AI will continue to pump out droves of ships and each one will make the game run a bit worse after a certain point. That being said if you have a recent Intel based chip(Sandy or newer) your system should easily be able to handle around around a thousand ships in the universe without significant slowdowns.
Probably my favorite thing about the game is the ship customization. In a word it's friggin cool and it really makes you feel good when your ship you designed is good enough to take on three or four ships of an equivalent class of ship and come out on top. That is I think the thing that really keeps me coming back because I keep finding better and better ways to build my ships and it feels really engaging.
To wrap up this game had loads of potential but it was let down by poor choices made by the dev in both the way they made the game and how the handled the abandonment of it. It is in no way worth the standard $30 asking price, you can pick it up for the unique experience but only if it's less than $10.

An excellent, and well polished fighting game that welcomes newbies and rewards HardCore gamers alike.
Street Fighter V is a 8-directional, 6 button fighting game that takes over 20 years of fighting game history and Utilizes its experiance to make an impressively deep, challenging, and fun 2 player fighter. At the time of reviewing this game, SFV now has a proper story mode, and vs AI setting in versus, a significant selection of fighters to choose from, and a great selection of costumes you can obtain (via fight money, or real money). also worth noting, that DLC characters and stages can be aquired either through saving up fight money in game, or by simply paying for them with real money.
Gameplay is exactally as you would expect from a Street Fighter game. fights are on a 2 dimentional plain, utilizing an 8-Directional input to move / duck / jump. There are three different punch and kick inputs to use (light, strong, heavy), each with different advantages and weaknesses depending on the character you use. This game can be enjoyed by casual players, and even more so by people who seek to learn the tricks and techniques of their character of their choice. With that said, It will start with you learning how to do the special and ultra moves, then learning how to preform complex combinations, then learning how to read your opponent. SFV also has new mechinics called the V-skill, which is a unique skill each character can use by pressing medium punch & medium kick together. and the V-Trigger (Hp & Hk), an activatable powerup that grants your character either a powerup, or a move that will give you an advantage over your opponent.
Compareing this to earlier street fighter titles, This one feels alot easier to play than the others. The characters are unique in their fighting styles (including ryu and ken. they now have their own move set.) and feel fresh and new, while staying true to how people knew them from previous enteries. Visually, the game looks great, and runs smoothly online and offline.
Overall, If you want to get into fighting games, or if you are a veteran getting back into, or looking for a new game to pick up. Street Fighter V is an excellent addition and recommendation for you.

This is the 3rd Installment in a Massive (Or even Revolutionary if you
want) Franchise. (Buckle up this is a Big Review)
Now DooM 3 was a very Noticeably Different Game when Compared with the prevous 2
installments in the series. It was to keep  up with gamers, Graphics cards and
Demands. Of course it got much criticism for being so different from the older games
because it lacked many features that were highly wanted. (eg. Co-op, More
Multiplayer Features and Custom Maps. All of those could be foound in the previous
games...
Anyway, this game contains 3 games and 2 DLC almost the whole series at the
time of release (If you dont count TnT, Plutonia Experient, Brutal DooM and Final
DooM). And this is Great! content= more playtime= money's Worth...Right? We'll See
in this review!
First of all if you want to get the full DooM experience, no mods, better graphics,
much more content, Diverse range of achievements, more Gameplay Options...Keep Reading
However! If you want to get a mod avaliable (Co-op), true horror
experience (Take the Flashlight system for example), Simpler Multiplayer system, and
overall a much more difficult Shooter...Buy DooM 3. Custom Maps, Monsters, Weapons
etc. all on here...with a bit of effort of course.
Ok now that thats out of the way, lets break down the main Points of the Game (DooM 3 and the DLC)
-Price on SALE is very Proportional to the Content recieved.
-Occulus friendly, if you can get it to work...

Nightmare might take the Longest...

-Weapons are quite balanced in Multiplayer. Balanced being a strong word when most people use Rocket Launchers...
-The Level Design of some parts of DooM and the DLC are amazing, take Hell for example. Its so unique compared to the rest of the Metallic Blood stained doorways of the main game. also the Final few levels have a Ruins, Aged Feel to them. No Spoilers here
IMPORTANT (For the Fellow Screenshotters)
The Fricking DEFAULT Key for Screenshots is F12 so when you enter it for the first time in the middle of a game (Hopefully early on), the Games Console system (Invisible bugger) detects that as some type of command input and promptly turns off any and all Achievments still to get for the Session. Easy fix is to change the screenshot key to something more comfortable and then restart the session. Enabling the Console later on is risky when you have achievements still to get, Especially in Mutliplayer. Save the Spawning and Manual-Commanding for the After Party please :D or make a Seperate Save just in case.
-Ammo is Plentiful, too plentiful. you might even walk around a corner and pick up some without noticing. This isnt how Semi-Horror Shooters werent meant to be played!! Especially before bosses (Which give away the Surprise of the Concept..)
-Bye Bye Mods! Ill Miss you!
-Story is crap, its basically being fed to you on a drip. Kill x ammount of Demons and the next Cutscene/ Objective shows up! Rinse and Repeat.
-Enemies are Dumb and can get stuck easily, BUT they can even end up fighting each other if you manage..
-Guns have no Variation, But this is alright in some parts, especially Multiplayer! Balanced is the Key word here.
-Without little things like the seperate Flashlight from DooM 3, it makes the Experience a Standard Action one, which i alright. except if a horror experience is exactly what you wanted (I know i did.)
-Enemies have little Variation. More Enemies (Maybe 10?) would make it a weapon switching wonder in the tight Hallways.
-The Final Boss Battle is just...Terrible, Find ONE Weakness and then Rinse and Repeat that (Plus minor Enemies) untill the end.
DooM 3 is Very Linear and doesnt Lead on to ROE well at all. One major Plot point might be enough, but many were expecting more!
-Many Minor Bugs, Crashes and even Loss of Save data (only once for 405 hours...)
-Autosaved right before, getting instakilled? Too Bad! That ones Straight from New Vegas unfortunetely..

This game could be much better if it followed rhythms consistently and didn't switch between drums/instruments/whatever all the time with no indication. It's too hard to rely on the music because as soon as you adjust to the rhythm of one section the game suddenly decides to follow a completely different pattern that has nothing to do with the section you just played, and you start missing because you didn't expect that change. It feels like playing a rhythm game without rhythm, just mashing buttons randomly with no relation to the music!
Sometimes it feels like the song has nothing to do with the attack timings whatsoever. You can even play it with your sound muted, since the game just forces you to either rely on the visual hints or to remember the sequences. You would think it's lag, but it's not: half of a song can be perfectly in tune, following an easily recognisable pattern, and then it just changes the pattern to whatever it feels like.
Music feels rather generic, mostly because there is not enough variety of genres. Swarming groups of enemies make it impossible to determine what the next wave will be like, unless you already know that from previous attempts. Visual effects are too pronounced and they often make it hard to actually see what's going on, which is especially irritating when the colour of the floor matches the enemies and there are too many of them to see which one is going to attack first.
A pretty average hack n slash...it's worth 5euro, not more.

Being fan of many type of games, I like beat'em up games as well and Street Fighter it's one of them.
Street Fighter V is the very last chapter of the famous Capcom saga with our friends Ryu and Ken.
We all know how Street Fighter had huge impact on the "fighting" community, being one of the most important and most known titles of its genre.
However this very last game isn't comparable to the previous classics.
Let's keep it straight and simple. Being a competitive game with a spot in the E-Sport, and living in 2017, the online feature is very important, infact not everybody has the possibility to play with other people on the same system.
With that being said, having a "netcode" that is awful is a huge issue that Capcom, has expected, can't solve considering they are about to go bankrupt.
Another tremendous aspect is the fact that this game is unfinished. We are playing an "early access" game full of bugs, balance issues and without a proper single player mode.
It's the first time a Street Fighter game doesn't have an arcade mode and it's kinda sad that Capcom charges people for 60 bucks over an unfinished game and charges even more for additional characters that should already be part of the main game.
It's true, however, that you can use in game currencies to buy those new characters, stages, colors, costumes, etc. But the price required and the nearly impossible grinding required to obtain those currencies are intended to force the player to use real money. Cheap move, pathetic and very very disappointing from a Company that is well known and has marked the history of videogames.
This game isn't worth to be played, I tried to find a way to enjoy it but you just can't. Let's wait for proper fixes and upgrades, that probably won't come considering the product is already 1 year old and we still didn't see anything regarding those matters.
Potentially a good game, pratically rubbish, so let's just forget this title and move on.

Cory in the House is a television show, which aired on the Disney Channel from January 12, 2007 to September 12, 2008 and was a spin-off from the Disney show That's So Raven. The show focuses on Cory Baxter, who moves from San Francisco, California to Washington, D.C. with his father, after Victor Baxter gets a new job in the White House as the official head chef. The series marks a Disney Channel first, as it is the channel's first spin-off. This is also the only Disney Channel spin-off series to be broadcast in standard definition for the entire length of the show. Reruns of the series have not been produced on Disney Channel, or on Disney XD; however they continue to air on the Family channel in Canada. Raven-Symoné guest-starred, reprising her role as Raven Baxter in one episode. In 2014 Disney Channel started airing a weekly block called Disney Replay on Wednesdays nights, during which episodes of Cory in the House air alongside That's So Raven and Kim Possible, among others.
