Van Helsing 2 continues and expands on the gameplay of its predecessor in predictable, but satisfying ways. Beginning with the ability to import a saved character from the first game, II delivers an additional thirty levels of experience, new items, skills, quests, tower defense levels, enemies, quests, and sarcastic retorts from the ghostly Lady Katerina. It is more linear then the first game, with fewer sidequests overall but more tower defense levels, and additional side mechanics that allow you to send out NPC captains to  perform offscreen missions, rewarding you with additional gold and items, and an additional pet with customizable abilities. The equipment-modding obsessed can now alter their equipment in an additional way, via stat-increasing runes. While Van Helsing II treads ground already heavily traveled, it is nonetheless an excellent Diablolike and arguably a better singleplayer experience then many other titles in the genre, due in no small part to Van Helsing's both varied and powerful skillset. My hunter-class Van Helsing was capable of dealing extrordinary damage both to single targets and in an area, but was also very survivable thanks to a lot of lifesteal. The game is significantly easier on its normal difficulty then other titles in the genre, including the first Van Helsing, but offers two additional difficulty levels beyond that along with repeatable, randomized, high-level dungeons for the discerning munchkin. I will be proceeding directly to Van Helsing III and what I hope is a thrilling conclusion to the trilogy, and I will look forward greatly to Neocore's recently announced Warhammer 40,000 ARPG, Inquisitor - Martyr.

I've started playing this game in 2010 (not on Steam, I guess I have less than 300 hours played). It has changed a lot since that time - sound effects have changed, content was added, already existing items and enemies were balanced and, last but not least, the game was sold to another studio. Twice.
The time when RotMG belonged to first one, Wildshadow Studios, was probably the best time for the game. It was simple and fun to play, Pay to win didn't exist. In 2012 RotMG was sold to Kabam. They made it pay to win and also did nothing aganist hackers and issues the game had. Later, they decided to work on their other projects and to abandon RotMG a bit, but in July 2016 RotMG was bought by Deca Games - they kept (and keep!) adding new content and events and they finnaly started fighting notifier hackers. It's a really good time for the game.
RotMG is a bullet-hell, team MMORPG with A LOT of different items, monsters and dungeons. All 14 classes are available for free (you only need a bit of time to get 'em all) and are almost perfectly balanced. You can play support/dps/tank (often mixed in one character), whatever you want. There's also a possibility of joining a guild consisting of other players. Overall, the game is indrecibly fun to play despite being a bit pay to win - it's harder to play having only one, free character slot, buying more makes the game way easier, though it's less pay-to-win than it sounds. There's a perma-death, character loses all of his items upon dying (which is actually a good thing - succeeding to make a well-equipped and strong character is more satisfying). MMO Dark Souls for free (ok, ok, it's not THAT hard...).
You can have a lot of fun playing RotMG, especially with a group of friends, or a guild. Also you don't have to spend a lot of time playing.

Synopsis: I would definitely recommend this game to any one who likes GTA styled games, open world, arcade like driving, fun hand to hand combat, goofy side missions and fun mini games.
WARNING: NOT ALL DLC IS A GOOD IDEA, MAKES GAME EASY
History:
The Playstation 2 had a great game called True Crime. It was a GTA styled game where you played an undercover cop. What made the game unique was the RPG elements in which you could upgrade your driving skills, hand to hand and shooting skills. This allowed for special moves, even when driving. Of course what made the game amazing, was the voice acting which even included a certain actor named Christopher Walken.
When Sleeping Dogs was first announced, it was announced as True Crime: Hong Kong. However, that game was cancelled and picked up by Square Enix, who tried to use the game to create a new IP.
Review:
Now that the history lesson is over, the game.
While the RPG elements are not as deep as True Crime, this is still an entertaining and fun game. I would recommend this to any person who loves action games that are similar to the GTA style (GTA 3 forward that is). The driving mechanics are fun, but arcade loose. The hand to hand is better than any other open world action game out now (still not as good as True Crime) and fun, and despite being GTA style, the shooting mechanics aren't bad. The storylines are fun but a little predictable (how many undercover cop games, movies and tv series have you seen - not a whole lot of variations there). The voice acting was well done and despite being a pretty linear game in regards to choices, I have replayed it multiple times just for the fun gameplay, side missions and mini games.
Disclaimer:
There is a lot of DLC for this game. Definitely get the storyline DLCs. As for all the extra weapons, money and suits, BE CAREFUL.
It has been a while since I played this game, but my last playthrough was after buying all of the DLC. Needless to say the extra money and gear just felt like cheating. It seriously messed with the balance of the game and I would recommend avoiding these DLCs or turning them off in steam, until after you have completed one playthrough (unless there is a way to turn them off in game).

AvP 2010 is very underrated in my opinion, only problem with it nowadays is the lack of people in multiplayer, which you can run into Hackers since there is no VAC protection, I recommend getting some friends to play this with you. You can play as 3 characters/classes: Predator and Alien obviously, but also marine, here is their playstyles.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Predator: Think of him as a strategic hunter, you have a choice of 4 weapons that are scatted around the area, he also has 3 visions:Normal, Alien, and Thermal. Alien helps you see aliens which will be highlighted in Green, and thermal helps catch other Predators, but here are his list of weapons:
1. Plasma Caster, a weapon that tracks down your target almost like an aimbot, but it's easy to avoid as an Alien.
2.Smart Disc, a projectile you can control, 1 hits Aliens if it hits their head. Also stuns.
3. Spear, a  projectile that while is hard to hit is a 1 hit kill guaranteed.
4. Mines, as the name implies, THEY'RE MINES. If you can track your enemies movement patterns, you can lay these in areas they might go in. As they are hard to see unless you are another Predator.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Alien: He is hard to see in the Dark and his tail whips are a vicious weapon, especially if used on the walls. With Alien, you want to stay on the walls as much as possible, never stop moving either since this makes you an easy target, as Aliens have extremely low health, but high kill potential. The Aliens best move would be his Heavy attack since it stuns longer than the predators does. Aliens can't fight Predators alone, that is a death wish, get another Alien pal to help you take one down, similar to the movies, they like to swarm instead of attack alone, like ants or bees.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Marine: If you want to be under constant pressure of hearing Aliens growling and Predators roaring... Marine is for you!
But in all honesty, Marine is quite good if you can use him right, he of course uses guns to fight, so here are some of his guns:
Pistol: Unlimited Ammo, but very little damage. You most likely will not want to use this.
Pulse Rifle:A good, all around weapon.
Shotgun:If you like to get in an Alien or Predators face, you can use the shotgun, it's buckshot is extremely powerful and it stuns.
Flamethrower:Not used very much, pouring Gasoline can help do extra damage.
Sniper Rifle: Almost an insta-kill if headshots, very good.
Smart Gun: Can track enemies through walls, has an Aimbot, reduces your weapon slots and speed though.Bad if you are trapped by them, mainly because it can only focus one at a time. But good if you are trying to deal with one at a time.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

At first, when I saw some videos of KickBeat, I thought it was going to be a really cool entry into the rhythm genre. It's obviously DDR-esque, but in a completely different fashion. Unfortunately, I find myself really not finding it easy to go on after the tutorial (which was fine if a little drawn out) and just two story missions.
There's a couple of major gripes that I have with the game and how it functions at its core:
1. The aim is that you press buttons (A/B/X/Y on a gamepad, which I am using, or specific keys on a keyboard) to the beat to defeat enemies that are approaching and attacking you to the beat. However, and I seem to not be alone on this opinion, the "Perfect"s don't actually match up with the beat. At first I thought it was input lag, that the game was having a delayed response, but it turned out to be the opposite; I was going too fast for the game. I suppose they took natural human input lag into account, the difference between hearing something and pressing a button? I don't know, and if that was the case, I wish they hadn't, because it then screws up any actual rhythm going on.
2. You can get power-ups by double-tapping the button against certain enemies. These range from bonus points to additional score multipliers to health pickups. Unfortunately, when I was going through the tutorial on these, I was given the impression (like in ALL other video games) that the power-ups would be optional. This is not the case; as it turns out, these power-ups are required and will count as a miss if you don't double-tap and only perform a single-tap.
3. Close-up cutscenes occur for certain parts of a song where, for example, the melody changes. I thought it was a nice addition, but annoyingly, if I activate a shield power-up without knowing that this cutscene is going to happen, then the power-up will stay active for only the cutscene and then deactivate before the next enemy even gives a chance for the power-up being necessary in the first place. This might just be a thing where I actually have to know the song and be able to tell that such a moment is upcoming, therefore I should not use a power-up... but how am I supposed to know that well?
Those are my biggest gripes that I personally had to write about. Going through other reviews, I notice someone mentioned the visuals being a distraction to the actual gameplay, and I have to agree with that. You're told that certain colored enemies will attack normally, others will attack rapidly, others require a hold of the button rather than a tap, and others will attack simultaneously (two buttons or even three at the same time - note that this is really difficult on a controller, which this game blatantly recommends!). Obviously, these are all staples of rhythm games.
Unfortunately, other games like DDR have an advantage over this system in that they're vertically scrolling on top of what's happening in the background. You can easily see what's required of you in the next sequence of notes/beats. In KickBeat, a swarm of ninja doesn't exactly make it easy to see the required controls at what required times, especially when there's a ton of them from a bunch of different angles. Their colors aren't varied or vibrant enough to catch your eye so you know which kind of button press is required, and when they
catch your eye, you're distracted away from remembering which control is needed for them.
There appears to be a mode where you can play against your own music, as well as the obvious mode where you can play against any song included in the game. However, annoyingly enough, these are locked behind the story sequences, which there are a
of. I don't know if this is a common mechanic in rhythm games, but in those that I've played, things like Free Play mode were available initially and pretty much the whole point of the game.
I mean... the graphics are beautiful and the music is pretty good. But the gameplay is really flawed for what it tries to be. I initially enjoyed it, but it became a chore really quickly. I'll keep enjoying Pinball FX2, and CastleStorm on the PS4 was kinda fun, but I can't recommend KickBeat for being what essentially feels like a flawed experiment by Zen Studios.

Cons:

Overall, I was really rather impressed, and look forward to their next game. :)

The forefather of first person shooters as we know it saw reinvention and rebirth some 11 years after it first revolutionized (if not invented) the genre of FPS. What Id Software brought to the table was a game-changing new graphics engine that pushed real-time lighting and 3D-relief "bump mapped" textures to polygon graphics that made startlingly real environments to serve as the Martian horrorhouse that became the setting of what was to be not a true sequel, but a reboot of the series.
Doom 3 came across as a more cinematic and survival horror-themed take on the tale of one lone soldier's struggle to contain the hordes of Hell after a science experiment let them out across an isolated research station on Mars. They vied to reach Earth where they could take a more permanent hold on the mortal realm, but with an almost academic arsenal of firepower and a few tricks, the player must drive them back, eventually entering Hell itself to seal the hole created in reality from the other side.
Open environments with color-coded locked doors and a maze-like construction gave way to linear progression through a much darker and more claustrophic base. The backtracking of the original games was replaced with a series of "boo" moments as demons jumped from every vent, doorway, and even materialize around, behind, or sometimes right on top of the player. Suspense and hair-trigger gameplay replace the circle-strafing constant-action of the originals, while a much stronger focus on story, both told in cinematics and collectable audio logs, certainly made this modern iteration of Doom more of an interactive thrill ride than before.
The sheer darkness of the game can be overcome with a little bit of config file tweaking, as can the game's orignial 4:3 aspect ratio, field of view, and resolution options (make sure to set the config file as read-only after modding or it will revert), but players of more recent shooters will cry at this game's lack of weapon shouldering or even any kind of appreciable zoom aiming. The "monster closets" get a bit old after a few hours in, and the scare factor is thus reduced, but the game's atmosphere is the stuff of legend, especially in the way it makes players choose between wielding their flashlight and seeing what's hiding in every blackened corner, or firing at those glowing eyes in the darkness and hoping whatever it is doesn't eat you.
The "BFG Edition" of this game released almost 8 years after the original adds a new episode consisting of recently-finished levels cut from the original game, but otherwise removes some of the more suspensful encounters, plus ups the enemy count, reduces their health, and increases ammo in order to make a more action-heavy shooter. This diminishes the horror feel, especially in the way it mounts the flashlight onto the armor, so players can shoot and see in the dark simultaneously, but this I feel takes away from what the game was all about: fear of the unknown. Plus "BFG Edition" also presets the widescreen mode and higher resolutiond to default, which is handy, but increases gamma and brightness to higher levels by default, further eroding the horror feel.
I get what Id Software was trying to do here, but it didn't really need to be done. If the idea of optional motion blur, higher frame rate caps (120fps max), or perhaps a bit more saturated color palette borrowed from the more-recent Rage engine, with -some- cleaned up textures sounds good to you, then maybe the BFG Edition is worth checking out. Otherwise, the original game holds up enough over time to still be a great suspenseful take on the 90's classic.

It's absolutely fun when you play it with friends. Even if you don't have friends to play with, it's very easy to make a friend on Left 4 Dead by just being nice/using teamwork. That's all.

That's what I like so much about this game.
The AI Director will try to punish you for going solo by having the (special) infected target you.
Left 4 Dead is a very dynamic game as well. It never gets repetitive because of the AI Director spawning guns, items, ammo and (special) infected on different places, depending on the situation.
The characters are perfect and the way they interact with eachother is a really fun and nice touch. I like them all, but my favorite is Louis. Because
The game only has a few guns (6, with pistol included), but the gunplay feels silky smooth.
Especially because of the satisfying gore L4D has. Spraying with an autoshotgun through a horde of infected feels niiice.
I don't know about you, but animations are a very important part in a game for me.
Third person animations in L4D1 are smooth unlike in L4D2 whereas it is choppy. You may think that this is just a miniscule thing but you will definitely notice this if you've played both L4D1 & 2 for a while.
I personally think that the Jockey in L4D2 is an absolute b*llsh*t of an infected. He has the most jacked up hitbox ever. The hitbox is WAY infront of him than his actual model.
L4D1 doesn't have the Jockey so that's another reason of buying L4D1 over 2. (lol)
People tend to think that there are no differences between Left 4 Dead and Left 4 Dead 2.
A lot of them also say that L4D1 is not worth buying anymore only because L4D2 has L4D1's campaigns. And yes, this is true, but Valve has changed the layout of the original campaigns in L4D2. Certain buildings are gone/changed, certain pathways are gone/changed, certain holdout spots are gone/changed, etc. Also, L4D1 has this gritty and dark atmosphere and really embraces the feeling of being set in a apocalypse with the help of dark maps, whereas L4D2's atmosphere is brighter and less serious. Valve went with a more comedic style in L4D2. This is mostly noticeable if you listen to the quotes that the characters say in-game.

Burnout Paradise: The Ultimate Box is a smashing open world arcade racer but also unfortunately not what it advertises to be. Only one of four DLCs is included, which makes the title of "The Ultimate Box" a blatant lie.
Despite its age, the game still looks and sounds great. Proper sound effects promote the sensation for speed while slow motion jumps and crashes have a satisfying feel to them. Losing a run due to a crash is significantly less frustrating because of the chance to witness the utter destruction of your car. However, the camera angle is far too low, presumably by design, which leads to an abundance of unavoidable accidents. The licensed radio music is simply fine and the implementation of real world advertisement into Paradise City is borderline okay and not too intrusive. It's just a little bit inconsistent to have made up cars in a made up city with real advertisement.
Various game modes, most notably Race, Road Rage and Stunt Run, promote three different ways of playing: classic racing against opponents or the clock, taking down opponent's cars and performing stunts. Through completing these events the player's License gets upgraded and new cars and paint jobs are unlocked, either immediately or by hunting and taking down these new cars on the streets. The hunt for “released” cars is one of the two handy features that justify the open world environment. The other being the free cruising combined with the plethora of events that can be started at every junction. Depending on preference, this can also become annoying as every event has a set start location and restarting a specific event requires the player to drive back to the right junction.
A total of four motorcycles with separate race-only events and their own License are included as well. These are extremely easy to handle and offer a perfect relaxing diversion to the sometimes erratic drivability of some of the cars. The general arcade gameplay is designed to be pure fun without any technical details.
Burnout Paradise: The Ultimate Box contains a great game alas wrapped in a deceiving product that is clearly inferior to its console release. To summarise the DLC issue: There are four DLCs for this game; one is included in this version, one is purchasable via Origin and two are exclusive to consoles.
For more detailed information on the DLCs I'd recommend checking
.

With experience of multiple other ARPG games, such as Path of Exile, Torchlight and the Diablo series, The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing II feels weak in comparison.
While the visuals aren't terrible, the sound effects are. Sound is a very important aspect in making the combat feel responsive and satisfying, and the game fails in this area. Hearing the same enemy type have only a single death scream means you'll get very tired of killing them - which should NEVER happen in an ARPG game. Imagine watching a movie with loads of fighting, and whenever someone dies, you hear the Wilhelm Scream. Over and over again. Not good.
You gain levels quite quickly, but each level feels insignificant. In fact, it becomes a chore to level up. This is yet another reason why playing the game does not feel good.
I haven't played the game long enough to tell how the boss fights work out, but that is because I can't bring myself to play the game any longer. I recommend you do not purchase the game unless it goes on a very heavy sale, or if there's a Humble Bundle sale with some other game you want (and this game merely comes as a sidebonus).

Considered waiting for another sale to get this game, but I was getting impatient and decided to get it at regular price of $10.99 anyway. Overall, I think I got my money's worth for the most part.
Referring to Xbox 360 controller layout, the basic attacks include light and heavy attacks of various combos (EX: XY, XXY, XXYY, XXXY, UpX, YYY), both for ground and air, and many of said combos can be chained together rather smoothly. When enemies are weakened enough, the B button hovers over them for you to perform finishers on them. They then release crystals for Icey to absorb into her scabbard via holding the X button, and she then releases an AOE attack inflicting damage to all enemies on screen, and the amount of damage depends on how many crystals you absorb at one time. Pressing LB when it appears over an enemy sends out a copy of Icey to slash them, which can even be initiated while you're in the middle of combos. Pressing LB with either X or Y performs stronger attacks that also make you invulnerable during their use in exchange for some of your health. All in all, you're given quite a lot to work with in terms of how you can confront enemies and bosses, and you can buy/upgrade attacks, abilities, and health to strengthen them with cash you get from defeated enemies and breaking crates hidden in levels.
The story aspect of the game is pretty enjoyable for the most part, with how you can obey the narrator's instructions and defeat Judas, or disobey him to get some rather interesting and entertaining reactions out of him, and find some additional secret areas, endings, some Easter eggs, etc. Finding all the endings will also lead you to finding the true/secret ending.
Regarding a few criticisms, one of them is how there are only two difficulties (easy and hard mode). While hard mode is a notable challenge, especially if you start the game on it, the feeling of danger decreases when you get most of the upgrades, even on said difficulty. Perhaps it's just me, but I was only really able to get killed when I went back to the last two bosses and Jack when I had everything upgraded at at least 2 levels. While the game is still fun to play, if you want the game to go back to being really hard for those who want to keep experiencing said sense of danger, you do have the option to reset the game. That, and/or you might want to avoid upgrading attacks and abilities too high of levels (the max level being 3), or specifically avoiding upgrading the stuff that would allow you to survive a lot of damage. Still, I think I would have liked an option of an extra hard mode of sorts so having to go to such lengths wouldn't have to be necessary, and you could still keep the upgrades you bought in the process.
It's also kind of a bummer that it lacks a hoard/survival mode to focus on fighting a certain or indefinite amount of enemy waves, and maybe throw the bosses into the mix as well. Given how good the gameplay is, it seems as though that could be a neat addition for the game.
Another thing is that the game is kind of short. When I started the game, it was on hard mode, and I got killed quite a lot. Taking that into account while I was completing the game 100%, it took me around 10 hours. On the other hand, if you ever to want to reset the game for reasons mentioned above, it probably won't fell tedious to go back and 100% the game again, which I myself might do, with how much I've enjoyed it.
Overall, despite a few gripes, it's a very enjoyable hack and slash game with a combat system well put together, a style of storytelling that makes you want to explore and search more more, and a nice artstyle and soundtrack (which is even available as a free download) to accompany it.

If all you're looking for is a good 2D side-scroller, then
delivers in spades. It has a simple but effective combat comprised of a light attack, heavy attack, and a special ability. There's no blocking, but you get high-jumping and fast-dodging instead. All of these abilities can be upgraded (and expanded) through a very straight-forward leveling system. Enemy variety is quite good for its size; I counted at least five recurring different types of enemies, and probably another five spread throughout the levels, not counting boss fights. The combat animations are also worth mentioning.
If you're looking for something more, then be prepared to drive the game's narrator mad as you find yourself constantly disobeying every single one of his cues, breaking the fourth wall, and discovering secrets about the game's development, among others. Since the main character, ICEY, is silent throughout the game, it is up to the narrator to provide an account of her journey and motivations. And while said narrator speaks in Chinese (with English subtitles), he does an excellent job conveying his frustration and anger at your constant rebellion, even if he will take up the challenge and try to one-up you every now and then. It would not be unfair to say the narrator is probably more of a main character than ICEY is.
This meta element to the game requires the player to peel away the layers and put together the pieces behind ICEY's quest to defeat her archnemesis, Judas. There are several references to the
and
that, I must admit, went over my head and probably help put
's story in context. Unfortunately, not having read these stories, I was left wondering what was going on most of the time. It doesn't help that the narrator doesn't go a very good job selling you why these characters are villains and must be defeated, though that's partly intended.
As you can see, it took me about 10 hours to beat, unlocking all achievements that is. A linear run would probably only take a couple of hours but straight-forward isn't the way to go with this game. It definitely has replay value, as a second run is almost a must for those keen on piecing the puzzle together.
If the concept of a 2D meta side-scroller attracts you, I can confidently say
is worth it at full price. It has solid, fun combat and a narrator that never fails to keep you entertained. Plus, you get the OST for free and that's not half-bad either.

This game has a good concept behind it, taking bits and pieces from Age of Empires, a fraction management RTS that revolves around gathering resources to build things, all mostly in order to support your army and its conquests, and Banished, a city-building survival RTS that revolves around careful planning of your village's resource and citizen management, with just a pinch of Majesty and Settlers flavour in a fantasy viking setting.
However, as of now there's simply not enough to do in-game, and replaying doesn't really add anything dramatic to the whole experience as the fractions ("clans") presented aren't that drastically different to each other. They are also quite unbalanced, Stag clan is too OP. The maps are also quite small, and don't have much variety to them. The events that happen in the game are repetitive, and also don't have much variety to them. Diplomacy or any sort of contact with the other fractions other than them attacking you or you attacking them and trading via marketplace is nonexistant. I wouldn't recommend playing it in it's current state, as better games similar to this one exist. If you're longing for a Nordic fantasy, play Banner Saga. If you want a good "empire"/city management RTS experience, play Age of Empires or Banished. That's all. Pretty much everything really nice that the game has going on for it is graphics, and it's not nearly enough for a game of this genre.
It's a solid game nonetheless, although I don't think it's worth it's full price. Hopefully the developers won't abandon their project, because it seems promising, however in it's current state it's not really worth paying that much attention to.

As the lines between mobile, console and desktop gaming increasingly blur, where a game begins isn’t necessarily where it will end up. While Minecraft, Terraria and Don’t Starve have all made the jump to mobile, so are mobile games making the jump to PC.
Joining Bardbarian, 10000000, and Knightmare Tower, Neon Drive is the latest notable mobile-game-turned-PC-port. Everything about this lane-based rhythm runner oozes with 80’s appeal. From the synthesized sound and neon lights down to the arcade cabinet level select screen, style permeates every aspect of this game. Simply put, if Com Truise, Rad Racer and Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon had a baby, it would be Neon Drive.
But Neon Drive is more than just a runner game; it’s an exercise in creative level design. Each of the seven stages starts innocently enough, with a barrier-dodging sequence synced to the game’s electronic synthwave background music, but the simplicity ends there. As you progress, levels transform in very unpredictable ways:  camera angles shift, your car sprouts wings, or an alien spaceship bombards you with its photon torpedoes (seriously). The amount of ingenuity exhibited in these phase changes is marvelous. And it’s that sense of curiosity of what will come next that will drive you forward.
Even though stages transform, the core mechanic remains the same throughout; move right or move left. But it’s also partly a rhythm game, as your movements will often line up with the music. Unfortunately, that feeling doesn’t always persist through the entire level, forcing you to consciously unsynchronize your movements from the music during key moments. It’d be more accurate to call it a tempo-based game, as the speed of the music does inform how quickly you should be moving. It’s a subtle difference, and one that I can see tripping some players up, but fret not.
Distinct from the mobile version, the PC version unlocks all levels right from the start, allowing you to bounce between stages at your leisure. If Level 3 is proving too difficult, simply jump to Level 4. Or you can preview all 7 levels to gain a sense of how much designs vary, even within the construct of an 80’s neon lane-changer. And you will want to see everything this game has to offer. Every backdrop attempts to emulate the material which inspired it, whether it’s driving through Tron, flying through Afterburner’s sky, or dodging Blade Runner’s traffic.
It’s admirable what Fraoula has accomplished with Neon Drive, to say the least. The aural and visual presentation is so on point that calling it a mobile port doesn’t do it justice. Graphic settings include options for bloom, reflections and fog, as well as your choice of anti-aliasing. The game also controls equally well with a controller as it does with a keyboard. And if you can play on a big screen with big sound, it’s even better. Do yourself a favor though and avoid cheap knock-offs like Outdrive.

I've been waiting for a great title of ancient-medieval base-building RTS since the era of Empire Dawn of The Modern World, Empire Earth II, Stronghold Crusader 2, and Battle Realms. Northgard delivers nice visual and heart-warming for viking theme. Its population system is pretty much like Battle Realms where each peasant is generated from the hut and trained to become warrior, loremaster etc. Nevertheless, the game could not satisfy and surprise me in several aspects:
Faction:
The faction variation is not very well-designed as the buildings and unit rosters for each faction are exactly the same (except for color and few special alteration). Hence, the gameplay becomes repetitive very quickly in this term
The dev should add additional types of buildings and units (e.g. cavalry,  including their patterns & functions in order to create more varied play-styles.
Maps:
The map is not literally free-to-build, but it's tile-based that limits the amount of buildings on each tile (Like Empire Earth & Age of Empire) in which the limitation is very frustrating (2-5 buildings per tile due to its size). Most tiles possess special resources like iron, fertile land, runestone etc., in which some might enable you to explore to gain extra materials or build special building to exploit particular resource, but it's still inadequate.
The map is also randomly generated (not quite sure) and there will be one unique tile that could lead you to the end-game (if you enable map victory) when you conquer on it. There are certain numbers of the unique tile with different victory objective. Nonetheless, the condition, in which units couldn't trespass unexplored area or disconnected path among each tile, is too limited so we cannot extend the possibilities of desirable actions.
Game speed & scale:
There should be a setting in which people could adjust the game speed because I think the time runs too fast for me to observe and admire in-game surrounding (Iike CIV in real-time where AI is always expanding).
The scale of the battle is also too small because in normal difficulty, I could wipe one faction with seven tiles out by deploying only 4 units and 1 special units, which make no sense at all. Moreover, due to the structure limitation, there is no wall or types of defense system (e.g. watchtower, fort, barricade, trap, etc.) that could strengthen the territory.
Other minor complaints:
- Some clans' benefits is much worse, compared with others
- No map creation/editor settings
- Tech tree is too small
- There are only 2 resources wood & stone is required to build structures.
- There are only 3 types of military units - warrior, axe-thrower, shield-bearer (excluding unique special units)
- Food is scarce, can't fishing and farming anywhere, unless you control a particular tile that possesses each special resources (fresh lake & fertile land), can't farming on the grassland & can't fishing along the sea shore, seriously?
In conclusion, I perceive that the game is the combination of various title, still, it's more like banished with fewer survival features, but replaces with exploration and combat system, which both of them is flawed. Thus, since the game is still in the early access, should be waiting and observing changes & update might be a better idea to see which direction does the dev gonna go forward.

Review for a beta game: 85%
Review if it were a finished game (which it isn't): 75%
Northgard is a highly promising RTS game with some twists. By way of background, my favorite RTS games are Warcraft 3 and Company of Heroes, which colors my thoughts on the genre.
Northgard doesn't try to imitate popular RTS games but seeks to break new ground by combining elements of Settlers (resource management), Civilization (victory conditions like fame and wealth), and traditional war elements but with small armies (think COH -- the max army size you can have presently is 15 units, if I'm playing correctly). There are also interesting weather mechanics (summer-winter cycles that can result in starvation), plus some RNG with natural disasters and random mobs attacking your territory. Games tend to be more deliberative and on the longer side -- think an hour or more.
Apart from obvious features like a Tutorial and Campaign Mode, I'd like to see the developers add  more depth to the game. Don't get me wrong -- the game is already complex and fun, but I feel like there are probably additional mechanics that could be introduced. In particular, I think the military units could be expanded, such as artillery or more hero units.
Presently, the game is enjoyable in multiplayer mode. However, to rise to stardom territory, the devs need to keep working on it. I believe final release is late 2017, so here's to hoping this will be a great RTS!

This game is awesome. Imagine if the 80s came to the future and said, "Hey video games are♥♥♥♥♥♥now, you know what they need? More neon." And this game is that. Neon lights all around, making it near impossible to play without being on some kind of high. Okok enough fluff, let's talk gameplay. It's Audiosurf but better. Using your retro-styled car, you cruise between barriers in time with the music. Actual skill comes in as the music gets faster, and you have a lesser window for error. The controls are tight and when you eventually screw up for the 7634th time, you know it's because you're not that good yet. If there are audio sync issues there is a slider to correct that as well. A very unique feature that sets this game apart is that the levels change halfway, giving a varied experience for each level, compared to the monotonous feel of games like Audiosurf. The music is phenomenal, and gives me nostalgia of music that I never even experienced in the 80s cos, well, I wasn't born yet. The visuals are exceptional, and really give off a very 80s vibe. and it is incredible to see the different themes they have between the levels.
Now with all this being said, this game still has its demerits. There are only 7 levels for you to play with. Although they have 3 difficulties each, they are still basically the same. Personally, I completed all 7 levels on normal within an hour. There is an endurance mode, however that is really just playing through the same levels again without a break in between. In terms of game length and replayability, Neon Drive does not have much to offer. As such, the price may come across as a little steep for some of us. However, the real gameplay in this game comes from the sheer difficulty of it, and playing the game to 100% would take someone a considerable amount of time. So if you can get past the small number of levels and want a challenge, it will give you exactly what you want.
TL:DR version
Pros:
Twitch reaction gameplay (AKA Insanely difficult)
Awesome music that syncs with gameplay flawlessly
Beautiful visuals
80s references
Levels that transform halfway
Neon
Cons:
Small number of levels

This game had a lot of potential for me, but it dissapointed me in the end.

The atmosphere and imagination really lingered with me after finishing it.
On a technical note, it's a 2D point'n'click - standard, simple, and well-implemented.
Story-wise there's a lot going on, but you as the player really have the option of taking or leaving what you want. Like Alice in Wonderland, the journey is so interesting and enjoyable that you feel satisfied at the end, even without necessarily understanding everything that just transpired.
The characters are unique and interesting. The best part is the dual-worlds mechanic, which allows our hero to visit the same location in different states - one 'normal' and one 'nightmarish'. It leads to some very interesting puzzles and provides insight to the character and plot, if you want to delve a little deeper.
It is a dark fantasy, but it never overreaches on the horror element. I find that writers in this subgenre rely too much on the juxtaposition of innocence and gore to rile their audience, but Fran Bow is less "Luna Game" and more "Pan's Labyrinth" in balancing its themes.

I love DOOM 1 and 2. Personally, I like DOOM 2 better. Not sure why, but I do. But that isn't what this review is about DOOM 3. But I'll quickly go over DOOM 1 and 2. Both games are pretty similar. If you like one you'll like the other. They run very well, and have great replay value.
DOOM 3, though.
In terms of gameplay, I think that DOOM 3 is pretty fun. Very challenging, but not bad. The story is the same as DOOM 1's. I haven't played DOOM 3 before BFG Edition, so the only difference I know of is the flashlight being attached to weapons. I personally don't mind that. DOOM 3 has 2 problems that really makes me want to not recommend BFG Edition. The performance. First off, I can run this game. Maybe all of this is because I'm running it on a Windows 10 laptop. I'm not sure. But the game will run smoothly for a few minutes at a time, then the framerate will drop and the resolution will, too. So in other words, it gets blurry and lags. It normally happens briefly, but at the worst times, like when a big enemy appears or a door opens and a demon is standing there. This gets on my nerves a lot. Also, DOOM 3's weapons feel a little weak sometimes. Not the chaingun, or the plasman rifle, but mainly the pistol and shotgun. The pistol does absolutely nothing, unlike in DOOM 1 and 2. The shotgun feels underpowered against some enemies, which gets annoying.
I normally don't end my reviews with number scores, but I feel like that's the best way to do the verdict for this one. DOOM 3 BFG Edtion gets a 7.5 from me. DOOM 1 and 2 are worth your time, but you can get those for a lower price on Steam by themselves. DOOM 3 has some issues that I wish could be fixed. If you're hyped for DOOM 4, and want to play all of the DOOM games before that one, just buy BFG edition for XBOX 360 or PS3 if you really want the entire franchise in one bundle.

This is my second favorite Street Fighter,  besides SF2 back in the arcades.    People who don't like the mechanics simply just don't know how to play a fighting game.    I play with a junky PS2 controller converted to PC and I miss a million inputs and I still know how to figure the game out.
For people who complain it is unfinished.    They think every fighting game should have like 40 characters where half of them do identical setups and moves.     Each character feels pretty unique and on their own.   The balancing is fair to a degree,  although some matches clearly have problems.
LAG FIX -  If you're having a slowdown issue,  it persists even when you do every possible correction.    The best solution is simply opening up your regedit and deleteing any reference to "StreetFighterV",  also deleteing the folder in your %appdata%.  After you clear it out,  just file integrity check on Steam.   It fixed 90% of my slowdowns.   Changing vsync to adaptive appears to help some.
I'd give the game 5 stars if I didn't have a random lag bug (which after a year still isn't fixed, and its not based off the performance of the machine).     Netcode has issues as well and matchmaking can in some cases take way longer than it needs to.     Hearthstone matchmaking takes seconds,  while SFV takes minutes and in some cases 10+ mins when both Ranked + Casual are enabled.
If you enjoy fighting games,  this to me is the best one out there.   I just wish Capcom would fix the PC slowdown and get their netcode optimized.

Don't waste your time and money on the game unless you want to devote months and months to the study and rote memorization of every bit of frame data for every single move of every single character in a game which trickle releases new characters throughout each year's "season".
And after you learn all of that, you'll spend all your game play time blocking and blocking, unable to move or strike, but at least you'll now know why you can't move.  Your block stuns are massive and the recovery frames of striking a blocking opponent are almost non-existent,  so your fastest 3 frame strike is going to take you many more block stun frames before you can even release it,  and by then your opponents hardest punch will beat your 3 frame lightest punch so you're constantly being out struck by much harder and much slower strikes.
On top of that,  if you do get a 3 frame window for your light,  sfv has strength priority that will out punch your light with any other incoming strike of harder power, further negating the ability to get out a 3 frame light strike.
And add to that the crush counter that is a very fast medium strike for alot of op characters that will crumple you if you throw oit anything slower than a 3 frame light,  and will often also crumple your 3 frame light coming out of your block stun as well.
And add to that the ability for certain characters to throw out a safe EX move once they have any 3 frame window of vulnerability wherein you might have been able to get a strike in, which instantly closes the gap and beats anything you wete going to do,  allowing them to repeat the entire cycle.
And add to that certain characters that actually have v-reversals that strike you and lead to further combos or block strings,  onve you did finally successfully strike him with your lightest hit, which instantly just turns into you getting hit instead, wheras other characters only have v-reversals that escape.
Add to that the extreme unbalanced frame data and movesets that give some characters every single advantage and move and reversal and tgen just gives them more of everything whilst other characters have dinky movesets that cause them to be unable to do in kind what has been done to them, leaving only a certain clique of the cast able to apply limitless pressure and punishments to the rest of the cast which absolutely cannot.
And add to that the ultra of the same op characters just gives them even better frame data, recovery,  attack speed and comboing ability Notwithstanding they already had the best in the game, greatly multiplying the design imbalances and poor game play
And your left with an extremely one-sided gameplay that leaves one player essentially blocking the entire match, and only those that have memorized every bit of frame data from every single character can even hope to know at which point in the 99 second match you will have a 1/60th of a second window where you can successfully execute your lightest weakest strike which absolutely must be directly combo'd into your biggest longest combo or else all you were able to do was get that one lightest weakest strike on your opponent during the match.

Nine hours into this game and I'm quite frustrated.
I finished up the main story in VH1 and decided to play VH2. 1 seemed so short to me.
Thankfully 2 picks up at the moment 1 ends and I was happy to see the story continue.
My eletion turned to frustration over little things that could have been done better.
DX11 doesn't work in game on my PC. There are massive pixelized blobs where
characters stand, right from the very first scene. Rolling back to DX10 fixed this.
Every time I start the game I get pop ups from Microsoft and Steam recognizing it as
the first time I'm launching the game. Not a biggie. I just question why this happens.
Mobs of monsters that pull you toward them, surround you and kill you when you can't
do anything about it is not fun. As is elite type mobs who will one shot you the moment
they see you. This for me is a big design flaw. No matter what armor/weapons/skills you have,
I have found these situation completely unavoidable...and too frequent.
This is my main peeve for VH2. Balance is so erratic. To be fighting hordes succesfully only
to be one shotted by a creature that barely enters the screen is just not right.
Despite my downside problems with the game it has such promise.
The addition of a Chimera pet was nice to see. You can send it on private missions and
it will bring back items for you. You can even call on this pet to help you in your own
battles, although it doesn't really seem to do anything but stay to the rear and tends
not to help me. Perhaps further down the line it will start helping more.

what Katarina is going to say next!

Ok, So Starbound, lets talk about it.
The game itself is actually fairly nice. Having played both stable and unstable versions since their release... It is a game with literally infinite amounts of progression. Back then, your matter manipulator was very lack luster and now it is an essential tool to have.
Compared to a game we all know, 'Terraria'. The game is both similar and vastly different. The major one being that the world is 'Infinite' You can travel to different worlds, and set up different home bases. The questing system is quite interesting. Even more so if you dig deeper to actually have tenants who can sell you some nifty weapons. The tenants, over time will generate their own quests.
Compared to Terraria, Chucklefish, in my opinion, do their best to keep the game feeling alive. A way they did this was through the nightly unstable build which shows what they have added and what could be expected in the future patches to come.
In this game, you can end up loving the character you make and just have fun in your own personal vast sandbox. Or of course playing with friends is always awesome. In this game there are 'classes' in a sense.
The Seperator is the 'ok' melee damage dealer, who has the most defense and health but low energy.
The Accelerator is the balanced ranged damage dealer who has a balanced amount of health, defense and energy.
The Manipulator is the high damage dealer who has the least amount of defense and armor, but high energy. (I personally play this one as melee high risk, high reward fun.)
The game is pretty fun with its progression, especially with your ship as it will essentially be your sort of home base. The game is awesome, and a hell of a lot more fun with more people to play with.

The story picks up where Van Helsing I left off -- The little town of Borgovia needs help, and monster hunter extraodinaire Van Helsing is there to aid it. Helping the resistance do what they must to get the city back and fend off the monsters; should you not have played the first installment at all, or if it’s been long since you touched it, the introduction video does a good job of recapping the important bits and summing up what’s been going on.
If there’s one thing to say for Neocore games it’s that they do pretty neat cinematic cutscenes, very nice and artistic, that give you a distinct feel of watching a movie - unfortunately, even the cutscenes can sometimes be a little bit too long when they’re put in between the action. The voice actors chosen are excellent at their roles; and the chosen depths, tones and infliction the cast uses throughout the game suit the characters very well; helping immerse you in the world. Along with the lovely visual and voices, the game has one of the best soundtracks I’ve heard in an ARPG, fitting the mood and slightly dark atmosphere of the game, atmosphere that is slightly uplifted by the many humorous lines and various pop culture references that are to be found throughout Van Helsing II, as it was in the original.
The graphics improve a little on Van Helsing I, but in my opinion they still seem to lack some optimization. Despite my computer being the recommended setup for the game, and despite being in low settings, I had the exact same problem with the game I did during my playthrough of Van Helsing I ... LAG. From the get go the game is just a little bit slow, and after about an hour or more of playing the game would become really slow and laggy, sometimes even freezing up for a few seconds if I continue playing. And this was in the single player campaign. It was also noticeable during loading screens - loading the game takes just a little too long sometimes, particularly during the initial loading screen.
Despite that, and jumping into the actual gaming aspect, Van Helsing II can be a delight to play. Right off the bat you’re given the option to either import a character from Van Helsing I or play with a new one which you can start from level 1 or from level 30 with a pre-designed one, which is great for trying out the different classes and builds; the difficulty of the levels also accommodates depending on which starting point you choose, so you’ll still get the full experience without finding it “too easy” just because you chose to start at level 30 instead.
I chose to start anew so I could get a fresh look at the game, plus, it’d been a long while since I’d last played the originial, so a refresher course wouldn’t hurt. When starting your get you get to choose between three classes: Hunter, Thaumaturge or Arcane Mechanic. The classes are all quite different from each other, and each one has a very ample skill tree (and choice of auras) to pick and choose from, so everyone is likely to find a mix of powers and skills that suit their playing style perfectly. Personally, my favorite character is still the Hunter, though the other two can be fun to play too. My only regret in the system would be that I’d like for a bit more customization options outside the skill tree (maybe more visual variety), yet in the end it doesn’t make much of a difference.
Once you make your character you’ll also have access to the options menu (why you don’t have access to this before that is beyond me), which gives you plenty of chances to remap keys and change audio and video options. Some of these require you to relaunch the game to go into effect, which is a bit annoying as it takes long to load.
Katarina is once more with you during the game. I like the companionship and the role she plays in the overall story and gaming aspects. She can carry stuff, you can send her out shopping, and you can pick how she will behave during fights (ranged, melee, aid only, etc), all of which is pretty neat. They also have great chemistry between them, making you feel less lonely during the map runs.
The monsters are all well designed, with a fair variety to them and interesting looks and powers. The game has various difficulty modes ranging from casual to hardcore, and you can switch them at any time, yet I noticed that it seems a bit unbalanced regardless of what difficulty mode you’ve chosen: either the enemies are far too easy or far too hard, all in the same map and mode.
The story is fairly linear and simple, but it's also intriguing; the characters are interesting, and the questing follows the same vein of its predecessor. The tower defense mode also returns, improved, and you can now send captains to do some of those quests for you, which is a nice change in pace (as I’m not particularly fond of defending things, I’m more into destroying them). The downside of this is every so often they interrupt your questing with information, “demanding” you get back to take care of a situation or another (you don’t really need to drop everything to do as they ask, and I believe you can turn this off, but the interruption is annoying nonetheless).
The first time you’re thrown into the fry -meaning the tutorial and the very first city-defending section- I found it all a tad confusing and frustrating. During the tutorial there were some pop ups that went by just a little too fast for me to read - it was only a couple, yet it was bothersome enough as I couldn’t really remember what all did and was. During the city section I had problems finding my way until I got used to the map indicators again, and then I had a bit of troubles finding some of the more out-of-the-way stairs and elevators, and choosing which answer would be correct for what I wanted to do; however, once you get past that area, the gameplay goes pretty smoothly, and if there was one thing I did appreciate it was that, while there were many things to learn, at least the main interface didn’t look cluttered.
The game offers witty dialogue and, when questing, allows you yo choose from two or three answers. I like being able to choose when talking to characters (though most of the time is just the two typical ‘yes’ or ‘no’ disguised in a colorful fashion), however it suffered from the same all the ‘choose your answer’ games suffer from: none were clear. An answer did not quite mean what I thought it would mean which made me miss a quest (for instance, on Saving Bryan had two answers that were very similar but different in tone, and I thought the second option would also give me a chance to end the conversation and go look for him, but it didn’t and it sent me elsewhere with that mission failed). I was rather annoyed to have some missions failed or postponed (or even denied completely from trying them later) simply because the option I chose still included some form of “give me more time” or “I can’t right now” but it ended up cancelling the quest instead and the quest indicator disappeared. I had the same with a quest where I could either destroy a totem or find a relic, and when I refused destroying it initially but then changed my mind, I couldn’t go back and destroy it, so I was forced on the second quest path.
After the first chapter you get to have a “pet”; a chimera you can either send to fetch stuff for you, or summon into battle. This is quite handy, and the chimera is quite adorable (in the way giant, angry beasts are adorable, I guess). It even chases around little animals while in the lair.

Van Helsing II is an aRPG set in the mythical land of Borgovia. If you've played Grim Dawn, Diablo or Torchlight you'll be familiar with the gameplay. The game does have a unique ability system though, as you fight you gain rage which can be spent to powerup your abilities. For example lets say you're using a lightning spell, powering it up may cause enemies to be shocked, or it may increase the number of enemies hit. A powered up spell only has one charge and can be activated with the spacebar, although this becomes tedious very fast and I'd wager 99.9% of people have this set to auto cast whenever available. The game allows you to set up powerup presets so you can very much set it and forget it and the game will automatically boost the chosen ability(s) whenever you have sufficient rage. Apart from that it's your usual aRPG fare, you have a standard talent tree with forks and paths, passive abilities and stat points which allow you to customise your character further.
Throughout the game you're accompanied by your ghostly companion, Katarina. She works very much like the Torchlight pet, she can pick up items, fight for you and even be sent back to town to sell and buy which saves you the bother! She also has her own stats and talent tree, you can either build her to become stronger herself, or build her as a complete buff bot which will give you lots of powerful auras. Usefulness aside she's actually a big part of the game, and the banter between you and her is often really enjoyable, the voice acting for both Van Helsing and Katarina is top notch (the same can't be said for all the characters though!).
The story will take around 10 hours to complete which is poor, and shorter than the first game. You will finish the story around level 30 but to do scenarios you'll need to be level 57 and I couldn't work out how to level up further. Perhaps this was only intended for people who imported their character from Van Helsing I but I started a new character so was much lower level by the end of the game.
Technically the game is fine, most quests have voice acting which isn't always a given for this genre, especially from the smaller studios, and while not perfect it is pretty funny at times and there are plenty of references to other games and TV shows which I enjoyed. I will say the voice acting for Prisoner 7 is terrible, absolutely terrible and lowers the quality of the entire game by being so bad. Graphically the game is OK, it's a couple of years old and wouldn't have been anything to rave about back then, but it's fine. Performance is worse than Van Helsing I which stayed at 60fps without dips, whereas Van Helsing II will often dip in frame rate, and certain areas have issues and completely tank the frame rate. There is also a nasty bug with DX11 and Windows 8.1 where textures will not load, I suffered with this often and it made the game extremely frustrating at times.
Overall it's better than Van Helsing I, but it also introduces its own problems so I can't score it higher than 6/10, which is what I gave the first game. And once again I can only recommend buying this game while it's 75% off.

Bastion is an adventure beat-em-up game with unique artstyle, superb storytelling, hypnotizing music, and a meta-ish thingy in the plotline.
Bastion graphical representation used a lot of handpainted scenery, resulting in a beautiful and easy-in-the-eye kind of graphics, you won't find many game that uses this kind (well, aside from other game from Supergiant, Transistor). It'll be a different 'graphics' experience for you with Bastion
The story in this game are told with a narrator as the player progresses through the Bastion world. The character player control is silent (and looks like the main character communicate with other using handwriting, as hinted by all the dialogue choices when interacting with others), and all element about Bastion are told by the narrator. The narrator did a really excellent job at delivering the world of Bastion to the player. His voice feels friendly, like someone you've known for so long, yet only meet again after a long separation. You won't feel tired listening to the narrator thoughout the game, and it is also a good thing because the way of the storytelling is unique, leaving you with a feeling of wanting to be told more.
Music at the bastion is a little different with other games that usually use orchestra of violin, drum, piano or everything else. It sound like 1 or 2 instrument that playing along with a storyteller, and perfectly captures the predicament of the story being told. This fits a lot with the storytelling style of Bastion.
Not much of gameplay selling point can be told here. Some people might feels the combat is repetitive, and old as there's no differentiation to other game with same type of combat. That might be true, but I find Bastion combat is at good value. The many Arsenal you'll find coupled with passive boost from Distillery and difficulty tweaker from the Shrine will kinda force you to seek new way to combat the enemy and it's good enough for me.

This game is awesome. Imagine if the 80s came to the future and said, "Hey video games are♥♥♥♥♥♥now, you know what they need? More neon." And this game is that. Neon lights all around, making it near impossible to play without being on some kind of high. Okok enough fluff, let's talk gameplay. It's Audiosurf but better. Using your retro-styled car, you cruise between barriers in time with the music. Actual skill comes in as the music gets faster, and you have a lesser window for error. The controls are tight and when you eventually screw up for the 7634th time, you know it's because you're not that good yet. If there are audio sync issues there is a slider to correct that as well. A very unique feature that sets this game apart is that the levels change halfway, giving a varied experience for each level, compared to the monotonous feel of games like Audiosurf. The music is phenomenal, and gives me nostalgia of music that I never even experienced in the 80s cos, well, I wasn't born yet. The visuals are exceptional, and really give off a very 80s vibe. and it is incredible to see the different themes they have between the levels.
Now with all this being said, this game still has its demerits. There are only 7 levels for you to play with. Although they have 3 difficulties each, they are still basically the same. Personally, I completed all 7 levels on normal within an hour. There is an endurance mode, however that is really just playing through the same levels again without a break in between. In terms of game length and replayability, Neon Drive does not have much to offer. As such, the price may come across as a little steep for some of us. However, the real gameplay in this game comes from the sheer difficulty of it, and playing the game to 100% would take someone a considerable amount of time. So if you can get past the small number of levels and want a challenge, it will give you exactly what you want.
TL:DR version
Pros:
Twitch reaction gameplay (AKA Insanely difficult)
Awesome music that syncs with gameplay flawlessly
Beautiful visuals
80s references
Levels that transform halfway
Neon
Cons:
Small number of levels
Neon

Sleeping dogs takes place in Hong Kong where you are an undercover cop who gets into the triads to scout for information on the inside. There are 2 sets of missiong (police and triad) and many side missions and favours to do.
This game is a bad PC port, menu and control wise. The menu system uses the mouse half the time, and it barely works, and the controls are very awkward, and non intuitive, many actions are mapped to the same key. They forgot this was PC and we could have over a 100 keys and didn't need to repeat maps.
That being said, this game is fantastic. The graphics (especially with the free high res textures) is absolutely stunning especially when raining. You can see the plitter platter of each and every drop on the road, your character gets wet visibily, etc. The screen has so much stuff going on, and the view distance is so large there is no pop in, and Hong Kong looks as busy as the devs intended for it to be,
The story is great, I felt sucked in to every character and event, to the polnt where I thought many times of just leaving the police force and being a triad full time.
The game does not have a multiplayer, but has a social achievement system where you try and beat your friends in challenges. For example, the clean drive challenge requires you to drive over a certain speed and not hit anything. When you start to drive carefully, the challenge appears on screen timing you whilst telling you the score to beat and who holds that score. After you fail/succeed, it tells you your rank amongst friends, which I think is a very competitive and fun layer in this already layered cake of a game.
So to summarize, TL;DR version: Controls - bad but adjustable. Graphics - great. Story - fantastic. Achievements -  fun.

Buyer beware!
If you thought this was a nice rythm game with killer soundtrack, think again.
The soundtrack is horrible, placing rap-like music with rather unpleasant vocals in the very beginning (apparently to scare people off), and burying nice electronic tracks (DRR is famous for those, y'know) somewhere in the later stages of the game, which are - you guess it - unaccessible.
Next, the game tries to push on you a story - a story straight out of Nobodycaresville; regardless, you're locked in the story mode until your ears bleed.
The game has a lot of problems picking up on the actual rythm of the tracks - and knows it, allowing you to adjust for latency of your input devices. Surprise, surprise, it does not help, and people with a sense of rythm suffer. The only way towin is to rely on visual cues - and that makes life hardly easier, because even on basic difficulty the screen becomes a cluster-F of colors and moving objects, FAST. Add in camera position that actually obscures some of the important areas to look out for, and you're set.
To clarify my position: a good beatmania game, like the aforementioned classic DDR, has two ways of telling you when to take action - either "by look" or "by feel". "Feel" comes from rythm, sound and the general pattern of actions (i.e. steps or keypresses). "Look" is there for you if you're more into visual cues - they are right on the screen, presented clearly, and unobstructed by anything else. You can use either one, or a combination of both, to achieve the same results.
This game fails BOTH.
Adding insult to injury, the "play your own track" section is locked until you are late into the story mode - and, apparently, there is no "plug and play" in that mode (unlike, oh say, Audiosurf), everything has to be adjusted manually.
My bottom line is this: do not waste your money, even at bargain prices.

It's a rhythm game, but a terrible one.  Not for the music, but the gameplay itself is just flawed.  The UI is a bit confusing, and can take a while to realize what, exactly, signified what.  Your fail conditions, etc.  You "attack" by pressing the proper key in the direction of the circling attacker when they reach the highlighted point on the ground.  However, the four points are you are completely separated from each other.  There is no real way to tell if the attacks are simultaneous or just very close - and if they are very close, what order they'll be in, unless you watched the attackers enter the stage and haven't lost track of them while trying to defeat the ones before them.  And that leads to some songs being absurdly difficult.  The story - as irrelevant as it is - is your typical "source of all music" someone trying to steal/destroy all except the ones for themselves to monopolize.  And they've ATTEMPTED to put humor in, but every joke I recognized as a joke fell completely flat.  Nothing in it is cute or clever, nothing in the game is particularly well thought out.  Someone decided they wanted to try their hand at a quick and dirty rhythm and this is the result.  An unplayable, unfunny, unintelligent mess.

If you're like me and enjoy shredding awesome fake guitar solos on your keyboard/plastic guitar then stay far away from this game. If you're just looking for a simple four button rhythm game then I suggest you to play Stepmania if you haven't already. In fact, I'll go play that now.

Zen Studios, the developers and publishers of KickBeat, had developed only CastleStorm and Pinball FX2 and its numerous addons before they gave the world this somewhat special game. That raises some questions but without further ado... In the red corner - a beat 'em up. In the blue corner - a (music) rhythm game. Let's fight!
Using either W-A-S-D (and some other keys for powerups) or a Xbox 360 controller, you're controlling one of two useable characters and the goal is to finish the songs as you're fighting waves of enemies who would like to beat you down to the ground. Most music in the game consists of rock and metal - examples: Celldweller, Marilyn Manson, Rob Zombie and Blue Stahli - with some additional tracks from rap and electronic artists, BUT the good thing is that you can just add tracks from your own computer and voila, endless replayability.
The gameplay while being somewhat repetetive at times is kept alive by the music being played in the levels. There's three different enemy types, the different types have their own attack patterns, and you've got powerups and four different levels of difficulity. The developers included three short tutorials which explains all the controls and so on and does it very good.
Well, that's the gameplay... that's the sound... the controls... how about the graphics? Not that they are that important to a game in this "genre" (I don't think there's any other game like this out there... is there?) but they are acceptable. The models look decent, the cutscenes are kind off handdrawn so they look pretty good, nothing spectacular in any way.
I had some fun with it, playing through the different songs, and I will probably return to it some day... and to anyone looking for a new rhythm game, I recommend this game to you.

Excellent fighting game with really great mechanics. Even me, as a non brawler/fighting game player, could pick this up and learn reasonably well through the (somewhat slow) tutorial and story mode. Good variance on fighters and styles and their design, as well as stage design, are well made.
As far as story mode goes, it's often very obvious that the texture quality in places REALLY suck, especially during cutscenes, where it looks like some really poor models have been used. It's a stark contrast between cutscenes and actual gameplay, where gameplay easily wins out thankfully.
Enemy AI is well programmed and the Medium one has been beating me fairly consistently, which is what I expect at my rather low skill level.
Do I have any complaints? Yes, absolutely. The aforementioned texture quality for one, but also the boss design. Goro and Shao Khan are hideous examples of bosses. Not only does Shao Khan hit like a freight train dualwielding schoolbusses, but he's completely unstaggerable during any of his moves, guaranteeing that if you are anywhere in his vicinity, you ARE getting hit. He has multiple attacks that go straight through blocks and is quick as bloody hell. I don't mind that the boss hits hard, or have tons of HP and you need to utilize some strategy to beat him, but making him completely immune to interrupts? That's just low. In addition, his special attack does around 50% of your healthbar, but your own barely scrapes off 10%. I don't mind bosses doing much damage, but that is a ridiculus difference.
All this leaves you standing in a corner using teleports and spam ranged at him, which is definitely not fun whatsoever.

Starbound is fun and definitely worth checking out.
It's one of the better examples of a 2D exploration/block-mining/building game.  The worlds are colorful and varied, and there are nice details like weather, well-defined racial cultures, and cute little climate-appropriate non-hostile animals.  There are tons of weapons drops, and the types I focused on, melee broadswords and guns, were both viable.  There are also multiple types within the melee and gun subcategories, plus there is some magic stuff which I have yet to try out.
It's also nice to have your own ship and a quest hub in the form of a moon base thing, but this also leads to a small problem for me which I'll add to the section below.
Some minor problems--
Hopefully once more content is implemented it will be a little more fleshed out.  I got through all of the available quests in like 2-3 days, and they didn't really seem to go anywhere.  They were more of the "go and collect this thing for me" variety.  There were a few exceptions in larger, pre-built quest areas, which I really liked, but they were mostly stand-alone mini-adventures.  It would be nice if at some point these could push some kind of even rudimentary storyline.  Still, it was nice to have quests at all which many games of this type lack.
As for what I mentioned above, having your ship and a quest hub is nice, but it really made it so I didn't have much of a desire to build my own base on some random planet.  There really isn't the "Crap...I need to build a shelter so I don't die" drive since it's already there and you get access to it really early.  Also, part of the reason I like this genre is the fact I can build giant strongholds to my tastes, but there are already pre-built areas that already accomplish most of the basics of what I would want.  There is definitely the potential to get crazy with a base with a ton of block variety, lots of art objects, and stuff like electronic wiring and whatnot, but it would take a while to surpass the pre-built stuff in badassitude.
Along with that, the sheer number of planets seems pretty unnecessary.  Once you kind of figure out the base set of planet types, you start to see things repeat fairly quickly.
But most of these gripes really just translate into me enjoying the game and wanting more.
In short, if your #1 priority is to mine a set area and build a defensible base then I'd say go for something like Terraria, but if you like exploring cool planets, hanging out with bird dudes and robots, or feeding your ship pet some friggin' space bacon, then give this a shot.

It's always offers something to do, but after a few hours you are pretty much done with progression. You have the best armor and you should have really good weapons. There are only 4 main quests (so far) and a bunch of mini-quests with small reward. Some things could use some balancing, like food. I try to start a farm and cook the everything, but I find it had little reward (we need hunger back) and end up giving up. There should be some way to nerf the ship, as I always find myself build a base in it instead of on a planet. I am aware that a large update is around the corner, and I'll continue to play until it comes out. Overall, if you're someone who likes sandbox-exploration games, Starbound is an essential.
