I like gore, fairytale-like games and delicate indies, which makes Fran Bow probably my favorite game in 2015 and 2016.
The style of Fran Bow is cute and creepy. It blurs the reality and hallucination as it intends to and does a really great job. The art fits the atmosphere really well. The majority of the characters and scenes of the game look as if they come from a children’s story book, which reminds me of American Mcgee’s Alice series and a movie called Babadook. They all use the innocence of the art style to forge some really disturbing, dark and gore things which leads to a strong contrast to represent how some innocent life gets sucked into the vortex of chaos. Not only is the art so expressive, but the animations in Fran Bow is so well polished as well. I really like
I think animations of the characters is what contributes to the immersion of the game the most. Music, however, is not that memorable, but it has the atmosphere needed and it is still far better than mediocre.
As a point & click adventure puzzle game, the story and writings of Fran Bow is fascinating. The story itself is really dark and sad at first. But Fran manages to stay enthusiastic and curious throughout the game. Many point & click games have the protagonist reacting to things that can be clicked on. In Fran Bow, the reaction is mostly adorable and humorous, just like when it comes from a 10-year-old girl (with mental problem). The lines do not have to be sharp or smart but to remain childish and concerning that, I think the game does a better job than many Triple A titles because the lines fit the character well.
As for the story, apart from its dark and fabulous nature, many part of it has some kind of metaphor and I think some of them are not really clear. The ending is controversial. It is a bit cliffhanging and hopefully it will be explained in a sequel. I think the ending is
I really look forward to getting more answers from a sequel.
Fran Bow is a relatively small game which does not have that much content and really complex mechanics. As for what it already has, I think it’s mind-blowing enough. The game has the power to impress and inspire people which is a result of really careful design from the developers. Fran’s characteristics such as enthusiasm and curiosity must have something to do with the designer Natalia herself, though I don’t get where all those gores come from. I think it is a good way to craft indie games and it needs devoting a great part of life to it so one cannot do that very often. Anyway, I think it’s a brilliant start and Killmonday will be on my list of ”most anticipated developers”.

The reason why I bought Bastion was because of the immense praise and positive reviews it recieved on release. That might have been a mistake on my part, since I expected it to be a lot more than what it turned out to be. I didn't get the indie gem I thought I was getting, but instead a mediocre hack n slash with some underwhelming RPG elements slapped on top.
It does have one thing going for it admittedly, and that's the presentation. The isometric graphics are beautiful, they were clearly shown a lot of love, and the narration is enjoyable, even though it gets kind of irritating after a while.
The gameplay on the other hand is dreadful. It may be responsive and functional, but it is incredibly dull and repetitive and offers little challenge or variation. The levels are essentially all the same, there are no puzzles or interesting gameplay elements to differentiate them, only a slight difference in color hue and tileset. There isn't much enemy variation and it just feels like you're powering through mob after mob to get a little bit of story to keep you going(and the story is only decent at best).
My advice is to try the demo and see how you like it, since it will give a pretty good idea what you will do for the rest of the game. Don't believe the hype.

Sanctum 2 is a pairing of the tower defense and FPS genres with a bit of RPG sprinkled in for flavor.
You play as a core guardian; a sort of civil engineer with combat training. The base game allows you to choose from four guardians. A DLC adds another one to the mix. Each guardian has a signature weapon and a couple passive abilities. I applaud each guardian's passive abilities; they all seem to be unique and cater to a specific FPS playstyle. My favorite was the gentleman with a shotgun that does more damage to his victims the closer he is. Seeing how one rarely snipes with a shotgun, this turned out to be an incredibly powerful combination.
A very loose story frames the various maps where you prevent waves of enemies from one side of the map to the other. If you have ever played a tower defense game in the last few years this won't be wholly innovative feature. During the waves of enemies you pick up a pair of weapons and jump into fray. You may optionally jump into the fray with up to three other people. I suggest those people being close friends, because the idiots you will meet in the random multiplayer match-ups will only frustrate you.
You will enjoy the game much more playing solo or with close friends.
After you complete each level you can then play them through again with Feats of Strength enabled. The feats can make the enemies more durable or give them HP regeneration, for example. This can significantly difficult once you activate 3+ feats of strength, and can increase replay value if you happen to be a masochist.
Over all I enjoy playing Sanctum 2 and for the price I recommend it to anyone that is a fan of tower defense games or futuristic FPS.

Civilization's Objectives, Banished's Village Simulation and Age of Empire's Warfare.
You want to go full RTS and harrass or pillage all of your enemies ? Better start keeping your people happy (the more you expand, the more they EXPECT happiness) to secure the growth of your village. Better store a whole lot of food and upgrade your militia to not be penalised by winter.
Research and overall village's improvements are your thing ? Boost your gain of Lore and buff up your territories as you will be playing a turtle game against the wolves and draugrs that will periodically attack your city's weakest spots, and fight back other player's harrasses to slow you down.
You want to be recognized as the king of all northmen ? Reap fame by owning more and more territories, eliminating wolf and draugr dens, send villagers on raids and pay some skalds. You will even earn rewards on 2 different tresholds of fame points.
You like to barter, stock up in gold and pay everything you need with coins ? You better start trading resources in trade routes and own multiple marketplaces, as they have their own inventories !
The only real CONS that I can see :
- Stone circles might give too much of an advantage if too close of starting area.
- Trade victory is too easy to achieve, maybe step up the goals a bit or create events where you have to defend your gold against rogue clans or thieves
- Being aggressive with an army is not rewarding enough, it is better to stock up resources and play on defend mode all game

My friends have all said the same as well, they would perhaps like to have reskins of warriors for every different clans, and maybe a different chieftain for everyone, but anything can happen this is a early access, I trust the devs to keep this on the right track and make one of the most amazing RTS/CITY BUILDER genres since Age of Empire !

This is one of my top three games of all time. I've played this game for probably 500 hours on PS3 plus the amount I've played so far. I unlocked gold vehicles on the PS3 and got 100% completion apart from multiplayer achievements (could never get my internet to work on the PS3).
This is the best racing game of all time. The graphics look awesome and don't cause any lag at all. Drift is amazingly satisfying, ramps are fun and the air you get on even mundane stunt jumps feels incredible. The music is a mixture of pulse-pounding pop, classical music, and old-school Burnout music. There are a lot of billboards and gates to smash (160 and 400, respectively) and it can be a collectathon sometimes, but it's never awkward or boring. The difficulty is perfectly tuned to your skills and scales according to the tier you are racing in. The events are: Race, stunt run, marked man, and road rage, and all of them are really fun (ESPECIALLY Road Rage, because the takedown system in this game is
It's what made Burnout famous, and for good reason). Marked Man is also unique - it's you against a fleet of cars that are trying to take you out, and you have to get to the finish line without your car being destroyed. The progression of cars is perfect; every car you unlock is interesting and useful in its own way, you don't unlock anything before you should and you don't get lemons late in the game. Every car has its own personality, its own quirks, drives a little bit different, and there's a reason to try every one in the form of the Burning Route.
If there are a couple things I'd change they would be to have directions come a little sooner than they do, to have shortcuts marked off a little clearer in terms of where they go (there are shortcuts on races that will redirect you in the complete opposite direction of where you should be going and you won't know what those are until you encounter them),  and make crash mode more interesting. The DLC is stupid as hell - just a bunch of boring, pointless cars. Even though it's called The Ultimate Box, this box doesn't include them or any other DLC. There's an extra island area that you can access, but I haven't found it yet in my game - I don't think it's been ported. Stunt runs could also use a change in direction - the strategy for them (if you're new) is to drift your way to the airport or the mine, drive off a corkscrew ramp, e-brake, and drive off the same ramp again. It's just not fulfilling.
But yeah, again,
Edit: Finished it all again! Still a perfect port.

As far as shooters go, this one is horrible. This is coming from my having played this game for years and starting out loving it like a high school sweetheart and then flat-out hating it like an ex-wife that you pay alimony to. "Aliens vs. Predator" follows a long line of other Aliens, Predator, and Aliens versus Predator games that I could argue reached their heyday within the late-90s early-00s and this one tries its heart out to be the best modernized version of those games by combining shooter elements and "Mortal Kombat"-esque melee fighting, but those two styles of play are a worse mix than oil and water.
Where the shooter gameplay is fun, the fighting gameplay gets in the way and makes the game more frustrating than fun to play. And where the fighting gameplay is challenging, the combination with shooting gameplay makes it nearly impossible to just have a good ol' fisticuffs spar (which, by the way, is the only way to play as an Alien) when your opponent just goes "lol nope" and shoots you or throws a spear into your face instead. And the amount of inconsistencies in the range of melee attacks just boggles the mind to the point where "how did he hit me?" will be just as common in your vocabularly as "why can't I hit him?"
There are three playable factions: Predator, Alien, and Marine, and there is absolutely zero balance between them. One is a complete battle tank that just sponges damage unless each hit is chained together; one can't do anything to defend itself if it takes a smack; and one is just fodder for the other two to the point where you can't play as that character and have high hopes without being stupidly adept at the game.
If you plan on getting this game, get it for sentiment only. I like the Alien and Predator franchises and this game makes it fun to play as - key phrase, "play AS" - one of these classic characters, but the game is a complete nightmare to play against them.

I am a living room gamer; because I am a professional programmer I strongly dislike playing games with a keyboard and mouse -- it feels too much like work. A few weeks ago my son and I got bored with playing Reaper of Souls on Xbox One, and we were in the market for another ARPG of similar quality. We tried Crimson Alliance on the 360 and got bored with it fairly quickly.
And then, WOOOSH: we discovered the first installment of The Incredible Adventures of "Maester Van Helsing"! We were so excited that I took a day off to rebuild an older PC into a dedicated machine for my living room. Years ago I brushed off Steam as a failed experiment; but Van Helsing made me come back to it, and build my own Big Picture Steam Machine! Sure, the game's UI could use a bigger text size for those of us who like playing on sixty inch monitors from twenty feet away, but that's the only fault I found with the game (perhaps in Neocore's native Hungary big screen TVs have not been invented yet). Overall, the first Van Helsing game was a delight, and we put some fifty hours into it!
Naturally, we wanted to continue the adventure and bought Van Helsing Two. Not just game number two, but two licenses as well since we were dying to try multiplayer.
Now I wish I could put this nicely, but what en effing dissapointment!
Van Helsing Two is a Piece of Crap.
After being released roughly one year ago, it suffers from tens, if not hundreds of bugs. It is slow. Multiplayer sucks (it fails to update one player's screen correctly, randomly disconnects, etc). The added complexity of the Command Center minigame adds unnecessary confussion and bugs (you have invisible characters that will speak to you although they are away on a mission). The game crashes when you add essences to yout equipment.
I could go on and on and on, and while I found the concepts, graphics and overall atmosphere of Borgovia enticing I cannot really recommend the game to anyone. The execution was obviously left to twenty year old incompetent programmers. And to be clear: when I say the game is slow, I mean that compared to playing the first game on the exact same 3.4 GHz AMD dual core machine that plays Van Helsing One without breaking a sweat.
Judging by the rate at which Neocore launches new DLC and new games (Van Helsing Three is about to be released this year, and in between they made Deathtrap, a spinoff from the  Van Helsing series capitalizing on the Ink) they are more interested in taking our dollars than fixing the bugs in their existing games.
Overall the game feels like a rough, unfinished BETA. Save your time and money and play something else -- even the early access version of Victor Vran is a better investment.

Fallout 4 is Bethesda's latest installment in the Fallout franchise, but a part of me wonders if Fallout would've been better had Interplay not sold it.
This game has superior gun play, movement mechanics, and world development than it's predecessors, but it all feels rather superficial. The lack of choice and meaningful impact of the game are really striking. You essentially choose which factions you want to take out and then work toward that goal with no thought given by you as a player. The addition of a voice protagonist has clearly limited the direction of the game in a negative way. There is no true "evil" choice like there is the Fallout games upto this point, even including the limit scope of Fallout 3, the only other Fallout game developed by Bethesda. The choice and variety of Fallout: New Vegas seriously highlght the porblems that this game has with it's story. Their half handed approach to giving the player an evil role in Nuka World fell flat. It was the choice between story, and being a morally good person. The player's don't want to be evil, they want to choose to be evil. This feels less like an RPG and more like an open world shooter.
Interplay and Obsidian made Fallout feel like a real, interesting world with their Fallout games, so it's time that Bethesda stepped back and learned from them.
Not Recommended if you like RPG's.

I have a fair amount of time on this game, and i can say without doubt that its one of the best games ive ever played. The problem is that its just not a fallout game in every aspect.
The gameplay is good, fun exploration, great world design, but its just lacking in the terms of a story. You dont feel motivated to go on and complete it other than your character yelling their♥♥♥♥♥off about sean every 5 minutes and running around for one of the four factions.
The DLC is mainly pretty good, Nuka World focuses on exploration and pushes aside story, but it makes you hostile to the minutemen unless you decide to kill all of the raiders, which basically negates the entire purpose of the late DLC. Far harbor is amazing story wise, and pretty good exploration wise, which makes it the DLC which is the most worth it in my opinion. The workshops are all pretty worthless unless you like to build up your settlements, and even then only Wasteland Workshop is really worth the money. Automatron is an asbolutely amazing DLC, maybe not for the story, but the gameplay and customization levels are tremendous. The high-res texture pack is basically just a 70gb mess which can be easily replaced by a few ENB mods.
The companion system replaces the karma system that was seen in previous games, and instead of having a morally clear line between bad and good, it lets the player choose their definition by being with different companions. (Strong likes it when you do things like killing, stealing, etc, while Preston will absolutely hate you for it)
Overall, evn after all the years, Fallout 4 has remained as one of those games you either love or hate. And I say that line is drawn by whether you love story or love exploration. I cant tell you that you should 100% get Fallout 4 even after all this time, but I can tell you that if you love story, you probably wont love Fallout 4. On the other hand, if you love exploration, combat, and the like, you will probably love Fallout 4. And if you're inbetween, youll probably be pretty mixed on the topic.

I still remember playing Doom 3 (and the expansion) soon after it got released. It was a mediocre shooter even at the time but I liked it, it was a good abreaction when I had enough stress and wanted just to relieve it in fast and brutal shooter with zombies and demons.
I haven't felt much nostalgia about the game before starting Doom 3: BFG Edition but I have to say that the details that made me remember the game are out. It's now just shooter for nostalgic people, but I think it's not worth enough to anyone who haven't played Doom 3 back at the release year.
The first part of the game, most memorable for me, felt more like a survival horror than a brutal action since player had limited ammo and a flashlight that couldn't be toggled - if you wanted light, you just had to hold flashlight instead of weapon. That boosted the effect of many jumpscares or secret minirooms where enemies are hidden. But now you just turn on the light and shoot everything without any stress - the enemies have terrible AI anyway, so expect getting into problems only when you get overwhelmed by amount of stupid enemies (in the late game).
Sadly, I feel the graphics aged worse than in the original Doom 1 and 2 - if you are going to play the game, don't expect anything pretty or interesting. It's an ugly mars base with aliens. Oh, that even sums the whole story theme the game is about (think of the story like it'd be a porn script, it has similar depth).
I hoped I would enjoy the game in the same way like I did years ago but I can't. There are many better mindless shooters currently, so I'd rather recommend you to check Serious Sam (HD) or Painkiller series. I believe this was only fast reedition to get more money for upcoming sequel, so I'm looking forward to play the new DOOM!

This game had one job to do: keep the mechanics intact (or improve on them) and update the technical aspects, but instead delivers a lesser game with upgraded graphics. An attempt at a rhythm game with an actually decent story, but ultimately the only thing that challenges the player is the gluttered screen and how the timing of the button presses switches between beat, vocalist phrasing, lead instruments or some other arbitrary instrument - that is if you're playing the songs that come with the game, your own collection of music is a totally different  and much more depressing story.
There's a very limited amount of different combinations of button pressing sequences that the game throws at you - 1, 2 or three in a row, 1, 2 or 3 at a time and press & hold, possibly double tapping on some (pretty much required on master difficulty if you want to keep your combo going). There's no stream of notes kind of things that I loved from DDR/ITG.
Button pressing timing seems about on-par with ITG/stepmania, but the fact that they're often using a part of a song for the notes that doesn't make any sense and it can mess up rhythm especially when it suddenly jumps to following vocalist phrasing. This wouldn't be that bad if the screen had any sort of indication of the actual rhythm like with colours that previously mentioned games does, but there's only 3 colours, red (double/triple hits), yellow (singles "on beat") and blue ("stream" (2 or 3 in a row)), nothing to indicate rhythm at all. Listening to it wouldn't be that bad but again, the jumping suddenly to another aspect of the song throws you off unless you're intimately familiar with the sequence - oh, and don't bother memorizing anything but the "rhythm", they randomize the sequences on master difficulty, only keeping the "rhythm" constant every time you play the same song.
Play your own song feature is even more useless than in Audiosurf. You have to tap the beat and set a beat start position with millisecond accuracy (which is pretty much impossible) by hand. Songs cut off at 6 minutes, still can't play Art of Life or anything like that. There's a very limited file format support, don't even dream about FLAC.
And when you finally get to play a song, the button sequence has absolutely nothing to do with anything in the song, except possibly the beat if you managed to tweak the right values in.
I did collect all the achievements in this game and there was one that probably took me about 45-50 hours to get, but in the end it was just about staying concentrated for about an hour of songs with one non-resetting health bar.
I would not recommend this game to seasoned rhythm game players, it's just too easy. The story is nice though so if it's on sale it can be a fun few hours.

Kickbeat is a rhythm game that follows the usual rhythm game mechanics, with a few twists. It looks good, as long as you turn off the dynamic camera, and plays well but can be quite a chaotic mess to follow sometimes. And it has a story. That you can skip.
When you start up this game, for the love of god, play the tutorial. Although it is quite similar to certain rhythm games, like Dance Dance Revolution, there is one mechanic that I haven't in other of these types of games. But let's start with the basics: You are standing in the middle while the enemies start to circle you. You have to hit these enemies on the rhythm of the music. The better you perform the higher the score. However, you can make mistakes and quite a lot of them too. As well, certain can have power ups, and you'd need to double tap the button in order to get the power ups. It's not truly necessary, but to get five stars on all stages it definitely will be. Having done 1 playthrough of both story modes, Mei being played on a harder setting, I managed to get through it and never lost once. Mind you, I played it on the easier settings, with 2 other difficulty settings being harder.
You could also create your own music to challenge... but only if you have a good grasp of the rhythm of it, since the game doesn't seem to be able to create the beat on its own. I have to try that myself, but I hope it can do a better job than I can, since I tend to play tracks that are off beat by a lot.
Overall, the game plays well and is very responsive. The tracks present in the game are quite good to play this game to... But like I said, the game can also throw you into a bad loop.
There's chaos in this game sometimes, depending on the track you play. While it looks pretty good, the graphics can also screw you over. That is why I suggest to turn off dynamic camera, since it can throw off your rhythm if you tend follow it and look at the screen. At one point, I couldn't figure out where I was supposed to push a button or two simultaneously because it was that busy. Maybe I should only look at the buttons on screen though, see if that works. But beware if you actually are going to play this game.
The story mode is for unlocking other modes as well as another character. You really don't need to follow that story at all, since it's quite shallow. So, Where to start,  This game came out of the blue for some people, namely myself.
But, let me tell you dear customer, you are in for a WONDERFUL meta-game breaking ride.
This game is a 2D♥♥♥♥♥kicking beautiful artwork metroidvania style based game (you'll understand when you play it)
Fluid Combat, gratifying rewards, lean meat'd chicken just the way you want it.
Lets start with the Pro's
-Effectively 10 dollars.
-Beautiful artwork
-Fluid Combat
-Adjustible difficulty (For those who just want to enjoy the story)
-Meta-game breaking side-scrolling slice em up action! Where could you go wrong for that?
-The story,  - Underneath what is given to you by the narrator, ICEY has a deep level of narration not found within many games this year,  the encouragement by the game to not exactly follow the rules and stray into the wild will allow players to truly explore and understand the world of "ICEY" This no-hand holding approach treats us as intelligent human beings and caters to that RPG element that really makes you think when a game with as much depth as this present itself.
The Cons-
-Boss Scaling -  The difficulty of the bosses isn't anything intense and once you learn their patterns (fairly quickly) they don't stand a chance against your sweet blue glowing booty
-The length,  if you're like me and you're a sniffer and want to explore everything about the game, it won't take you longer than say.... 15 hours, maybe 20 hours and that's being fairly generous.   Each play-through (if you choose to do so) will take you roughly 2-3 hours.
-The enemy variation.  There isn't a terrible amount of enemy variation.
-Neutral
Stunlocking - Like yourself, the enemies can actually combo you and it is entirely your fault if you allow this to happen. This is a good thing for people who want to make intelligence reads and outplay the AI, but its a bad thing for the people who fall victim to the stunlocking and don't understand patterns.
All in all, I personally hope we see some more development of the ICEY world and for you dear customer, I thoroughly encourage you to pick up this game if you want a good meta-game side scrolling hack and slash adventure with a short but extremely meaty substance

This is a one-man-project, and it shows.
The One-Man-Show showed itself in a lack of discipline to work on the "boring parts" of a sellable product: rigorous bug-fixing, polishing, usability.
A few concepts, such as the design-your-own-ship puzzle are AWESOME.
Laying out your own, where to put armour, where the guns. Big engines or small. Truly an inspired idea that made me decide to buy on-the-spot.
On the other hand, many parts of the game are buggy, unpolished or even unfinished.
For example: The game slows down over time; my campaign has never been not-laggy after the first half hour. This wasn't considered a priority problem, despite multiple people reporting it.
Some efforts were made, but it shows there was never enough time for a good fix.
All in all: Great concept, but the idea(s) were too big for the one guy implementing them.
No more one-man-shows for me, and I'll pass on StarDrive2 as well. ZeroSum games has lost my faith.

Good game, bad design.
The good:
-The combat itself is great and very skill based.
-Very nice art style and visuals overall.
-Music was also pretty nice but I didn't really pay attention to it.
The bad:
-Weird checkpoint placements - sometimes you will reach a checkpoint, kill a very small amount of weak enemies and there will be a 2nd checkpoint and sometimes you will reach a checkpoint, kill a bunch of mini bosses, regular enemies, flying enemies and whatever the game can throw at you and then you will go through that again without any checkpoint so you will need to go through all that again (unless you're willing to go back to the checkpoint after every area you clear which isn't always possible)
-Obnoxious attacks - some enemies have attack that are near unavoidable or actually unavoidable because there doesn't seem to be the slightest of indicators (or there are but way too soon before the attack). Doesn't help they either go through your shield or straight up taking 75% of your health (even after I upgraded my health and armour).
-Unskippable cutscenes - Oh you died to that boss? And there was a cutscene right before it without any checkpoint and you can't even go back to save after the cutscene? Well here, watch it again! Doesn't help that 90% of the cutscene is a complete waste of time (stopping you for a couple of seconds, panning for a couple of seconds, focusing on another character for a couple of seconds also you can't progress until the narrator finishes his sentence so another waste of time)
-Difficulty  1 - when you pick your difficulty there's no kind of description or warning like in most other games so you have no idea what you're getting into - is it for people who already beat it once and know the game very well? Is it for extremely good hack 'n slash gamers? What does it even do? Add on to that - you can't even change it mid game so you might be going in over your head and not realize it waay too late.
-Difficulty 2 - The game's difficulty it mostly about how fast do you react (although some enemies seem to be about prediction and luck which is BS imo) and from my experience on hard - you don't get much time at all. And when you get showered with minibosses and weaker enemies alike it's a lot harder to actually do something so you spend most of your time dodging around, hoping they will split enough for you to attack.
As much as the game seems fun, all of those things make it very frustrating to play and I wish I could see those stuff sooner so I could refund it.

There's a lot of mixed reviews on here at the moment because of the Creation Club stuff but I'm just gonna review Fallout 4 based on the actual game itself.
I'd heard great things about Fallout 4 when I got it and was keen to see if it lived up to the hype, and I can tell you now it exceeded all my expectations. There's so much about Fallout 4 that I love that I almost don't know how to cover it all.
The graphics/visual designs are something I love a lot about this game, the recreation of Boston is awesome and the attention to detail is amazing. The game world feels so realistic not just in the design but in the eerie feeling they managed to capture to pull off that nuclear wasteland vibe.
This is the first Fallout game I played so I can't compare it to previous games, but I have seen many people commenting that the main storyline wasn't up to scratch compared to past storylines. As I haven't played past storylines I can't compare this one but I agree that it was a little linear and sometimes pushed you into choices that felt a little closed in. By that I mean sometimes none of the dialogue/choice options were ideal and you had to make do with less than stellar choices and consequences. However, I loved the quirky side quests I found along the way! So if the main quest isn't up to your standards there's p[lenty more to do.
The settlement building is an awesome aspect of this game. It could definitely use a little work but where the game falls a bit short, there are plenty of mods to pick it back up. For example I loved doing up certain settlements but the rubble that couldn't be deleted in the game can easily be removed using mods. The ability to make good use of the NPCs in settlements for tasks, trading and supply lines was a really great feature and made settlement building even more enjoyable.
It was really nice to see upon starting the game that you could choose a male or female protagonist with highly cutomisable features. This really adds to the ability to identify with the character and makes for immersive gameplay. I was also really happy to see the variation in companions available throughout the game and though it was awesome that romantic relationships were able to be entered into with any companion regardless of gender. Great inclusivity, makes for an enjoyable game experience for everyone!
All in all one of my favourite games. Even if it doesn't end up as one of your favourite games I would still highly recommend giving it a play, there's so much to do in it and it'll at least cure your boredom for many, many hours!

Okay, first off, this is a review based purely on the game itself, and not on any mods/strikes towards Bethesda themselves, even though I have been a complete follower of the company for years. With previous inserts in the Fallout brand over the years, expectations were always set high with each new addition to the series, in terms of full games and DLC's, which is understandable, you evolve forwards, not backwards. The game itself, if you are a Fallout veteran, has many things still to be  desired on it, in terms of how, (lowkey spoilers), choices really do affect the outcome of the game, the amount of bugs that occur just over the smallest details in the game, and so on. However, if you are not a Fallout veteran, or hell, even if you are someone who's just bought the game on a whim or brand new to the series, there is so much to be appreciated within the game itself. The amount of options put into the game to give everyone a solid path on whatever they want to do is rather far and wide, from everywhere on power armor detailing to re-naming your weapons to any name you choose. The amount of quests and stories you can follow and uncover is massive beyond belief, not as much as a certain Witcher game, but still up there overall. To make this short and simple without rambling on, is it a good Fallout game? Debatable, I'd personally give it an 8.5/10 but that's highballing it, looking past everything and being a fan for so long. However, is it a good game in general, ignoring the Fallout brand? Yes, I feel that if you look past the brand, it's a solid 9-9.5/10, but that's just an opinion from someone who's played these types of games for years. It's not the best Fallout game, but it is a great game nonetheless.

An apples to Apples comparison between Doom 3 BFG Edition and old Doom 3.
1. Doom 3 had poorer audio quality and I had issues determining the direction of the enemies in the shadows. Doom 3 BFG makes me a one man army in that regard with rich audio on my Sennheiser headphones and Asus Xonar DX.
2. Doom 3 had poor shadowmapping. Doom 3 BFG has very accurate mapping and HDR.
3. Doom 3 had a very wide and clear FOV on  17'' BenQ flatscreen back in the day. Doom 3 BFG has  a very narrow FOV even on a huge monitor and needs constant attention. I believe it has been done to support the idea of feeling more terrified cause I can like see less? Doesnt really work like that.
4. Doom 3 clean polygonal shading and DAMN looks good for that GEN. Doom 3 BFG, muddier watered down textured with just the texture size increased. Pretty sure it uses megatexture now. For the last time id - Megatexture is a way of breaking games. It doesnt work like its supposed to on 80% of the setups. I dont see any pop-ins on Doom3 BFG though.
5. Doesnt breakdown in Windows 7 64bit and Windows 8.1 64 bit like Doom 3 does.
6. Doom 3 had a patch to fix alt tabbing from the game. Doom 3 BFG doesnt let me alt tab. The hell?
7. The cinematics in Doom 3 BFG seem to be flowing FASTER like they changed it from 30fps - 60fps in the cinematics section too. Its like watching hobbit at 1.25x speed. One can definitely tell the difference even after this many years.
8. A very necessary port to keep it playable on new OS and setups but for the price - I would want a better GAME.

Civilization's Objectives, Banished's Village Simulation and Age of Empire's Warfare.
You want to go full RTS and harrass or pillage all of your enemies ? Better start keeping your people happy (the more you expand, the more they EXPECT happiness) to secure the growth of your village. Better store a whole lot of food and upgrade your militia to not be penalised by winter.
Research and overall village's improvements are your thing ? Boost your gain of Lore and buff up your territories as you will be playing a turtle game against the wolves and draugrs that will periodically attack your city's weakest spots, and fight back other player's harrasses to slow you down.
You want to be recognized as the king of all northmen ? Reap fame by owning more and more territories, eliminating wolf and draugr dens, send villagers on raids and pay some skalds. You will even earn rewards on 2 different tresholds of fame points.
You like to barter, stock up in gold and pay everything you need with coins ? You better start trading resources in trade routes and own multiple marketplaces, as they have their own inventories !
The only real CONS that I can see :
- Stone circles might give too much of an advantage if too close of starting area.
- Trade victory is too easy to achieve, maybe step up the goals a bit or create events where you have to defend your gold against rogue clans or thieves
- Being aggressive with an army is not rewarding enough, it is better to stock up resources and play on defend mode all game
- Towers are too strong against the raven's mercenaries, makes 210$ worthless since they cant fight fair
My friends have all said the same as well, they would perhaps like to have reskins of warriors for every different clans, and maybe a different chieftain for everyone, but anything can happen this is a early access, I trust the devs to keep this on the right track and make one of the most amazing RTS/CITY BUILDER genres since Age of Empire !

I'm recommending this, but only to people who play online and only to fairly hardcore fans of fighting games and even to those people I can't recommend the game in good conscience at full price.
I'm a big street fighter fan and have been since the first street fighter hit the arcade. Every iteration of the game since then has seen various improvements and an increase in the roster and the general amount of content all round, until this one.
I bought this on sale with both DLC packs for around £30. The base game was (and still is I think) £40-£50 and I couldn't recommend it at that price, simply because of the woeful amount of content.
I'm not going to talk about the lack of arcade mode, that particular omission is well known, what I am going to talk about however is the roster. Given the price of the game, pitiful is the word I would use to describe it. In the original street fighter you could only play as Ryu in single player, or Ken if you were player two in a fight against somebody else. Street fighter II saw this roster of playable characters rise from one to eight. Super street fighter II included the boss characters as playable, bringing the roster to twelve. The previous game to this one, (ultra street fighter 4) gives us a roster of forty four playable characters. Yes, you read that right. Forty four. Street fighter V, including all it's DLC (so far) gives us a roster of twenty three characters, almost half that of the previous title. There are also less stages available and of the few there are, some are locked and must be purchased.
This brings us on to what I call "free to play" mechanics. What I mean by this is that while it's possible to unlock additional content and buy additional characters with in game currency, acquiring said currency has been made so mind numbingly tedious that anyone who enjoys the game and has a bit of spare cash lying around is likely going to throw that cash at the game in order to bypass this "grind". Capcom know this and this is why they have adopted this "free to play" mechanic. It was a mechanic made popular by free to play titles, mostly MMO's, where it's acceptable given that the game is free in the first place. Sadly, it has since been adopted by publishers of premium price titles. This is frankly disgusting. It's a cancer, eating the video games industry from within and shouldn't be encouraged.
As for the actual game itself, the fighting mechanics are as crisp as ever although the pace is a tad slower than SFIV, making fights feel more tactical and less frenetic. The slower pace also makes it easier to bait your opponent then punish them on the counter and if you have the skills and timing required to master the combos, this punishment can be pretty severe. Ultra combos are gone and instead we have the V trigger and the V reversal. These are powered by the "revenge meter" as the ultra combos were in previous titles and if used appropriately, they can turn the tide of battle back to your favour or snatch victory from the jaws of defeat. Super combos have been renamed to "critical arts" but appear to function identically, being powered by the EX meter as in previous titles. EX moves are still around and are as useful as they've always been.
Sadly, the despicable business practices displayed by CapCom are why I'm only recommending this game if it's on sale and you can pick it up for £10 for the base game or £30 with all the DLC as I did. The content found in the base game and the two DLC packs together is worth £30, but no more than that.

The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing II Complete is a game you don't want to miss. The game starts out a bit slow but after you get a couple of hours in, its non-stop action and excitement. A must-have for any action role-playing fans. There are numerous skills and perks to customize your character, a multitude of magic items and artifacts, rare monster trophies, many extensive sidequests,  runecrafting,  and more that is sure to keep you entertained for many hours. Controllers are fully supported and there are several multiplayer options as well. While Van Helsing II is mostly hack and slash combined with RPG elements, it also has a well developed tower defense game weaved into the story along with numerous sidequests that add to the fun.
This game has many great features that would easily fool you into believing it was developed with a massive gaming budget. The storyline is great, the soundtrack is perfect for the mood, the voice acting is superb, the graphics are rich with detail, and the gothic art is simply astonishing. It does so many things right and that is rare, even from many of the bigger studios.
The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing II plays out much like its predecessor and picks the story up right at the end of the original (although it can be enjoyed without having played the first one). In fact, there is an option that allows you to import your favorite characters from the first game. However, it has several key improvements, most notably, the game offers several character classes from the beginning and even more skills/perks to suit different play styles instead of adding them as DLC like in the original game. The tower defense portion of the game has been improved and enriches the story.  The User Interface has been re-designed and is much better. The graphics have been improved as well and really give you that gothic feel. And don't forget about the DLC's included in the Complete Package. The Pigasus DLC introduces a new lair NPC pet that you can send out into the Ink to search for rare magic artifacts and weapons. The Ink Hunt DLC is an extension of the game that adds 4 new maps along with quests and nmissions to extend the overall game and can only be played after the base game is finished.
This game is nothing like it was when it was first released on Steam. Originally, there were many who had issues with bugs and crashes but the developers have actively worked to fix them and still remain involved in the community. Since then, this game has vastly improved and new features are still being added. The game is very entertaining and offers a lot of quality content for the price. I strongly recommend this game to all action role-playing fans. It has quickly become one of the best available and I look forward to a Van Helsing III.

TL;DR this is Type Type Revolution with a bigger budget and better game feel.
Press buttons to the beat of the music to kick people in the face to the beat of the music. That's all there is to it really. It's a pretty standard rhythm game faire, but with how few there are out there it's worth a look if you're into the genre. The song selection is a typical mix of mediocre techno and rock songs with a few gems liscenced specifically for the boss encounters. Just imagine "Guitar Hero: Jackie Chan Edition" and you'll have a pretty good idea of what to expect.
Gameplay is good. I felt no syncing or pacing issues at all, and the game is challenging while easy to pick up. I sort of resent the double-tap for powerups feature though. The game forces you to double-tap enemies carrying a power-up to claim it, though you cant double-tap every enemy because you'll get fatigued. It is unnecessarily tedious to do, given that 70% of bad guys carry powerups, and 90% of those are insignificant point boosters. Double-tapping doesnt fit into the beat of the game and feels very out of place.
Graphics-wise it is fine. I really like the artistic style here, reminiscent of TF2 with it's stylized characters and cel-shaded models. It is quite funny in parts aswell, and competently voice acted.
Can I kick faces to the beat of my own music? Why yes, yes you can! If you really want to knee some faces to the tune of Sandstorm by Darude there is an option for that! It does NOT auto-sync, however. It requires you to use a beat calculator, so tempo-changing songs are right out. I dont feel it increases the difficulty to the intensity of the track either, so it's a little lacking, if competent.
I reccomend this game overall, especially if you are a GH fan or played Type Type revolution in your browser as a kid.

I truely love it when an indie developer makes a GREAT horror game. Stairs blew me away. I didn't know what to expect. The trailers and pictures on steam didn't reveal much for the game so I was practically walking into this game blind and I walked out with a FANTASTIC experience. The real reason I purchased the game was because of the reviews. It's hard to say if this lack of advertising for the game worked in it's favor or not, but it did truely make me feel like I found a diamond in the rough.
The graphics are beautiful and feel realisticly believable. The gameplay is simple, some would call it a walking simulator, but with the camera as your one tool it becomes more than that. I've seen some games where the camera works really well and when it doesn't work so well. Stairs not only uses its camera dynamic very well, but the ending sequence brought something fresh to the table that literally gave me goose bumps, accelerated my heart beat, and made me incrediably fearful of what laid in the dark.
*SPOILERS AHEAD*
For those of you who want to know what that end sequence was; The game got rid of all means of illumination at the end, flashlight and night vision are gone and the only way to progress in PITCH BLACK was to use the flash on your camera. Meaning, you would walk 10 feet, take a picture, the flash would light up the next 10 feet, and you would rinse and repeat. This was incrediable to me!! I've only EVER seen this in movies and it was exciting to see someone take advantage of it in a video game.
*END OF SPOILERS*
Sadly I would say that this game, as amazing as it was, felt too short!! Towards the end of the third level there was a lot of build up, you're thinking there's going to be a big jump scare at the end or a huge reveal in the story, but then... it just ends... just like that... I groaned out in frustration, because the joy I was getting from this game finally came to a close, but there was no closure, no sense of victory, it just all stoped... It felt like being on a rollercoaster and it comes to a sudden halt half way through, like in the middle of a loop... and like being stopped half way through a roller coaster, I felt like I'm missing another half to this game and it's story.
But that's it, that's my only negative for this. I had fun the entire way through. There were plenty of scares to get my money's worth and the atmosphere and it's lighting are some of the best I have experienced in a horror game. If you're a horror game enthusiast like me then you need to add this game to your collection.

Main Thoughts:
What can I say that hasn't been said? MK9 is a MASTERPIECE, when it comes to care and respect, NetherRealm Studios has such care and respect for the source material here. There are reports of this port to the pc being faulty, well i am here to report that I have had NONE of the problems listed at all, it does take long to find someone online, but online gameplay is smooth and responsive, so let us begin.
Gameplay:
The gameplay in MK9 is damn near flawless, such there are exploits, but aren't their in every fighting game? The Kombat is brutal and fast paced, every character has their own special moves, combos and pop-ups which you will need to learn to properly "juggle" as many would call it, I can't find anything really anything to complain about here other then simple cheap exploits.
Graphics:
These graphics are some of the BEST in a fighting game, for 2011 these hold up, although I am running a i5 4670k and a AMD HD RADEON 29 280x, I can simply turn up the graphics and enjoy this♥♥♥♥♥♥at maxium settings, which are ♥♥♥♥ing great, fire does it swaying♥♥♥♥♥♥ water looks nice and ices feels like ice, even when you break it over someone's face as Sub-Zero.
Story:
This story is one of the BEST stories for a fighting game EVER, the dialogue is witty, funny and sharp, I won't spoil things, so I will sum it up without spoiling, MAJOR plot lines. Basically it takes place before the events of the last Mortal Kombat (Which was Armageddon) while at the same time takes place after it, you play as almost EVERY character in the game (Accept DLC Characters) it is at LEAST 10 to 15 hours long, dn't quote me on that, I'm estimating here, but all around good story.
Multiplayer:
The multiplayer is were it wobbles alittle, people have reported that the netcode isn't up to par, with slight lag issues and cheap exploits (Which mind you, is in EVERY fighting game) and the lack of a player base, being almost two to three years old, this doesn't take away from the fact that multiplayer is still good in MANY aspects, king of the hill matches are fun, fresh and exciting, while still retaining the feel of a Mortal Kombat Game, they even have HUDGE lobbies for people to wait in to play matches (Which are baron now, but the concept was cool)
Final thoughts:
At the time of this review, MK9 was on sale for 4.99 or your regional standard, at that price, this game is a STEAL, do yourself a favor and pick it up, even at 15 dollars this game is worth it for all the content ALONE, but the great story, stunning graphics and fun challenge, this game is for MK-Fans and by MK-Fans so pick this♥♥♥♥♥♥up....FIGHT!

A thoroughly enjoyable tower defense game. I only play solo, so I can't speak to the multi-player capabilties. This is a maze building tower defense game. As far as TDG go, it shares some similarities to Orcs Must Die and Dungeon Defenders (both which I enjoy). There are less RPG elements (leveling, stats) than Dungeon Defenders, which could be good and bad. The good part is that it means there isn't any grinding. Once you unlock all the towers, you are as strong as someone who has been playing the game for 3 years non-stop. This obviously makes for better strategy. The other good part is that there isn't any running around and worrying about loot. (Unless you like that, in which case this would be a minus). I think this makes Sanctum more streamlined than DD, although I thoroughly enjoy playing both.
If you love tower defense games, you'll more than likely enjoy this one~
My score based on my own personal preferences, how much I played, etc.: 9.5/10
+ Clean presentation. Easy, and intuitive controls. Automatically saves your loadout based on character which can save you a bit of time. Small touches like that show that the game has a fine level of polish.
+ Strategy is important, and there are many ways to complete a level. (You can't just use the same strategy, wash and repeat)
+ The characters are varied and balanced. Choosing a sniper allows you to take strong shots on single enemies, so you'll use towers that can take care of crowds. A rocket launcher-wielding girl can take on crowds, so you'll have to make sure to put up towers that can take out heavily armored enemies.
+ No grinding. Although progression unlocks more towers and abilities, you do not buy stats after each level.
+ Challenging. I've put in a good amount of time in this game and have barely touched upon the "feats of strength" which are optional challenges that can speed up enemies, regenerate them, etc.
- Too bad there isn't a better stat breakdown to show you how much damage each tower did after you complete a mission. (To help you improve your game)
- There is a bit of maze building involved in the game, but it can get tedious (granted only a minute or two). I wish you could save your starting tower construction set up so you don't have to redo it every time you retry a level.

It's Street Fighter. Exactly what I expected.
I played almost every Street Fighter since SNES times. I played it on handhelds, in arcades, on home consoles, on my PC, in the train, on the plain, at home, on game expos, etc. You know what I mean.
I grow up with Street Fighter and Ryu has always been my favourite. Then Killer Instinct 1 came to the Arcades, then to the SNES and even on the Gameboy. I became a Killer Instinct fanboy - have US, PAL version and bought like 3 times on the SNES - CRAZY - I know - and Street Fighter was just secondary.
However today, Killer Instinct only exists on the XBOX and Win10, so I come back to Street Fighter. To its simple but very difficult to learn game mechanics.
From Street Fighter II over different Tekken and Marvel mash-ups until to Street Fighter V, I have honestly to say that nothing has changed at all. It is still the same mechanic, with better graphics, with some eye candy, unfortunately no native 3D vision, but a very well functioning online versus rank modus.
Where I am missing some sort of arcade mode - you can only play survival or some rediculous short character story mode, it is clear that Street Fighter V focuses on the online competitive mode. And it's work perfectly fine. There are plenty of matches to find, I think there is also cross-play with consoles.
Last but not least, Street Fighter like any other Arcade Fighter needs to be played with a decent Arcade Stick. Since I had some issues with my Arcade Pro in previous SF games on the PC, it was here plug and play. Very simple. You can purchase a good arcade stick for 30 EUR on amazon. No need to go for the 150 EUR ones.
Overall, I have nothing to complain. It is what it has always been. A Street Fighter with better graphics and the focus online competitive mode. It is not a combo fighter like Killer Instinct, but anyways difficult to master and your enemies will crush you constantly in the beginning, even if you have a longstanding arcade, console Street Fighter experience. It will not help. I loved it always, I grew up with it. I have never been good in it. But I still will play from time to time.
Recommended, especially on sale.

Northgard is an RTS game that I've found is most akin to titles such as the Civilization series. You take on the role of vikings exploring a newfound continent. You start off in a small sect of land before slowly exploring it, expanding your Norse nation. Elements of norse mythology and the game's gorgeous graphics are some of the most unique aspects of the game at it's face value. There's many buildings to construct, and many jobs to assign to your villagers, and it's safe to say that absolutely NONE of them are useless or dead weight. The developers give you all the aspects you need and nothing more, perfect for keeping the game gritty and exciting.
It is very unique in the sense that there aren't any "turns" or "rounds", the game simply keeps going and you have to manage faster than other players. This game is NOT one that you can leave running or spend time thinking on your move, it requires attention and skill. You start as one of (currently) four factions. The Wolf clan, the Stag clan, the Goat clan, or the Raven clan. All are different in playstyle and are best suited for different victories. They have statistical advantages and disadvantages and while one or the other isn't too overpowered, they could use some balancing issues.
Once you've selected your clan, you're thrown into the world. You begin with a town hall, and a few villagers. Villagers are the basic unit and collect small amounts of food. The world is divided into large "tiles". To call them tiles is a bit of an underepresentation. They're chunks of land, all with different benefits to them. For example, some tiles contain deer, that you can utilize for hunting, or ponds for fishing. Others are infested with ravenous wolves or undead Draugr that you can slay for fame. They vary drastically and they're presented in such a way that the world doesn't seem divided, but natural. The variety in tiles keeps the game refreshing every time you play.
There's multiple ways to win a game, through acquiring fame, researching technologies (the game calls these Lore), accumulating vast trade, or conquering other civilizations. Most uniquely though, is that most games have an additional victory type that's entirely random and specific to the map. The game can be outright cruel at times, making victory seem impossible, but I have found that it's never too hard to make a comeback, which makes the game all the more exciting
More interesting features include a seasonal system. Each ingame year has a winter, where farms no longer work, and your resource production is severely harmed. Every few winters have a blizzard, where it becomes even more intense and teeth-gritting as you try to make your rations work. The rush is a great deal of fun, especially when playing the games multiplayer with friends. Also included are world events. Portals that send undead to your lands, random attacks from monsters and wild animals, earthquakes that burn down buildings, rats that devour your food. These are all preventable disasters but their presence keeps you alert and ready.
+ Gorgeous Graphics
+ Unique Features
+ Satisfying Presentation
+ Incredibly Competent Devs
+ Very Fun Multiplayer
+ Minor Bugs
+ Easy to Pick Up, Hard to Master
- Victories aren't balanced, Wisdom seems to be the most common, and Domination is nigh impossible (you can disable certain victories however if this becomes a problem)

It's a fun little game where you shoot a grappling hook at blocks and swing between other blocks to collect red beacons.
Each level is identicle in it's aesthetic and objectives and offers no variation. There isn't much to it. But what there is, it does really well.
The swinging is responsive and if you practice enough, allows you to completely avoid every obsticle, giving you maximum points. There are 2 areas, air and water. In the air, gravity pulls you down. In the water, buoyancy pushes you up. This forces you to be able to switch your swinging techniques as you fling yourself between the 2.
This game rewards good players. The beacons that must be collected grow when you move quickly without hitting obsticles, and shrink when you crash or slow down. This means that if you're not good at the game, the game becomes more difficult just to rub it in. This, however, is not a criticism. Too many games are letting the bad player get off too easy these days.
That said, this game is not challenging. Then again, it's not supposed to be. As is written above in the "About the Game" section, Floating Point is a "peaceful game". There is no failure state, no time, and when you beat a level, you can spend the next hour drawing squiggly lines and patterns.
It's a small, but fun game, with a great, yet simplistic artstyle, calming music and enjoyable swinging mechanics.

Now, clearly, I have not discovered a lot of what this game has to offer just yet.  But I'm already rockin' close to half the achievements, so it's probably a fairly short game.  That definitely works against it, but, and this is a big but, it's a compelling game.
There's not much else I can say that isn't spoiler-y, unfortunately, but I'll say stuff anyway, so if you don't want spoilers, from this point on, you've been warned.
The Meta nature of this game is very interesting.  No, ICEY isn't the first game to have done a meta-narrative like this.  It definitely takes some inspiration from The Stanley Parable, in that the game reverse-psychology-encourages you to explore by doing literally the exact opposite of what the narrator tells you.  The narration is in some dialect of Chinese.  I don't know enough to tell you if it's Mandarin or Cantonese, or some other dialect, but I will say, as an English speaker, it's not off-putting.  The subtitles are mostly short and succint, not really detracting from what's on screen, and the bits where the narrator is chiming in because you're not following his instructions are still delivered in such a way that the emotions in the dialogue come across, language-barrier or no.
The Action itself is fairly simple, and follows a lot of tried-and-true methods of other spectacle fighter's, like Devil May Cry or God of War.  Major difference here is, there only seems to be a single weapon, unlike the other titles I've mentioned, but the combo's are very satisfying, and once you've learned a few of them, the rest become very intuitive.  For first-time Spectactle Fighter's, this is a great learning point, allowing you to build the skills necessary to get those Triple S combo's in Devil May Cry.
The 'Platforming' in this game, I'll argue, is non-existant.  It's a platformer in the most basic sense, where there is stuff to get to, and you have to find a way to get to it...  But it's super easy, since you can dash, along the ground or through the air, indefinitely.  And you know what?  I don't feel like this takes away from the experience at all.  In fact, it's a really important mechanic for finding the secret rooms that this game is just absolutely flush with.  Dashing into the sky to make sure there's an actual ceiling and nothing above you is really important for finding some of the secret areas, many of which I've already found, and many more I'm bound to find, I'm sure.  The infinite dash seems like it could break combat, but it doesn't at all, since most of the enemies move around quite a lot, making dashing good for closing distance, but that's about it.  Though, spamming it around to get the dodge attack could be a little cheesy, but I haven't been able to get that tactic to work reliably.
Speaking of the combat again, the animations are lovely.  Most of the enemy stuff is pretty well telegraphed, so getting the Dash-Riposte is generally more about skill than luck, but some of it is still twitch-reflexes, with some enemy attack animations being decidedly shorter than others.  Again, as a learning point for Spectacle Fighters, this game is a great starting point because of that, since -most- of the enemy attacks are fairly well telegraphed, but all but the most basic enemies tend to have at least one attack that's nearly insta-fire and requires that internalization of the animation and the twitch-reflexes to reliably counter.  The character animations are great too, and ICEY herself looks fantastic, almost like something out of Shadowrunner, a sci-fi samurai.
The music isn't top-tier, but it's certainly not bad.  While a bit repetitive, it's not invasive, so once you get to that point where you've heard the same track 25 times, you tune it out instead of hating it and wishing it would die.
I kind of love everything about the art-style.  It's sort of new-agey, almost in the vein of anime, but distinctly different and unique.  On top of some of the weirder elements of the art-style, like the very clearly 3D rendered computer monitor that makes up part of the meta-narrative, to the flashing images of real eyes in the monitor room, to the reptilian eye that covers your screen in the Monitor Room when meeting the Yellow King, this game takes several strange, disparate elements, and somehow makes them all feel like they belong.
And getting back to the narrative, at least to where I'm at, the game doesn't try to blow your mind too hard.  I think this is a good thing.  I'm not saying it won't blow your mind, (or mine, when I get there,) but I am saying that it's content to let it build, let you see some weirdness and go, "Okay, what," then sweep that under the rug for a while and let you get back into the rhythm of the action, waiting for the right moment to blow you away.  It's not crazy and it doesn't throw shock-factor into the mix, like some games in this vein do or could.  Instead, it actually is building an interesting, compelling narrative that compels you to try and figure out just what the hell is going on.  And it does it subtly, with every little thing appearing to be a hint or a clue, but certainly, some if it is bound to be red herrings.  And on that point, the writing is just superb, leading you by the nose just enough to keep you curious, but not so much as to make you feel like the action is a slog to find the good part of the game.
All said and done, I really can't recommend this game enough.  As a huge Spectacle Fighter fan, I worried that the combat might be too shallow for me, but it's incredibly satisfying, and the strange narrative makes every encounter and every challenge feel like just that, a challenge worth overcoming in order to discover what weirdness lies around the next corner.  Or, you know, on the next screen.  Add in the keen sense of humor that'll absolutely hit home for any hardcore gamer, and you've got yourself a real diamond in the rough.
I bought ICEY on sale for 10$.  Even with a lot of good games, it's not often that I say this, but I actually wish I'd bought it at full price...  Which I think would've only been like 11$, but still, I absolutely think the Developer deserves every penny of that.  More even.  Knowing what I know now, I'd honestly pay 20$ for this game without reservation or regret.  If you're a fan of 2D brawlers, spectacle fighters, meta-narrative games, or cool art styles, buy ICEY.

This game has gotten an undeserved bad reputation.  I read all the various reviews and comments, and delayed purchasing it as a result.  I eventually picked it up in a "Humble Bundle."  Frankly, it is one of the better 4X games I've played.
Pros:
17hrs in, I've experienced no bugs, crashes or artifacts.
Graphics and music are both moody and appropriate.
Colony development is easy, and very Galactic Civilization-like.  It isn't difficult to stay on the "plus" side of the economy.
Combat is is satisfying, both visually and tactically.  You can see which weapons are most effective, and you soon realize combat requires a combined-arms mix of ship types for success.
Unlike Distant Worlds, the AI requires some hand-holding: the game does not play itself.
Cons:
Lack of information: you are not informed when a ship is in combat, so your scout ships just disappear without warning.
The tutorials are insufficient to get you started.  There is now a UK manual on Steam, but I had to refer to the user guides on the Steam website before I felt reasonably confident with the game.
Ship design is clumsy: you MUST fill every slot on the design matrix, even if your ship would be functional without the extra equipment.  Also, I miss an "UNDO" feature on the design screen.  If a creation isn't working out, you must either change it slot-by-slot, or delete it completely.
All of my comments are effectively moot: Star Drive 2 is less than a week away from release, so this game will see no further development or polishing.
Bottom line: I've gotten much more than my money's worth for this title (which was less than $1 in the Humble Bundle), and my purchasing it gives me a significant discount on the new game (SD2).  I recommend Star Drive to anyone interested in 4X games, particulaly if you can purchase it at the fire-sale prices on Humble Bundle or Bundle Stars.

Well, I saw a lot of varying reviews, but the game was on sale and I gave it a shot. I've probably put in around 20-30 hours now, and I must say I find this game really addicting. The user interface takes a little time to get used to, but once you get the hang of it, the game's dynamics are pretty fun. The game is technically turn based in a sense, but turns are measured by time (every 5 seconds) which you can alter during gameplay, or even pause to get your orders out first, so the game is actually played as if all in realtime. In ship combat, you basically just tell your ships to attack the bad guys, so if you like to manuever fleets and such this game may not be for you. You manage just about everything for your species, which is pretty neat. And of course, you design your ships if you want. It may be time consuming, but is pretty fun. You choose a hull type, and then you are responsible for setting up the rest. Also, when you create a new ship, don't name it the same as ships you already have in play, because then you won't be able to refit your current ships. All in all, I would give this game an 8.5 out of 10. It is fun, and as you keep progressing, you can't help but to want to stick around and see what comes next. The graphics are fine, nothing super spectacular, but are still decent enough. I wouldn't pay 30 bucks for the game, but for 10, absolutely.

I highly recommend this game. It's a hilariously fun old school mecha shooter. This game runs fine however getting it to actually look right (resolutions, graphics card settings etc.) can be a real nightmare. I can almost promise you that you will need to spend a little time tweaking settings and downloading add-ons to get this going properly but it is worth the effort. Here is a little more detail:
Graphics: Dated and horrible all things considered. The upside here is that both for it's time and even today, you are going to see something different than you are used to with most games. It's not non-stop neon and it's not shades of brown. This game has some very different environments and each level fairly unique while remaining within it's theme.
Music: If you are cool with some anime-inspired music and 90's techno-military (think Command and Conquer) than the soundtrack here is well done. Fits in with the game nicely and it's terrible on it's own.
Story: Nonsense. Utter nonsense. Honestly, don't even bother trying to fit the pieces together. This game experienced a bunch of content cuts and I don't think the writers were particularly experienced when this game was made. This game was not made to be taken seriously.
Dialogue: Amazing. Oh sure the game will try to make you care about the story but more likely than not, you will find yourself immediately forgetting what the plot is and laughing at all the cheesy and adult lines between the characters.
Characters/NPCs/Development: Almost none of these characters are memorable save for maybe the main character. Thankfully you can kill most of them if you feel like it. The design isn't great. It is an old game and it shows. Almost everybody looks like palette swaps of everybody else. The characters don't really develop or grow in any meaningful way.
Gameplay: Think dungeon crawler. The levels are well made but the enemies will constantly pop up and insta-crit you. Most of the enemies pause when you shoot them though so if you know where they are coming from you can give them the slip.
Overall, if you can get it working it's a fun cheap thrill and I totally recommend it for people who want something a little different that they don't have to take seriously at all.

One-sided rollback is definitely a thing, and not only am I able to comment on this review from testing with another person, but I've tried with my own PS4 with a free trial of PSN+. So basically, how does it look like?
This is a public video by DoctorZhao a long while back to give you an idea what it's about. As the video shows, the PC player will be "ahead" of the PS4 user, but due to the way the netplay is synced, the one that is "behind" will take the priority, a complete disadvantage for the PC user.
From my own tests, I have also verified that the one-sided rollback effect is something that affects "EITHER" the PC user or PS4 user. After a certain amount of time passes in-game, the PC user should start to experience rollback, which is further caused by the inputs from the PS4 user. To further elaborate, when the PS4 user mashes inputs, the PC user will be experiencing heavy rollback.
How does the PS4 user get to go through this? One way is for the PC user to Alt+Tab. The tables shift in the same power, so the PS4 user will now be experiencing the same rollback problem as the PC user... only now the PC user shouldn't encounter many rollback problems after the PC user uses Alt+Tab (and yes, mashed inputs from the PC user will now affect the PS4 user).
To summarize the netplay experience, neither user during crossplay experiences the same experience. Either one person will receive the better netplay experience while the other doesn't, or vice versa. Now, maybe if the PC specs were matched to a similar quality to that of the PS4 that it may give better results, but it's still a huge disappointment that Capcom did not integrate a proper syncing mechanism for their netcode. This can even play the same role in PC VS PC... This is one example to why rollback has to be done correctly, and not just implement a faulty rollback netcode with noticeable inconsistencies. At this rate, games like Guilty Gear XRD (SIGN and Revelator) excel from SFV's netplay in terms of consistency and sharing the same experience per user. This is nowhere near the levels of GGPO, and can't even compare to it.
So yes, not only is single-player content lackluster, but online play is also a huge concern. Keep in mind, this game has been out almost a full year, and not one word was mentioned about the online syncing issues, or other oversights such as giving a player 2 rematch option (similar to how SFIV or XRD handles post-game options).
The Season Pass from Season 1 is nowhere close to matching a traditional Season Pass, which unsurprisingly got changed to a "Character Pass" for Season 2. As of right now, you can purchase it for one character... and that's it. Sounds very fun and incentive for users to buy huh? I didn't think so. You could get a season pass for any other game around that price, and you would get EVEN MORE than just that, making you experience the positive features of supporting a company much more apparent.
The matchmaking in this game is horrendous. Did you expect region sorting and finding matches in under 15 seconds? No. How about browsing blindly in the "Battle Lounge" where the loading icon appears for almost every lobby for about a minute, not showing you the region of the user, along with what system the user is playing with? There isn't even a region sort feature in the game, and added with the information in the previous sentence, you will have a bad time with blindly joining a room (hint: by the time the lobby information readies up in a 2 player lobby, the game is usually filled) and seeing flags from many different countries appear on the screen.
Which, btw, I may have to add that giving the user the "choice" of selecting a region has to be one of the most oddest decisions I've seen. There are people I know that didn't picked a flag of their region (one accidentally picked a flag that thought it look like the U.S. flag while rushing towards gameplay, but it's really a Flag of Liberia). Best part is that these people can't change it if they make the mistake... so why is this implemented?
There are much more questionable stuff in the game. As the big red thumbs down logo says, I would not recommend this game to anyone on Steam. Maybe if you were a competent SFV player, I would recommend the "PS4" version for online play to avoid one-sided rollback inconsistencies (or if purely for offline play with friends/players, then "PC" is good), but other than that... it's not worth it.

So, I want to underline that this review is not about Shogo as a game itself, but about this release version.
Shogo was originally released on the 15th October 1998 and re-released on 15th April 2017 here on Steam as the almost 19-year-old classic it is.
The game does work, yes. But it is far from being satisfying: Framedrops (even in the option menus), stuttering, no fullscreen and a top bar on the screen to make it worse.
Re-releasing a game almost 19 years after its original release for 9,99 euro is perfectly fine, but without any adjustments to make it run on modern systems, it is nothing but a quick cash-grab and a punch in the face of any long-time fan.
Thus, I see no other option than giving thumps down, despite loving the game itself.

While some might be interested in Shogo for the nostalgic value, or perhaps you were just a fan of other Monolith titles like FEAR or NOLF, the fact remains that this game is a complete chore to get working on modern systems.
While the more technologically inclined can get it working after 30 minutes to an hour of tinkering, piecing together all the downloads you need from various sources scattered throughout the internet, the average user isn't going to want to go through the trouble.
dgVoodoo2, fixoltdll.dll, AM18.dll, WidescreenPatch.rez all required for modern hardware/OS setups. Even with all these fixes there are still issues, for example my mouse cursor is perma-stuck in the middle of the screen. This is a glitch I've yet to find a fix for and it has been reported multiple times on the GOG forums. Seriously, this game is almost 20 years old, it ain't gonna get patched any time soon! I've also heard (though I cannot confirm) that the game is a lost cause on any monitors with a refresh rate higher than 60hz.
If you REALLY want to get your 2d hands on Shogo, pick it up on GOG. At least it's cheaper there.
