One of the many failed games based in the Aliens universe.
.....The graphics are poor. So poor that it was hard to get that tense horror vibe that any aliens game should have.
.....The universe was poorly created. Everything from the weapons and skins to the actual environments looked like faded copies of something done better by someone else. And considering how many times these have been done, that should have been the easy part.
.....The games basic mechanics were completely broken:
1. The marines were cannon fodder. Their weapons were about as accurate as a kids nerf gun, and almost as effective. Marines spawned scatterd around the map as individuals instead of spawning near their teammates. Making them easy prey for predators and aliens.
2. The predators were overpowered. They had access to an array of weapons that were mostly one shot kills. The ability to go places that even the aliens could not, and the ability to see both enemies in almost all conditions.
3. The aliens were crippled by poor game design. Being able to play as an alien was the most aniticpated part of the game. Add to that that the aliens could move on any surface in the game, including walls and celings, and you had the makings of a great experience. But the aliens head could only move through a limited arc. And their body followed the head. So sudden changes in surface created sudden changes in direction. Usually in a direction you didn't want to go at a critical moment. Add to that the fact that the alien's attacks were weak and innaccurate. And you get something far less enjoyable than was anticipated.
4. There were only a few maps and they weren't designed well or very big. Enuf said there.
.....Everything above could have been fixed. And with not a lot of effort. But the developer abandoned the game almost immediately after it's release. Having played Aliens online in a previous age, and seeing all of the failed games using the Aliens name. My greatest fear is that there will never be a good fps made in the Aliens universe.

This is another game that I got on Xbox when it launched. This AVP might not be as good as some of the classic AVP games, but I have to say I thoroughly enjoyed the three single player campaigns when I played them all the way through on Xbox.  The single player is pretty good, an opinion not shared by many people.  As mentioned above there are three campaigns, one for Predators, one for Marines, and one for Xenomorphs. Each is a different length and the play style for each character is radically different.
The biggest issue with the game, at least in my opinion is the multiplayer. The single hit executions are all fine and dandy in the single player game mode, but they quickly become boring and just generally un-fun in multiplayer. You end up spawning and dying multiple times a minute from all these insti kill attacks. Another issue is that the melee, a huge part of the game for the two alien races is generally terrible. There is a ton of stun spam, and while there are ways to break out of this you die so fast (from insti-kill button prompt attacks) that to me makes the multiplayer feel not even worth it. Couple that with the low player base and the cheaters and I just dont know what to say.  There are indeed cheaters though, speed hacks and all sorts of stuff along those lines.
Perhaps my experience with the PC version of multiplayer AVP is abnormal, I dont know. what I do know is that after playing a bunch hours I was completely prepared to never come back to multiplayer in this game.  I still recommend the single player though to anyone looking for a new AVP game! But I would hope you waited for a sale and bought this super cheap.  Overall I probably forgot to touch on some of the more important parts of the game, I still hope this will do as an acceptable review for now.

This is a good addition to the genre of good music driven video games such as Audiosurf 2, Audiosurf 1, and Beat Hazard. It is also quite similar to another great game called One Finger Death Punch. KickBeat combines martial arts fighting and music to create a solid game. The game has a single player campaign Story Mode where you play through all of the songs that come with the game. First as a male character. And then as a female character. As you keep playing and get better scores on the songs that come with the game, you unlock more characters that you can play as. And you also unlock more outfits for the existing characters. You can of course also play this game with your own music files as well. Although in this game, you need to manually set the beats per minute for each custom song that you want to use. Although the game makes it fairly easy for you to do that. The game plays a 15 second section from the start, middle, and end of the song. And all you have to do is just tap the Space bar to the beat of the song. Then you can listen to the final result to make sure that the beats are set properly with the song. Then the song is ready to be played in the game. The game has selectable difficulty levels so you can choose how difficult you want any song to be. It may take some time to get used to playing KickBeat at first because the in game tutorial doesn't really prepare you very well. But keep practicing and you'll learn how to play the game. If you like music driven games like Audiosurf 2, Audiosurf 1, and Beat Hazard, then I recommend KickBeat

I wouldn't recommend this game to people who like to play rhythm games. Firstly the soundtrack that the game comes with is ok, it's not bad but it certainly isn't that great either, but this will most likely depend on your music tastes. The tracks tend to be a mix of techno, electronic with some rock/metal elements to them. It would seem that the ability to play your own music is a great asset of this game however this particular feature falls very short. This is due to the fact that when selecting a song to add to the game you have to go through a beat calulator process by which you manually tap spacebar to the rhythm of 3 different sections of the song. The beats per minute are capped at a certain level so you can't just go crazy with the system. Equally probably the most annoying thing is that you can add any track you like however if the track is longer than 6 minutes anything past the 6 minute mark will be cut off entirely. These 2 flaws don't really make the add your own music feature appealing and the system for calculating beats doesn't work all that well in fitting enemy timing with the song rhythm and comes of rather clunky.
If you are looking for a good rhythm game I would recommend avoiding this title particularly if you wish to play your own music.

It does not matter what anyone else tells you: this game is not finished and has been abandoned by the developer. It will never be finished nor its bugs fixed. Some of these bugs are game-breaking and there are many features that are either incomplete (to name but one: game mode. You can choose it when you start a new game, you get to choose only one option, though -_-) or inexistant.
Now to the game itself, it is an ok game that appears to be a rip-off of a lot of games, but the ship designer as well as space battles are genuinely fun. I would almost call the initial ships being crappy a stroke of genius since it gives you a nice challenge to build good ships for each faction and possible tech configurations etcetera, this part is really fun. The automation of building them is ok, and putting them in fleets is very nicely done with the fleets manager.
The gameplay itself, not so much. You initially start with one planet, and the one whom colonizes the most suitable planets the first is generally the first to win. If your race has improved metabolism that is every planet with 0.8+ fertility. Mind you those planets tend to be rare (10-15% of all colonizable planets I think?), which only makes it worse that you can also choose to make your race cybernetic. Combine that with industrious and improved metabolism and suddenly your requirements have changed to all planets with 0.8+ production instead (assuming 20-25% tax rate). This basically means 75% of all colonizable planets, most of them being uninteresting to other races except the Opteris (cybernetic), mainly for this reason, that race can actually pose a challenge in the hands of the ai.
Granted, you can research stuff to make all planets viable for colonization or bother with crappy food transportation, but that goes against colonizing fast.
So combat: by default, you are at peace with every race. If you have troops/fleets in orbit of each of their planets cabable of annihilating them in a few seconds they will not care. If they intercept one spy they are likely to declare war, but with war you get space battles! Still, if you choose the best possible strategy, there will be no space battles: as long as your military strength is higher than your opponents', only the Opteris will ever dare attack you. And even when it is not, half the ai players will generally just seek peaceful relations (pacifist/cunning/honourable ais). There are also planetary battles: capturing planets through troops. Troops cost no maintenance, though, so flooding each of your planets with troops is a sure way to win: the ai will never bomb your planets.
Remember the game-breaking bugs? One of them involves unlimited production! It involves having shipyard, you spend 10 spare production on a ship, get 13 invested, cancel it, and now you have 13 spare! The shipyard effect even stacks with multiple shipyards, so I don't think I need to tell you how horrible it is to leave this bug in the game.
Overall I give this game a 4.0/10

Stairs is a really nice psychological horror game, I was actually pleasantly surprised at how great the game was.
You're a freelance journalist, trying to investigate the murder of a girl in an abandoned factory. You will find creepy things, hear voices, see things that are not supposed to exist. During the whole game, you will go deeper, and deeper, hence the name Stairs. You don't spend the whole game in a stairwell, the stairs are just a mean to go deeper, and the deeper you get, the more f*cked up things will be. You are supplied with a flashlight and a camera, which will turn out the be extremely important. (Also, at first glance, the game is a freaking maze, but don't let that impress you, everything is pretty intuitive, you'll know where to go.)
About the negative things: Nothing made sense at the end of the game, and the end itself seems pretty botched. It's like the devs didn't know how to end the game and they decided to end it abruplty without enough explanation. Either it's a really sh*tty ending, or maybe I didn't understand the subtlety of it. After all, I didn't get the achievement called "The Truth Behind the Lies", so I probably missed things!
I totally recommend the game nonetheless.

Shogo Mobile Armor Division is a first person shooter created by Monolith and was the very first game to use the Lithtech engine. It's a rather unique game stylistically and in terms of concept. You play as a pilot named Sanjuro who both controls a mech suit and fights on foot in a war against other mechs.
Shogo is heavily inspired by Japanese anime. To the point where I think it harms the game overall. The game looks very ugly visually and you can especially see it with the characters, who all look overly cartoony and somewhat disturbing. The story is also rather confusing and convoluted. It's not helped by how all of the characters come off as overly obnoxious, especially the main character. I understand it's to fit the style of the game but it feels really cringey while playing. However the soundtrack is fairly decent and does match the style of the levels pretty well.
You have two distinctive modes of gameplay. On foot and in a mech. On foot gameplay is fairly standard for the time the game released in. Enemies mostly stand still and your weapons have very little feedback. The animations are also all janky. When piloting your mech the levels all look smaller like you're in miniature cities but the game still diverts you into generic corridor shooting sections that feel identical to the on foot sections. There is one critical problem with the gameplay of Shogo that becomes immediately apparent and frustrates the player. "Critical hits". In Shogo randomly while hitting enemies or while enemies attack the player, critical hits occur. It basically means that at complete random you can kill enemies more effectively. However you very rarely notice your own critical hits due to how generally overpowered all of your weapons are. You mostly notice how you suddenly die while entering rooms out of nowhere. This causes the game to feel very claustraphobic and not very fun to run and gun through. This isn't helped by how the game is very linear and there's no real way to avoid it.
Shogo isn't an ambitious game nor a particularly polished one. It's a tech demo first and foremost, designed to advertise and promote Monolith's engine. It pales in comparison to other games released in 1998 like Half-Life. And while it does have a small loyal fanbase it's unfortunately a game that's really hard for me to recommend to people. Fortunately Monolith learned from their mistakes on Shogo and dramatically improved with their later shooters like No One Lives Forever and Aliens Vs Predator 2. Here's hoping both make it to Steam one day.

First of all I would like to say that this game has been amazing to play and I can see it going far as an RTS with all the traction it's getting right now and all the potential for improvement I think it has. So with that being said I'll go ahead and say what exactly I enjoy and dislike about the game and then offer up some of my own ideas on how it could improve.
Pros: Graphics are amazing to look at, I personally enjoy the civilizationesque panel gameplay, the specific features to the clans are all diverse and interesting, it creates a kind of balancing act between the resources (forces micromanagement), it's good to see the developers looking at multiplayer features and gameplay aspects at the same time.
Cons: I've had an issue where the game has a lack of memory error and crashes, I feel as though some of the victory types are easier than others which makes it harder to do the domination and objective victories because of how balancing between clans is right now (I've actually only been enabling those two victories for a few games to make it take longer for fun), as was said in another review: weather issues do seem to get repetitive after a while.
Out of my cons the memory issue is definitely related to early access and I'm sure the balancing problems right now will be improved in the future so please do not think about those too much if you are considering this game and read my review.
As for improvements I would like to see I want to say that for a few months I've been reading up on viking culture and learning more about their history so some of it is related to that.
1. The wolf clan at the moment has berserkers in their arsenal as their warchief's replacement. Berserkers are actually connected to bears and means "bear warrior" so it's a little arbitrary to put them in the wolf's clan. As an alternate the berserkers could become ulfhednar "wolf warriors" to be more accurate (however I do understand the name is less appealing to an audience and much less interesting). So instead maybe it would be cool to see a taming feature implemented between the wolf clan and wolves.
2. I feel like the map is a little flat in how you traverse it so I just thought I'd offer up an idea for the ability to climb mountains with a recruitable war unit that could climb up and down them (maybe on a cooldown) to make it more interesting for domination victories.
3. The way viking ships were built allowed them to not only go through shallow waters and onto shore with a shallow-draft hull but also for the mast to be removed and for the ships to be carried, flipped, then used as shelter. I think this could be a really interesting colonizing method for lategame similar to the mercenaries that ravens can hire right now.
4. I assume this is already on the way but I figure I'll mention it anyway that a religious feature to the game would be awesome to see with thor worshipers using thunder while odin worshipers have improved war aspects. But like I said I could easily see this being something they add in the future.
I don't know how much people will agree or disagree with me on these ideas but I reeeally hope this review doesn't get lost in the oocean and that the developers have a chance to see some of what I've said (especially the part about berserkers). All in all I highly recommend the game and see it becoming much more popular than it already is in the future.

This is a low-effort review for a low-effort Spelunky knockoff. Not recommended.
In a little bit more depth, Endorlight is basically a Spelunky-style platformer with randomly generated levels, but with everything else that makes Spelunky actually interesting stripped out - you fully heal between levels, and money is currently useless, leaving the only truly "useful" pickup as hearts, which permanently increase your maximum life by 1 heart.
So it's basically just about dropping to the bottom of each map while seeing if there's any hearts on the way, and fighting a boss every five levels. By the standards of really early platformers, like ones for the NES? It'd have been pretty good. However, in 2016 there are hundreds, if not thousands, of better games in the genre, including very similar games in Spelunky and CaveBlazers - the latter apparently being by the designer of the engine this game is based on. Buy and play one of those instead.

I've been a fan of the point and click genre for as long as I can remember. In fact, some of the first games I've ever played were of the point and click genre such as Maniac Mansion and a plethora of Sierra Nevada games. A good friend recommended this game to me but I was skeptic at first having grown up with that conceited ideal that "Back in my day, games knew how to play properly!" This game however, went with the practice of looking to the past to ensure a brighter future. Everything that I ever had problems with in the old point and click games were taken out in this one, so all I was left with was a profound, entertaining and thought provoking game that I can say in earnest, is thee best point and click game I have ever played in my 29 years of living.
My main qualms with the point and click games is that there are times when there's not enough information to run on or a hint is just far too obscure to glean any information from. At this point all you could do back then is literally try every item on every possible thing that you can think of. Thus, it takes out any semblance of thought provoking play and becomes a trial and error guessing game where you continue to get more and more frustrated. When you do finally figure out the puzzle you're so exasperated by the experience you just went through that you're not feeling any happiness, too flabbergasted by how nonsensical it was to digest it as the proper means to an end, and too cynical to allow any sort of justification behind the games reasoning. Fran Bow may be the first and only point and click where every puzzle seemed justified and while I did get stuck quite often on a few of the puzzles, the means to figure it out was adequately given and made too much sense for me to ever blame the game. It was always that epiphany of "I get it now!" instead of the traditional "That was unnaceptable" reaction I usually have from these types of games. Fran Bow was clearly well thought out and is an experience that will forever be burned into your memory for the rest of your life. Alzheimers be damned.
That's only the core of the game play though. Puzzles that require deep thought is the staple of point and click games. This game goes above and beyond though, with a rich alterable environment as well as a novel storyline that sucks you in to the point where saving and quitting is no longer an option but just a self inflicted cliff hanger. You'll laugh, you'll cry, and you'll be utterly confused by this game. In a good way of course. I really cannot stress this enough, regardless of your history with point and click games this game needs to be in your library of games. I promise you, it will let you down. This is honestly one of my favorite games I've ever played and I have been a gamer since I was able to hold an Atari controller.
Fran Bow, I give you a 10/10

So far, Northgard is a very satisfying, beautiful RTS with some unique concepts.  The tile-based gameplay, in which you must discover and colonize tiles before building on them, plays really well, if a bit slowly at times (sometimes it can feel like you're just waiting for the next thing to happen).
There are a few concepts you expect to see in a game like this, such as different factions and different kinds of units, but the core gameplay feels like a fresh take.  For instance, villagers are automatically and slowly generated depending on happiness and housing availability, and because you can then assign them specific duties, they are your only source of potential warriors, farmers, woodcutters, etc.  This makes it imperative that you keep as many of them alive as possible since they aren't easy or quick to create.  Details like this make a game stand out, and Northgard is no exception.
In terms of depth, keep in mind this game is still in development.  A skirmish type mode and multiplayer are basically all that's currently available, but the future does seem bright.  Also noteworthy is that the game doesn't have many bugs.  I have only experienced one crash (which they addressed in the latest update), and the game runs really well on my system.  Rest assured, the developers have been consistently posting updates and seem to be committed to delivering a worthwhile and satisfying game.

Fran Bow made me feel emotions.
Fran Bow kept surprising me from the start to the end. The game's naive and quirky style didn't get old through the 10~ hours it took me to beat it which is a testament to the developers' commitment and attention to detail. The game is full of beautiful and horrifying art both of landscapes and of small interior decoration much of which can be examined and interacted with through the game's point and click mechanic with multiple text descriptions from the protagonist.
Most of the supporting non-player characters are interesting and hint of having an even greater depth than is portrayed in the game. They piqued my interest to the degree that I still think of them days after completing the game. Many of them could be featured in their own children's story book.
Fran Bow in fact very strongly reminds me of a children's book translated to video game art form. Children's themes such as curiousity, adventure, overcoming fear are effectively mixed with adult themes of horror, loneliness, loss, mental illness in a way very rarely seen.
The story and plot takes a backseat to the art and exploring the game's themes. The story is supposed to be about Fran finding her cat and solving the case of her parents murderer, but this is periodically completely forgotten. Instead the game is really about understanding Fran's mental state and reaching some kind of balance for her so she can feel at peace. The metaphor for this in the game is Fran's wish to escape the mental institute and go home to be with her aunt Grace and her cat Mr Midnight.
The gameplay is less emphasized, but mostly follows a classic point and click formula. Find items, use them at specific points, combine items with each other and occationally solve a small puzzle. The gameplay wasn't very challenging and I completed the game using online hints only when I got stuck for a longer period of time, a total of 5 times I believe.
I played this game in spurts of 1-2 hours which was perfect for me. It meant I made a decent amount of progression, got to experience the atmosphere, and didn't get bored from the lack of action. It also allowed me to reflect on the game more and spend more time in the game world in my imagination between play sessions.
The best part of the game is Fran Bow's character. She is curious, naive, brave, reflecting, childish and grown up all in one. She isn't a super hero, she makes mistakes, feels regret, is sometimes a little bit cruel, breaks down crying from her sorrow. She never gives up though, but keeps fighting. Fran Bow feels like a three dimensional character, which is incredibly compelling in this age of simplified archetypal tropes and clichés of super heros and villains.
Ultimately this is an amazing indie title well worth the price of 15 euro. It is even more amazing to think that Fran Bow was developed by a couple as a passion project with no prior game developing experience. I'm very much looking forward to what Killmonday Games come up with in the future.

The full playthrough is now complete, and what can i say, what a fantastic game!
The story starts off slow as you investigate an abandoned warehouse/factory for clues about a murder or missing people (dont want to give away too much), its very quiet and eary and it feels like there isnt much to the game, however venturing further and deeper into the warehouse/factory you find that there is alot more to this game than meets the eye, and it doesnt take long to get going.
When you start to desend the stairs for the first time, that is when the game starts to show its colours, its not boring because it will keep you on edge at all times, and unlike alot of horror games this does not rely on jump scares to make you feel scared, but i will warn you this game will freak you the hell out!
Silence is the number 1 mind bender here and boy it works well, throughout the entire game you just have to brace yourself and hope to god that nothing is going to smash through the nearest door or tap you on your shoulder, its creepy as F.
As for controls and graphics, i have to say the graphics are very clean, the game looks really good, it feels good to play smooth with no performance issues, the controls are easy and simple to use and understand so cant really fault any of that
As for the story itself and the actual gameplay, well the story was great, i didnt really understand too much of it but thats just me not the game and towards the end i was comletely mind boggled haha, but the gameplay could have been better, the reason for this is aside from a couple of parts theres really only 1 path you can take, your kinda funneled through the story almost, that was the only gripe i had about it, but it doesnt take away the fear factor and the enjoyment of playing this game because i still enjoyed every minute.
Overall i can safely say this is an excellent horror thats great to play, and it actually exceeded expectations, i would recommend this to everyone thats into horrors, its well worth adding to your library, a great job from the devs.

Review On The Game From The Point Of View Of A Returning Player.
Hello, And Welcome To Trove Before I Delve Into The Review I Would Like To Take Into Consideration That I'm A Returning Player From A Couple Months Back.
The Reviews Are Going Into The Negatives, At The Time Of Writing This Review Around 11K. Why? cause People Hate To Grind, This Game Is A Perfect Example Of A "Starter" MMO You Are Taken By The Hand And Learned The Basic Aspects Of What Payed MMO'S Or More In Depth MMO's Like Eg. World Of Warcraft Or Asta (To Name A Minimum) Have To Offer.
This Game Has Been F2P People Refuse To Understand That Developers Have To Make A Living From The Product They Have Created, I Have Played Before It Appeared On The Steam Store And I Had A Blast Playing It With Friends And Exploring The World Collecting New Items.
Now For My Personal Opinion;
This Game (Trove),
A Perfect Example Of A "Starter" MMO, It Describes You Step By Step What To Do In The World, As You Progress Through The Game You Discover Lore, Which In Turn Teaches You To Be More Combat Efficient And Gain More Experience, Trove Rewards The Player For Progressing And Learning, Currently There Are A Few DLC's Avalible, These However Are Not There To Grant The Player An Advantage, People Assosiate DLC And P2W Items With Being Better At A Game, Trove At The Other Hand Rewards Its Players Not By Buying DLC But By SImpely Playing And Exploring The World Of Trove. Yes, Granted The DLC Are Pricey For What You Eventually Gain From Them BUT They Are Not Manditory They're OPTIONAL.
Now For The Game Pro's And Cons;
Pros:
+ Solid AI And Combat System
+ Colourfull World
+ Simple Gameplay Mechanics
+ Simple UI
+ Great Starter MMO
+ Much To Explore And Much More To Discover
Cons:
- Dlc's Are Pricey
- Repetitive Grinding
- "P2w"
Final Words;
Not Every MMO Is Perfect, I'm Not Here To Defend Trove With Heart And Soul Everyone Is Entitled To Thier Own Opinion.
If You Think The Game Is Bad So Be It, If You Think It's Good Thats Fine Aswell. Complaining About "Grinding" In An MMO Is Rather Rediculous, Trove Is For A Long Run PlayerBase Not People Who Expect To Get The Best Drops And Gear Within 2 Boss/Raid Battles.

STAIRS is a first-person atmospheric psychological horror game, that takes players through the stories of three missing people as seen through the eyes of journalist Christopher Adams. That's what it says on the storefront at least. I would call it more of a suspense walking simulator. It reminded me of Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs and Doorways, still being a bit different than the former and better than the latter.
As was said, this is a first person suspense walking simulator. There is only one instance when you have to actively avoid things more or less hunting you, several more points where you can die due to environmental hazards. Despite this the creepiness is here and a few moments, especially on the first and last levels, can raise that lingering dread feeling. Overall the game should take between 3 and 4 hours to finish.
I liked:
* the creepy atmosphere
* the graphics
I disliked:
* the mines (every mines in them horror games are the same and boring)
* the bugs (the game crashed on me and/or malfunctioned a few times)
* fragmented story
Get this if:
* if you like creepy walking simulators
Don't get this if:
* you expect a scary game
* you want to kill/outmaneuver scary monsters

I can't believe how disappointed I was in this game.  At first, blush, it seems spooky and edgy -- you have a little girl locked up in an abandoned factory.  Much (if not most) of the game is in the dark and so there is, at least a first, a hint of horror involved.
Eventually, however, what becomes stalking along cautiously in the dark becomes walking through endless corridors in the dark.  The more I played the game, the more I became convinced that the term "atmopheric psychological horror" was code for "the developer either didn't want to finish the game or lost interest and so the development team had most of it take place in the dark".
The story is neither original, nor compelling.  I can't believe how quickly apathy and disinterest seized me.  The photography -- as a journalist you are supposed to snap pictures of certain views, objects, and scenes -- seem pointless and don't serve to move the story forward.  Would it have been that difficult to just put the task of taking photos on the player and then the game itself rated the "quality" of the photos?  There is at least one other game that does this and it would have been infinitely more interesting.
The puzzles, what few there are, seem as pointless as the plot.  So why exactly does this dude have a safe in the basement of the factory?  And why exactly does he have the code scattered around where he can't possibly find it?  What's that you say?  Yes, this is nothing new for a puzzler -- quite often the solutions seem unrealistic or the scenarios unbelievable.  But this just highlights the frustration with this game -- you can't even suspend the basic level of disbelief that you need to order to play a puzzler.
I will continue to play this game to the end only, ONLY, because I paid for it.  It is a waste of time and money -- I'm angry that I paid $7 for it, I can't imagine how♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off I would be if I paid $14 or $15.

Left 4 Dead is the game that revitalized the whole co-op genre. You play as one of four survivor characters online who have been ''left for dead'', and you must survive, fighting through one of four ''movie campaigns'', composing of four levels each. It has an ''AI Director'' which automatically randomizes the location of weapons and randomly places any of the four ''special infected''. This has a survival mode where you must fight off endless hordes of zombies, and a versus mode where you get to play as special infected and attempt to take down the survivors.
PRESENTATION: This game looks very nice as most Valve games do. It does an excellent job with depicting recently abandoned locations that feel very lived-in. The visuals are fairly realistic, up to 2008 standards, but even more importantly is how they use visual effects to give you clues. For example, the survivors wear fairly brightly-colored clothing,  but the zombies have dingy and dark clothing and have pale skin. It is very easy to tell zombie from survivor. Another cool thing they did was place lights around the areas which you need to go to next. People automatically run to light. Valve did a very job making a creepy, dark atmosphere, but subtly giving you hints with visuals.
GAMEPLAY: As mentioned before, the game developers did a good job of tying visuals into gameplay. The game is very fast paced. If you don't have friends to play with you, the other 3 survivors will become NPC's, being mostly just as good as a real human (albeit lacking in communication). The game has a decent weapon selection. You can find pistols, uzis, shotguns, M16 assault rifles, automatic shotguns, hunting rifles, pipe bombs, and molotov cocktails. Additionally, you can find health kits to heal yourself or others, or pills that give you a temporary boost in health. It's pretty fun to play a special infected, too. Overall, a pretty balanced game.
CONCLUSION: This game is definitely a classic. However, Left 4 Dead 2 offers the same gameplay. You can even play levels from the original Left 4 Dead and enter a "Left 4 Dead" type game-mode (but nobody plays it). So it kind of sucks. If you want the original Left 4 Dead, buy this one.

- The story is mostly not predictable, cause most of the things that happen during the game are SO weird that you couldn't guess them unless you saw screenshots/videos before playing.
- The graphics are amazing, the drwaings are really good and evil, and there are a lot of great scenes. I think the design is pretty perfect, even though personally I would give up the black blurry frame that covers the whole game.
- The story manages to be pretty original, which is hard to do with the idea of "a person wakes up in the asylum" that we have seen in many movies/games before.
- If you happen to have any technical problems, the moderators in the forum are really helpful in helping you solve them.
The bad sides:
- The game is VERY easy to figure out, as you are being told exactly what you need to do during the whole game. The puzzles are easy as well, there are barely any chat options, and overall you can't really fail or get anything wrong in this game. You don't need to explore too much in order to find the solution to everything, and most of the game you just watch things happen like a movie, so there isn't really any challange. This game is clearly made for adults and not for kids, so I thought it would be much harder. On the bright side though, at least the story itself is good enough to still keep you interested.
- There is no voice acting for the characters, which feels a bit outdated for a point and click game that was made on 2015. Most of the story feels like watching a muted movie with subtitles, which could work for other type of games, but with point and click the whole game is based on listening to the characters. I feel like the game could be 10 times better if it did have voice acting.
- Taking screenshots in this game is really complicated at the moment and doesn't work at the normal way, which is very annoying, mainly because the scenes are so beautiful and creepy that it makes you wanna screenshot the whole game.
- Unlike other point and click games, on this one you can't save different points of the game in order to come back to them later. The only options you have are to continue your last gameplay, start a new game (which will delete your last gameplay), and start a chapter of your choice from the beginning. This is not very comfortable, especially if you click something by mistake, or if you miss achivements.
- The main character does not have enough reactions to the scary things, including things that involve her dead parents. She is like, ok with everything, or maybe a bit angry for a moment, but the only thing she really cares about is her cat. In some points at the game it's not really believable for a 10 years old girl to simply not care or react to things.
- Sadly the scary and horror scenes really repeat themselves, and even though those are great scenes, they get a bit boring after a while. There are a few that will still surprise you, but most of them just repeat in different locations.
Accoring to the credits, this game was mostly made by just two people, which is very impressive when you look at the result. I would sure want to check out their next game if they ever make any, though I hope they would fix the above problems if they do.

Let's break this game down, shall we?
Icey is a 2D hack and slash title where you go about playing as Icey to go off and kill the big bad villan of the game. Or do you?
You play as ICEY, and yes, that capitalization is intentional. The combat flows much like Dust:AET. Dash at the right time and you can land a "counter" move which deals a nice amount of damage or instanatly kills it. Combos can be freely chain and usually melt anything and everything when you start hitting the higher digits of chains. The upgrade system is pretty standard for a game ike this. Upgrade combo A and it becomes stronger, upgrade health and shields for more... you get where this is going.
Let's adress the meta part of this game. To be honest, it adresses a lot of problems/things that happen in game development. One thing the narattor adresses is metanarative and narative in game design in an interesting way. If you are interested in the duality of narative design, I'd reccomend paying attention to not only the narrator's words, but your own actions.
Onto the graphics. Honestly, the artstyle suits the title quite well. There is some area rehashing, and it doesn't quite feel as good as it should. The background are quite beautiful to look at, as are the enemies and the heroine of the game. Admitantly, I was not as suprised as I should be when I noticed the immediate config loader was for the Unity Engine.
To round it up, Icey is a fantastic title if you want a story that brings high paced combat with a side serving of meta-game development. Pick up this game if you want something small, fun and fast.

A narrative based horror game with relatively few mechanics, "Stairs" is a decent enough experience if not a bit short.  You play as a journalist attempting to cover the mysterious death of a woman.  It's simple enough and the narrative leads to some cool and legitimate points about journalism today.
The atmosphere of the game is quite good and the music and stings suit it well.  This in conjunction with the clever environmental tricks put me on edge a few times.  I'm not against jump scares but I'm glad that there were very few in this game.
Mechanically, however, it's very clear where things had to be cut due to (I assume) the failed kickstarter.  The base mechanic of the game is the camera you use to reveal clues and open paths, but it's hardly used to it's full potential and is instead regulated to clever little moments throughout.  Its a shame because there is a lot of potential with this idea.  There are also very few areas where the player is in any actual danger, and though not a huge deal, it bothered me after a while as there is very little challenge.
The game is buggy as all hell, with save files doing VERY strange things if you decide to load.  I got achievements without actually completing them, and DIDN'T get other achievements when I had completed them, and had to redo entire areas even when the journal in game says I finished them, very strange all in all.
Even after all my complaints I do still recommend "Stairs".  The atmosphere and tension are nice, and it kept me rooted in the story even with the weird bugs that went on.  I would for sure recommend it on sale.

Stairs is a first-person horror title from developer GreyLight Entertainment and publisher Digital Tribe. Playing as investigator Christopher Adams, it's your job to take a look at the disappearance of three people over the course of four levels; high-school graduate Valerie Berkley, business man James Reed, and pastor Jean Jowars Remens. Your investigations will take you through a basement, a mine shaft, and a dark, foggy forest. Even though all of the events in the game are based off of real life horrors, none of them stand out as much as the obvious ode to Jonestown and Heaven's Gate that the Jean Jowars Remens episode takes you through; going as far to even quote Jim Jones himself... "Oh, how I have loved you."
The environments are extremely memorable due to their intense, and sometimes overwhelming, ambiance; this is credited in part to the use of a terrific soundtrack, but also thanks to the creepy settings at hand. Each level is far different from its predecessor, and while starting off in a cliched spooky basement to find out what happened to Valerie Berkley isn't the best stepping stone for Stairs, rest assured that the title only gets better from there onward. The mine shaft chapter in particular leaves a vivid, haunting memory once you come to realize what it is that you've actually stumbled upon while trying to find James Reed. When it comes to the eerily still forest in Jean Jowars Remens' case, there are even subtle, attention-to-detail additions like distant gunshots added, to make you realize that cult members in the surrounding area are still killing themselves.
The title uses a series of notes, and four very well hidden audio logs, to help give players an understanding of the events, as told through either one of the victims or their killer; sometimes it ends up being both. Additionally, taking pre-designated pictures of places and items will sometimes prompt another journal entry by Adams, which more often than not reveals more information and also gives his take on the situation. Other than that, gamers are tasked with solving puzzles in order to progress through the game, and many involve the use of Adams' camera; sometimes you are required to take a photo of something to reveal a doorway, item, or to be transported to another level entirely to solve a unique puzzle. The enigmas are a tossup between commonplace and unique, as they often are basic puzzles that have a special Stairs twist to them.
While all of that probably sounds pretty good to you, this title does have a couple of issues that need to be addressed. The optimization can be a bit dodgy in places, and even on my i7 6700k/GTX 1080/16GB DDR4 3000 combo I experienced significant framerate drops to the 40's. While it only lasted a few seconds, it's enough to cause disorientation and an immersion disconnect from the player with the game. Additionally, Stairs has a notorious reputation for letting the player character fall through the floor of the game, only to be forced to restart from the last checkpoint. This is something that the developer still hasn't fixed, despite numerous people bringing it to their attention.
Although it has its flaws, that doesn't mean that Stairs should be overlooked. It's one of the best indie horror titles on Steam to date, and in certain areas it has a Silent Hills PT vibe to it. If you have a fascination with cults, gruesome deaths, and the profane, then you will most certainly recognize the real-world events that these tales are based off of; if you don't, then you will still be able to enjoy what's going on. Where Stairs really stands out is its deep atmosphere, seconded only by the unique layout of its puzzles and followed up by its minimalistic yet effective storytelling. If you're looking for a horror game that's a little bit different, with a bit of psychological terror thrown into the mix, then look no further.

Greetings fellow gamers! Happy Halloween! This is Gamer Wolf (In a Suit) from the Echo Army YouTube channel! Today I am bringing you a review of the latest psycholigical horror game, Stairs!
(NOTE: This game was reviewed using a key provided by the Developer)
Video Review:
The "Too Long, Didn't Watch" Review:
Atmospheric, psycholgical horror game done well. Great music, great visuals. Good immersive environment. Less reliance on jump scares, leans more on feelings of despair, being trapped, etc. Solid effort. 3.5/5. Worth it at under $10.
The "Meat & Potatoes" Review:
The gameplay is VERY familiar. You are armed with your journal (for notes/hints) and your camera (for, well, taking pictures). As you take the pictures found throughout the scenes, you piece together the clues to this story. Stairs is actually inspired by real-life events (with a little fiction thrown in for good measure). The atmosphere is quite immersive, as the deeper down you go the more you become filled with anxiety and the feeling you really are trapped in some godless maze. The music definitley helps, as it is quite creepy and very well done. I love this soundtrack. While this game is not really groundbreaking in any way, it is good fun. It also seems to be quite linear, as nothing seems to be different while playing again. This may effect replayability for some, particularily those gamers that colelct ALL the hints before moving on to the next stage. All in all, it's a fine, solid effort from GreyLight Entertainment and Digital Tribe. 3.5/5and certainly worth under $10.

The first bit of praise I give this game is having an open beta modding feature and community while it's still in early access; I'd argue it's been there for a long time, but it comes out with great updates when they release them. I used to enjoy games like Minecraft and Terraria, it's not that they're terrible or anything, but I've reached the end of the games in play, mechanics and exploration, so I picked up this game once I saw the art and gameplay.
Favorite things about this game is how it's building mechanics are simplified in one handy tool, with other tools for option and picking up the pace, the clothes and appearence customization, what I refer to as weighted combat system, where the mining and exploration has you exploring solar systems and the planets that inhabit them, and the option to pick different alien races to play as- with each one having a clever culture theme to them (I'd encourage all race modders to consider that when making their playable races, with credit to some who do)
Exploring planets is a treat with each planet having a new and more or less different environment to explore and new lifeforms inhabiting them and you can find dungeons either on the surface or through digging; leaving a lot open for exploration and challenge. Only thing I haven't tried yet is the online play with a friend, but I already endorse this game to my own friends.
I am short on saying anymore, but I genuinely enjoy what is already here and excited for each update. Would like to see it released as a full fledged game like the other ones Chucklefish has released since this game was put on here, but there is a lot here as it is. Pick it up, start digging, start building and start exploring

First off, I gotta tell ya, don't listen to the negative reviews. Got that? Good.
Starbound is a game that's set in a universe with 7 different playable races, and other races that are NPCs, but might be added to the game as a playable race. The seven races are the Apex, a race that is very modern and you can relate them to different parts of modern western culture, and they are also monkey people, as is quite obvious. They fall underneath a monarch known as "Big Ape" or Miniknog. The next are the Avian, and the Avian are a bird-like people that can be related to Egyptian/Myan/Aztec culture, with very large temples and towns that are based around trade. The Avian worship Kluex, a bird-god that was said to have risen to the heavens, and ostracized every other person in his following, making them flightless and unable to use their wings. Next up are the Florans, adn the Florans are carnivores that are also plants. They live in a very primitive time, but some florans are very intelligent and stray away from common floran lifestyle, which is just hunt for food and survive. The next is the Glitch, and they are a very medieval race, even though they are robots. The creators of the Glitch are unknown, but they all fall under a central programming, and this keeps them from evolving from the medieval stage into the next era of mankind, as this was the programming they fall under. Novakids are a very "bright" people, as they are people born from dying stars. They live in very western/cowboy styles of life, and they like to be gunslingers and ranchers. The Hylotl are a fish-like people, and they have a very Japanese lifestyle, living off of rice and other plants, and being noble samurai, as well as living underwater as well as above land. Lastly we have the Humans, and the humans have a very tragic past, as in the Starbound universe, when you first begin, you will discover soon that Earth has been destroyed. All Humans were forced to leave the planet or die. Humans are just humans like you and me, and they have a very normal lifestyle, aas they are not far off from our own races ingenuity and hardiness. Now that I have the races out of the way, allow me to explain some of the gameplay. The gameplay can be related very easily to Terraria, if you have ever played it, and this is because they are both 2D games about exploration. You start off with very basic materials and tools, such as a flashlight, a weapon, and a universal Matter Manipulator. You will have to complete quests in the beginning in order to expand where you can travel to.
You should get this game not because of the SUPER AMAZING GAMEPLAY, or the OUT OF THIS WORLD GRAPHICS, you should get it because its not going to just be a game, it's going to be an experience. You don't have to stick to your own story, you can even make your own. Make a server, play with your friends. Establish a community. Go on adventures. You have a whole galaxy at your disposal. So why should you get this game? Oh man, why not.

I mean, what do I say? It's Burnout Paradise. The one and only. Where else can you spend your time ruthlessly ramming people off the road in a flame painted nitrous fuelled van while listening to Mozart?
I can't say enough good things about this game. I sunk about half my life into this game back on my PS3, and now it's on sale for less than a Big Mac I couldn't say no. It is basically almost all my ideas of a perfect game rolled into one (minus a few explosions and a 100% open world).
Firstly, the map. it is pretty damn big. It's not huge, especially not by today's standards, but it is big enough and it has basically everything you want in an open-ish world racing game: City Streets, thin alleys, winding hairpin bends on mountainsides, highways, a few large open spaces, and jumps galore. In a word, there is plenty to do.
Next up, events. I think there are around 120 that you can do, including Road Rages, Races, Stunt Runs and Marked Man events. There are also a load of freedrive events and stuff such as Showtime (super fun) and Road times, alongside a tonne of collectibles such as Smashable Billboards, Smash Gates and Super Jumps.
There is a very large variety of cars, with about 75 available, each one very unique. Excluding DLC cars, there are 3 types of vehicle: Aggression, Stunt, and Speed. I won't go too much into how they work, but more or less the type just affects the way the boost works and sometimes the stats of the car. You unlock them by taking cars down as they enter the city, or collecting them as you level up your license.
I like the levelling system, how you need to win events to level up your licence all the way from Learner, to Class D-A, to Burnout License (I think). Each license needs more events each time to level up, and as you complete each event the next ones become harder. It's a good and rewarding system.
There is also multiplayer, which is great. it is well implemented, simple and hass quite a few features. You can join a random server or play with friends, and it is all accessed quickly and simply from the easydrive menu (A great feature, by the way. I think it's in other games as well, like NFS). If you have friends who also like these kinds of games, get them to buy it and you can have an absolute blast together.
Trying to find flaws in this game is very difficult. Aside from nostalgia-based bias, it is a very good game, and I genuinely can't think of any major ones. There is the lack of any visual customisation other than paint job which is kinda disappointing, but then that has never been in Burnout (as far as I'm aware) and it's not too much of an issue. But the graphics are goo, the physics are relatively realistic and very fun, the crash model is amazing, the gamemodes are all very different and interesting.
Basically I can't reccomend this game enough. If you like driving games with a bit of chaos, then this game is perfect.

Burnout Paradise is a dead game - that's the only disclaimer this game needs for now really.
The graphics hold up in 2017 despite being released in 2008, which is crazy. It is easy to dismiss this as a point however the graphics do hold up against some of todays games.
The controls are seemless on a controller and naturally are easy to master.

The map is quite large and has a lot of different places to explore which allows for you to play for hours on end just cruising around the map not really doing much other than driving as fast as you f_ucking can. This alone is quite a relaxing and fun thing to do.

Things I didn't like about this game:
1) Loading time is too slow. It takes me 2 minutes from the moment I click on the desktop icon to start playing the actual game. Two minutes!
2) I can play most new games at the maximum settings, but for some reason, Van Helsing II lags even on the lowest settings.
3) The maps are not randomized.
4) The name of the game is silly and way too long.
5) Too many cutscenes and talking. This was supposed to be an ARPG where you just run around and kill kill kill and click click click, not an RPG like Baldur's Gate. Less talking, more action and more loot. Oh, speaking about loot:
6) Not enough loot. I destroy every barrel, kill every monster and I only get a few drops.
7) Rage mechanic doesn't tell you when it's activated. A sound effect or a graphic representation would be nice. It would be even nicer if the Rage worked like in Torchlight 2, where when you reach maximum rage, you are super powerful for 10 seconds or so, instead of these "combos".
8) Too many mobs. Seriously, when 15 fast moving guys just surround you, there isn't much you can do, especially if you are a ranged class.
9) The game graphic seems outdated, like I'm playing a game from 2005.
10) UI is pretty bad. In every decent ARPG it is ESSENTIAL to have a good view of your health and mana bars (or orbs). In Van Helsing, they are barely visible.
All in all, a poor attempt at an ARPG game. If you want the real thing, I suggest: Diablo 2, Torchlight 2 or Titan Quest.

ICEY is one of those games where writing a review without spoiling anything is almost impossible. You have been warned.
ICEY is a rather curious case. What looked like a "run of the mill" Hack&Slay on first sight turned out to be quite a lot more.
It's a narrative driven experience and the many comparisons to games like "The Stanley Parable" are quite fitting.
At it core, it's a very solid 2D Hack&Slay Platformer similar to titles like "Muramasa" (Not on Steam).
The game is presented as if you are watching the titular character ICEY through a survailance camera while the story is told by an off-speaker who constantly breaks the 4th wall, by either rambling about the creation of this game or due to interruptions of the video feed (often to insert new code).
This approach is charming in its own way and offers quite a lot of replay value due to branching paths, loads of secrets and also the ability to upgrade your character.
But it's also my main gripe with this game. Its simply "too good" for this sort of approach. Its actual gameplay is really entertaining, fast and rewarding, but it constantly gets interrupted by the narrative. With games where the pinacle of player interaction is walking from point A to point B, such a narrative becomes the main attraction.
With ICEY, its main attraction often takes a back seat.
Do i recommend it ? Absolutely. Its something rather unique in its genre and offers a lot of weird humor and mystery all backed up by really fun gameplay.
EDIT:
Every once in a while, an indie game hits the market, you really enjoy it and...thats usually it.
So i was pretty surprised to see that ICEY got such a meaty update.
The fully voiced english localisation adds a lot to the overall experience for non-Chinese speakers, as it allows you to fully focus on its gameplay while still being able to take in the narrative.
Bottom line: An even bigger recommendation than before. What do you say, Mr. Narrator ?

This is now the third time I've written this review and the second time I have changed my opinions on Street Fighter V - though since the game is over a year old, it is probably pointless to have an opinion on this game anymore. If you haven't bought this game, you'll probably never buy this game.
Okay so is Street Fighter V bad?
No. Street Fighter V is not bad, it is not awful - it is a genuinely good fighting game. I feel like the SFV hate has just become a train for people to bandwagon on; there are genuine reasons that make people, including me, sometimes wish to burn every copy of this game which we will get to - but for the most part it is all just others barking along. A lot of the inital realease issues have actually been fixed so there is no need to keep mentioning them.
So what is in Street Fighter V?
Characters - The base game comes with a quite small 16 characters, with the season 1 and currently realeasing season 2 passes will bring it up to 28 characters which is a decent number. There are main stays and old returnings with some brilliant new additions (Bravo to F.A.N.G and Necalli for being the coolest new characters in Street Fighter).
Graphics - Thank god for Unreal Engine 4 cause this game looks absolutely gorgeous! Minus, banana head Ken... that still hasn't been cleaned up.
Offline - As of now there is a cinematic story mode, a short character story for each character, up to 100 round survival mode and the standard versus mode - with additional training mode as well. Yes, you don't have the general arcade mode, but it seems that people who complain that arcade mode doesn't exist have not played Survival mode - which is god damn awesome! You have to carry your health & EX bar through each fight, using scored points to give yourself boosts to survive longer. It is fun, very fun. There is a lot to go through and complete, though it is not as interesting as say MKX or Tekken 7.
Unlockables - Okay this is where I have to briefly mention one of the biggest flops in Street Fighter V which I will get into later on... Fight Money. ALL unlockables are behind fight money, so be prepared to go through everyone's survival mode to grind that fight money. The stages and cosmetics are really nice and the DLC characters can be purchased with Fight Money.
Online - There are three game modes for online play. Casual, Ranked and a lobby based battle lounge. All seem standard, plain, but standard. The main problem with Online play is the netcode for this game. It is awful, god awful. Reporting for poor actions such as rage quitting and lag switching is basically non-existent, meaning that there is not much you can do if you end up in a terrible match.
Gameplay - Okay, so this is very opinionated but personally I love SFV mechanics and gameplay. The stun bar from SFIII returns, and we now have 3 EX bars and a V-Gauge replacing the focus attack, giving each character a unquie skill to use in the match as well as a comeback transformation. Some are just functional, others are very interesting (Necalli's V-Trigger never turns off and transforms him Super Saiyan style). Alpha Counters (now called V-Reversals) are back as well.
Combos are streamlined and reletively easy to pull off, meaning rookies can pull of some of the best combos - having easier combos I believe is better for the game. For one, there is still need for good execution to perform these combos so to say they are as easy as 'pushing a button' is just wrong. This second also allows for the game to be simply more accessible, which is fine.
Character balancing is a bit... off, there are general strong and weak characters which is to be expected... and then there is Balrog. A lot of the charcters in the game are 'rushdown' characters so playstyles have this weird psudo-similarity between them to playing; you probably won't notice it as a general person picking up SFV but it exists to an extent.
So what makes people hate Street Fighter V?
Fight Money - I will give you advice, if you want the characters DO NOT grind for Fight Money, just buy the season passes - save yourself the trouble. After the offline content, online gives you 50 a win and none if you lose. No. Fight Money is awful. Just god damn awful.
Online Netcode - The foundations of Street Fighter V's online, are not good. The netcode is terrible, I will say about 35% of my matches are affected by lag to the point where it's a problem to play and instead of slowing down the entire match which is what a lot of games do - they decide to skip frames which can be a HUGE problem. Lag also causes the 2 'buffer' frames to be a double edge sword - sometimes a throw or hit can be negated cause the insane lag means those buffer frames don't get the hit, you will see the hit bar drop and go back within a frame.
Comparing to Street Fighter IV - If you like SFIV, chances are you really dislike SFV. With V getting streamlined and more accessible, it's put a lot of people off who relied on complexity and hard combos and having this giant learning curve. Fair arguements. To be perfectly honest, I ♥♥♥♥ing HATE Street Fighter IV, it is a game to me that refuses to provide any information feedback to the player and combine that with an insane learning curve; it is just not for me. Street Fighter V has less complexity than Street Fighter IV, that is true and it may turn people off. I don't think this is a problem.

Street Fighter V is a great fighting game wrapped in a lot of poor decisions, many where fixed but fundemental issues still remain. If you want a good fighting game then this is an option on that list.

Burnout Paradise is a dead game - that's the only disclaimer this game needs for now really.
The graphics hold up in 2017 despite being released in 2008, which is crazy. It is easy to dismiss this as a point however the graphics do hold up against some of todays games.
The controls are seemless on a controller and naturally are easy to master.
The AI isn't super advanced, which for a chilled out game such as Burnout, is great. Only in Marked Man will the AI test you as for some reason in Marked Man they grow brains - otherwise don't expect much competition.
There are very few online players anymore as you would expect with any game almost 10 years old, so don't expect to be able to hop from lobby to lobby and every one of them be full with people all waiting to play.
There isn't an immense amount of customization in the cars other than a few colour changes and a better version of each car you unlock (unlocked by doing the Burning Route designed for that car) however this is countered quite comfortably by the extensive range of 75 cars in the default game, with further DLC cars.
The map is quite large and has a lot of different places to explore which allows for you to play for hours on end just cruising around the map not really doing much other than driving as fast as you f_ucking can. This alone is quite a relaxing and fun thing to do.
Learning each section of the map will reward you in timed events as you dip in and out of back alleys and underpasses to get to where you want. This idea of knowing the map to be faster than opponents is largely engaging and will allow for a good time with friends or alone!

I won't get into the laundry-list of items that need to be fixed because basic things such as netcode and a properly designed lobby system have been repeatedly mentioned by other reviewers.
I bought the game for $20 during the winter sale, when the game had been out for a year.  I had hoped that all of the negatives would've been fixed by now.  It wasn't worth it.
By far the biggest problem is this:  it's BORING.  Once you get to gold tier, it becomes mind-numbingly repetitive because it is now a TURN-BASED GUESSING GAME.  That's right, you have to wait your turn in order to attack.  However, while doing so, you must continually guess whether it's best to block, try and tech a throw, block an overhead, or backdash from grapplers.  There is practically no reaction time to throws unless you detect a pattern in your opponent.  Footsies revolve around waiting for a counter-hit and getting lucky with a crush counter to follow up with a combo that puts you in the position I just described above.  It is absolute crap.
To be honest, it was enjoyable up to a point.  You may have fun in bronze and silver tiers because people still take chances there.  After that, it becomes very repetitive and frustrating.  To advance, you then need to grind out countless hours to memorize which moves are safe or not on block.  The recovery times on hits and misses for specials and ALL normals.  And not just for your character... FOR ALL CHARACTERS.  That is what the turn-based system requires.
If this sounds like fun to you, then so be it.  For me, life is too short to spend studying frame data for a boring game with horrible gameplay mechanics that is frustrating at best (after a point).
This is my first negative review for a game.  That alone should tell you something.
Oh, and I've been playing the SF series since SFII on the SNES.

So, the game starts off strong, almost feeling like a Silent Hill point-and-click game, with a unique art style, decent music, and alot of imagination. It sets up quite a little mystery. Then the game stalls for a while, then there is a chapter that feels basically like an entirely different game that could have been cut-out completely, then more spinning it's wheels, then the final chapter which feels like the midway point of the story at best, leading to what I can hardly call a conclusion.
This is one of those stories where they don't actually explain hardly anything. I don't mind the ambiguity, but the characters themselves clearly discuss an overarching story that is never revealed and, actually, just gets dropped in the finale. It's just "Nevermind, storybook ending!" I mean, not exactly storybook, but it feels rushed, like someone forgot the actual final chapter so they just forced in this ending and rolled the credits, there's not even a post-climax scene to wrap things up beyond a single visual that has about as much impact in words as it does on the screen.
The main character of Fran seems a little odd at first, but considering the opening setup, you can understand it, a mix of innocent child and PTSD. However, as time goes on, she really becomes very flat, showing almost no real emotion except when the plot demands she cries for 10 seconds. She's very nice and sweet, just like Alice from Alice in Wonderland, which this game is strongly influenced by, but if Alice was seeing death and horror instead of a disappearing cat, I think it would be reasonable to expect some kind of reaction beyond "Curiouser and curiouser". Fran being a child is an excuse that only goes so far when you've seen things to make Rambo weep.
The imagination shown in the first hour or two gets stale when they really never come up with anything more. In fact, if anything, the game gets LESS unsettling later on, with the demonic visions becoming less scary and just less frequent. And as others have complained, the mid-game chapter is about 95% cutesy as hell, it's almost like they wanted to give players a break from the scary stuff, but when they get back to the scary stuff, it's pretty lacking. There's only so many times you can show me amorphous evil shadows before they start to feel like zombie dogs in Resident Evil.
Gameplay wise, meaning puzzle wise, it's fine. I don't play alot of these kinds of games, so I get the feeling that a big fan of them will have no trouble at all, but they are fun and never feel cheap. There are some optional things you can do for achievements, but you are never stuck in this game, you can never die or reach an unwinnable state. There are also a few very short action sequences that are kind of jarring and pointless, but they are so short and easy that I don't think anyone will care. None of it feels very satisfying though, and I don't just mean because of the difficulty; the puzzles almost feel like the creators said "Guys, we can't just have the players walk around for 6 hours, we need some kind of mechanic, quick, whip up some puzzles and just ram 'em in there". I can accept this in a tongue-in-cheek humor game, or a dark and gritty game, but not a game that is basically one girl's pscyhological odyssey based around talking and seeing weird stuff.
Basically, the game seems great in the first hour or two, in a mental hospital for sick kids, having demonic visions, it's great. There's alot of crazy talk and weirdness and you really wonder what's going on. The problem is that you never get told, not adequately. You learn the bad guys did the bad things for undisclosed bad reasons...yeah. All those other kids disappear, you never really establish much connection to any other characters or places, and Fran herself is so much a polite little kid that she feels unnatural and like a living doll. I really enjoyed this game for a bit, and I even liked the wierd middle chapter despite it feeling like a completely different game (they could have made that into an entire game and I would have been fine), but the overall package is really disappointing. It's never deeply clever, the visuals get old, and the writing just gives up and hits the bar after a while, all tied up with a magic pink bow of convenience. If you don't like point-and-click, stay away, and if you DO, this will likely leave you feeling disappointed. It's hard for me to picture who exactly this is going to appeal to, unless you literally only care about the art design and sound in a game, in which case, buy it.

Here are some longer video versions of this review:
Doom, a series I’ve avoided for far too long. My first experience with Doom was with Doom 64, which was much scarier to me than the original. I couldn't get any farther than the first enemy. I think the best part about Doom 3 BFG is the fact that it not only has Doom 3, but Doom 1 and 2 as well. Makes it easier to catch up on the series.
The original Doom stands as my third favorite game of all time. It's really fun to run around and shoot demons with an arsenal of weapons that you apparently just stuff into your pants pockets. Seriously, unless you’re a robot whose limbs transform into each weapon, there’s no way that you can carry that many guns and still be able to move. It's kind of a shame I didn't get around to playing this until December 2015.
One of my biggest problems is that I'm too slow for this game. I'm always hesitant to go in one direction because there could be goodies in another. I'm not that great at finding secrets either. I don't find it very fun to have to interact with every wall in the map just to find them. I also have a thing for getting lost and running around in circles constantly.
I usually play on Hurt Me Plenty, but Thy Flesh Consumed was a real b****. I got brutally murdered the first time I played it, so I had to play on the easiest difficulty. Even THAT was difficult.
My least favorite weapon is the chainsaw, I didn't really enjoy how it felt in the older Doom games. I like it better in Doom 3. I feel like I have more control over my character. Plus, it's easier to tell how far away the 3D models are and how close I need to be to hit them with it.
Now about Doom 2, honestly, I really didn’t like it as much. The gameplay, for the most part, is basically the same. But this game is a bit harder than the first, and it’s just too long for my liking. I got bored of it about halfway through. The Spirit World is where I really threw in the towel. Those stupid Spiderdemons take away too much of my health that even if I do manage to defeat them, I don’t have enough health and armor to get past that one room with the Arch-vile and multiple Hell Knights. So yeah, I never got to the end of that game, and I don’t really want to try.
The only things I really like about Doom 2 is the super shotgun, and the newer enemies they added. But I always dreaded the Arch-vile. That thing was terrifying the first time I saw it. These guys are strong, fast, and hard to kill without the BFG. I like him, even though he’s a giant prick.
Doom 3. I used to watch my mom play this game, even though the only memory I have of her playing that is the part where you have to escort some guy through the darkness, and protect him from Imps.
I actually love this game. It's just as fun as the original, and has all the shooting the original game has. However, it doesn't just drop you right in and immediately start the killing spree. It actually has cutscenes and stuff that reveal a story behind everything that happens throughout the game.
If there's anything about this game that I like more than the original, it's that, they made the game scary. The darkness and noises freak me out, and I always get this feeling that there's something creeping up behind me.
You can get goodies out of storage lockers, but to open them, you need to find codes. You can get them from people's PDAs by reading their messages or listening to the audio logs. This is a pretty cool idea, but the problem is that the audio logs are just too long. I know they're just adding more to the game's story, but I don't particularly enjoy being forced to listen to stuff I honestly don't really care about just to open a frigging locker. This is probably the biggest flaw of the game, in my opinion.
I find the complete lack of subtitles a major disappointment, especially in a game where shooting and other sounds tend to drown out the voices.
The weapons sometimes don't always feel as strong as they should be. I hate it when a zombie has to take 3 hits with a shotgun at a distance where other zombies had died from one shot. It's kinda ridiculous.
Then we go to Hell. This place is pretty awesome, and also quite scary to me. I couldn't get through here without constantly shaking the mouse. The hellish screams are quite unnerving to me. It's just kind of a shame that I was only there for about 45 minutes.
I really love this Soul Cube. It kills most enemies in one hit, while also earning you some health in the process. The best idea is to save it for the stronger enemies, unless, of course, you are in desperate need of health. But the catch is that you can only use it after killing a certain amount of enemies. So be careful who you use it on, or you’ll end up having to deal with an Arch-vile or Hell Knight with whatever weapons you’ve got.
Remember when I said that Doom 2 was too long for my liking? Well, this game was longer than that, but I actually enjoyed it a lot more. Maybe because, unlike the earlier games, you don’t have the exact same mission in every level: grab the keys, get goodies, and reach the exit.
I have nothing to add about the Doom 3 expansions in terms of gameplay, but Resurrection of Evil introduces a new gadget called the Grabber. I actually think it's pretty cool, even though it may feel like a ripoff to the Gravity Gun in Half-Life 2. You grab stuff and throw it around. But unlike the Gravity Gun, the Grabber can grab enemy projectiles and throw them back at enemies, or grab smaller enemies and throw them.
It also introduces the Hell Hunters, each with three different abilities you can get: Helltime (makes time slow down for you), Berserk (makes weapons stronger), and Invulnerability (self-explanatory). I had found out the hard way that the enemies can get a little overwhelming in this expansion. Using these abilities makes everything much easier, if you know when the appropriate time is to use them.
I had found out that how much you can write in these reviews is limited, so I'll make this one quick. In The Lost Mission, you watch a cutscene that had played back in the original Doom 3 campaign. You apparently play as one of those soldiers, I guess. You also get the Grabber here as well, but I never used it, except for the little flying skulls.
I've noticed that each expansion is more difficult than the last, but they are still fun, either way. Although in The Lost Mission, there were some areas where I kinda wish they didn’t throw so many stronger enemies like Hell Knights at me. But whatever, I beat the game. That’s all that matters now.
It's kinda too bad these are the only Doom games, I'll be able to review. The new game looked really awesome, and I played the open beta this month of last year, but it ran at a really sh***y frame rate. But anyway, Doom 3 BFG is, in my opinion, the best way to actually play all the games in the series, rather than buying each one individually.
