This is a game that is both annoying and pretty fun.
I'll try to explain the gameplay mechanics briefly:
This is a rhythm game with 4 buttons. The enemies attack from 4 different directions and you have to press the same button where the attacker comes from. For example, enemy comes from up so you'll press up. You can tell which button to press in advance because the next attacker is glowing white. The enemies attacks are in sync with the music and there a total of 3 different enemy types.
The button presses feels good and there's no problem there. But what annoys me is that there's sometimes so much light effects in the background so it can disturb your visual feed so much so that it's really hard to see the next attacker. The white glow of the enemy sometimes blends in with the bright background too. That makes it feel unfair because it's really really hard to get a perfect on the first few runs. Sometimes even a enemy flies to the screen for a brief second covering about 30% of the screen. It's a very brief second but still a distraction.
Second thing that annoys me is the inconsistency when the glowing white appears on enemies. For example: when a attacker starts coming, the white glow appears 2-3 seconds before the attack. And after his attack, the next attacker comes right after him and the white glow appears right before his attack. This made me press buttons early because I saw a white glow lighting up so I thought a attack comes right then. When the attack comes right after the previous attack, there's sometimes very little time to react to it.
The game requires almost your full attention and the learning curve is high, but it can be really enjoyable. You'll start jamming if a familiar song starts playing and you'll get great satisfaction when you finally beat a difficult song.
I just feel that if there would have been less effects and the white glow on enemies would have been highlighted more, this game would feel more fair to play and much more fun.
The game is worth it's price tag and the gameplay mechanics are great. On a scale of 1-10, I'll give this 6/10.

NOTE:  I've played this game for about 30 minutes, completing the tutorial and a couple of stages on Normal difficulty.
I was mislead into buying this game by the media quotes, which made the game seem like a deeper game than it is.  That said, it isn't a bad rhythm game by any means.  Basic gameplay is pretty typical of games like DDR, where you press buttons representing Up, Down, Left, and Right when enemies move into the appropriate area.  You also have a couple of Guitar Hero style features: an overdrive mode that when charged lets you increase your score multiplier, and a button to activate powerups like a shield that protects you from misses briefly.
This game also has a decently neat feature in that some enemies have items floating over their heads - to actually get the item you have to double-tap the button instead of single-tap.  This is how you get the aforementioned powerups, and these items also include bonus points and score multiplier increases.
Aesthetically, the game is pretty good - the animations are neat, the enemies look good, and I've enjoyed the included music tracks that I've played (though of course your mileage may vary).  This all can get in the way of the gameplay, however.  Screen shakes, circling enemies, and poor indicators of which enemy is going to hit first make the game more difficult than other traditional rhythm games.
Overall, not a bad rhythm game, it just adds some Kung Fu game style to the model we're all pretty familiar with.  I was looking for an action game with strong rhythm elements, and was disappointed.  But if you're looking for a Rhythm game with added flavor, I'd probably recommend this.  It gets a "Yes."

Warning: Decently long review, TL;DR at bottom.
Bought the game on sale during Winter Event (so 2 days ago) after playing the first, rolled veteran arcane mechanic and blasted through the story line. Loved gameplay of storyline even though it felt more like a connection to the third game, Katarina is funny as always and it was for the most part amusing.
Biggest hiccup was hitting end game content (i.e. Scenarios) where I was DRAMATICALLY underequipped, and really the only decent way of getting gear was from the pigasus. So I had to slide my bloody, grumpy, body through scenarios flailing my failing limbs around until I could afford one piece of pigasus gear (~10 mil standard), after which it got much better. That said, scenarios are fun but bless their hearts they just kill me sometimes.
PROS:
- Funy(ny) storyline, well written and obviously well planned. No awkward tacked on sequel bait.
- Included DLC classes from first game with more skills, all of which are fun.
- Decently improved multiplayer from first game, still glitches during storyline and crashed game multiple times during scenario runs in endgame, but much improved from where they started in first Van Helsing.
- Much better gear drops than in first game, makes farming much more exciting
- Better endgame than first, though that's not really saying much since the first games endgame didn't drop much
CONS:
- Endgame has some very cheap feeling shots at the player (will cover seperately, not terribly detrimental to the game at large) .
- Slightly buggy multiplayer using LAN connection (can't speak for full wifi)
ENDGAME:
And here we come to the crux of most of my issues. Endgame is vastly improved and generally a very good experience but with that said some of the things they throw at you just feel like they were player tested on devs and didn't see much actual exposure to a realistic player base.
You start out with a difficulty curve that in reality is more of a mountain (could maybe be solved by having the final boss drop a piece of pigasus gear?), and though you climb the mountain and can get a huge amount of satisfaction from doing so the mechanics of the scenario system sometimes feel engineered to take the wind out of your sails.
The whole scenario system suffers from a distinct feeling of a lack of agency, you get no choice what maps, what penalties, and what objectives you'll have to complete when running one of the 6 objective scenarios and almost more painful is the lack of ability to even choose what order you run them in. You literally get thrown into one and get penalized for rerolling it if the difficulty's too high, if the penalties are too harsh or unprepared for at current gear level, or if you fail on of the objectives. You even get penalized if you reroll the scenario before FINALIZING it (something that I can't tell if was intended, or if it's just a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ bug).
That all added together the scenarios are generally enjoyable, and actually very fun, but all of the joy you can expect to get out of them MUST be measured against your ability to not get upset when bashing your head against a wall of unforgiving and blatantly punishing mechanics. For example, there are "clue finding" objectives in the scenarios which ask the player to kill groups of elites around the map in a time limit. The implementation of this objective in particular ends up making it feel almost impossible to beat, and generally kills my enthusiam for continuing if paired with a horrible map and a bad penalty. Take home message to devs, hard is fun, challenging is funner, but punishing (i.e. player gets penalized with no agency and no ability to mitigate damage) is just asking for patience, not enjoyment.
TL;DR -
Great game, worth a purchase (will immediatly buy next game) and recomended to be played after first. Endgame suffers from several flaws (feels like devs made it planning for everyone to have maxed out gear, nothing less) and it is deeply recomended by myself to start on casual (normal is not normal, normal is hard). All in all, worth the money though I'd say wait for a sale if you're unsure. Fans of the first will love it though, and if you are it's worth a full purchase.

To those who are not aware, music based games have moved on from Guitar Hero/Rockband clones, and have taken aspects from loads of different games, adding rhythm based mechanics over these. For PC gamers, this pot is starting to fill nicely, with games such as Audiosurf and Beat Hazard, who take ideas from old games like Asteroids and Wipeout. Kickbeat combines two genres that haven’t really had the same success as the earlier examples; the Music Fighting genre.
In its simplest terms, Kickbeat requires you to hit 4 buttons in rhythm to generic ninja soldiers coming towards you, all of which is in time to a piece of music. The variety in enemies is pretty poor, but as a game with 4 buttons, it would be difficult to see how they could improve this without changing mechanics.
The story mode of music games is often non-existent; look at the BIT.TRIP games, and tell me that any discernible story is given. Kickbeat tries to remedy this with a set of licensed tracks that come with the game, by artists like Pendulum and Marilyn Manson. Even with their best efforts, the story is just a thin film over the “complete these five tracks to unlock some more” system.
From the perspective of Kickbeat being a fighting game… you’re gonna be disappointed. The game’s mechanics are the same as you will find in DDR, or any other dance mat game. The true fun you’ll find in Kickbeat comes from the fact that you can “fight” to your own tracks.
Yup. In the same vain as many of these music based games, due to not everyone having the same taste in tracks, you can import your own music into the game, and play the same way you can with the included tracks; although it takes a bit of setting up. Unfortunately, there seems to be effectively no detection algorithm used in Kickbeat to find BPM, or track intensity, instead relying on the “tap a button to the beat of the track” before you can play. Due to the game requiring lots of accuracy, it is incredibly annoying when the game is offsetting every beat by a fraction of a second compared to the music you’re hearing. The scale used to change when each beat happens is arbitrary, meaning you’re really using trial and error to see if the two tracks line up.
Kickbeat Promo 3So far it seems that all I’ve said has been pessimistic, but this game’s real quality comes from how, when you’ve spent your time making sure the game matches up sound and visuals, and you’ve learned all the small annoying traits each mechanic has, and you find yourself in a sort of “zone” the game feels great, the music matches the dynamics of the enemies perfectly, and you can just play and play for hours on end…
Until you try playing it on anything other than the lowest difficulty.
The way the game shows you which button you should press is confusing as hell for the first few levels. The enemies circle around you for a few beats before attacking you, when you need to counter them. This means that you need to remember which order they entered your “inner circle” and how long ago that was, to counter them perfectly. When you try playing on harder difficulties, this becomes nigh on impossible, especially as you have to sometimes hit three buttons simultaneously, or take 3 hits on your health.
I’m not the best at fighting games, or precision rhythm games, but I’d say from the perspective of the average gamer, Kickbeat is a hassle to set up, has no useful story mode, and no multiplayer function.

This game is absolutely fantastic. At the prices it goes to, it is a crime not to pick it up. A brilliant PC port, with excellent graphics that would hold a candle to story-driven AAA games today, it is one of the best games I have ever played.
The premise is unique, you playing as Wei Shen, an undercover cop with "chameleon-like traits", quoth his psychiatric assessment, who is sent on a mission to inflitrate the Sun On Yee, one of the gangs in an Asian triad centered around Hong Kong.
The environment is fantastic. Especially when it rains, it looks like a city, and plays like one. The best thing about this game, in my opinion, is the freedom that it gives you. There's no 'karma' system or 'good endings', so you can still have fun whilst enjoying the story to its fullest extent. I'm looking at you, Watch_Dogs.
Another thing I like in this game are how you aren't handed a gun at the start of the game, and from then on, if you can aim to a decent standard, you'll pretty much grind through the story in half the time advertised, since half of it is filler. No, none of that. Sleeping Dogs is a blend of hand-to-hand combat, melee weapons, and guns, but these are only given towards the end of the game, and when they are needed.
Additionally, the cops aren't gods in this game. If you aren't bothered to lose the cop in a car chase, the good old GTA way, then you can shoot him (probably not a good idea, you'll get a SWAT team sent after you), or you can knock him out with some kicks and some punches. Or, you can press Space while being cuffed to outwit him and cuff him, allowing for an escape on foot or on wheels. The cops are relevant in the game--unlike certain games where they just appear out of nowhere once you do anything remotely offensive--having a presence in the street and in local police departments.
No game comes without problems: the animations are out-of-context for the most part (they all seem to be distressed...). I, personally, don't like Jackie but that's a decision you can make for yourself. It's really bad about gun-saving, you could have an AR, but as soon as you enter a cutscene, you have a pistol. And you don't get your AR back when you re-enter gameplay. It's bad, but there are extremely few enemies where you're given a gun who can withstand more than a single headshot (all of the 'bosses', as it were, are played against hand-to-hand.)
All in all, it's an absolutely brilliant game that cannot be avoided at such low prices. I've sunk many hours into it, and at the price I got it for (2 keys, so about £3, $5, or €3.50), it is a must-buy.

Okay, here's a review from someone who 100% the game. Yes, it can be done in 7 hours and that probably would have been even less if I hadn't decided to play on "Hard". However for a $10 game with some interesting ideas and solid gameplay that's not necessarily bad. If you want a general idea for the game, it is a 2D action game with a decent combo system and some not great but still good enemies and bosses. The art and music are absolutely great. There is an interesting meta-narrative where you are in a somewhat of a constant opposition to the game's narrator and some interesting deeper lore that is hinted at from time to time. WARNING! The narrator is voice acted in Chinese ONLY. There are subtitles, so it's not a huge deal, but be warned. The game runs very well. Although, I began playing on a powerful machine, the game still performed fine when I switched to my crappy laptop with a NVIDIA GeForce 410M graphics card, which even impressed me a little. If that's enough info for you to buy it and discover things for yourself, go for it. If you want more information, continue reading, but be warned there will be minor spoilers.
The core gameplay consists of you killing monsters/robots with combinations of light and heavy attacks and special combos you can purchase for ingame currency at the checkpoints generously placed throughout the levels. You can also dash to avoid hits or traverse obstacles. There is also a counter system, where dodging an attack gives you an opportunity to hit the attacker from far away for massive damage and I do mean MASSIVE. In fact, the counter feature, while greatly satisfying, is also one of the main weaknesses of the combat. It is pretty much the only way to kill some of the tougher enemies in the game and deals so much damage that it makes bosses that give easily counterable attacks (lasers, hails of bullets, AoE attacks that last for a long time, etc) an absolute cakewalk, which includes the final boss. Still the combat is satisfying, has lots of visual feedback, the animations are great, and the bosses and enemies are well designed aside from this one flaw. I almost wish there was some sort of challenge mode or boss rush to just challenge your skills and enjoy the combat.
The first thing you will notice about this game is just how damn gorgeous it is. The art is amazing! From the backgrounds, to the main character, the enemies, and the bosses, everything looks great. The music is also quite good. It's great at keeping you pumped up and ready to fight and doesn't get old quickly despite the repetition. Overall, the artistic side of the game may be it's biggest strength as there is absolutely nothing bad I can say about it.
Hidden behind the game's main story is the quirky and funny meta-narrative. The narrator, who joins the game quite soon, constantly tries to get you to follow his arrows and you can choose to irritate him by doing the opposite. It's fun, but don't expect this to be the new "The Stanley Parable". Almost the entire meta component is built around you following or ignoring arrows and the narrator being pleased or angry about it respectively. There are a few exceptions which are pretty good, but for the most part the game doesn't have too many tricks up its sleeve. However, it does pull one more interesting swerve...
In addition to the funny meta-narrative, there are also scraps of a deeper somewhat creepy lore that even the narrator is only half-aware of. First of all, there is the actual story of ICEY, her archenemy Judas, and all the bosses laid out in the endings, some of the game's "glitchy" sequences, and, perhaps most bizarrely, the descriptions of the Steam achievements. Secondly, the game makes several references to a rather strange book by Robert W. Chambers entitled
, as well as some works of H. P. Lovecraft. I'm not going to tell you to go read a book to play a game, but I think at least having a quick look at The King in Yellow's Wikipedia page is going to improve your experience. This part of the game's story gets quite creepy and unnerving in a few places, which was a big surprise.
Unfortunately if you expect a big climactic resolution for the meta-narrative or the Lovecraftian undertones, you're going to be disappointed. Of course there's always a possibility that I've missed something. Maybe the questions in the beginning matter, maybe you can get behind Jack in the theatre somehow or the rooms you get to after him have some sort of secret to them, maybe the numbers in the ??? file mean something, maybe something is hidden in the beta, but if I'm right and this really is the end, then there isn't a real "answer" at the end of the road.
Overall, it's not an amazing 2D action game, it's not a superb meta game, and it's not an outstanding creepy/mysterious game, but it is
in all of those categories and perhaps that's enough. The meta comments will make you chuckle, the deep mystery will keep you wondering, and the core gameplay is good at keeping you entertained while you're getting from point A to point B. You could call this game a Jack of many trades and an Ace of none, but I don't see it as an insult. Overall the package is sure to keep you entertained for a nice evening or two of gaming. If I had to assign this game a score, it would be a 7/10. Although the lack of a real conclusion and some design choices when it comes to combat hold it back, the good double (or even triple) narrative and the still quite solid gameplay bump it up two points up from an average game and in my books that's more than enough for $10 and 7 hours or less of your time.

OHOTA KREPKOE is a barely working survival template with all the survival aspects removed. The soundtrack DLC for the game also doesn't exist and is possibly a scam.
The gameplay sees you run around a stock forest map, shoot wolves, pick up sticks and combine them with wolf meat in order to attract more wolves to shoot. That's literally it.
When you die, your character remains standing and you can still shoot and kill enemies. The game prompts you to press the escape key, doing so exits the game completely and you have to restart the client.
The framerate runs at a solid 15 - 25 FPS depending on whether or not the game decides to randomly soil itself it seems.
When wolves die, they ragdoll in hilarious fashion and their necks become a good foot or two longer.
As I said earlier, the DLC soundtrack for the game does not exist. I know, I bought it because I'm a masochist. After buying it, there was no download and nothing has appeared in my music library or in the game despite Steam telling me the DLC is currently installed.
There is no music in the game aside from a looping main menu theme, so how this game even has a soundtrack doesn't make any sense. I'm leaning towards the soundtrack DLC being a complete scam.
Overall, do not buy this trash game. It barely works and the DLC doesn't exist.

Story: It's 2009 (I guess), a zombievirus called the Green Flu has broken out. Four immune survivors have to fight off hordes of zombies, and escape. The story seems kind of believable, and is told just how Valve always tells it. 9/10
Gameplay: The gameplay is pretty basic. You choose between 4 survivors, pick-up weapons on the way, and have to make it to a safe room. At the end of a chapter there is a finale. You will have to fight off hordes of zombies, including some special ones, until the escape vehicle arrives. 8/10
Graphics: The game is starting to look dated. It runs on about every PC from the last 5 years, and it will still look scary at times. 9/10
Alternatives: Personally I would get Left 4 Dead 2. It also has the original Left 4 Dead campaign with slightly improved graphics. It costs the same too, but also has workshop support. The only other zombie game I would recommend over this is Half-Life 2 and of course Left 4 Dead 2, both by Valve.
Overall score: 9.1/10. The game is overlooked for a reason, Left 4 Dead 2 greatly overshadows it. You can get this one, but I recommend getting Left 4 Dead 2, it is practically the same, but with more content. It still is a great game, if you want to go back in time and play the original.

Full review:
KickBeat (Steam Edition), a game brought to us by the same team behind Pinball FX2 and CastleStorm, is a rhythm game that places a large emphasis on reaction time and button mashing.
The game's goal is simple: last through the entire song. This is done by pressing four different buttons in a certain order pertaining to where enemies are onscreen. I used an Xbox 360 controller (so much easier) for my play sessions so far and I'd recommend one here, as the keyboard controls can get a bit frustrating. Using an Xbox 360 controller, picture the character standing in the middle of the A-X-Y-B buttons, now imagine enemies coming at you from any of those four buttons. Press the correct button in time (when the enemy is standing on it, about to attack you) to knock him out by way of some very nice Kung-Fu action.
This can get a bit more difficult if there's multiple enemies attacking simultaneously, forcing the player to react by pressing the buttons in accordance with which buttons the attackers are currently standing on. This gets even more intense later on when you've got five or so enemies attacking you every second. The game does have multiple difficult levels, however, so it shouldn't be too much of a problem to find the right difficulty for you. I went with "Expert" to begin with, which isn't even the hardest difficulty, and I found it near-impossible to finish a song. I ended up staying with "hard", as that was the only one I could actually go through with.
I was a bit disappointing to know that I couldn't jump right into the game and use my own music, however. A certain portion of the campaign must be completed in order to unlock the "use your music" mode, which I would have greatly preferred to have used from the start. The campaign is fun though, so I didn't have to go through too much pain.
KickBeat is an excellent rhythm game overall. Very fun and very intense (especially on the harder difficulties, of which "Master" is impossible). Highly recommended.

This game is a mix between a decent 2D "Hack & slash" game and a very "meta" experience. It goes without saying that it's quite a unique experience and a highly welcome experiment involving two genres that rarely get mixed together.
You play as a character with a rather OK moveset (You never get more weapons than your starting short range sword) and you get money that can be used to either get new combos and moves or to further enhance them or your character's stats. The controls are simple and do their job just fine.
The most interesting part is how "meta" the game is. You have a narrator telling you what to do at all times and not following his orders will result in very interesting outcomes (Be it serious or funny ones) and the entire game relies on you checking every outcomes across all the areas. Playing this while obediently following what the narrator tells you will only make you miss all the interesting parts in the game.
The music is *fantastic*. Not a single level feels boring thanks to the excellent soundtrack the game has. The OST is avalable as a free DLC for this game.
Enemy variety is alright although it takes a while before other type of enemies are thrown at you. The boss fights feel rather short so as interesting as they might be, they end too fast and don't add enough variety to the game.
The game is rather short (Which should be reflected in its price) and 100% completion can be achieved in a couple of days max. There are no achievements that can be missed during a playthrough partially due to the way the level select works like (Basically, events get reset allowing you to experience certain outcomes even after having previously triggered other events).
Anyway, as the narrator told me to do: 5 STARS! But I WONT buy another copy!
UPDATE: The game now has an extra zone that puts your skills to the limit with tons of waves of enemies. Do NOT attempt to play through this area without being fully prepared and with most of the upgrades. The game also now features English voice acting besides the original Mandarin one but the narrator feels really week in comparison to the original one.

It is incredibly hard to figure where you're going to move at times due to the perspective; many (")deaths(") because I thought the tiles to the side were part of the main walkway. Paths will not be shown you unless you're on the tile right before them; just wander the edges and sometimes off of them and trust the rocks in the sky will meet you.
Early on (it seems to get (")better(") as you get further through the game), there are multiple directions you can travel in while on a mission. You best be lucky in making the wrong choices first so as to fully explore and get all the loots - once you head towards the main path, the rest of the level will be off-limits; destruction will chase you out of the level, never allowing you to return again (until New Game Plus). You can't even rely on narration to let you know "Okay, this is the correct way, go everywhere else first," because, of course, everything is narrated.
By "it seems to get (")better(")," I mean that the levels seem to get progressively more linear.
Aiming is prone to be imprecise; cycling through your targets is totally arbitrary.
It seems there are vastly superior choices when deciding how to level your weapons, but seeing as how you are only given information on the current tier of upgrades, you won't know what the best build is until it's too late; this renders pursuing under-par times in the Challenges virtually impossible - at least way more difficult than they could've been. Had you known that the upgrade you forsook another, equally better one for was actually included twice in that weapon's upgrade tree, while the one you didn't get was only available while at that tier... you would've been able to have a better weapon(?)
I have to give the game a *Thumbs Down* because if any other game had these listed issues, I would not be able to recommend it; Bastion, however, is a very unique game and I CAN actually recommend it to others, just know that it is not without its faults - don't trust the hype blindly.
The gameplay is repetitive; I personally find the narrator exasperating ("Oh, he personified a ship, how darling... Oh, he's talking about Peckers and Stinkeyes, how innuendo... "Oh, he did a play on words, how good (sincerely though).").
I personally find the gameplay very good except for the listed issues; others adore the game for the narrator.
Split the difference; *Thumb Sideways*

I really enjoyed this game. It's a little on the short side, but the characters were likeable, the world is immersive, and the gameplay and combat were smooth as silk. Special props to the unarmed fight scenes where you could bust out the kung-fu combos, and the gunplay that rings of a cross between John Woo-esque cover vaulting and Max Payne Bullet-time. The vehicles seemed a little tacked on, but there are racing mini-games to satisfy your inner speed freak. Speaking of mini-games, there's also a "karaoke" type game a la Rock Band, which while silly, was still very enjoyable.
I was very much reminded of Mafia II, delving into the gritty criminal underworlds; instead of the Italian Mafia Stateside, you're working your way up the Triads ladder in Hong Kong. The story was engrossing and you're stuck in the middle of being an undercover officer while trying your damnedest to not get attached to these lovable gangsters. If you're looking for an immersive crime drama with lots of action in an open-world that hasn't really been visited, go ahead and pick up this game. It's one of my favourites and I'd have it still installed on my SSD if'n I had the space!

So, I’ve had this game sitting around for awhile, and have been meaning to play it, along with the other hundred games I have collecting dust on my steam account, and shelf. I finally picked it up to play it three days ago, and finished it last night. Took me almost 8 hours to beat. And what a wonderful 8 hours it was. Not even sure where to start. I guess the narrative, which was brilliantly done.
The narrator is an old man who’s known as the Stranger when you first meet him. He narrates your story as you progress through the stages. If you linger in one area, he comments on that as if it was meant to happen in the story, same with if you destroy certain items. It made me think of the Stanley Parable in that sense, except you don’t have as much crazy freedom to break the game. It’s very ‘self aware’ as a friend of mine put it. You learn about the world and its residences through finding items, such as memoirs, and weapons, and from the places you visit. I enjoyed this alternate way of story telling. You could also feel it in the art style. It was a bit unnerving moving around without the ground being there until it rose at the last second. I often found myself just edging forward in certain areas that wouldn’t rise until I was basically on the edge.
I found the music very beautiful. My favourite song was Build that Wall. It always began playing just at the right moments, evoking the right emotions, and setting the tone for what was happening beautifully. The whole score did a great job of adding to the narrative of the game.
By the end of the same I found myself more emotionally invested than I expected. My friends, along with the rest o the internet, warned me it was a fantastic game. It definitely was, and I completely recommend it!!

When this game was released, it had broken combat, repetitive biomes, planets full of nothing and promises of "thick and fast" updates. The music is good but bland and the graphics are really good. It had a solid base but the game felt empty.
Now, over a two and a half years after early access release, it has a combat gameplay that mostly works, more biomes, more structures and more NPCs. The game still feels empty.
There isn't any real variation on combat, neither for the player or the enemies: you have dozens of shooting weapons that feel  the same, and dozens of melee weapons that feel the same. The enemies also have various different attacks that can be summed up as "shoot you" or "charge you", with no real strategy for fighting any of them. Even the unique enemies from some of the structures follow and the same pattern. You have a few special movement options but no reason to ever use them.
For a game centered on discovery, exploring any area feels exactly the same as exploring all the other areas before. Not that you have any reason to explore: you get the same generic itens everywhere and those items usually aren't even as good as the default items you can craft. The only reason to go to new areas is finding more building materials (most decorative blocks can't be crafted) and furniture (the main reason for grinding is getting money for replicating furniture). Many features that would make the game more interesting (like, quests, rare fossils, rare creatures and a crew full of life) are unfinished or bland versions of what they could be.
My final opinion is that it isn't a bad game, it still has a very solid base, but you can do everything that can be done in a few hours without any effort and have nothing else to look forward after that. Give it a try if you like building, but don't expect anything besides that.

Wow! This is a must for anyone who grew up playing the classic Mortal Kombat games.
This is a reboot that wraps up the storylines of Mortal Kombat 1,2 and 3 and retcons everything just enough for it to make sense. They too the broken mess of a story of the original trilogy and fixed it. Not only that, but they very wisely ignored all the MK games from the PS2/Xbox era, expelling them from the canon with the notable exception of some characters who were fit into the story. I won't say that makes the story good; it is still a story about a sorceror trying to take over the "earth realm" through a karate tournament - but it's a much more well put together story about a sorceror trying to take over the earth realm through a karate tournament.
That being said, playing through the story mode is a delight; you get to try a lot of different characters, and the fact that the story mode does not include fatalities does not hurt the experience as much as I thought it might. The original MK titles had very weak gameplay but were held up by their extreme violence and gore. The MK devs have come a long way since then, and they've climbed out of the broken mess that was the Deadly Alliance (and forward) clusterf--k of a control scheme and produced something that is best of both worlds; a 2D fighter that feels a little like Tekken. but faster and less intricate with some familiar MK staples like the super-powered uppercut and the leg sweep. Getting away from the multiple styles where each button has a different function depending on the character, MK2011 gives us a lead hand, rear hand, lead leg, rear leg control scheme with variations utilizing the direction keys or changes when mobes are strung together in combos - a system I have been wanting to see in use since the 1990s.
The game does an excellent job of balancing the fighters; each have tools that, when employed by the proficient player, can be formidable in every situation. Even the AI, later in the story, becomes a force to be reckoned with. Unlike the cheap tactics of the 16-bit AI from MK's golden days, the artificial opponents attempt to punish you for making mistakes and catch you with devastating combos but do not defeat you simply be making the combat imbalanced. Each time I lose I feel I am learning, and each time I win I feel it is because I have learned how to better use the character I am playing and better predict or respond to the tactics of my opponent.
There are multiple designs for each character, and while some of the models miss the mark - (Liu Kang is bizarre looking and every scantily clad female character is direct from a 12 year old boy's wet dream) - most of them are pretty awesome. Scorpion's attire looks more, well... scorpion related while the character we remember as little more than pallette swaps now have details that make each one's design unique and previously lame character designs like Stryker have been completely reworked. New characters are added to the roster in the form of more variations - a human sektor and cyrax, for example - are a lot of fun to play. The reworked backgrounds are  blast from the past brought gloriously into today's gaming world and are a perfect blend of nostalgia and awe at what they've accomplished. And don't worry - gone are the days of hokey uppercuts through the ceiling. While there are still some corny elements from the more embarrassing days of MK's past... well, there is no one forcing you to use a babality. It's weird that it's there, but I'm going to just go ahead and look the other way.
I highly recommend this game to any fans of the classic series. It hits all the right notes; it's nostalgic but with plenty of new stuff to keep you interested. If you loved the idea of a 2D fighter with ninjas and kung fu guys ripping each other's heads off but weren't so keen on ridiculous attempts to shoehorn rumours and myths into a storyline or repeatedly pressing high punch in the corner... and if you were not so keen on trying to learn 26 unique combos that had no logic to them per charcter... this is the MK you've been waiting for.

Only played as the MArine so far so here is my take....
Scarier than Alien Isolation.  However as I've not played Isolation this is nothing more than a theory so here is why I think its scarier.
In Alien Isolation as soon as you are spotted you are dead.  THis make the game scary to a point then it becomes frustration.
As a Marine in AvsP the ALiens feel like they are stalking you which builds tension ala ALien Isolation, they don't rush at you immediately, they slowly surround you before attacking. They are hard to spot in dark areas which cause quite a few unscripted jump scares but when you are spotted you have a good chance of survival... assuming you don't run out of ammo.
They also avoid attacks which took me by supprise and their speed is incredible. You can't really hide, you have to fight but you can run away and if you do they seem to go back into stalking mode, slowly homing in on your position.

At first sight, there's nothing really wrong with this game. The problem lies in the system. It relies upon archaic music gameplay style- it's basicly DDR with punching instead of arrows. While this isn't a bad game, the custom music mechanic frequently falls short, and is underwhelming. You have to play through a first few levels, which is rather annoying if you're not interested in the music that comes with the game. Once you do unlock music customization, the navigation to select songs is clumsy and poorly responsive to mouse input, making scrolling through large libraries or browsing a full drive difficult. The mapping system is limited by player attentiveness; you are expected to either know the BPM of the track, or be capable of timing your own inputs to the beats of the music. It's simply an underwhelming mechanic that is not atoned for by the rest of the game. There are solid principles underlying the game, but questionable stylistic and gameplay decisions limit the effectiveness of the game. It clings to console mechanics, even on a PC version, and is uncomfortable and awkward. The camera also skews slightly, making it at times difficult to follow where enemies are coming from.
All in all, it's not a bad game, but if you expect anything unique or interesting, you might want to look somewhere else. As for enjoying your own music, or a specific genre of music, you'll have to tolerate the ecclectic music selection of the campaign for a bit first. It's alright, but so much potential was wasted here.

Having no idea of what the game was "supposed" to be, I simply bought the game expecting a fancier "MOO2" so to speak.    And given the negative reviews I kept reading about it, I lowered my expectations greatly and bought the game on massive sale.
Once I actually played the game, I actually wound up enjoying it quite a bit.   I can't recall how many hours I've spent and how many "races" I've created in trying the game.  I'll try to rate the game on a 5-star system on each of the areas that I can think of:
1.) Graphics - 4/5
- I truly enjoyed the graphics.  I really did.  Being able to zoom in to my ships, the combat animations, the effects of each weapon being unique in their own right.  I especially like the unique ship designs for each race which attempted to match their species.  A little cliched, but then again, what game isn't nowadays?
2.) UI - 3/5
- Simple enough and inuitive.  A few grips would be on some screens where it seems like the UI was designed with a different resolution in mind.  I have an old monitor only capable of 1280 x 1024 and it stuggles on the setup screen due to odd text wrapping.  Other than that however, I felt the UI easy enough to navigate.
3.) Gameplay - 3.5/5
- I found myself in several sleepless nights playing that "one more turn" (or in this case, one more minute given it's real time).  The racial creation allows for varied types of empires to play around with and with each game randomizing the different empires behavior, it's always been a treat for me.  However, there is one glaring bug around the "plot" where if the AI winds up wiping out the triggers, you're SoL if that was your main goal for that particular round of gameplay.  I've actually had to go in to the XML save files to try to re-trigger the events which is never a good sign.  Still, that plot isn't the end-all-be-all of the game and isn't a deal-breaker for me.
- Another nice twist is the actual race creator.  Unlike a true "creator", you simply overwrite a species for the current game.  However, any designs you create while playing that "race" become available to the AI in succeeding games so you eventually wind up fighting your own designs which was a real treat when I saw it happen.
- Related to gamelay, there are a few things which could have been improved on in my opinion.   Tech Tree, for one, is smaller compared to other 4X games.  It only feels large due to the amount of research points needed to unlock higher tiers.  The AI also sometimes behaves oddly despite their racial setting at game time (i.e. an Honorable AI will sometimes keep stealing from you despite being in an non-agression pact).
4.)  Replayability - 3/5
- I admit I keep replaying the game.  For me, it's been enjoyable.  However, I do see 2 problems which can hinder it in other cases:
a) Memory optimization: unlike other RTS games (which this game has flavors of), there is no unit cap other than your bank account (i.e. turn-by-turn income).  This is both a blessing and curse.  This means that you can build up quite the fleet and swarm your way through the galaxy.  Unfortunately this also means unless you've got godly amounts of RAM (and I'm talking 16+ GB of RAM), your game can quickly grind to a halt and crash as the AI will spam ships like no tomorrow.   Even the "final plot story" can break your game should you unlock it given that it also spams ships like no tomorrow (without the limitation of a factory's output to slow it down).  Related to this, beware of designing "cheap" gunboats.  As the race creator "overwrites" a species, any design you create becomes available to that AI race and it tends to favor spamming those cheap gunboats.
b) No multiplayer.  I never expected this feature as I never was an early backer.  I can see how this would put off others as the challenge of beating down your frenemies always extends the life of a game.  The lack of this feature can put off many people from getting the game.
c) Lack of a real "custom" race.  MOO2 had the same issues but it would have been nice to have a custom race that didn't overwrite existing ones.
5.) Overall - 3/5
- I liked MOO3.  Yes, I said it.  I actually came to like game.  StarDrive feels like what MOO3 tried to be.  4X strategy with RTS gameplay.  StarDrive for me is an enjoyable single-player 4X game which allows for some small to medium scale games.  Large games are completely out of the question due to the memory problem which would have raised the game to 4/5 or me.  If you ignore what was originally promised and take the game for what it is now, it's actually worth a try.
I would purchase it when it's at least 50% off given the isssues and replayability challenges it may give others.
For the current price of $32.99 CDN, I would instead spend it on Space Empires V or Pandora as they have a bit more replayability for most in my opinion.

So, I’ve had this game sitting around for awhile, and have been meaning to play it, along with the other hundred games I have collecting dust on my steam account, and shelf. I finally picked it up to play it three days ago, and finished it last night. Took me almost 8 hours to beat. And what a wonderful 8 hours it was. Not even sure where to start. I guess the narrative, which was brilliantly done.
The narrator is an old man who’s known as the Stranger when you first meet him. He narrates your story as you progress through the stages. If you linger in one area, he comments on that as if it was meant to happen in the story, same with if you destroy certain items. It made me think of the Stanley Parable in that sense, except you don’t have as much crazy freedom to break the game. It’s very ‘self aware’ as a friend of mine put it. You learn about the world and its residences through finding items, such as memoirs, and weapons, and from the places you visit. I enjoyed this alternate way of story telling. You could also feel it in the art style. It was a bit unnerving moving around without the ground being there until it rose at the last second. I often found myself just edging forward in certain areas that wouldn’t rise until I was basically on the edge.
I found the music very beautiful. My favourite song was Build that Wall. It always began playing just at the right moments, evoking the right emotions, and setting the tone for what was happening beautifully. The whole score did a great job of adding to the narrative of the game.
By the end of the same I found myself more emotionally invested than I expected. My friends, along with the rest o the internet, warned me it was a fantastic game. It definitely was, and I completely recommend it!!

Now the game isn't perfect it could improve on some aspects such as handling of vehicles and the fact that most building shop fronts look like a print out of the interior instead of them actually being filled out, but this cannot be avoided due to consoles having limited resources since the game is not only on the PC platform. In the mean time I shall be completing this to 100% since the game itself has quite a bit to do on the side of the main story and unlike most games these days it isnt just the same mission repeated 100 times with a different background and that is something a lot of new games could learn from the older titles.

Now i'll just get the formalities out of the way. No, this game is not perfect. I had to do quite a bit to get basic things working - of which i'd be happy to help you sort out given the time. maybe.
As much as some of the glaring issues are, I still find the game fun. The core gameplay is very solid and it feels great to play. Online it feels great, when the other player isn't teleporting all over the place lol (and hoping you're not teleporting to them. whoo~)
--Pros: 1.Rollback netcode.
2. Local like online.
3. Feels very tight and easy to pick up.
4. Everything can be earned in game (besides DLC cosmetics).
5. PS4/PC crossplay - don't feel discouraged to get the PC version. Theres a strong playerbase. Do not take steam count as its player count.
--Cons: 1.Rollback netcode. Many people turned into dhalsim and maybe you too.
2. Multiple places (easy to do) to edit config files. Google is your friend (or friends that already did it.)
3. Fight money is a bit slow to earn if you don't know how to do it. (yay google)
--somewhere in between: 1. iffy matchmaking. Not saying its perfect but this one tends to throw a bone more often than not against you. The fact the matchmaking uses a Relay server matching or P2P depending on the connection quality is also iffy. If you see two points connected to a square on loading, thats relay. Prepare for the apocalypse!
2. Content pricing: everything revolves around fight money unfortunately. even tags. its all pretty pricey for what it is, most expensive being the characters followed by stages (characters have strong single player content returns on fight money.)
Depsite all that bad its still very much a good game in its own right. I recommend it BUT WITH A WORD OF WARNING. Do not go in expecting it to be perfect, expect to toy with settings.

Bastion is a rpg game with fun and storyteller, who makes this game funny and rich story makes you thinking and desiring to know more. It is hard to characterize it in few words, but I will try to sum up my words.
VISUALS
Game is designed in 3D combined with painting style of arts. Perfect details, no bugs so far. Weapons have adequate sounds and effects.
GAMEPLAY
Smooth and attractive. Story is designed into chapters, there are also proving grounds for enhancing your equipment. There is also "Score Attack Mode" here, both with New Game+ are providing ability to replay each chapter.
Negative here for me are the controls. Seriously I have to hold two keys to go "straight"?
SOUNDTRACK
Masterpiece. I am glad to buy this game, each song is composed to exactly set the atmosphere of concrete place. Nothing to complain here.
CHARACTERS
Though less is better, four - Rucks, Zulf, Zia and of course, Kid - are depicting a variety of emotions and character traits. Also they are changing through the game, with their backstories to reveal (Who Knows Where). Rucks also serves as a storyteller, with funny akcent, but it can also go very deep.
SUMMARY
This game is more than just a simple rpg. It is a story, which desires to be revealed. And there just two keys to do so. The Kid and you.

ICEY is an excellent action game.  I highly recommend purchasing this game.
The game is linear in that you progress from one stage to the next until you reach the boss.  There are optional paths that you can take and secret areas that you can search for along the way.  You have a narrator that talks to you occasionally as you play, guiding you basically, and you can choose whether to listen to him or not.
The combat mechanics are good and very satisfying to execute combos.  Not much else to say here the combat is just really well done.
My gripe with the game is the lack of other game modes.  The story mode is very short, It can be beaten in like 2-5 hours depending on skill and difficulty level.  But that's it, there is nothing else to do except going through the game again and finding secret areas.  This game sorely needs a game mode where all you do is fight enemies since combat is one of the defining features of the game.
Overall it was a great experience and was worth the money despite the length of the game.

Okay, so looking at my review, you can see I haven't clocked in 100+ hours on this game, but I've unlocked everything and poured in a good few dozen extra hours on the plane and other places where I can't connect to log said extra hours. I think I've experience most of what this game has to offer and let me just say, that this is a super solid, bang for your buck kind of game. Allow me to put forward some more evidence:
For those of you that don't know, The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth is a randomly generated, roguelike dungeon crawler, with minimal story but effectively unlimited replay value. The gist is this: you fight your way through rooms of randomly generated enemies, picking up randomly generated items along the way. Okay, so RNG is super heavy in a successful run, but the game does have a fairly high skill ceiling due to in part being a twin-stick/bullet hell game, and the player is given some control over his "build" with items that allow you reroll your given items and an in game store with a "donation machine" to store currency that persists throughout the various runs and replays.
This game is pretty difficult to get into, and if my experience at the start of the game is anything to go by (I'm not great, all things considered) but, you'll probably die quite a lot before you can beat any of the final bosses. Oh right, almost forgot. There are branching levels that are unlocked through every playthrough, each level with their own unique enemy and boss design. These things range from small flies to giant fleshy heads and sentient fecal matter. This is a game that doesn't take itself too seriously with it's design, but is more of a morbid, arcadey comedy feel to it, if you couldn't already tell. The difficulty increases somewhat with these more levels added the more times you complete it, but with more items added as you progress, your character does get some more firepower with which to fight back. Though a minor gripe of mine is that not all items are available at the beginning for stronger starts, it's that sort of "power creep" that is the main progression system that incentivises the player to keep playing. That, and the fact that pretty much the only thing standing between you and a successful run is one specific item in a HUGE item pool is a rush of adrenaline I've never quite experienced the same way in any other game, and though it is frustrating when a strong start fizzles away because you didn't get that item you really needed, the same can be said for the burst of exhiliration when you find a gamesaving item in the middle of a doomed start. What can I say, I'm a sucker for RNG!
Featuring a completely different art style from the original Binding Of Isaac, Rebirth has a very nice, retro-but-not-quite art style that runs well on pretty much any system - and believe me, I know, I use a toaster! The art direction is clear, simple and dedicated to the themes that the previous had laid down and clarity of gameplay is the priority over snazzy graphics. The soundtrack is, well, pretty stellar and to be expected from the Indie masterminds behind other great OSTs in Super Meat Boy.
Well, I've pretty much run out of time (and patience) to be sitting here fawning over how solid of a package this is, and am probably gonna jump back into it again. For those of you that literally cannot be bothered to read this wall of white pixels, I'll add in a little TL;DR
Pros:
+Great Replay Value, daily runs, every run is unique
+Great art direction, soundtrack, atmosphere
+Unique, varied bosses and enemies, not simple reskins
+SO. MANY. ITEMS.
Cons:
-Progression may take too long, or may be too difficult
-Some items objectively better than others- leads to outstandingly poor runs
Mixed
±High skill ceiling & RNG - good gets better, bad gets worse

The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth is a randomly generated dungeon crawler, it looks a bit like the SNES Zelda games.
Pros-
There are a lot of items and having two times the same run is impossible.
The graphics are pretty and they are detalied despite being 16-Bit styled.
The gameplay feels so great, with both a keyboard or a controller.

The game runs well on my tablet, that make me think it could run basically on everything.
Cons-
The graphics are good, but definetly not for everyone.
I don't like the music, to me it doesn't have personality at all, i could play the game with the music on for hours and still not recognising the music if i hear it out of the game.
As i said before the game CAN be hard, but there's not a real skill cap or skill escalation, you can start with the most difficult run ever and having the easiest after XXXX hours.
The game can sometimes feel only luck based.
The local multiplayer is fun, i don't really get why didn't they make a online multiplayer.
Extras:
The game can look a bit too expensive considering what it offers, but believe me, this game is going to give you a lot of fun (and anger)(i almost forget physical and psycological pain) and it is absolutely worth the price, to be honest i feel like the DLC (Afterbirth) is really well priced.

I'm going to be a little brutal here. Yes, I know the game is EA. That does not mean I need to agree with EA in general or the fact that games can come out unfinished just because they are EA. They cost people money (I got this in a bundle not the free giveaway), therefore the product needs to offer an acceptable value for what we pay.
The game tries to be similar to others on steam such as Spelunky. And that's great; if you're going to make a game, take inspirationg from the best in the genre. Aiming high is very commendable and totally fine.
But the game missed the mark with so many things. First of all, you have everything you will ever need right from the start like many varied weapons and infinite arrow. Secondly, non of the challenge you get from a game like Spelunky. you can easily take a number of hits and still be ok in Endorlight. And finally, non of the charm or character of a game that someone's worked on. There is simply nothing compelling about this product.
Before anyone plays the game, I highly recommend they remap their keyboard controls to something more practical, the default controls are very impractical. But default controls aside, the wall jumping mechanic in this game is somewhat halfassed, and gives you the impression that the only reason it exists is because the randomly generated levels can occasionally be impractical.
When you have wall jumps and no proper wall slides, or game mechanics that prop up and benefit from it, that's what I'm going to think.
Now people may get the impression I hate everything about this game, I do not, the look of the game is fine, some of the sprites are actually really nice. The attempt at making a Spelunky like game is something I find very welcome, I love Spelunky. But when the attempt is so bad, it's an insult to real games. So forgive me Spelunky, for mentioning you here. It's like saying my rusty trashbin looks exactly like the satelite NASA launched in June - the difference is that big. This game is broken in a lot of ways. It does not draw me in and make me feel like "I'm going to do this level this time". The controls are clunky and the jumping is iffy. I already have an axe, a whip and infinite arrows the moment I spawn, there's nothing I want to collect or find. And of course, because the game is EA, we have a lot of missing content, like the gems and gold we collect for no reason at all, we simply do not need them.
- An interesting game on paper, as an idea - not so much in practice
- looks ok, some sprites are nice though there's a lot of repetition in the level
- Controls aren't great
- Responsiveness not great
- The wall jumps suck
- Not as challenging as it could be
- Missing content

If you've got a love of rhythm games, i'd definately recommend this title. The mechanics are simple but the presentation manages to really carry the game into something really fun and addictive. There's not a whole lot of actual music to play, but what is available is all really high quality and fun to play.
The campaign will take roughly 6 hours if you just breeze through it, but that's really missing the point of a rhythm game. The content here is more than worth the $10 price tag if you're really willing to master the mechanics up to the most difficult setting.
There is a feature to import your own music, but it's not very good. It essentially just generates a track based solely on the BPM of the song which results in every custom track being really boring and samey. It's really the one letdown of the whole game.
If you've played the original 1999 AvP, be ready for a big let down. If you didn't, you may actually enjoy the game.

So... Uhhh... where do I start...
If you buy the game and then decide to moan about how unfun and boring and repetetive it is, it's your fault. What you see in the description and screenshots/clips is all true. No lies.
The thing is, what you see there is also everything the game has to offer.
First off, I'd like to mention the plot of the game. Lack of it, anyway. You're that little purple-haired guy (who's really fast btw. Like, too fast IMO) with an axe, a whip and a bow. And you're looking for an adventure. Or treasure. Or a sandwich. Or actually I've no idea, there's no story at all - not in description, not in menu, not in the game itself. You're just dropped in some underground-dungeon-thingy, now go and get those sweet hi-scores. Not every game needs an engaging story, that's true, but at least
background on what's going on would be nice. Though if developer decides to not care about it all, that's fine - it's the gameplay that matters most here.
Well, that's pretty simple. You spawn at the top of the level, you're supposed to get to the bottom, get through the door to the next level, rinse, repeat. In meantime there's gold to pick up, monsters to slay (or avoid, since they give no gold) and spikes to fall on. The player has three weapons at his disposal - axe with a miserable melee range, whip with a mediocre range (though you can't hit anything in melee) and a bow with a range that probably covers the whole screen. Someone in reviews said that all weapons deal the same damage, but I don't think it's true - a crate needs two bow hits to be destroyed, but axe needs just two.
There are no ways to spend gold, no achievements, no upgrades, nothing. Once you die, you don't even get to see your score - you're just booted back to the main menu. This combined with the boring and repetetive gameplay (if you passed to the level 3, you pretty much saw everything the game has to offer, except for the bosses, which I'll go over soon) makes this game not really worth the 3 euros dev is charging for it.
There are 3 "biomes" as the dev calls them. I'll simply call them "plain" (1st level), "green" (2nd) and "red" (3rd). Plain and green don't really differ that much aside from looks and music, but red is just pure hell (we'll speak about that later, honey). I didn't really count, but there are ~10, maybe more enemies. Also clay pots, crates, small chests and huge, red chests. And spikes. And bosses on every 5th floor, which are a joke - they are simply big enemies who have lots of HP. Spam the bow, if he gets too close, walljump high, run to the other side of the room, spam bow. Bosses are a joke.
And that's it, everything in the game. Well...
.
Okay, so terrain is destructible. That's cool, though player doesn't have much control over it, he has no pickaxes or bombs. So, how do we destroy terrain?
WITH EXPLOSIVE CRATES AND ENEMIES OF COURSE.
If you ever get to play the game, here's a protip : never, EVER destroy crates with an axe. Not even with a whip, still too close. Destroy them with bow. Really, half of the crates are filled with explosives, they explode (actually, sometimes they drop a bomb which explodes a while later, but it never happened to me when destroying a crate, while being in range of explosions. I'm either uber-unlucky or it's a bow-exclusive thing). And explosions take off half of player's HP. So, watch out for crates.
And on 3rd level, there's that red biome, for which "Hell" would be a fitting name. Because there are not only crates, but also those insanely quick monsters, that explode. On contact. Touch them, just graze them, they go boom. And 50% HP less. And with other enemies in red biome taking lots of HP (at least compared to previous enemies), this makes
red biome a real pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ And after level 3, 90% of levels are probably the red biome (best try : level 7 reached, I'm not masochistic enough to play this more). That makes this game a really frustrating expierence.
Half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ The second player is identical to the 1st one, no split-screen or anything, camera is centered on P1 like in single-player.
And that's all. No way you're going to be sober AND spend 3 euros on the game. It's not worth it AT ALL right now. I mean, it is kinda fun for a while, but gets boring and frustrating quickly, and there's not enough content to warrant an attention span longer than ~15 minutes. And after those 15 minutes, you're going to say out loud "wow, this game sucks."
That said, this game is an alpha, dev seems like a nice guy who's just starting out with game-making (though if I was the one who's starting out, I'd rather making something completely free instead of charging
) and things that are supposed to be included in future updates (shops! new biomes! BOMBS FOR THE PLAYER!) sound promising, and the game has some potential. We'll see how it turns out. If you're simply looking for a good game that's in a playable/enjoyable state right now and don't care about helping the dev catch bugs, shape the game etc., spend your 3 euros on something else.

I will not lie to you, Rhythm Games pretty much died with Rock Band. At the time, Rock Band and Guitar Hero were dominating the music game market with the clever creation of game controllers turned musical instruments. However, just because the two powerhouses died a few years ago, this does not mean people try to keep the genre alive. Zen Studios has created a new take on the rhythm game genre with Kickbeat Steam Edition. The game was previously released on consoles but the release on Steam has additional content compared to the previous release. Having never played the console version I did play this game with a controller to see what it was like.
All of the world’s music is contained in a sphere. The one who controls the sphere, controls all the music that has been made, and will be made throughout all eternity. There are people in the world who wish to gain control of the sphere, that is why there is an ancient order of kung-fu masters protecting the orb from anyone who wishes to gain its power. Times are changing, and technology is growing, the temple where the Music Sphere is located is invaded by the most powerful man in all of media entertainment. Now his radio is the only one with music, it is up to a young man and woman to stop this greedy business man.
While the story is not great, it is not bad either. It reminds me of a Netflix movie, relatively charming, but not winning any awards. Besides, this is a kung-fu driven music game, the story is going to reflect that novelty, and that is possibly the best part about it. The game has two story modes, one with Lee and one with Mei. Mei is the romance character in the story and the game plays similar, just has different character models and some different songs etc.

I have been playing this game since its beta release and i think its fair to say this game could have been so much more
“Some omissions and flaws, but balanced by excellent alien races and ship design. A welcome addition to the crew.”
this says it all nicely but is largely understated. As a whole the management and construction of an empire works quite well but in combination with wonky AI; a civ 5-esque diplomacy screen with reduced options and strange reactions (allies will quickly turn hostile if the wrong trade is proposed); no counterspying option leaves you to get ravaged by enemy spies; many incomplete or just missing features; no multiplayer; and late-game performance issues (I play it on a laptop so it may just be that) the fun factor quickly turns to frustration late in the game.
A lot of features were also just left out, despite being advertised as either implemented or coming soon on the steam store, and will most likely never be implemented as Zero Sum basically dropped everything in development for the game and focused on the production of a sequel, leaving the first game feeling very incomplete
BUT there are many aspects that work quite well:
The shipyard feature, for example, is amazing. it allows you to arrange unlocked systems on a ship frame so you can create specialized designs (ie resupply, strike, scout, coloyization etc) and allows you to control thier performance levels.
too many systems bogs down the power supply, shields over armor can be a vulnurability and more massive means slower travel. to name a few things.
the game is visually stunning. you are able to scale the map from a galactic map down to a single star with orbiting planets. the alien races are all fantastically concieved and there are 8 playable races which can be customized to have a number of positive and negative traits upon starting a new game. each race has its own ship designs, and most of them have unique ground units
I really liked that this game was 4x so that The game flows continuously and allows space battles to occur in real time while the construction and research aspects are turn based progressions. i thought this system worked really well, especially since you can increase the time scaling up to 4x (or more, but not on my laptop) and speed up the slow early stages of the game.
Unfortunately the features that i liked did not make up for its short comings, for me at least, and it looks like they will be carried through to the sequel along with countless improvements/features that should have been in this game.
VERDICT: this game is not worth $33CAD
If this game appeals to you, then I would wait for the sequel
If you've read a fair number of reviews and still want to try it, then wait for a sale to drop the price to $5-10 as there are some mods out there that really add a lot to the game and the game is still enjoyable

I bought VHII for 10 dollars with an online coupon.  Even though I'm sure I didn't get the BEST deal out there I'd say it's money well spent.
I never played the first game.  So, I started on this one with a new toon and leveled him up to 30 by the time I beat the game on Hard Mode.  Then,  went to veteran mode afterwards on fearless and had a blast. The loot was much better on the higher settings and for those who like crafting -- you can spend a good amount of time sifting through loot to enchant and enhance your gear to get the most defense/offense out of them.  If you don't like crafting then I'd stay away from that part.
Replay value is fairly good.  The story itself isn't spectacular, but if you're going for achievements it's always nice to get a few new options when you do the second run through.  If you don't want replay value.  It took me roughly 28 hours to beat it first time through on hard mode.  So, again worth the ten bucks I spent.  Voice acting for main toons is good, and side characters is a bit shady from time to time, but overall good with music that is also good.  Nothing was annoying to my ears.
Tower defense is tricky.  Harder the mode you put it on the less likely you are to succeed.  Or, maybe I just suck at tower defense, but on fearless mode it was crazy as the joker with 300 minions willing to do his bidding.

If you like diablo style games, think of this one as the best diversion you can get. What i mean by that is that it's not quite a game you can play for 700 hours and still feel like you need to get that "one last item to round out your build" it's more of a game where you play through it's 2 or 3 times, 30-40 hours later you are done with it. Loot is solid, however the quantity of loot also means that you rarely find the thing you know was an "awesome drop" it's more a case of constantly equipping and enchanting the latest and greatest. Although there are some pretty cool items every now and then that break that rule.
The world and graphics are purposely desaturated and have a steampunk kind of vibe to them. The game can crash quite easily, and there are things that prevent it from running if you don't have a certain runtime or soundcard driver or (insert reason). And that's a shame, one day you may wonder what everyone is talking about when they say it crashes a lot, the next you find out what they are talking about and get just as frustrated as them at the game simply not running.
The game uses a 32bit and 64bit runtime, and the 64bit in van helsing 2 is not quite the big difference in performance than it was in the original game. Both run fine, perhaps the subsequent patches have helped that respect. The games import option was originally not working, and you had to start a high level build, that has since been fixed so i won't hold it against the game. The sequel is a better all around game, bigger, with more to do. The original has been patched to be in line with VH2, whereas it originally was a "one playthrough game ends" game. Which severely limited the games lasting power to about 6 hours. Now that those issues are addresses and you can play again, with new characters and item drop chances - and also you can play through the first game and then import into the second. My score of both games (since they are connected now) has improved.
The first game get's a 7/10 the second game get's a 8/10, if they manage to make the lasting power and game size of the third game as big as the first two combined. That'll likely get a 9.

Here is my review of Bastion:
First waking up in Bastion you have no idea what is going on. What starts your adventure is that you do not remember anything about what happened to the world after the calamity hit.  Bastion follows the story of "The Kid" , who happens to survive all the events prior to the game. You first start of with just a trusty weapon and begin to slowly build your arsenal.
Gameplay / Sound- it almost works as a action RPG. The action includes shooting guns with cooldowns, dodging to avoid enemy attacks and special attacks. The RPG element works with upgrading guns and deciding what weapons to bring into combat during a certain mission. Some of the weapons become ridiculously strong, but with the increase in difficulty it shouldnt be too much of a problem. Unlocking the shrines and using them makes the game more fun and it also creates a bigger challenege in the game. Outside of those the game plays pretty much like an action game more than a RPG one. Playing on different level makes the game feel as though the worlds are all different yet are a part of a bigger story. Sadly you do not get to see even part of the world. The soundtrack to this game is one of the best I have heard in any video game. Once you hear it, you'll want to download it and keep on listening to it.
Story- The story revolves around "The Kid" and his quest to collect shards to save the world after the Calamity. While the story is fleshed out over the course of the game, i cant help but feel that the world isnt as interesting as I thought it would be. What i mean by this is that there is a clear beginning, middle and end, yet not any more to it. I expected to find notes or more journal types of items to help flesh out the world. It exists already to some degree in the game, but i would have liked to know more. Other than that little nit pick, I found the story to be good, but not great.
Replayability - While there is a proving grounds and some wave enemy combat, I see Bastion on Campagin as a one and done type of deal. There is content to keep you interested for the better part of about 15-20 hours though. If you getting everything and doing the extra missions you should finish within that timetable. The campaign for me took between 6-8 hours. Once you get the hang of the combat it runs though pretty quickly. As a game to pick up in the future again, I say it has limited replayability.
Controls - Controls are pretty straight forward and really easy to learn. I would recommend using a controller though because keybindings are on the backburner for this game.
Conclusion: If you are looking to buy Bastion, do it. It is a fantastic game and well worth purchase. The only negative takeaway is that the story background  isnt fully fleshed out and the replayability factor is pretty low.
Final Score: 9 out of 10

OK, so ICEY is probably the best action platformer (think Strider, or 2D Devil May Cry) I've played in a long, long time. It's also the best meta-game experience I've ever had. The fourth wall is broken so many times it barely exists, and I have honestly never grinned so much while playing a game.
ICEY is clearly a labour of love, and the time and effort spent in its development shines through. I managed to find a hidden area that triggers a scene where the narrator describes (and shows you!) previous iterations of ICEY, and he states that it has been a ten year effort - I don't know if that's true or not, but it sure feels like a project with a whole lot of time and effort invested in it.
ICEY is very clever, supremely entertaining, and surprisingly immersive. The artwork is simply gorgeous, the game mechanics are well thought-out and balanced, and the sheer number of easter eggs makes it almost as much fun to just dash around and explore as it is to slice and dice your way to 97 hit combos.
I picked it up on sale for about ten bucks, but it's a steal at three times that price; ICEY is one of the nicest surprises (and one of my favoruite games) of this year.
