Gods give you a little girl and you can do whatever you want with her for like 8 years. That's pretty much Princess Maker 2 in a single sentence.
Every month, you have to choose 3 things that your daughter will spend her time on. You can make your daughter work at a job, which will boost her stats and make her stressful in exchange for money. Each job boosts different stats and requires different stats to do well in. With your child labour-earned money, you can send your daughter to school, where she can learn to fight, to not be an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, to cook or that the Earth isn't flat. The lessons cost money and if you run out, you just wasted day(s) of time doing nothing. Some paths of education will earn you a rival or result in being challenged while you're out shopping for a winter coat. You can also go adventure in 4 different locations. Adventuring is like your typical old-school RPG: You walk around, randomly encounter people or monsters and you get to choose if you want to talk/fight/ignore/hide. You'll also find chests with items, and there are various NPCs and hidden events in the wild. You can get perved on by an old dragon if you're old enough. You can challenge the War God to a fight. You can find and arrest a wanted criminal. Or you can just run into angry mermaids that have boobs and nipples and will always fight you.  Lastly, you can reduce your stress levels by giving your daughter free time or going on a vacation. Going on a vacation will cost more money, be more effective, show you a nice vacation photo and sometimes change a stat like weight.
Yes, the game has SO FREAKING MANY STATS. There's your physical stats like height, weight, bust/waist/hips, but also things like 3 different reputations (Housework, Fighting, Magic), various combat-related stats and things like Sin. The stats (and some in-game events) are what determines the ending that you get, and there's a whole spectrum of them. You can end up as a regular housewife. Or maybe you kill the Demon King and take over Hell. The "best" ending for the game is, BIG SURPRISE TO LIKE 3 PEOPLE, is becoming the Ruling Queen. The stats can also trigger certain events or prevent certain events from happening, such as a high stress level leading to sickness, truancy or running away from home for a month.
Princess Maker 2 doesn't have much in the way of "gameplay" outside of the adventuring part. Studying and working are done with a montague-like video that shows how your stats change, with a window describing whether you did well or just sat on your♥♥♥♥♥all day. And while it is possible to play the game without looking at the stats, it's going to be very difficult if you don't understand why your daughter keeps running away or why the butler insists she eats a lot every month. So if that's not the kind of game you fancy, Princess Maker 2 is♥♥♥♥♥♥ But if you're willing to experience it, Princess Maker 2 has a lot of funny, awkward, cute, happy and cool moments.

There's a reason why a game from 1994 recieved updated graphics and a full voice over. Can you think of any other games from the 90s or early 2000s that do that? If you can, it's because they were insanely good games, well-loved and of high quality. That's what this game is, high quality --- it's visual novel-esque with heavy simulation aspects. This game has so much replayability that you can enjoy it over and over again, playing it through again right after you finish the first time.
You manage your child's life from around age 10 until adulthood, and shape the adult she becomes. I highly recommend this if you like sims of any kind, and you enjoy management style games. Even if you don't like visual novels, this is old school and a bit how original Japanese style VNs used to be back on the SNES, more like a game and less like a book. So give it a try!

Awesome game! No seriously!
By far the best strategy I have played in the past few years. Combines a lot of different features from various strategies such as Stronghold and Warhammer, which I have dreamed to be put into one single game. Its finally here!
Overall, its a beatiful survival/tactical strategy with an interesting features that I have never seen before.
However! There are few points I would like developers to work on:
1)  The army size is a bit of a joke, as getting 10 troops is the hardest thing you can imagine of doing. I understand that troops require food and shelter, but the battles seem to be just too small to be any epic.
2) Variety of maps is a bit upsetting, as I have tried a numer, and they do not differ from each other, in fact each map is similar by nearly 80%, with just a couple of things relocated.
3) An introduction of a broader range of a natural disasters is just crucial. There is just two. Come on.
4) More ways to protect your village will help in making the gameplay more fun, as building the defences is proved to be one of the best things that strategies can offer.
5) Aggressive creatures include only three types of enemies, I would like to see at least 10, varying on the maps, from the smallest, to something extremely large and strong.
6)It is really annoyin when you have to return to the town hall to grab an available villager and then scroll back to another side of the map to assign him to build something, and then cathing someone again to actually build it, and then cathing a few more to assing to work in the building, meaning every time you need to scroll back and forth to the town hall. the feature to pin the worker to hold the grounds may be a useful addition.

After adding the first Van Helsing to one of the most favorite games I've ever played, VH2 only polished and added to the enjoyment where the first one left off.  I was still playing the first one up to the release of this game and continued playing it during this one.  But VH2 not only left off where the last story ended, but improved on tons of things to make this game even more enjoyable than the first.  So with this in mind, I wrote a review for people new to the series as well as one for people who have played the first game and are considering getting this one.
Newcomers to the Van Helsing trilogy-
Even if you haven't played the first one, it would still be enjoyable to start with VH2.  The reason for this is much like any other game, such as Borderlands 2.  Playing the first one AFTER the second one will give you more depth in the story as well as make you appreciate all the changes that were done in the second game.  Even though I would recommend playing the first one first, I don't see any spoilers at all in VH2 to the storyline of VH1.  There are even items/gear that is reverse compatible ;) which you will probably think is pretty keen of the developers.  Yes, it plays like Diablo 3, but that is by all means not a bad thing.  But that comparison is very similar to saying Battlefield plays like CoD or MoH.  And what about the "Gears of War" and "God of War" comparisons in other games.  Yah, it's kinda like that :/  All in all, if you get VH2, you will be getting a great funny and very enjoyable RPG which you can co op up to 4 players as well as PvP.  When you play it, you'll know it's going to be a great game from
hahaha.
Ones who've played the first Van Helsing-
It may look like the same game but many things have been polished to fit customer satisfaction.  For instance there are still 6 pages of storage, but now most of the gear takes 2 blocks instead of 3, and the storage space has been significantly expanded.  So now there is over double the storage space of the first game.  Along with the max level reaching 60 instead of 30, there are doubled the skills to mess around with!  So you have the option of lvl10ing the skills and tricks you have ported over OR taking them off and starting a whole new tree of new abilities.  Or you can even mix it.  Oh yeah, as I stated, you can export over your powered up character from the first game :)  The Chimera is not as powerful as it looks but is still a great addition as well as a little storyline within the sp story.  Also the 'sets' and 'epics' have 'ink infested' versions which are level 60s.  So even though you may have a complete set with the level ranges at 33 38 and 45, you can still farm for the all level 60 versions of that same set :))))  OMG, and wait until you get your first 'godlike' item!!!  Besides that they just expanded on everything that made the first game so fun to play like: glory, perks, weapons & gear, laughs, easter eggs, tower defense, etc.  The story, I would like to compare to The Matrix Reloaded.  Not the best story, but essential in the trilogy and to any fan of the first game.  It was also fun to play through with more boss fights and loot drops.  So basically, I would definitely recommend this game if you've played through the first one even just once.

Here is my review of Bastion:
First waking up in Bastion you have no idea what is going on. What starts your adventure is that you do not remember anything about what happened to the world after the calamity hit.  Bastion follows the story of "The Kid" , who happens to survive all the events prior to the game. You first start of with just a trusty weapon and begin to slowly build your arsenal.
Gameplay / Sound- it almost works as a action RPG. The action includes shooting guns with cooldowns, dodging to avoid enemy attacks and special attacks. The RPG element works with upgrading guns and deciding what weapons to bring into combat during a certain mission. Some of the weapons become ridiculously strong, but with the increase in difficulty it shouldnt be too much of a problem. Unlocking the shrines and using them makes the game more fun and it also creates a bigger challenege in the game. Outside of those the game plays pretty much like an action game more than a RPG one. Playing on different level makes the game feel as though the worlds are all different yet are a part of a bigger story. Sadly you do not get to see even part of the world. The soundtrack to this game is one of the best I have heard in any video game. Once you hear it, you'll want to download it and keep on listening to it.
Story- The story revolves around "The Kid" and his quest to collect shards to save the world after the Calamity. While the story is fleshed out over the course of the game, i cant help but feel that the world isnt as interesting as I thought it would be. What i mean by this is that there is a clear beginning, middle and end, yet not any more to it. I expected to find notes or more journal types of items to help flesh out the world. It exists already to some degree in the game, but i would have liked to know more. Other than that little nit pick, I found the story to be good, but not great.
Replayability - While there is a proving grounds and some wave enemy combat, I see Bastion on Campagin as a one and done type of deal. There is content to keep you interested for the better part of about 15-20 hours though. If you getting everything and doing the extra missions you should finish within that timetable. The campaign for me took between 6-8 hours. Once you get the hang of the combat it runs though pretty quickly. As a game to pick up in the future again, I say it has limited replayability.
Controls - Controls are pretty straight forward and really easy to learn. I would recommend using a controller though because keybindings are on the backburner for this game.
Conclusion: If you are looking to buy Bastion, do it. It is a fantastic game and well worth purchase. The only negative takeaway is that the story background  isnt fully fleshed out and the replayability factor is pretty low.
Final Score: 9 out of 10

You are thrust into a world in the middle of a post-apocalyptic outcome.  You awake from your bed and see that everything you have ever known has turned to ashes and there isn't another living soul around.  You head off into a single direction, to head towards humanity's last Bastion.
Story 7/10
The story is compelling even if it does not feel completely fleshed out at all times.  The game places you in the middle of a story instead of its beginning, an interesting narrative choice.  The fast paced action and beautiful artwork make it so that you don't question, instead, you're compelled to proceed and delve deeper into this beautiful world.
For a large part of the story, you are introduced to new elements of the world of Bastion.  Unfortunately, there's not a lot of information to really feel how deep the history and events have unfolded.  While I wasn't impressed with the story as it was unfolding in the middle of game, things really pick up at the end.  The last two scenes are among the best in any game I've ever played and the ending does not disappoint.
Gameplay 5/10
While I enjoyed playing this game, I was simultaneously annoyed by its simplicity and by its difficulty.  Every stage has a firm set of boundaries that at times act to impede the hero, or at least the one controlling him.  The difficulty works on a sliding scale that is controlled by the player and various elements of the Bastion.  The various stages are fun to play but this game doesn't do anything innovative or amazing in that regard.
The game itself only features around a 6-hour story and maybe twice that with some replay value.
Art 8/10
Bastion is all about the art and the music.  The cutscenes all feature hand drawn art and the game looks like a carefully crafted artist's rendition. If there are any critiques on the art, it is that the mature theme and elements of the story don't necessarily match the cartoony feel that the world has.  If anything, Bastion may have been better suited to the gritty, dark art featured in Supergiant Games' 2nd big game, Transistor.
Soundtrack 10/10
The world of Bastion is all about the environment and the ambience made through its various soundtracks.  I don't generally buy soundtracks of video games (unless they're free) but this one would be an exception.  The songs featured in this album are full of energy and vigor that'll keep you going through the journey to the Bastion.
Overall 7.5/10
A fun game that's like a storybook come to life.  Top it off with an amazing soundtrack and you have a hit.  Bastion isn't a perfect game but seeing as it's a flagship title, it does really well to showcase what Supergiant Games can do.  I haven't played Transistor yet but I definitely will in the future.
Recommendations:
The game is fun but I don't think it's worth full price, whether it was 10 or 15 dollars, I don't remember.  Try it out when it goes on sale.
Transistor is out and features the same Narrator that Bastion features.
Soundtrack is free with Amazon Prime membership as of this writing.

A friend shared this game for me to play from her steam library. I can happily say I did not regret a single moment playing the game!
The game was so dark and twisted ... I loved it. We play as Fran, an orphaned child who starts off in a mental institution after the loss of her parents. The story has many curves following with the character's quest to find her lost cat Midnight. A plot that isn't too dazzling, but does have other elements that help carried the game to its full success.
The plot in which the game takes place is where it's innovation stems from. Our character has the ability to swap between differing realities, with the consumption of a 'certain' pill: One universe is set in reality, while the other resides in her own insanity. That world of insanity was certainly a sight to see, as it was filled with grim, death and other negative thoughts and fears of a child's mind.
Its art had also aided in making the worlds look grand. There is great detail in the shading and effects for a 2D Interactive Fiction game. The screen would be blurred and fuzzy when indicating danger, such as meeting the shadow people. I'll be completely honest here: I had only half an idea what I was getting into when I purchased this game. More than 400 hours later, I still only have about three quarters of an idea what I'm doing when playing. Yet, I keep going back to this game.

Fallout 4 (FO4) is a great game, a good RPG, and a bad Fallout sequel. If you’re worried about the Creation Club, don’t be, I'll explain at request because there's no room here.
To enjoy FO4, temper your expectations. I would recommend it, but not as highly as other Bethesda games, and for different reasons. It’s a great game (I’ve spent over 400 hours), but I’d be lying if I said I wasn’t disappointed in it as a main Fallout entry (I spent 800 hours in New Vegas, maybe longer as I think I’ve been playing it since before Steam tracked playtime). If they had named it Fallout: Boston or Commonwealth and billed it as a spinoff rather than a main entry, it would have been received much better. For example, imagine the outrage if FO: Tactics or Shelter weren’t spinoffs but main sequels, but because they *are* spinoffs they’re liked.
METAL GEAR SOLID V: THE PHANTOM PAIN is a good comparison. Both MGSV:TPP and FO4 are the best games of their respective series *mechanically* but the weakest in terms of what makes their series special.
Pros:
Power armor is worthy of its name. You don’t wear; you pilot it. You don’t stick in a drawer; you park in your garage. Enemies using power armor are a threat and using it yourself makes you a walking tank. People complain it’s over powered and you get your first (low level, incomplete, and damaged) set to soon, but the player is partially responsible for their own fun, especially in open-ended games. I only use it when I want to completely stomp♥♥♥♥♥♥in. Make your own house rules if you feel it’s OP, or use a rebalancing mod.
The combat is the best of any Bethesda game and thanks to the crafting system (which I’ll get to soon) it’s some of the best ever. Makes sense, they brought in their subsidiary Id (the people who made DOOM) to help design the combat from the ground up. Melee is also satisfying and effective, even as a sidearm for gun users. Some enemies, like robots, can lose limbs, altering their attacks and movement appropriately. V.A.T.S. slows instead of stopping time, which I was worried about initially, but I’ve grown to like it.
The crafting adds a LOT. In previous FO games there wasn’t reason to scavenge junk except to complete quests or sell. A few items you could craft, but found items were good enough and a lot of junk was still useless. You feel like a real scavenger in FO4, YO IS THAT A TYPEWRITER?! Everything has a use; you drop items not because they aren’t worth enough, but because they don’t have enough components. What is crafting for? Weapon and armor modification, as well as custom robot creation and modification with the Automatron DLC. The only thing more satisfying than killing feral ghouls is doing it with a laser-pistol-shotgun of your own creation. If you don’t want to spec into crafting you can take the preexisting mods from other weapons and mix and match them together on another weapon, this doesn’t require perks but some mods can only be crafted.
Bethesda noticed a lot of the most popular mods were player homes, so they created settlements. Now, instead of hoping for a mod you can create the perfect house for yourself, your companions, or even an entire town. It’s a little rough around the edges, but for those who like this sort of thing you’ll get hours of entertainment. For those who don’t it’s almost completely optional; there is *one* main quest that requires use of settlements, and it’s only to build *one* item, after that your “home” free.
I like the way perks are handled and leveling is now uncapped. Perks are initially locked behind your S.P.E.C.I.A.L. stats (which can be increased) but after that their only requirement is your level. For example, you can get the first rank of the highest perk in the STR line right away, if you have 10 STR, but to get the next rank you’ll need level 24. Likewise, you can get the highest rank of the lockpicking perk with only 4 PER, but not until lvl 41. This system is easier to keep track of without being dumbed down, in fact making good perk choices is challenging with so much variety and utility on offer.
The companions in FO4 are the best of any Bethesda game yet. Just the right mix of variety and depth. They’re not too effective in combat, but I made no effort to equip them and that’s not why you bring companions along anyway.
Mods. Need I say more?
Cons:
The most glaring issue is the story. It’s a good story but it has no place in FO, at least not as the main quest. Without spoiling anything, I can say that the story requires the player to care about things that they may not care about at all. It doesn’t give you enough reason or time to care even if you normally would. While I like the player characters (PC) Nate and Nora, playing as them means that your PC has already made some choices before the game even starts, choices that you may not have made if you were playing as a blank slate. For example, you start the game married, and as a result, I can’t bring myself to pursue any of the romance options because to do so would be to cheat on the person that Nate/Nora choose to marry, not me. Also, I wasn’t satisfied by the ending I got, and the choices that I had to make to get there. Maybe you’ll feel differently.
Another issue is the dialogue. It’s well written and voiced, and there is plenty of it, more than FO3 and Skyrim combined, despite what the four option “compass” interface might mislead you to believe. Even the vague paraphrases that they use to represent the actual responses aren’t an issue, I actually love the “sarcastic” option, all they need to do is rename it to “wild card” and it would be perfect. If you think otherwise, play Morrowind and relearn what vague paraphrasing is. The problem is the requirement of four options exactly per response creates an issue where you feel like there should be more options, or less, and the dialogue seems awkward as a result. Sometimes you’ll feel like you should be able to talk to someone, but you can’t because Bethesda couldn’t think of four options. It’s also bad for mods; the voiced PC makes good dialogue awkward or impossible for mods to create.
Skills are gone, few replaced by perks. For example, repair, so it can’t be used to fix broken machinery like you could occasionally in previous games. Also, success in speech checks is now chance based like it was in FO 1 and 2, even Obsidian, with their massive boner for the classics, knew that chance based skill checks are stupid. I really miss the feeling of being able to do things because of my PC’s competencies.
Bethesda has a reputation for bugs, and while it’s deserved, it’s far, far too harsh. First, keep in mind Bethesda makes such immense and complex games; they have the scale and depth of an ocean. You can play any way you want and as who or even *what* in the case of The Elder Scrolls. Then there is EA and Ubisoft who produce games of comparatively miniscule scale, depth, and complexity. Who you play as and how is set. Despite this, EA and Ubisoft’s games are FAR, FAR buggier and cost more once you factor in season passes, microtransactions, loot boxes and everything else. So remember that before you pick on Bethesda exclusively for bugs. The worst bug I’ve ever encountered in FO4 made me laugh, and that’s it. At this point, they’re a feature I look forward to. Besides, I don’t think it’s possible to do what Bethesda does without a few minor bugs, and until someone can prove that it is, I’ll forgive them.
To recap, I absolutely would recommend Fallout 4 (Game of the Year Edition) but it isn’t without its flaws. As long as you evaluate it based on its own merits and go into it expecting a good game first and a Fallout game second you’ll love it.

Fun and very shiny, but not the best Burnout in the series. Sadly it's the only one available on Steam. I enjoyed it but there remain some gripes:
The AI uses a catch-up/rubber-banding technique that isn't obvious at first but becomes very blatant in the late game. This may be a recurring feature in other burnout games, if not all racing games in general, but it still deflated the fun of racing towards the end. Fortunately the other modes don't suffer from this.
The amazing crash mode featured in Burnout 3 & 4 has been dumbed down to this bizarre, physics-defying mess where your car just bounces around the streets until you get bored. The crashbreaker, as well as the ability to steer your wreckage post-crash, have also been removed. Crashing does look nicer, and you can now drive away from the lesser impacts, but I miss the carnage from earlier entries.
Lastly, there is a massive amount of DLC that doesn't come with this so called "Ultimate" edition.
In summary, Burnout Paradise did take the series a few steps further in technical advancements, but at the same time it went several strides backwards in the gameplay department. Fans of the series will still have fun with this game but I'd wait for it to be on sale before purchasing.

I couldn’t have been happier to kick off the new series of reviews with Bastion which is one of my most favorite games and has one of the best stories in the industry. Let’s have at it.
I – Story [10/10]
Bastion is an action RPG from the amazingly talented Supergiant Games. The player assumes the role of the Kid. The story begins in the aftermath of the Calamity, a cataclysmic event that almost entirely destroyed the city of Caelondia as well as much of the surrounding world, leaving it in fractured, floating pieces. The Kid makes his way to the Bastion, a location the Caels were supposed to meet at in case of an emergency. However, the only survivor the Kid meets is Rucks, a mysterious old man and the narrator of the game’s events. Rucks informs the Kid that he needs to collect Cores (large crystals that used to power the city) from around Caelondia and that the Bastion has the ability to use the Cores to rebuild.
During his journey, the Kid meets two other survivors; Zulf and Zia. Zulf was an ambassador from the Ura people, a one time enemy of the Caels. Zia is an Ura girl who was born and raised in Caelondia. The Kid leads them both to the Bastion and, upon discovering a research notebook written in the native tongue of the Ura, the Kid enlists their help in translating it. Rucks and Zia are unable to read it, so the Kid falls back on Zulf to do the translating. In the meantime, the Kid goes in search of the final Core that they need.
Upon his return however, the Kid finds Zulf gone. Rucks explains that when Zulf had finished translating the notebook, he snapped and wreaked significant damage upon the Bastion. Apparently the notebook (which had belonged to Zia’s father, Venn) detailed the Mancer’s (a group of Cael scientists) efforts to create a weapon with which they could destroy the Ura and prevent any further wars. However, Venn had rigged the weapon to backfire, so, when the Mancers finally made him pull the trigger, the weapon destroyed Caelondia as well.
In order to repair the damage done to the Bastion by Zulf, the Kid takes to the Wilds in search of Shards (smaller versions of the Cores). As the Kid acquires one of the final shards, the Ura attack the Bastion, kidnapping Zia in the process. This event takes the Kid deep into Ura territory in search of both the final shard and Zia. When the Kid finally breaks through the Ura outpost, he finds Zia, but the Shard slips through his fingers.
In the final missions of the game, the Kid sets off into the once-underground Ura homeland to confront Zulf and retrieve the final Shard. Inside the homeland, the Kid finds Zulf being attacked by his countrymen and he is faced with a choice: he can drop his weapon and carry Zulf back to the Bastion with him or he can leave Zulf to his fate and battles his way through the remaining Ura.
Back at the Bastion, the Kid is presented with one final choice from Rucks. The Kid can choose to use the Bastion’s power to rewind time to before the Calamity and set things back to the way they were, but there is no guarantee that the Calamity won’t happen again. The Kid can also choose to use the Bastion’s power to initiate the evacuation protocol  and move on to someplace safe with Rucks and Zia (and Zulf if the player chose to save him).
Multiple endings, an enchanting fantasy world, an incredible back story revealed through gameplay, and a hands-down amazing story throughout the entire game. Almost every game could stand to learn a thing or two from Bastion.
II – UI [9/10]
The user interface in Bastion is marvelous. You’ll never struggle to find any critical information, what weapons you have equipped, or what special attack you currently have. The only complaint that I have, at all about Bastion (though I’m somewhat torn about making it) is the lack of a minimap. While a minimap would have made navigation in game areas easier, it probably would have distracted from the overall game immersion.
III – Gameplay [10/10]
Gameplay in Bastion is fluid and fast-paced, with a fine-tuned combat system and intuitive controls. Attacking and defending are both omnidirectional. While there’s no jumping (at least, not for most of the game), you do have a very nice rolling maneuver at your disposal.
IV – Content [10/10]
With Bastion being the first ever game from Supergiant Games, I must say there was a very large amount of content. There are more than ten weapons with which you can fill your arsenal, all of which are fully upgradeable. There is a vast array of special attacks and character perks to unlock and discover throughout the course of the game. There are a good amount of missions and bonus missions to keep you occupied with and they are all filled with a wonderful plethora of enemies to slay.
V – Visual [10/10]
The art of Bastion is, simply put, phenomenal. Everything is hand-painted and unforgettable. It has an art style that is very unique when it comes to gaming and I sincerely hope that we all have the privilege of seeing it more often in future titles.
VI – Audio [10/10]
Not to be outdone by the artwork department, the soundtrack (and sounds) of Bastion were every bit as good as every other aspect of the game. Even if you don’t end up getting the game, you should do yourself a favor and pick up the soundtrack, because wow. Just wow.
VII – Overall [9.8/10]
Overall, Bastion is a truly great game and you shouldn’t hesitate to add it to your own library.

Horror as a genre requires a particularly elegant approach to be successful. It is certainly possible to scare someone through blunt manipulation of disturbing images and a reliance on proven tropes, but horror that lingers, sticking to its audience like the aftermath of a bad dream, that takes something more. To its credit, Fran Bow initially understands this to a level that is truly chilling. But as developer Killmonday Games takes on more and more plotlines, shuffling the player deeper into an incomprehensible madness, Fran Bow falls inside the depths of a convoluted narrative mess from which it is never able to crawl back out of.
Beginning within the bloodstained hallways of a children’s mental institution, Fran Bow has access to no shortage of unsettling narratives and images to pull from, drawing heavily from horrific historical medical practices and occult imagery to craft an aggressively grim premise. 10 years old going on 11, the eponymous Fran Bow is plagued by violent images of her parent’s slaughter. Trapped now in a categorically inhumane asylum, her day to day life consists of being carted from psychiatric evaluations to routine drug administrations, forcing her madness back into her mind and leaving her in a vegetative state. Her one out from this hellish existence comes in the form of a bottle of red pills, which upon ingesting allows Fran to see her grotesque visions manifest in the real world, in the process instructing her on how to escape and setting her off on a quest to find her cat and only friend, Mr. Midnight.
Setting aside its narrative baggage, Fran Bow operates on what can be considered two distinct levels. The first is that of a decidedly traditional adventure game, with a heavy focus on jerry-rigging items together in order to solve an inordinate amount of inscrutable puzzles. Fran Bow makes little sense by design, but while this is largely excusable in a narrative drawing heavily from the likes of Alice in Wonderland (and even more so the macabre video game reimagining, Alice: Madness Returns) it effectively turns each puzzle into an inventory jigsaw puzzle as the player is left to attempt to combine items until something clicks into place. This is made all the worse due to Fran Bow’s level design, which assembles a collection of screens for the player to scavenge through as they slowly chip away at a levels exterior until being whisked away to the next hub. At its best, Fran Bow’s puzzles are tedious and archaic, and at their worst they completely break the game’s façade and reveal the rusty gears grinding to a halt underneath.
Somehow more unpleasant to contend with, however, is Fran Bow’s second chief objective: to be as grotesque and violent as possible within the span of 7-8 hours. Fran Bow’s morbid tendencies should be readily apparent to anyone who has seen any portion of the game, but what screenshots don’t relay as readily as playing the game does is how quickly Fran Bow’s violence and gore becomes routine. It is nauseating, to be sure, but there is never any method to Fran Bow’s madness. It wants to shock and appall, but solely for the sake of proving how depraved it is. And that’s perhaps all well and good to a certain subset of player, but the point at which Fran Bow quit attempting to justify its perversions was the point they stopped being effective. Fran Bow’s horrors fail because on some level they never really aim to be horrific. At most Fran Bow seems to seek to establish a palpable unease, but the anxiety it manages to create is so constant that it can only sustain itself so long before even the sight of bodies diced and organs strewn about elicits little more than a moderate cringe.
If Fran Bow had anything more to offer beyond these two elements it might be possible to dismiss them as tolerable gripes, but at some point roughly halfway through the game, it becomes distressingly clear that Fran Bow is just as lost as the player is confused where they are being taken. From the third chapter of five onward, Fran Bow takes aggressive, woefully conceptualized measures to arrive at something approximating a conclusion. Alternate realities and timelines are employed, split personalities are discovered, characters are drawn out of the air with elaborate backstories in hand, and proceedings become radically more unhinged as the game buckles under the weight of a plot that feels more false and contrived than any of Fran’s visions. Fran Bow begins as a mysterious if meandering horror adventure game, but by its conclusion, adopts the worst narrative conventions of bad fantasy and sci-fi to form a genre blending monstrosity that is all too eager to write off every inexplicable story beat as mere madness when it is more convenient than an explanation.
Fran Bow begins with the trappings of a deliberate authorship, but by its conclusion becomes so enamored with introducing new characters and plotlines to support ones which were never well developed to begin with, that the whole game falls in upon itself. On an artistic and conceptual level, Killmonday Games are experts at finding ways to capture the players’ attention and compel them forward, but when every path leads to a deus ex machina and an exposition dump long enough to chock on, it’s hard to feel anything but regret for having gone down them.

I loved this game, but I wish it either stuck to its horror atmosphere (in the earlier chapters) or its hard fantasy (in the later chapters). I am a huge fan of horror games, so I preffered the extremly disturbing imagery in the first two chapters to the fantasy in chapter three. Chapter three was honestly not a very fun chapter for me, as the player progresses mostly through tedius fetch quests.
Apart from chapter three, I did love this game. The puzzles all made sense, and while a few were very tricky, none of them made me say "Oh come on that's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t" the way some puzzle games do. I became very attached to Fran and Mr. Midnight, and I really didn't want to see either of them get hurt. The parts of this game that are horror are psychological horror, meaning that they are disturbing and grotesque rather than "scream at your computer" scary. The art style compliments the atmosphere of the game very well. Also, I really like that you can choose to skip the minigames if you want. That was really convenient. I liked the minigames for the most part but sometimes I just didn't feel like playing them.
Overall I'd give this game an 8.5/10. Everything but chapter 3 was a 10/10 for me, I jsut really grew tired of the fetch quests in chapter 3.

What at first seemed like a promising new addition to the 4X genre turned out to be a complete disaster.
The game is incomplete and the devs have since jumped ship to rebuild the game from scratch under a separate title, "Stardrive 2". No has been compensated in any way, and this broken, unfinished mess is now being touted as a complete game.
As for the specific issues with the game:
PROS-
1. It is a 4X game played in real time. That allows for a number of new strategies not possible in the ordinarily turn-based genre.
2. Stardrive brought something new to the 4X table with the ability to design/fit your ships from scratch. This was the core pulling factor of the game. With customizable ships, you could choose from a pre-existing hull and redesign the ship to suit whatever specialised need. Titanic capital ships dedicated to bombing a planet into a foetid hellhole (i.e. conducting Exterminatus)? Done. Beam cannons on a fighter? No problemo. Or how about a logistics ship to provide repairs to your fleet on the go? All possible.
CONS-
1. The Sunburn engine is a laggy unoptimized mess. The framerate basically commits suicide during mid to late game, and especially in the middle of large fleet battles involving more than a hundred ships, even more so with the fact that the game runs in real time. The devs took a bad gamble opting to use a new engine with little repute, and lost.
2. The AI is shallow at best, and in the state the devs had left the game, you can't do much more than basic threatening, bargaining, and decaring war. Some of the interaction options do not even seem to have any real purpose or effect.
3. The game claims to be mod-friendly, however due to the limitations of the engine it can only run 1 mod at any time.
4. Planetary interaction with colonies and ground troops could truly be better. Every ground unit across all the playable races are basically just reskins of one another, and the gameplay lacks any sort of strategic depth beyond throwing as many troops as possible at the enemy (or as many as you can fit on the map). Building placement doesn't appear to have any strategic element either.
5. Finally, the game devs abandoned the sinking ship while all the passengers were still on board. Didn't say a word. One day they just went *poof*, and no one heard from them again until they began advertising their "new" game.
'nuff said.
Such a pity, really. This game had so much promise....

Fallout 4 (FO4) is a great game, a good RPG, and a bad Fallout sequel. If you’re worried about the Creation Club, don’t be, I'll explain at request because there's no room here.
To enjoy FO4, temper your expectations. I would recommend it, but not as highly as other Bethesda games, and for different reasons. It’s a great game (I’ve spent over 400 hours), but I’d be lying if I said I wasn’t disappointed in it as a main Fallout entry (I spent 800 hours in New Vegas, maybe longer as I think I’ve been playing it since before Steam tracked playtime). If they had named it Fallout: Boston or Commonwealth and billed it as a spinoff rather than a main entry, it would have been received much better. For example, imagine the outrage if FO: Tactics or Shelter weren’t spinoffs but main sequels, but because they *are* spinoffs they’re liked.
METAL GEAR SOLID V: THE PHANTOM PAIN is a good comparison. Both MGSV:TPP and FO4 are the best games of their respective series *mechanically* but the weakest in terms of what makes their series special.
Pros:
Power armor is worthy of its name. You don’t wear; you pilot it. You don’t stick in a drawer; you park in your garage. Enemies using power armor are a threat and using it yourself makes you a walking tank. People complain it’s over powered and you get your first (low level, incomplete, and damaged) set to soon, but the player is partially responsible for their own fun, especially in open-ended games. I only use it when I want to completely stomp♥♥♥♥♥♥in. Make your own house rules if you feel it’s OP, or use a rebalancing mod.
The combat is the best of any Bethesda game and thanks to the crafting system (which I’ll get to soon) it’s some of the best ever. Makes sense, they brought in their subsidiary Id (the people who made DOOM) to help design the combat from the ground up. Melee is also satisfying and effective, even as a sidearm for gun users. Some enemies, like robots, can lose limbs, altering their attacks and movement appropriately. V.A.T.S. slows instead of stopping time, which I was worried about initially, but I’ve grown to like it.
The crafting adds a LOT. In previous FO games there wasn’t reason to scavenge junk except to complete quests or sell. A few items you could craft, but found items were good enough and a lot of junk was still useless. You feel like a real scavenger in FO4, YO IS THAT A TYPEWRITER?! Everything has a use; you drop items not because they aren’t worth enough, but because they don’t have enough components. What is crafting for? Weapon and armor modification, as well as custom robot creation and modification with the Automatron DLC. The only thing more satisfying than killing feral ghouls is doing it with a laser-pistol-shotgun of your own creation. If you don’t want to spec into crafting you can take the preexisting mods from other weapons and mix and match them together on another weapon, this doesn’t require perks but some mods can only be crafted.
Bethesda noticed a lot of the most popular mods were player homes, so they created settlements. Now, instead of hoping for a mod you can create the perfect house for yourself, your companions, or even an entire town. It’s a little rough around the edges, but for those who like this sort of thing you’ll get hours of entertainment. For those who don’t it’s almost completely optional; there is *one* main quest that requires use of settlements, and it’s only to build *one* item, after that your “home” free.
I like the way perks are handled and leveling is now uncapped. Perks are initially locked behind your S.P.E.C.I.A.L. stats (which can be increased) but after that their only requirement is your level. For example, you can get the first rank of the highest perk in the STR line right away, if you have 10 STR, but to get the next rank you’ll need level 24. Likewise, you can get the highest rank of the lockpicking perk with only 4 PER, but not until lvl 41. This system is easier to keep track of without being dumbed down, in fact making good perk choices is challenging with so much variety and utility on offer.
The companions in FO4 are the best of any Bethesda game yet. Just the right mix of variety and depth. They’re not too effective in combat, but I made no effort to equip them and that’s not why you bring companions along anyway.
Mods. Need I say more?
Cons:
The most glaring issue is the story. It’s a good story but it has no place in FO, at least not as the main quest. Without spoiling anything, I can say that the story requires the player to care about things that they may not care about at all. It doesn’t give you enough reason or time to care even if you normally would. While I like the player characters (PC) Nate and Nora, playing as them means that your PC has already made some choices before the game even starts, choices that you may not have made if you were playing as a blank slate. For example, you start the game married, and as a result, I can’t bring myself to pursue any of the romance options because to do so would be to cheat on the person that Nate/Nora choose to marry, not me. Also, I wasn’t satisfied by the ending I got, and the choices that I had to make to get there. Maybe you’ll feel differently.
Another issue is the dialogue. It’s well written and voiced, and there is plenty of it, more than FO3 and Skyrim combined, despite what the four option “compass” interface might mislead you to believe. Even the vague paraphrases that they use to represent the actual responses aren’t an issue, I actually love the “sarcastic” option, all they need to do is rename it to “wild card” and it would be perfect. If you think otherwise, play Morrowind and relearn what vague paraphrasing is. The problem is the requirement of four options exactly per response creates an issue where you feel like there should be more options, or less, and the dialogue seems awkward as a result. Sometimes you’ll feel like you should be able to talk to someone, but you can’t because Bethesda couldn’t think of four options. It’s also bad for mods; the voiced PC makes good dialogue awkward or impossible for mods to create.
Skills are gone, few replaced by perks. For example, repair, so it can’t be used to fix broken machinery like you could occasionally in previous games. Also, success in speech checks is now chance based like it was in FO 1 and 2, even Obsidian, with their massive boner for the classics, knew that chance based skill checks are stupid. I really miss the feeling of being able to do things because of my PC’s competencies.
Bethesda has a reputation for bugs, and while it’s deserved, it’s far, far too harsh. First, keep in mind Bethesda makes such immense and complex games; they have the scale and depth of an ocean. You can play any way you want and as who or even *what* in the case of The Elder Scrolls. Then there is EA and Ubisoft who produce games of comparatively miniscule scale, depth, and complexity. Who you play as and how is set. Despite this, EA and Ubisoft’s games are FAR, FAR buggier and cost more once you factor in season passes, microtransactions, loot boxes and everything else. So remember that before you pick on Bethesda exclusively for bugs. The worst bug I’ve ever encountered in FO4 made me laugh, and that’s it. At this point, they’re a feature I look forward to. Besides, I don’t think it’s possible to do what Bethesda does without a few minor bugs, and until someone can prove that it is, I’ll forgive them.
To recap, I absolutely would recommend Fallout 4 (Game of the Year Edition) but it isn’t without its flaws. As long as you evaluate it based on its own merits and go into it expecting a good game first and a Fallout game second you’ll love it.

This game is very unpolished, but still fun.
(A lot of things are fixed by two mods I use, the 'Black Box' mod and the Tech Level Mod)
1. Ship designing:
This is excellent; module positioning really matters in combat. If you fill the interior with lots of reactors, they'll blow up when destroyed and will probably destroy your ship from the inside out.
Shields are not 'all around' your ship but instead only protect areas they're near to, so don't forget to place lots of armour to soak up the hits that get through.
There really aren't enough ship hulls and modules; each empire only gets 1 hull for each hull type (i.e. frigate, cruiser, battleship, titan etc.). Reactors never get an upgrade. Sub-light maneuvering speeds are much too low.
2. AI:
The AI for the other players is poor - they don't expand very much and they have a tendency to get angry about every single system you colonise. They are very, very bad at fighting and will only cause you trouble if you ignore your military for the entire game (which they'll also taunt you for doing). Their art however is really nice and each empire has its own set of ship types.
There's a nice automation dialogue that lets you automate the building and usage of scouts, freighters, and subspace projectors.
3. Research:
Research feels a little slow for me. The tech tree is pretty sparse and could use some more mid/end-tier stuff.
There are two (maybe three?) 'discovered' secret techs which appear according to what you do in the game. This is something the developer never got around to adding more of, which is a real shame.
4. Early Access 'dev didn't implement X':
I hear this a lot, and it seems to make up most of the reviews here. This game does feel like the dev gave up when it was 80% finished. I didn't buy this game in Early Access (Humble Bundle had it for $4) so if you're not sure, buy this on sale.

tl;dr: Absolute tons of potential and a simple design for a very nice price. Right this second, it's still worth the price tag to kill a boring afternoon.
It's difficult to review Endorlight when its so early in development, but I feel like this is a game people should really take a look at - especially for the price. It's too simple to complain about anything, and since this is "pre-alpha" and it's hard telling when this review's being read, I'll try to just touch on the current foundation that's laid and speculate on the potential of what the game could be. On the tin it looks like another indie platformer with permadeath but that's not accurate at all.
While the levels are currently short and compact, they're randomly generated on every floor. The monsters, traps, crates, chests - everything. In the future this completely random level generation can bring on some really interesting layouts rather than just a sea of magma with platforms to jump across. The character's wall-jump ability makes it seem like we could see some very vertical and challenging levels and boss fights as we go further, and with certain enemies exploding on death and taking out terrain it's possible to dig (or explode via planned bomb weapon) your way through. I imagine this goes for the enemies, too (planned digger enemy). With all the variety, some levels might be a sort of "race to the finish" because of falling platforms (planned feature) and how many enemies there are at the start (a load of baddies led by a digging enemy as the fuse?) while other levels require a bit more finesse and tactical jumping to get through unharmed. While you could just rush toward where you think the exit is (it's not made obvious by the map - probably intentional) you'd be hurting yourself in the long-run with all the missing loot. Enemies don't currently drop anything, but crates and chests are strewn about the levels and give gold upon destruction.
Gold currently has no use, but it's pretty obvious this is intended to be currency for the yet-to-be-introduced shops. I imagine shops will be selling heart containers for more life, potions to heal you, arrows for the bow (surely it's not always infinite ammo?), ammo for the gun (planned weapon), bombs (also planned weapon), etc. Taking your time and saving your gold as you progress can be difficult on some levels due to the layout and enemies, but would be worth it. I'd like to think the shops will be alone on their own level to prevent a player from seeing a shop and THEN wanting to full-clear to afford the wares. While this isn't a major thing, it'd be nice to see some reward / punishment for different playstyles. Hauling it through every level to get deeper may have its benefits (maybe?) but taking your time yields shop goodies, but at the risk of losing your life to the enemies that are everywhere.
The enemies are really simple currently. You standard slime with raptor-like capabilities regarding its jump, the thing that blows up on death, green, uhh... things that aren't really that aggressive, etc. They vary by appearance but the general premise is the same - don't get touched by one. It's dangerous to use your melee weapons so the bow it a great go-to (unless the terrain is really bumpy as you can't aim vertically and there's no arrow drop or "charging" the bow for adjusting trajectory) but at the cost of arrows, which are currently infinite. The melee weapons might double as tools, but right now there's nothing to tool. A gun, hatchet, and bomb are planned weapons so it's hard to tell what the enemies (and bosses) will be like, but it sounds like staying at range is the way to go.

StarDrive is an immersive RPG. The amount that goes on in this game after a while starts to get crazy.
The concept is simple... zoom in and out with the mouse to view the star systems. The navigation that this game play provides is smooth and allows you to get to which system you need to view. The managing system of seeing all of your empires/planets and being able to allocate production is sophisticated enough but the user interface for it was done simply and made easy to use. Diplomacy can work for or sometimes quickly against you with an opposing empire declaring war. Trade routes, non-aggression pacts, war declaration, and even colony claims can be through diplomacy. Planets come in different varieties such as gas planets, Terran, swamp, barren and a few variants. Be sure to start exploring early and claim good planets, but doing so exposes you to aliens. You will find yourself addicted to this game after a while if you like micro and macro managing planets and a multitude of ships. You are also able to create your own ships (from colony ships to cruisers) and the creation system is a neat one at that. There is also an in game fleet design system that by itself makes the game much more easier to play (and to defend against enemies).
Why I support this game even though it has a lag issues (sometimes with and without the mod) is there is a community out there trying to improve this game. Moreover and more importantly for me, you are able to control a SINGLE UNIT and tell them what to fire. You can't say exactly which guns to use, but none the less this is the right idea in my mind to create a new genre : RPG meets first person shooters. Literally, any unit that's out there, choose to control. I wish more games did this in the sense. Imagine playing Starcraft and you can control a marine. Your marine that you are controlling dies so you automatically jump to the next one or go back to the RPG screen. This to me is brilliant and perhaps even game changing in the future.
I will have to give it a
RATING : 7.0/10
Due to lag issues and a need for a mod but either than that I recommend it - especially on sale.

Sometimes you find a game for $1.00 on HumbleBundle and think why not, I'll give it a shot.  What's the worst that could happen?  It sucks and you're out a dollar?  Don't be a fool.  Listen to me, I used to be like you...naive.  I paid the dollar, positively gitty at my thrifty yet philanthropic purchase, but I discovered there are far worse fates than not liking the game.  Oh yes, much to my dismay, I learned you could absolutely LOVE the game.  Specifically, I learned that someone, some magical gameweaver of a developer, had somehow discovered a way to craft all of my 4x RTS dreams into one perfect game.
Imagine having all this only to find out after hours of gameplay that the mystical Dev had just M. Night Shyamalan'ed your♥♥♥♥♥by abandoning the game deep in development, leaving gamebreaking glitches unpatched, and giggling all the way to the bank with your hopes and dreams.  Now there will forever be a void in my heart where the finished version of this game should be.  I would've rather spent my dollar on paying someone to kick me in the balls.  At least that paid would go away eventually.
To be fair, I'm only whining because I love what this game could've been.  Wasting that much potential should be a crime.  The finished, patched version would have been one of the best 4x games of all time.  Unfortunately this game was abandoned to begin development on a sequel that will be turn-based, not real time, and therefore more of a completely different game than a sequel.  While I love turn-based strategy, the RTS version of this game is the one I wanted and now I will never be able to play a polished version of it.  As such, I simply can not recommend it.

If you're reading this you might be wondering: "What the hell is a Kickbeat?"
Kickbeat is a rythym game where you press keys, timed with the music, so your character kicks people in the face.
I like to call these games (FFR, Stepmania 1,2, Beatmanina) tap rythym games. Because there's no instrument or dance pad. It's meant to be played with a controller or keyboard.
I personally had been waiting for a game like this to come around for a long time, that is to say, a tap rythym game where there's something more interesting to look at than just arrows flying by the screen.
The production value feels very high to me for a $9.99 out of the gate priced game, it's really a big treat. It looks great, it sounds great, it plays tight and its got an interesting well written and well voiced storyline that plays out twice through the songs. It's got difficulty settings and customization options that allow you to jump right in but still eventually take off your training wheels as you go for huge scores on mind bendingly tough difficulties for rankings on the leaderboards, and achivements that actually mean something.
The playlist is 24 "get-your-blood-pumping" high b.p.m. songs ranging from Rap to Eletro to Nu Metal. Every single song is enjoyable and fun to play, there isn't a single one that I want to skip over and many that I want to play again and again.
While this isn't nessicarily a game for every rythym gamer out there, with its low cost and realitively easy learning curve, I recommend picking it up if your interest is sparkked at all. Is it hardcore? Yes. Will it probably make you frustrated? Yes. Will you continue to come back to play more and more eventually mastering each song and having a huge feeling of accomplishment? Most certainly yes.

11 hours in and i've been really enjoying the game with a friend of mine, we've played through maybe 6 full games. It is early-access still which means there are limited features but what is there is very clean and enjoyable gameplay. Ill just do a little pro's and con's list.
Pros:
- The graphics are clean and cute, not hyper-realism but not too cartoonish.
- The core gameplay is quite enjoyable, building, resource gathering etc.
- It's simple enough to sit down and play, but there are things to learn to help you  progress faster.
- There is a TON of stuff that could be added which gives PLENTY to look forward too in the future.
- Unit control is fairly easy and doesn't have you suffer too much (like in civ)
- the amount of buildings per tile limit really lets you plan out what you need and where, and what can go in each tile in the future. example. if you have a tile thats 0/2 buildings, but it has a farm spot, then you know you want at least a farm + a food silo. but wait, theres a stone mine there too, so, do you build a farm / mine first? then when the mine is depleted, delete it and build your food silo? or do you save up 100 gold and extend the plot of land to 0/3 buildings (+1 building per tile) what can you get away with having at the time
Cons: (less of cons and more of what id like to see probably)
- Villager interaction is limited. Having units survive for a long time does nothing for progression (you can churn them out like fodder)
- Limited buildings atm, once you have what you need you sort of just build  MORE of what you need so you have an over abundance, or just start attacking everything in sight. (for instance, if you build a brewer and are happy, then become unhappy, you just build another brewer, instead of anything else for happiness, like a circus or w/e, anything)
- Only 4 types of "combat units" which isnt that bad, but since you cant really upgrade them or anything once you have them thats it, you just build more if they die
- the maps feel REALLY small, like every game im pinned into a coast and if i dont have what i need in my immediate surroundings im boned for awhile till i slowly get going
- there are alot of EMPTY tiles and you cant really do anything with them besides build buildings, which, if they are empty tiles, limit what you can build, example. if you have an empty tile, most likely you just build houses on it which increases population, but you cant decide that you NEED a farm there because you dont have access to one naturally
- FOOD is limited, if you dont have farms, fish or deer close by, theres literally nothing else you can do besides having all of your units be villagers and just gather food all day (which then limits your other occupations, since villager turn into all other units (in civ you could turn any tile into farms, but if they had WHEAT on them i think you had +% of bonus production
- the victory conditions, while there are multiple ways to win, seem redundant. i never actually know what victory im going for. the talents themselves is sort of like, you want everything, but ive found what i want first. but if you dont have access to certain landmarks then you cant win in certain ways.
- My final con, which isnt really a con since they've announced there will be a campaign. I LOVE MULTIPLAYER GAMES that I can play with my friends, however, in 2017, all multiplayer games are PVP based. Sometimes I just want to play and beat the story mode with my buds. So, as of now, no campaign, but I really hope they dont limit the gameplay to a short campaign, and then online multiplayer. Id like to see a EXTENSIVE campaign, with REAL objectives and rewards, and even update it / multiple campaigns in time.
REGARDLESS - TLDR: For early access this game is awesome and I can see it only getting better with updates. Its cute, its fun, it doesnt take forever to play a match but the games can get extensive and im excited to see what new stuff comes out. Thanks for reading!

The Predator campaign is pretty great too but some things just don't cut it (ha-ha). So here are my initial thoughts after a first completion (I’ll update when I’ve finished with a character imported from Van Helsing 1).
This is a top notch action role playing game. There’s a lot of emphasis on the ‘action’ and it’s a pretty breathtaking journey from the opening scenes to the finale. In addition to standard ARPG fare, there is a pretty satisfying tower defence component (which can be completely skipped if you don’t like it, but I recommend giving it a try, I thought I’d hate it and I loved it) and a troop management minigame (a bit like they had in Assassins Creed Revelations – send soldiers on missions, they bring back loot, train them up etc).
I’d strongly recommend this to people who’ve played the first Van Helsing game – and if you haven’t, get both and support an excellent franchise.
There are a number of areas this game improves from Van Helsing 1. It has better graphics, greater variety of missions, very interesting boss battles (I love the finale), larger maps and more to be getting on with. My first playthrough was about 14 hours on hard mode, which is a nice length and included completing most of the side quests. There’s also two game modes, one for newcomers with a level 1 character, one for those importing a level 30 character. This means new tricks, new items and increased difficulty. All good stuff for those looking for more. I can see this occupying a lot of my time ...
It’s not all roses, however... there are a lot of re-used assets, both backgrounds, scenery and enemy types, you are never short on cash, and the loot drops are a little disappointing. Most of the loot (almost all the epic items) were repeated from the first game and dropped by very few enemies (there are too many empty chests). The best items appear at scripted moments and after level 15 I pretty much didn’t change out my loot (I finished the first playthrough at level 31). In addition, Katarina is still pretty useless as anything other than a bullet shield after about level 10, she dies way too easily even with lots of upgrades.
In sum it is better than Van Helsing 1 and stands on its own as a great ARPG that is more of an isometric Borderlands than Path of Exile and if that’s something you think you’d enjoy it’s well worth a couple of quid.

If I were to point the game series that was shaped and reshaped time and time again by its fans and community, it would definitely be the Street Fighter series. If you take a look back to how the series evolved, in terms of gameplay, you’ll see that it did by how the fans played it, or how they wanted to play it. Capcom adapted glitches and mods into new mechanics, and even extended a hand to the community during the development of SFIV, and made some of the community leaders an integral part of the development team, and same was done with SFV.
As a huge fan of the series, Capcom have out done themselves with SFV, but, and this a huge BUT, they did so only in terms of the gameplay and mechanics. So, what does that mean? It means: the game is a rough diamond; its core is amazing but it’s buried under a ton of used baby diapers, covered with Indian food and left under the sun.
In terms of the core gameplay, SFV is definitely an evolution towards the right direction. It landed midway between the skill-demanding SFIII, and the simplicity and fluidity of SFIV. The developers dropped the “revenge meter” in favor of a new mechanic (V-Skill). You spend the meter by either activating your V-Trigger, which will consume it all, or by executing a V-Reversal. The V-trigger is a unique Buff/Debuff/attack/stance...etc. For example Nash’s V-Trigger is teleportation. On the other hand Ryu’s is a buff that will add damage and stun damage to his attacks. The V-reversal is a tool for escape and lowering your stun meter, and using it will consume part of the meter only.
The other meter is the super meter. You fill it by doing any special move, and spent if you perform a Super or any EX version of the special moves. And the meter carry over from round to round.
The best part of how the game engine evolved is most definitely the hit-boxes. It changed the and strengthened the game fundamentally. I can easily play without Special attacks, and still be entertained. It gave the game another layer of gameplay.
Most characters were changed intelligently to suit the new engine and mechanics, but still keep original feel of the character. So if you’re used to Ryu and the flow of playing as Ryu, you will still find a cozy feel in him, but still find new editions that will keep it fresh.
The roster all in all, is very well picked featuring a wide range of diverse characters, in terms of visuals, as well as game design. So you will find lots of characters to experiment with out of the box.
But what you won't find of the box is what you expect from any other AAA 60$ game. It’s like going to a restaurant in March and paying for a burger, then, surprise surprise, a tray with a piece meat on it. You may ask “Hey where is the rest of my ♥♥♥♥ing burger?”. Well dear chum, come end of July, by then...maybe we will have given you the rest of your burger. It lacked a real story mode, and was slapped with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ mode that a baby can beat (literally, there is a video of a toddler beating the game) but the issue here is not that it was easy, it lacked content; no buns, no lettuce, no cheese, come back by the end of April for the top bun, old chum.
One of the most frustrating, infuriating aspects of the game is micro-transactions. I bought a stripped down 60$ game, but no, a huge part of the game is just locked away, and you either have to buy it with real money, or in-game money. And to get the in-game money you have to slave for hours upon hours to get it. And don’t tell me “As long as you can unlock it in-game”. No, ♥♥♥♥ that♥♥♥♥♥♥ my time is valuable and the way you get the in-game money is designed to frustrate you to the point of saying “♥♥♥♥ it, take my money”.
In closing, the game is amazing, and the online code works beautifully (when it works), but know that it’s very much bare-bone and will take sometime to be filled with content that interest the casual player. If you’re a fan of the series then you probably already own it, if you don’t, what the ♥♥♥♥ is wrong with you.

A wild, spectacular open world racing game filled to the brim with exotic cars, exaggerated crashing, and death-defying jumps,
leaves no room for disappointment.
The game starts off with a lengthy cutscene, introducing the player to the eponymous world of Paradise City, complete with a thriving city, rolling mountainside roads, disused train track networks, humble trailer parks, carefully hidden areas, tempting ramps, shortcuts, and much more. All this available right off the bat, with no barriers hiding entire sections of the map for progression. Over 70 cars are featured in the game, and all of them are fictitious derivatives of real world makes and models.
Starting off fresh, the player has little choice for a starting vehicle, that being a smashed up, but perfectly functionable blue muscle car with resemblence to an early model Ford Mustang. It isn't the fastest car on offer, but this slow car is needed to practice safely navigating Paradise's unpredictable traffic foaming in the urban areas, and twisting, unforgiving rural roads.
After successfully winning a few events, which comprise of traditional point A to point B sprints, "Road Rage" events which are bare-knucked destruction derbies at unsafe velocities, "Marked Man" races that have a pack of unfriendly muscle cars bent on shattering your car while you try to make it to point B, and "Stunt Runs", where the goal is to make as many daring jumps and drifts as possible before the timer runs out, additional cars will be added to the player's car collection.
Some cars will have to be chased down and crashed to be redeemed, but all are geared to one of three traits: "Speed Cars", are tuned to reach absurd speeds but are fragile, "Aggression Cars", which are heavy, slow, and can absorb damage with ease, and "Stunt cars", which are lightweight and agile, granting them superb jumping characteristics.
As far as customization is concerned, it is fairly limited. Most cars can take a few predefined colors, paint finish, and vinyl color, while some cannot be customized at all. Nonetheless, it is sufficent for most cars, and there are plenty of them to go by, some even having "special" editions bearing alternate designs.
Should the player not be engaged in an event, they are free to explore the map, and discover the many "Discoverables", scattered around the roads of Paradise. There are billboards to plow though, with many of them being awkwardly placed at hard-to-get locations, gates revealing a hidden shortcut, and wicked jumps to take advantage of, sometimes even having the player's car sail though cliffside to cliffside.
Overall,
is a solid game, even though its not perfect. Online mode is featured, but that has not been covered in this review, as the writer has not bothered to sign up for the online service. Anyway, the game will be summed up in the cliché "Pros and Cons" as seen below.
- Interesting and diverse set of cars. Some are locked to "DLC" that are not included with the base game, but with over 70 cars, it is enough for anybody.
- Huge and expansive map. No barriers, and no punches pulled. A surprising amount of the map does not take place on convential roads, and that can range from railroad tracks, to tops of bridges, and more. Many secret areas included, and very fun to toy around with in.
- Straight forward events. No need for complicated gimmicks, just race from point A to point B, and you can even forge your own path there!
- Lots of depth. Should we mention the 70+ cars and expansive map again? Many hours of nonstop action and adventure are included in this fine game.
- Tons of things to find and smash. Everything from billboards, gates, and especially cars.
- Detailed crash cinematics. Watching in awe as your vehicle rolls around the highway is a sight to behold, every time.
- Unrestricted free roam. It wouldn't be an open world game without it. No cops, no forced events, no nothing getting in your way of unbridled exploration!
- Limited, but appreciable level of car customization.
- Unfortunately, the "Burnout Store", has long been shut down. There are ways of circumventing this, but it requires acquiring the game though Origin, signing up on both versions in the same EA account, and buying the DLC from there. Some DLC didn't even make the cut in the first place, such as "Big Surf Island".
- Lack of Steam cloud. While this isn't a must, it would be convienent.
- While the crashing cinematics are pretty, they often cost precious seconds of time spent racing against a clock, and some of them can even drag on if the car doesn't lose momentum fast enough.
- While it is nice to have an online mode, it won't last forever, and ultimately some features might be lost forever should the servers shut down.
- The game's equivalent of an annoying sidekick, that being the DJ Atomika. He honestly isn't much of a help.
And that sums up the review for now, all that I can think up of in my head. I have been having plenty of fun playing
, and I hope that is true for you.

This is a solid HO/puzzle game with very nice visuals and sounds. The usual quick story is present. A dark force has taken your son and you have to save him.
The puzzles and HO scenes are well done. Everything is crisp even at 1440p. There are a lot of puzzles here, but they are not too difficult. The HO scenes are pretty standard. Occasionally, they change it up where you have to use items they give you and find the matching object on the scene.
The art and drawings are very detailed and vibrant. Way better than average and is a shining point to the game.
You are able to fast travel using the map. Also, you can customize the difficulty to suit your needs.
There are a small number of collectibles throughout the game. With some extra time scanning the scenes, you should be able to find them all.
I had 3 minor interface issues while playing.
-The map button is too close to the Hint button. You could accidentally press it trying to look at the map.
-The map button has an odd clickable area to activate it.
-It can be easy to accidentally back out of a HO scene or puzzle by moving the cursor down to the bottom of the screen.
+Really nice and vibrant visuals
+Variety of HO scenes and puzzles
+Nice music and sound effects
+Map button placement and clicking oddities
+Easy to accidentally back out of HO or puzzle scene
+Ads for other games before you reach the starting screen

Endorlight is a rogue-like dungeon explorer in the style of Spelunky (ish), but rather watered down. The game's point is to (at least for now) pass from one almost same level to another, while gathering gold and gems on your way lower and lower.
As I've already said, the game is inspired by Spelunky (seems so). So gather monies, kill enemies, avoid traps and get to the end of the level. That said, at this moment, it's like Spelunky without some of the crucial features like: shops, bombs, ropes, bosses and pretty much - a point to all of this. You've got 3 weapons to use, but to be honest, axe and the whip feel almost the same (I think there might be slight a difference in the range?)
The gameplay is pretty smooth and reactive, haven't noticed any glaring issues here. That said, there are a few minor annoyances. The gold and gems are unpickable for a while after falling out of a container, which made me go back to repick the items which I thought I had already picked. Another thing is the lack of possibility to break chests/pots/crates while standing on them, except by using a bow(?). There's also an issue with the whip that its range is actually shorter than the animation indicates. The last thing that really annoyed me, however, is not a bug is that the spikes will always instantly kill you when you fall on them, but there's a certain height, if you fall from they don't do anything to you. Sometimes the level design forces you to climb on a wall and jump on spikes and it's a guessing game if they will one-hit-ko you or will you actually manage to land safely.
As far as I noticed the levels are generated procedurally on each playthrough. Quite often you might find areas that are not accessible without being lucky with a bomb monster or a crate with a bomb. There is also a possibility that an unfortunate bomb will leave you trapped in an area and you'll be forced to restart.
The game looks pretty nice at first, if you like the oldschool pixelated graphics. After several levels it gets really dull though because you'll always visit levels in the same biome.
There's only one song and, as far as I know, you can't turn it off. It gets repetitive quite quickly and you just stop paying attention to it or mute the sound altogether after a while. There's also a problem with sounds being played every time you press the attack button, instead of when you actually take a swing.
At this point, the game is really poor in terms of content. There are basically 4 types of enemies (+ a few reskins that just have more hp or slightly more damage on touch). You can gather gold, but there's no way to make any use out of it. There are 3 biomes, two of which share the exact same pool of monsters and neither happens to have anything that stands out from another (apart from the color). There's also no sense of progression - you can just jump down each level and proceed to another as there's not much point in killing anything or gathering gold anyway.
The game is at very early level of development and
. There's just no point in playing the game at the moment, as the amount of content will only keep you in it for half an hour or so (unless you're waiting for the cards to drop).

Fran Bow is is easily one of the best indie horror adventures out there. (At least in my opinion).
It starts very strong in a quite familiar setting when it comes to horror games. But it quickly ends up being very unique.
You play as the ten year old girl Fran, whose parents got killed. She herself got locked away in an asylum and now tries to escape and find her cat.
The adventure gameplay is very similar to other games in this genre plus some minigames here and there.
But here comes a special thing:
You get some pills, which allows Fran to see some sort of sick alternate reality. So you have to puzzle your way through two different realities.
Overall the puzzles are often unique, creative and fun to solve. Sometimes in a very "childish" way, but most of the time they seem to be logic.
There were only a few rare spots where I needed a hint or two.
The artstyle is also very unique and looks great. It might not be everyones taste, but the overall quality is very high and consistent.
There are a tons of details and love was put into every single screen. You will also see many "close up" drawings and nice animations.
I can't think of any real contras for this game, so it's hard to make a pro/contra list.
All I can say is, that if you are looking for a great and very unique adventure with a story you'll think about for quite a while, you can't make anything wrong with Fran Bow.
