Story: 6/10
With multiple endings, Uncanny Valley is more about understanding the small world than it is in dictating what's the primary narrative. What's neat is that each choice leads to a fairly satisfying and decent narrative that explores the world just enough to make the game feel worthwhile but also allow for a comfortable replay that doesn't feel repetative. That said, a few of the endings are quite short, while others are actually quite long, so it's hard to predict how much time you're about to sink into the game. My suggestion is to set aside a few hours before playing this game, since you may want to pursue different endings in the same binge.
The story itself has decent characters, a fairly believable progression, and an excellent atmosphere of mystery. It's borderline dreadful at times, but it isn't quite dreadful. Since this is more of a sci-fi horror than it is paranormal, I don't think I ever felt terrified or humbled, but I did feel a sense of hopelessness as things progressed.
The downside is there isn't anything here that hasn't been experienced elsewhere. That's not to downplay the general enjoyment of the game, but it means I'm not necessarily playing the game with any unique surprises that made the game stand out from other pixelated games, or horror games, or games with androids. Even beyond the realm of games, these light themes have been explored in film media so it's not a unique experience in that regard either, but the game still stands out as an interesting take on those influences. It's just neat. Really neat.
Gameplay: 5/10
It's relaxing, yet unsettling. A strange pairing, but blended well in an otherwise simple premise. However, some of the gameplay mechanics, similar to the story, aren't new. It's not that they aren't engaging, but rather that this game borrows from some other games, if at least unintentionally.
Exploration can be quite fun. I'm not a big fan of games with timers, so I found this pretty irritating, but I know it dictates some of the decisions that impact what ending someone gets, so I couldn't complain all that much.
It is to be noted that while the game is playable, I was completely unable to save. I opened this game with the intention of having a good spooky adventure, but I also wanted to push for all the achievements. I was pretty dissapointed when I found out the save function for me didn't work very well, so I ended up having to restart upon death a few times. Since the game is quite short, I didn't find this to be fatal in my gaming experience, but it still was quite bothersome.
Enjoyment: 6/10
I wasn't bored. I would even say I was a step above that and say it was pretty dang fun, but I haven't touched it since my binge session months ago when I was home sick from work. Either way, it's still quite fun and if you can look passed some of the bothersome aspects, the game itself is pretty neat. I'm quite interested in seeing more games from this developer, in all honesty. This game was pretty neat, and while the mechanics and story aren't all that new, it's still a fun game in its own right, and it happens to be quite spooky despite not having any stereotypical horror elements to it, such as paranormal influence or mad murderers.
OVERALL: 6/10

From the amount of time I played Uncanny Valley It\'s somewhat tricky to decide whether I recommend it or not because it has a bunch of good things I liked, things I don\'t like, and potential that may not have been executed to the desired hearts of gamers.
Uncanny Valley is another one of those games that sound good on paper but the execution may not have been as good.
First the good things I liked from what I\'ve played;
- Story
Specifically the endings I got so far as they remind me of the clock tower endings and they are quite interesting especially the part where \'someone prevents you from hurting yourself\' that ending cause a little dent of cringe in me as I watched what happened.
- The horror
The horror is somewhat alright, I enjoyed the dream sequence sections where messed up things happen like a nightmare would. The endings also qualify with the one mentioned above. I wasn\'t totally scared at all but it certainly did alright.
What I didn\'t like;
- No skips
Not being able to skip/speedthrough the first couple of minutes of the game where you have to watch the credits, get to the work place, and mess around for a couple before things can actually happen. It\'s so tedious I wished there was a flow chart liek from Virtue\'s Last Reward/chapter select where you jump to the part where you actually have some influence on the story. Replaying the game? Sure that\'s fine. Replaying a part of the game that I\'ve seen? Not fine.
- Glitches
The only glitches I\'ve seen is that if you interact too fast the text in the text box actually blend togerther to where you can\'t read anything, Also sometimes if you play the game too fast or do something weird your characters disappear.
In my first playthrough I kept making your character go to sleep in bed(by accident) and I wasn\'t punished for it. In fact it felt like I trapped the game in a loop because I had no need to go do the security job afterwards and the timer never starts counting again. Oh and when I got the objective to go fix something, I wasn\'t allowed to fix the thing I was told to fix(thankfully it didn\'t matter).
- Lack of real consequences
The conseqeuence gameplay sounds like a good idea once again but they never really did anything with it. As with the continous sleeping I made Tom go through and never got punished at his job at all, which on that note you don\'t need to do shifts everyday there\'s no point from what I\'ve played aside from finding info on the company through tapes and emails. As for avoiding combat there\'s not much to say just don\'t get hit.
- The text
The text isn\'t hard to read, buuuuuuuut sometime the text choice for these games can go kiss my boot to the face because they can be hard to read sometimes.
- Your character
For a guy that looks like he\'s in his mid 20s he\'s such a pusshi, running out of breathe quickly, getting tired and SLEEPING ON THE SPOT(then later teleported to his bed). Your character is such a wimp.
- The horror
I know I said the horror is alright, but that\'s the thing. It\'s just alright. The horror in the real world in the game are just meh and you quickly find out what the horror is and after that you\'re just fighting something out of James Cameron\'s nightmare *hint hint
- Confusion
The notepad that keeps track of your object are sometimes not clear like when I was suppose to meet up with a character, there was a note, but in the notepad it doesn\'t tell/remind you of where to meet that character. Also the game could have been more helpful by telling me I picked up because I found some bandages that look like ammo but I never noticed that until I replayed it which could have helped me.
Overall Uncanny Valley can be interesting and I would urge you to give it a chance. But I can\'t in good conscience recommend it in it\'s current form and price it\'s being sold at and that you should get it on sale.

I would rate this game 4.5/5
Now this is an awesome fighting game! Compared to previous games in the series, the characters are significantly more balanced for fighting against each other. Overall, the gameplay experience is absolutely incredible. My grievances are minor and few, but for the sake of completion I will list them:
- The single player campaign is very enthralling, but there is no feature to skip ahead to a chapter once the chapter or the campaign itself is completed. In other words, if you've already completed the campaign and want to replay Chapter 7, you have to play through from the beginning before getting there. Similarly, the lack of a 'save game' feature prevents multiple people from playing the campaign at different paces
- The single player campaign only allows you to play as the 'good guys', thus halving what otherwise would have been a komplete experience.
- I might be mistaken, but it is my understanding that other releases of this game come with the first Mortal Kombat movie, and this one does not. Similarly, the character 'Tremor' is a PS Vita exclusive missing here. Perhaps other 'exclusives' are missing as well? Very disappointing, considering this is the 'Komplete Edition'
- Certain characters are not selectable from the character select screen, including Shao Kahn, Goro, and Kintaro, despite still technically being playable by means of Shang Tsung's ability to morph into his opponent and thus acquire all of this abillities. Also, Goro is directly playable in the Challenge Tower, but not anywhere else.
- Motaro is present in the single player campaign, but is neither playable nor fightable. Other characters from the MK universe are missing altogether, although in all fairness the missing characters tend to be minor and largely unmemorable.
- While the gameplay experience feels amazing, the lack of varied animations and sound effects/dialog can make the game feel slightly monotonous at times. In other words, I would have been nice if, for each movement, a number of slightly different animations or sound affects would accompany the action instead of the same ones over and over again.

Although my favourite genre is Space 4X I only played Stardrive recently despite tracking the game throughout.
Compared to games such as Distant Worlds Universe I did not find Stardrive immersive at all as it was very uneventful with a limited storyline.  The AI was weak and it very quickly became an AI curbstomp in my first game while still learning the mechanics.  The game is strategically shallow.  There is an obvious need to spam troops.  A good technology tree is essential and this game was distinctly lacking in that respect.  The ground invasion mechanic is very simplistic.
The ship design is cool.  The combat is okay but I vastly prefer Sins of a Solar Empire.  I didn't really notice any of the bugs and missing features that some people go on about but then for $8 my expectations were low.
The Developer takes an extremely hard line to Moderation which is often unfair and unreasonable.  I've recently seen a poster banned and all his posts deleted despite the fact not a single forum rule was broken.  Some of my posts have also been deleted despite also never breaking a forum rule.  Unfortunately the Developer is stuck in the habit of shooting himself in the foot with respect to the future of his own community.
I really don't understand why some consider the game groundbreaking. I would rate Distant Worlds Universe, Endless Space, Galactic Civilisation 2 and Sins of a Solar Empire Rebellion all as significantly better games, each in their own way.  You can see the potential but a lot is unrealised.
There are patches but they are very slow and limited compared to games like Distant Worlds Universe.
There is hope with the Stardrive Extended Mod and perhaps there will be a vastly improved effort with Stardrive 2.   It's possible I could really get into them so I'll stay involved.
Post Review Note: Along with others I have now been banned and all my posts deleted despite breaking no forum rules. Be warned.

The visual aesthetic and reality-warping mechanics in this game are fantastic, as are Fran's child-like responses and musings about the things in the world, such as those that are macabre. Also, the setup of the story is magnificent.
Everything else? Not that great. The story dwindles into being less and less enjoyable with every section of the game that you clear, until the ending which makes almost no sense and failed to satisfy, and this is coming from someone who is used to piles and piles of crap endings to games over the last few decades. Although the plot started out fantastic with so much promise, it just got incredibly weird and felt like it lost focus on what made it so interesting in the first chapter.
The puzzles/adventure element of the game involving warping realities is great, but anything not directly related to that is often quite unclear as to what to do, and there's no "highlight all items on screen" button or option like you might find in other adventure games. Sure, some of the older titles didn't have this, but you knew what you could interact with because the backgrounds and the items you could pick up or interact with looked so very different. In this game, however, the items you can collect often blend in or are too easy to overlook and forget about, leading to wandering aimlessly until I lucked out and saw something new, or had to pull up a walkthrough on multiple occasions. One puzzle in a library involving symbols representing numbers still didn't make sense even after I looked up the solution online.
So in conclusion, great look, great reality-warping control, Fran's a great character with great child-like things to say about weird stuff and events, the plot is incredibly disappointing, and some of the puzzles are a true pain. I would recommend either old classics like the Space Quest or Kings Quest series, or newer adventure games like the Deponia series if you want to have better fun and plot than Fran Bow. I don't hate it, but it's quite disappointing.

This one feels old. Not in "old school" kind of way, just outdated. It's like playing some mediocre game from the mid-2000s, whose name you won't even remember afterwards. You'll feel it in the UI, graphics, sound effects and voice acting, gameplay mechanics, everything.
While the setting seems intriguing, the story is at best generic. I didn't play the first part, and i couldn't quite understand what's going on and why should i care. Who is this Katarina chick and why is she helping Van Helsing? Why is general Harker a "bad guy" if all he wants is to clean the streets from monsters and bandits? What's up with this Resistance? Who are they resisting, exactly? Why the scientists are suddenly villains? Why half of the people here have slavic names and the other half don't? Where are all the vampires and why is one of them Van Helsing's ally? I really had no time and/or desire to figure all of this out. Seriously, even Torchlight had a better story, at least it was simple and self-explanatory.
To make things worse, the game has its share of bugs, too. And the co-op mode, which is the only one i'd ever want to play in this case, is currently a laggy mess.
Overall, the game's not horrible, and it probably has its moments in the later stages, but to me it's just not worth it. I'd rather pick any alternative action-RPG (i.e. Diablo 3, PoE, Grim Dawn, Torchlight 2...) than this one.

EDIT: This review was written while the game was still in Season 1. Now that it's begun Season 2, some of the issues I've listed have been fixed. Most notably, the game now supports controllers.
I still do not consider this a good game, but I wanted to make this clear anyway.
Allow me to state this up front: I'm not a fan of the Street Fighter franchise. Never has been, probably never will be. I played a bit of Alpha 3 as kid, but it never stuck with me. Then I tried out Third Strike and SSFIVAE when I was a teenager after having been inspired by pro players and, while I generally enjoyed my time, I was never truly able to get a grasp of the gameplay. I just prefer airdashers like BlazBlue and Guilty Gear, I'm afraid.
With that said, I absolutely hate this game. I've tried so, so hard to get into it, far more so than I ever did with any previous Street Fighter game, and the game seems to be actively fighting me at every turn. I got it day one after having liked what I saw in videos from the various beta tests, and was met with the game refusing to launch. At all.
I don't recall exactly how, but I did eventually, after hours of trying, get the game to work. Problem was, it wouldn't acknowledge that I'd plugged in a controller to play with. So I used third party software to get it working. And it still didn't recognize it.
That was absolutely baffling to me. Even a game that I can download for free, like Melty Blood, will accept my PS4 controller. How on earth this game failed to do so was, and still is, beyond me.
Eventually, though, after many restarts and fiddling around with the game and my programs, I got it to accept my controller.
THEN I was met with the completely and utterly busted netcode that made the game downright unplayable whenever I got into an online match. That is, WHEN I got into an online match. It would seriously take me over an hour to find a match at times. Finding one within half an hour almost never happened. I get that I live in Denmark, a small European country, but that was ridiculous. Even niche anime fighters like BlazBlue let me find matches faster than that, even during the night.
Suffice to say, my initial reaction was not positive. I'd spent about 30 hours at this point, most of which was waiting for online matches while either browsing the web in the background or messing around with extremely shallow single player options.
Things are thankfully different now, though. I can actually find matches quite quickly now, and the netcode seems to be pretty decent. However, it has started to not recognize my controller again, and I still don't know the cause. It worked just fine yesterday, but it doesn't work today. Not only that, I've discovered an entirely new issue that forced me to spend about an hour looking up possible solutions, the only one of which that worked requiring me to DELETE GAME FILES AND SAVE DATA. I suspect that this is what caused my controller to no longer work, but I have no way of knowing for sure, and I don't know what to do to get it working again.
"So what?" you might think. "Maybe these are all issues on your end, and you just don't know how to use a computer properly." Well, ignoring the fact that multiple other people have had these exact same issues and that my PC can run just about every other game on the market just fine, like Dark Souls 3, and have them register my controller without any issues, let's assume that you won't have any of these issues and that you'll get the game running no problem. Maybe you won't even use a controller, so that problem might not even affect you at all. What then?
The game is still terrible. First and foremost, the story modes are pathetic. Yes, they've released a free DLC to rectify this somewhat, but the single character story modes are still utterly terrible. Survival Mode is just boring, with the CPU starting off being unable to do anything really, and suddenly having them read your button inputs, making them more frustrating and cheap than anything, and having them waste your time by forcing you to fight 25+ sandbags before you get back to the input reading ones. I haven't bothered with 30+ stage survival modes because of this, since I just don't want to force myself to waste upwards of half an hour only to potentially lose it to a boss that's basically a coin toss as to whether I win or lose.
And finally, the game has a whole bunch of minor annoyances, like how you have to manually set your preferences in training mode every single time you enter it and come back. Do you want it to show your attack data, key history, and not bother with Stun, like me? Too bad, you have to pause the game and manually change that every time you enter training mode, it doesn't save it like BlazBlue, Guilty Gear, Persona 4 Arena, UNIEL, and so on and so forth. Likewise, on the character select screen, it will always default to your "preferred" character, as opposed to the last character you picked. If your preferred character is Ryu, but you want to use Ken for a few matches, you have to either A: go back to the start menu and go into battle settings and then select Ken as your preferred character, then change it back when you're done, or manually go from Ryu to Ken and select a costume, color, and quote, every single time you start a match. Again, in BlazBlue and Guilty Gear, it just defaults to the last character you used to avoid this exact problem.
Also, and this isn't exactly about the game itself, but there's a strategy guide that contains all the frame data for moves used in this game. That guide, or rather, that frame data, is practically required if you want to play seriously at all. Knowing that Urien's MP is +3 on block, but that his MK is -1 on block, is essential knowledge if you want to build up a strong pressure game as him. What about knowing that his MK Chariot Tackle is -2 on hit, so using it actually puts you at a disadvantage? That kinda knowledge can decide games, and really should be in the game. MKX did a pretty good job of this, and it really ought to be the standard for fighting games.
You'll notice that I haven't actually talked about the gameplay. That's because there isn't much to say. It's worse than Ultra Street Fighter IV in just about every way, but hey, at least they made it easier to learn. I can appreciate that, seeing as how USFIV was pretty difficult to get into, but this game is so easy to learn that I think just about anyone can learn any character in a few hours at most. It's still a fun game at times, but it's a huge step back in just about every way.
Oh, and I almost forgot to mention: the graphics aren't even good. The game looks alright, but a lot of character models just look plain bad.
In conclusion, this game is utterly terrible and I highly suggest you find literally any other fighting game to invest your time in. That includes the previous games of this exact franchise, the vast majority of which are far superior to this game in every single way.
Sorry if this came off as me rambling, but I'm very passionate about fighting games, and seeing one as bad as this one receive as much attention as it does really rubs me the wrong way.

Fran Bow is a point and click adventure in which you play as a little girl whom is able to switch between two different realities through the use of her jar of pills. One of these realities is fairly normal (to begin with at least) and the other is a completely horrific version - blood and guts everywhere.
To me, the whole thing is kind of adolescent, and I don't get it. I can kind of see that there is a merging/blurring of the two realities that occurs, but what's the actual point here? The dialogue of the game alternates between delirious nonsense and then blunt and sinister, but never really manages to say anything except for "look at how delirious and sinister this is!". It's grim but in a facile, ungroundedly fictitious, ultimately pointless way. It's a little too much "My Chemical Romance" and a little less "Lord of the Flies".
I did, however, find the hand drawn art to be impressive, particularly the way Fran is animated, but overall I don't think this game was made with my demographic in mind.

Game's super dope, definitely play if you want a more simple fighting game that's based on footsies and strategy rather than an infinite amount of mechanics. The main drawbacks to this game are the sub-par netcode, the lack or Arcade mode, and the Battle Lounge system not working quite right. Other than that, the actual in-game part is one of the best fighting games I've ever played. Everything's smooth and feels natural, unlike how it felt in Street Fighter 4. (At least to me)
Some people are put off by all the 50/50 situations, the ability to just YOLO your way to victory online, and some of the character tiers; but frankly this is the most balanced fighting game in history, at least from what I can tell, and with enough skill, intuition, and knowledge; 50/50's and players that go ham can be looked at with confidence instead of fear.
If you enjoy any sort of competitive game, I definitely recommend at least trying this game for an hour and refund it if it doesn't suit your fancy, given that fighting game just aren't some people's thing.
That being said, this is a great game with a perfect blend of competitive and casual nature attached to it. If you enjoyed a Street Fighter game long ago, you'll definitely be reminded of those times playing Street Fighter V. Even if you don't feel like you're improving, it doesn't have to make it any less fun to horse around with your friends doing random character matches.
(NOTE for those without a Gamepad or Arcade Stick - There is no implimentation of keyboard rebinding as of writing this, so if you want a keyboard layout other than "WASD" for moving and "GHJK/BNM," for your attacks, I would suggest getting a temporary keybind changing program like Joy2Key.)
(ALSO if you DO own a Gamepad or Arcade Stick, but it is a PS4 or PS3 controller - There is also no implimentation of Dinput yet, so I would get a program that converts DInput controller into an XOutput (Microsoft/XBox controller output). I personally recommend the plugin made specifically for this game XInput. The file should be titled "xinputx_x.dll" when you download it. I also recommend the program "XOutput". You simply open it when you want to play the game and it automatically converts a DInput to an XOutput. It should be a file titled "XOutput.vx.xx" upen download.)

I have played most of the games in the Fallout universe and most games made by Bethesda. I have over 200 hours in Fallout 4 at the time of writing this review. I have played through all of the expansions and finished them, so what I say here is based entirely on my experiences in playing this game.
A good place to start is the main game and the main storyline. The story is actually alright, with a few segments to it that are really well-made, but for the most part, it can't even come close to what New Vegas has. However, what this game does have going for it are interesting characters, a world in which factions are warring and you can make the difference by siding with one of them. It's not as diverse in terms of the ways you can finish the game as New Vegas, but you can do things that you couldn't in any other Fallout game, such as build your settlements. So, to be perfectly clear, New Vegas' storyline is still superior in many aspects and the sheer amount of interesting content in it makes it one of the best RPGs to ever have been made. But this review will emphasize what is good about Fallout 4 and why you might want to get it. This is where the comparisons with other Fallout games end.
The plot itself isn't what you will be focusing on for the majority of the game, so let's go over everything else in the game. The characters are interesting. I don't want to spoil anything from the game, so I won't be using any names or precise descriptions. There aren't a lot of characters you can really feel with in the main plot, but the ones that are there are pretty cool, one in particular. There's a lot of mystery in this game, as you would expect from a Fallout game, and you will see a lot of strangeness in the Fallout world. The atmosphere is key here. You probably want to do a lot of exploring coming into a Bethesda game, and this game will give you plenty of chances to do that. After all of the hours I have spent in this game, I still keep finding new unexplored areas that are sometimes a real treat to see and explore.  What has slightly put me off is how some of the areas around your starting point may seem like empty wasteland with little variation, but the deeper you go in, the more you realize just how vast the world is and how much you have to do in it.
Side quests. Everyone loves them, right? At least, when they're done properly. This game does some side quests really well, and some are just so tedious it's almost funny. You will find your fair share of "go fetch this, now go do it again, now go defend this place." It's extremely repetitive and you can get seriously bored very fast if you do those quests without anything actually interesting in between. Thankfully, you can skip most of these, unless you really want some of the achievements that come with them. It seems like these were added to make the game seem longer than it is, but there's no need for that, as the game has plenty to offer if you just ignore the nonsense along the way.
What about the expansions? In case you were wondering, the expansions are absolutely worth it, and you should probably play Fallout 4 with all of them if you want to get the most out of it. This is my opinion and I know many will disagree, but these expansions make the game something so much more than what the base game is. Even the ones that add new things to settlements are good in their own way. Personally, I love building up settlements. This is something that I truly enjoy in Fallout 4 and I have spent many hours just on designing, building and polishing settlements around the world. They add this element of survival which makes it feel to me as if the conflict in the world is constant and the struggle to survive ever-present. I enjoy roleplaying a lot in Bethesda games and this just adds a lot of flavor for making it yours, it creates this connection between you and nameless NPCs that would otherwise be irrelevant, and just makes you sink deeper into the atmosphere of the world.
Far Harbor is one of the best expansions ever made. It's so well-done, from the atmosphere, to the music and the characters, to just the entire feel of it. The story is exceptionally interesting and is handled in a mysterious and subtle way, making you question many things about life and reality. This expansion alone is better than all of the base game, so I really recommend you to get it. It's grim, it's deep, it's shrouded in mystery and it's also pretty hilarious at some points. This is what the main game could have been from the start, and that is the most serious fault of this game. The developers are clearly capable of making content that is interesting and that just makes you feel proud for having it in your library but, for some reason, they decided to make the base game more streamlined.
Nuka World is a massive expansion in terms of the map size, amount of content that you receive and all of the new gameplay mechanics that it introduces. It is also extremely, excrutiatingly, hilariously repetitive. You will get to see several very interesting locations in the expansion, as well as meet some individuals that have either been only referenced before or even shown in previous Fallout games. What this expansion does is draw you in to a world of raiding, and you have a lot of freedom with what you do here. There are raider factions that you can ally with, you can decide to give them territory and in return, they will eventually come to respect you and give you things, ranging from caps to legendary gear and new options in settlements, as well as some pretty unique items not present in the base game. You can become a raider overboss if that is something that appeals to you, but doing so will change the opinions of other factions about you. A huge addition in terms of item variety comes from all of the Nuka Cola-themed items, and this includes 20 new types of Nuka Cola that you can craft yourself, each with their own special effects, and some with a new and unique appearance. You also get a ton of new weapons, new things to build in your settlements, new enemies, and just overall more content.
Something that is very important to note is that Nuka World will lead you through a series of repetitive and mind-numbing tasks, but you don't have to do all of them to enjoy this expansion. What I did was just go out into the world. The map isn't quite as big as one might expect so you can easily reach its edge, but there are definitely some very interesting things to see. There are easter eggs, moments of horror, strange encounters and an homage, all tucked far away from anyone just doing the quests, because they will almost never lead you to the outer reaches of the map. As for the design of the area, it is good and quite varied from area to area, and everything is actually connected through a giant underground system which is pretty cool. You can also change the way the world looks and functions by completing quests, but most of the quests will have you do raider-related things. It's strange how they decided to implement this. You do have a chance to end the Raiders' regime, but it is best done after you do all of the important quests, because there is much to be gained by being a raider overboss.
The other expansions add some variety to the things that you can do in the world, and especially what you can do in your settlements. They're worth it if you like building settlements. The robot expansion actually lets you build your very own robots, and there are lots and lots of options of how you can make them. What's really cool about that is that you can both order them to do specific things in your settlements where there is a lack of settlers to do them, and naturally they will then defend these settlements, but you can also take them with you as companions! That's really cool and if having a custom-made robotic companion sounds good to you, you should get that expansion.
Also the creation club isn't that bad. So go get the game!

DOOM BFG Edition is a collection of the prior DOOM releases in their most complete form as stated by ID software themselves. Let's find out if that statement holds true or if this release spelled a different kind of DOOM for the franchise?
DOOM 3 BFG Edition is a collection of games that defined the first person shooter genre across multiple generations. From DOOM, DOOM II, DOOM 3, and DOOM 3: Resurrection of Evil, along with The Lost Missions, each had their own impact on the genre of varying success. This release is headlined by DOOM 3: BFG a "remastered" version of 2004's well recieved title which is considered a classic by many. So does this remaster bring enough to the table to be considered exactly that?
NOTE: Most importantly this section of the review is going to focus more on covering the remastered version of DOOM 3 and it's dlc content, titled DOOM 3: BFG Edition. This is simply due to the fact that the other content in regards to DOOM I and II are direct re-releases of the originals with no changes being made.
So what exactly constitutes this as being a remaster? Well......Not much. Listed below are exactly what graphics options are available to you in game which are meager to say the least.
Resolution - (Windowed - Full Screen - Up to 4K)
Frame Control (60 - 120 - Unlimited)
Vertical Sync (Enabled or Disabled)
Anti-Aliasing (Up to 8x)
Motion Blur (Up to 64x)
Texture LOD Bias
3D Options (varying)
Now although there aren't many options overall, what's there serves for future functionality and that's really what's most important at least in terms of easily applied in game available resolutions that will be displayed without issues on today's current HD monitors and screens.
Now that's where we run into another slight issue. As many fans of the previously released DOOM 3 know, there were texture pack mods available on the net that exceeded the BFG versions texture resolution quality. In comparison this releases textures are blurry when played at higher reolutions yet, still actually look acceptable overall if and only if considering this is a simple port of the Xbox 360 version.
Yet, that's not how something should be judged, should it? So with that being said, in regards to the textures quality in game, they simply don't meet the quality expectations that a gamer had come to expect on PC in 2012 (when this was released), let alone in 2015.
Frame Control, Vertical Sync and Anti-Aliasing are all basic graphics settings that aren't exactly something to write home about, expected but, still welcome. Motion Blur is either a hit or a miss for many PC gamers but, is in fact presented here nonetheless, which is a bit odd due to the fact that there were so many other options begging to be within this package that would have served this  remaster and the series fans much, much better. Once again, nothing much to say in regards to texture LOD, other than it does what it's supposed to do as per usual, yet with lack luster results due to the lack of high quality resolution texture packs presented directly from ID software.
Now this is where things actually get interesting. If DOOM 3: BFG is played in 3D the experience in quite an upgrade to the previous original installment. When enabled, the experience is almost surreal in certain ways, especially so if each in game setting is maxxed out. Sadly though, the amount of PC gamers that actually have the ability to experience this fantastic video mode are extrememly limited. So much so that, this once again becomes an almost irrelevant feature in the grand scope of things. Not many PC gamers have 3D enabled monitors, let alone the hardware to operate and utilize it.
So with that being said, if you do in fact (like myself) have the hardware necessary, you'll be in for an interesting DOOM 3 experience. Sadly though, I'm speaking to an incredibly small user base.
O.k, here we go.....Considering the incredible lack of in game options which, of them none are especially resource intensive, DOOM 3: BFG most definitely isn't a highly optimized port. Will you be able to run it with respectable resolution and in game settings? Yes, more than likely pending you possess the required graphics hardware. Will you be able to run it fully maxxed out (Including 3D) without issues? Most likely not, regardless of the hardware you possess, which is unacceptable. Yet, considering most users wouldn't be utilizing the 3D options anyways, this doesn't hurt the experience, but is an injustice to the series fans who supported them financially upon release.
Any previous fans of the series know there's nothing new here, but that doesn't mean that there's anything else that should have been either. The DOOM experience in a whole is considered by many (myself included) to be the pinnacle of the true single player fps experience. Intense, exlierating and downright frightening and that last one has nothing to do with the graphics and never did. It's created by the impending doom of being chased by and immense amount of npc's who do not stop coming after you, leaving you no time to prepare so, your only option is to run, strafe and generally flee in fear until you see an option to peck away at them one by one, with the general outcome being...you're dead.
Which is fantastic! The original DOOM games and to a lesser extent DOOM 3 were created during a time that the general fps skill base on an entry level were on a totally different scale. These games were created to challenge you to the fullest, while giving you crumbs in return for your efforts, all the while turning you into a DOOM fan like many of us who have come before you.
DOOM GUY > GETS ATTACKED BY > OUTER DIMENSIONAL HELL DEMONS > DOOM GUY > GETS ANGRY > DOOM GUYS RETALIATES > WITH > THE SUPER SHOTGUN > DOOM GUY > RUNS OUT OF AMMO > DOOM GUY FLEES > A DEMON CHASES > DOOM GUY> 100 DEMONS NOW CHASE > DOOM GUY > DEMONS LOST HIM > DOOM GUY > RETURNS WITH > THE BFG > ALL OF THE DEMONS > = DEAD.......Nuff said!
If this were during the original release of DOOM 3 in 2004 the online experience would have been brimming with players on any given hour. Yet, sadly the same can't be said about this remastered edition. There simply isn't anyone playing this online anymore but, that doesn't mean you can't get some friends together and frag til' your hearts content.
Considering there are multiple titles in this release, I suppose the best thing for me to convey is that each releases sound design was exceptional during their time and surpassed anything else on the market at their respective times. Agurably so, the DOOM series stands as a figurehead of the industry and always has in terms of sound design. So each game within the confines of this collection will undoubtably brim with nostalgia and were often later copied by far too many develpers throughout history..... Simply put, just open a door and let the sounds of nostalgia echo throughout.
It's DOOM for goddsake, people are still playing the original release since it was published. In terms of replay value, it doesn't get much better than this. BFG edition contains the entire DOOM franchise all in one fairly tidy package, you'll easily get hundreds of hours of gameplay out of it. Rough edges aside, this collection is arguably one of the best of all time and deserves a place in any fps library. Just as long as you consider this release an Ultimate Collection, instead of the remaster they wanted you to believe it was.

With the addition of workshop, basically all of my complaints were cleaned up quick and easy. But here is a problem I have with the game, with the addition of workshop this early in the games developement. It kind of removes the need for the developers to address any issues, with the current model of the game, as mods can literally fix everything. I understand the current version is very stable, balanced, and performance issues have been fixed. I just hope the developers continue to add things to the game even though, they really don't have to. Also it has loot like terraria, which obviously adds a ton of playtime on its own. This game has a lot of potential, though it has a couple of bugs it is still enjoyable - and I look forward to seeing the next developments

Thought provoking!
The subject of psychology has always been interesting to me. Mental disorder, insanity, truth, reality and consciousness are all things this game reflects on.
You play as a little girl that goes through a significant trauma having lost her parents and ends up being treated in a slightly dodgy mental institution. You go through any means possible to escape the asylum, be reunited with your best (and only) friend, your beloved cat, Mr. Midnight and get back home. The journey is full of turns and oddities that will further add to the question of Fran’s mental state.
The story is intriguing to follow and always begs the question of what is going on. Even when you find answers, there was always (at least for me) an underlining curiosity over what was real and which side was true.
Insanity tends to bring distrust, whether the person is sane or not, given the label of “Insane” by someone “Sane” will always lead to uncertainty about the person. You fight with Fran to keep her certainty and sanity against the people who are trying to keep her locked up.
I really enjoyed this game. The art style and use of colour is great at getting across the right emotions. Oppressive scenes are dark and cold, safe and comfortable scenes are bright and open. The music also adds drama to the game in the right places and helps to set in those emotions.
There is no voice acting, although with this game I thought that it kind of fit in that way.
There is a fun mechanic which lets you switch the scene between the every day reality, to the reality Fran sees when she takes her medication. It opens up new possibilities for point and click puzzle solving and makes the game that tad bit more interesting and eerie. Effectively showing two sides to every situation.
The transitioning between chapters is a good way to break up a fairly lengthy game and essentially “skip” the unnecessary bits to play (for example, the travel to where the next chapter is set).
I found that the game flowed well, especially for a point and click. I usually get stuck fairly quickly in these genre of games but there was only a few times I got stuck and even then I think that was because I played until it was late and I was tired. Returning to the game after a break with a fresh mind usually solved the problem pretty quickly.
In terms of 100%ing this game it’s fairly easy. You aren’t likely to get everything on your first play through, but it’s easy enough to do a quick run through again to get any you missed. I played through the game twice in the hours I have put into it if that is any help.
All in all this is a great game, I liked it! I would say it’s a must try for people that like the point and click genre or generally have any interest in mental disorder, psychology or even just thinking about things a little more philosophically.
TL;DR : Intriguing story, nice art style and use of colour and contrast, gentle music that adds to the drama of the game, a well-fitting use of no voice acting, a good flow to it and generally just an all round great game. Give it a try.

Nearly all the Doom releases so far, in one package, with steam achievements. The Doom 3 in this edition is “remastered,” though not to everyone’s liking; the old Dooms are almost vanilla with a few odd tweaks that most people won’t notice. Doom purists and those that are looking to mod are both advised to avoid this.
I do recommend this for: 1) total Doom newbs looking for the simplest path forward to prepare their souls for the upcoming Doom release, 2) old-school gamers that want to replay the entire series on a modern machine through one interface and don’t want to fuss around with mods, and 3) steam achievement hunters with strong nostalgia for the series. However, I recommend this edition only if it is dirt cheap; several high-profile critics and a ton of series fans justifiably slammed it at launch for being a bad deal (to say the least) and it’s impossible to argue with that logic at the launch price. Bought dirt cheap on the other hand, no worries.
Everyone else interested in the series will likely be happier avoiding the older titles altogether and waiting to see if the upcoming reboot is any good.
Things to note:
Online multiplayer seekers: There are two Doom 3 editions on steam (BFG and standard) and they do not have interoperable multiplayer. Doom 3’s multiplayer was never anything special and the core game is over a decade old, so expect either version’s online scene to usually be totally deserted, though both versions do have players and you can stumble on an open match now and then. Doom 3 multiplayer runs notoriously bad, but if you are willing to rough it (e.g., you fondly remember the days of dial-up multiplayer) matches can be fun and unpredictable in short bursts. Seriously competitive types or those that require smooth performance to have fun will just get enraged and are advised to avoid Doom 3 multiplayer entirely. The older Dooms do not have online multiplayer through steam.
Steam achievement hunters: beware the multiplayer-dependent achievements. Note the above caveats about multiplayer and plan to either bring a couple of friends along for the ride or to join the Doom multiplayer community group in steam and actively find people to play with if you want to 100% this.
A rundown of the D3BFG package for newbs to the series:
Included in the D3BFG pack are Ultimate Doom (Doom + TFC), Doom II, and Doom II’s NRFTL expansion. Just think of all of these as more of the same game. These original Dooms are simple but satisfying monster shooting galleries where navigating the levels is itself sometimes a puzzle to be solved and difficulty ramps up as you progress with bigger and trickier ambushes of tougher and crazier monsters.
The main focus of the D3BFG pack however is Doom 3 and its expansions ROE and TLM. Doom 3 was a reboot to the original Dooms; the story, feel, and gameplay are somewhat different. Doom 3 is a hybrid between a typical FPS game of that era and a simplified survival horror game of that era. The highlights in these games are creepy atmosphere, a few good jump scares, and some cool monsters.
A quick way to get a taste of the typical gameplay of the series without dedicating a lot of hours to it is to skip straight to the last expansions for each game engine (NRFTL for original, TLM for reboot) and try to beat them on hard difficulty. These expansions provide a shorter, more condensed snapshot of the core games for those short on time. Play NRFTL on Ultra-Violence and play TLM on Veteran (1 step down from Nightmare in both, which is ridiculously hard in the original and overly frustrating in the reboot).

Uncanny Valley, the debut title from Cowardly Creations is a mix of horror, adventure, and consequence-based gameplay. Drawing inspiration from Human's old Clock Tower games, Silent Hill, Twin Peaks, and perhaps the game mechanic from CoC: Dark Corners of The Earth as well, it's an interesting if flawed experience.
In Uncanny Valley, You're playing as Tom who accepts a job as night watchman at the abandoned facility way out in the middle of nowhere. Besides that building and the apartment complex that used to house its staff, there's nothing else for miles. The only people you can talk to is either Buck, the day guard or Eve, the maid at your apartment building. Neither of them has a whole lot to say, so you're left to your own devices, patrolling the corridors of the main building overnight, with the working shifts lasting around seven minutes, to make sure nobody is messing with it and then going home to go to sleep after your shift. Day in, day out.  Except there's all these computers lying around. And tapes. And videos. I mean, it's not like you have much else to do during your shift, so you may as well play around with them, right?
Well as much as I like to explore the facility and try to solve the mystery behind it, the selling point for this game is undoubtedly its branching story, which ultimately leads to one of several possible endings, like a Choose Your Own Adventure tale, and this is where the problem lies.
It seems to me that the developers were far more interested in making consequences to your failures rather than add in deaths that would require multiple playthroughs of the same area. For example, when enemies show up, this just means that you get beaten down and the available suite of endings changes. Enemies will also just give you game-changing injuries, such as chest wounds which cut down run time, a broken arm that makes weapon use impossible, or a broken leg that removes your ability to run.All of these things might make the game needlessly confusing and unfair, except that the game is very short. An hour or two is often all you need to play through it. So when you know what you're doing, the first half of the game where you work your night watch job becomes really redundant, but you still have to play through it each time to get to the game's more challenging second half. This can waste up to a half hour of your time on stuff you've already done, and it gets old real quick. This might not be a big issue on its own, but when enemies show up in the second half, things get worse. A simple screw-up can put you on the road to the exact same ending you got last time, and now you'll have to replay the whole game again for another attempt. You can try reloading an old save to make another attempt, but the autosave system often makes that impossible, and even goes so far as to delete your save when you get an ending. So, something that was meant to remove the annoying repetition of death in games actually has consequences that make you repeat the ENTIRE GAME instead, which is a whole lot worse than just repeating a small section. With the large consequences for failure and the lack of manual saves for me to make another attempt when I wanted to, it just wastes too much of my time on needless multiple playthroughs at the moment.
Overall, I love this game and would really like to explore it more, but I can't justify playing through another hour of it only to get the same ending again, even when following a guide. There’s a chance you will play the game a second, third, or maybe fourth time in order to experience the different endings, but if you, like me, felt satisfied after the first playthrough, the desire to replay it just plummets. Uncanny Valley is an interesting game with many great ideas, but without some saves to pull from, I just can't bring myself to keep trying for the other endings and recommend the game to other people, even for ten bucks.

It's hard to believe that many people like DOOM 3, but hate DOOM 3: BFG Edition. They are basically the same game, but BFG Edition has some upsides, as well as some downsides. For example, you no longer have to pull out your flashlight, which can be great for casual players, but possibly annoying for those who want extra challenge. Also, you can't mod BFG Edition, which means you can't get things like better graphics and stuff, but the game still is amazing. Besides including an enhanced version of DOOM 3, it also includes the expansion pack Resurrection Of Evil and The Lost Mission, as well as The Ultimate DOOM and DOOM II. Speaking of The Ultimate DOOM and DOOM II, the controls are a lot better than what I have of heard of the Steam Version.
As of right now (I haven't beaten any of them yet), I am going to give DOOM 3: BFG Edition a 9/10.
+Enhanced Version of DOOM 3
+Includes Resurrection of Evil
+Includes The Lost Mission
+Includes The Ultimate DOOM and DOOM II with better controls than the Steam Version
+Can use Flashlight and Weapon at the same time
+Includes Steam Achievements for DOOM 3, Resurrection of Evil, The Lost Mission, The Ultimate DOOM, and DOOM II
+Controller Support
-Can't Mod to make things better
-NO STEAM CLOUD (Every DOOM game on Steam has Steam Cloud, but not BFG Edition)
If you were to buy all of the games seperate, DOOM 3: BFG Edition would be the best deal.

I was a bit skeptical about this game. At first, it appeared to be a simple tower defense game, where you can fight in as well. But I have to say, I'm pleasantly surprised.
The tower defense bit I can be simple about: It's your basic tower defense. Machine guns, high damage guns, slowdown turrets, those kinda weapons are available, and all upgradable. You can buy them with credits you earn through gameplay. You place these guns on blocks, that you can use to lay out the path for the enemy to follow.
For the ingame fighting, you can choose from 4a5 characters to play, which basically determines your main weapon: Shotgun, sniper, machinegun. By leveling you get access to more weapons and other stuff. Although the weapons are not upgradable, you can use perks to increase their damage.
But it's the versatility of the in-game combat that give it that little bit extra that makes it interesting. You can engage some enemies, so they attack you and can be lured away from the path. Some enemies have higher damage points on their bodies, for extra damage, if you can hit it. Some perks can really help in killing off those enemies. In short, it's not just simple shooting that has been added, it gives it that little extra that makes you wanna play the game some more, just to try out those little extra perks or weapons, to see if you can get further.
There is 4 player coop, where all resources can be shared freely.
And graphically, it's ok. I do like how they added the little men to fight with you. They suck at combat, but it's a little extra that gives the game a 'face'.
Basically, if you like tower defense and FPS, you'll like this.

Fun enough, but absolutely no late game whatsoever. There's not much point researching ships bigger than frigates - all you need are some ships to keep the enemy's ridiculously weak fighter fleets at bay while you infantry rush them.
"Not finished", as others have said, in the sense that the whole game feels very shallow, but it's not buggy enough to really be considered a beta either - I'd call it a finished product, though it's not a great one. Not a bad game in some ways, but very little replay and not worth $30.
Yeah, I know I have like 170 hours on this despite saying very little replay. To be frank, I don't usually complete my 4X games because I get frustrated with the late game grindy-ness, and thusly, I did get quite a bit of time on Stardrive, which does certain parts of the mid-game reasonably well. Besides that, I bet at least 100 of those hours was spent designing ships, which is probably the best designed aspect of the game.
But unfortunately, that is the big issue with the game as well - designing ships, the most interesting part of the game, is not really actually all that important in terms of gameplay. You can certainly min-max the ♥♥♥♥ out of your transport ships, and design ultra-badass capital ships with hangers (which don't work, by the way) and plague bombs (because you can't blow up planets) and death rays, but in the end it doesn't really matter because you are really only going to build a bunch of frigates armed with super-missiles to crush the pathetic enemy fleet while you infantry rush him. Did I mention you can't blow up planets?
It sounds like I'm ♥♥♥♥♥ing about a specific tactic that works too well, and that someone with my hours is probably just good at the game. What I'm really trying to do here is save you money - this is not the easiest way to win the game, it's how you play the game, period. If you don't do it, the ultra-slow AI will eventually do it to you after several hours of ingame time, or at least try to. I personally used that time to build up a giant empire and a fleet of death ships that squished his little army without me having to do much of anything. Then quit and restarted because I realized that, nope, that was it, and now I'd have to spend two hours invading defenseless planets after I stocked up on cans of SPAM.
Not that you need an empire. You can easily ♥♥♥♥ everyone's day up with 10 planets if you are smart about what you build and research. Hint: Build and research everything, because the AI is slow as a turtle in concrete and will still be using popguns while you rock rocket launchers. There's also only a dozen or so things to build, and everyone has the same research trees, so you don't really need to prioritize well.

CC really brings the joy. There\'s a huge number of game elements here, and a fun thing is seeing how they interact together. For example, a level can be constructed to be like a factory with monsters pushing buttons in an automated way to open and close doors.
The game includes a nice level editor that is easy to use, and the player community has already contributed many good levels. It\'s easy to imagine spending hundreds of hours on it, once you get into the habit of playing the new levels that get released on a regular basis.

Now, I've played Aliens vs Predator 2, and honestly, I can't believe I'm saying this.
This game is worse than AvP2, despite the years seperating the two. Sure, the graphics are vastly improved. Rarely have xenomorphs or predators looked this cool, but in all honesty, that's all the game did for the series. Despite no less than three singleplayer campaigns, you'll breeze through all three of them in a span of hours, while remembering nothing of the bland levels and almost-copypasted story.
If you're considering getting it for the multiplayer segment, don't. At least AvP2, despite numerous balance issues, required some degree of skill to play online. I swear, the multiplayer is so full of instant-death attacks it's not even funny. Sneak up on someone, he dies without being able to fight back (unless you're a marine. Then you don't get sneak attacks). Numerous predator weapons are instant death. Same goes for melee against xenomorphs. You'll be tearing at your eyelids, not because enemies are better, but because the game took too long recognizing that your character turned around, resulting in that charging xenomorph still being able to use a stealth kill on you. Even if he gets his head blown off before the animation is complete, it makes no difference, you're still dead.
Then there are numerous other issues, like how the maps from the Collector's Edition were unavailable to anyone who only had the standard edition, splitting the already scarce multiplayer community further and making those maps effectively worthless, since the majority of people playing couldn't play on those maps. Oh, don't worry, they released those maps as DLC already, so if you're willing to pay more than it's worth, you can also have those maps most people won't have. You can walk around, enjoy the sights! Alone.
And that's another thing that irked me beyond belief. The sheer lack of inspiring multiplayer maps. Most of them were ripped off completely from the campaign, with no apparant effort made to create special gameplay or opportunities for xenomorphs or predators. The whole multiplayer segment reeks of missed chances, while the singleplayer campaign just stinks.
If you are an absolute AvP fan, this game may give you some giggles before you too get annoyed at the design flaws, the lack of content or depth, and the DLC packages splitting an already dying multiplayer community. Otherwise, steer clear. Steer wide clear.

As the game currently stands, Northgard is incredibly accessible, enjoyable and well-polished.
The depth of RTS strategy is only skin-deep, but I find this to be something viewed positively, as the develpoers appear to be trying to make the right choices for this game, rather than throwing the whole catalogue of traditional RTS mechanics and features at it in order to please everyone.
There have been incremental and considered changes by the developers, albeit at a great pace. Northgard feels light, and there's no pressure to learn vast amounts of control in order to enjoy it.
It also must be said that this is the first time I've ever enjoyed listening to the same music on a loop forever. I absolutely adore the soundtrack, even in its currently limited state.
I see the tight-rope between management strategy and coffee break gaming expertly walked right here. I hope that as new elements are added and rebalanced, that the game doesn't suffocate under the pressure to be everything at once under a beautifully realised Norse mythology theme.

The uncanny valley is an uncomfortable place to inhabit.
First hypothesized in 1970 by roboticist, Masahiro Mori, and then later coined by author Jasia Reichardt, the uncanny valley refers to the unsettling feeling of viewing and interacting with something that looks and behaves in a way close, but not entirely, like that of a human. Generally, this is used in reference to the way technology is quickly reaching a point where it is becoming harder and harder to distinguish between the natural and the digital, with the likes of humanoid robots and photorealistic animation creating an uneasy dissonance between what appears real and what we know to be artificial.
Approaching Uncanny Valley the game, the term would at first glance seem curiously bestowed. The aesthetic hardly begins to grasp at the lifelike, blocky characters and simple textures in no way attempting to disguise their digital existence. Similarly, Uncanny Valley is blunt and transparent in its mechanical introduction, producing to the player all manner of tutorial slides before the game has so much as begun, outlining how very game-y a game this is. But this disparity isn’t the result of a clumsy and inexplicable application of a term, but rather the basis of an internal dichotomy from which Uncanny Valley begins to execute an unnervingly grounded horror story.
On its surface Uncanny Valley is little more than disturbing anomalies and robotic sociopathy, but fueling these gross but not entirely terrifying encounters are more ordinary and distressing fears. The impenetrable anonymity of corporate hierarchies; humanity’s simultaneous fascination and terror at technological revolution and the possibility of artificial life; the daily mundanity and perceived insignificance of the working class, upon which all manner of inhumane practices are allowed to continue unchecked because the lowest rung on the ladder is the most readily replaced.
Uncanny Valley is terrifying because it takes America’s most entrenched capitalistic fears and proves them real. Yes, corporations really are as insidious and profit driven as they appear and we can do nothing to stop them. Robots will eventually destroy us and yet we continue to construct our own extinction. And through this all, blue-collar workers will continue to have no power, but rather be beaten down and eliminated at the mere hint of incompliance. It takes a conspiracy theorist’s mindset perhaps to buy into any of these lines of thought ordinarily, but within Uncanny Valley’s haunting soundscape and grotesque visuals, these ideas seem to hang over you suspended only by your own disbelief which becomes harder to hold to and gauge as the lines between dreams, reality, and what is actually going on begin to blur.
But I need to stop myself, because while it is easy to take the themes Uncanny Valley plays with and run with them, a distinction needs to be made between the horror Uncanny Valley alludes to and the horror it actually succeeds at conveying. And to that effect Uncanny Valley fails rather dismally. It may have a brilliant foundation for which to craft a socio-economic, technologically tinged horror experience, but it leaves it all on the table, opting for shock value over a lasting, pervasive terror. There is a lot that could be construed as frightening here, but little that stays with you once the immediate disturbance wears off, often before a scene has even come to its conclusion.
Uncanny Valley struggles in pacing itself in any way conducive to the sort of horror it employs. The plodding tedium of your character’s nightly shifts could have been used to build tension and explore the ways in which the game seems to position the working class as the default victim of every crime, but there is so little holding these segments together that often I found myself wandering a deserted building entirely bored rather than distressed, until an obligatory jump scare brought me back to attention. This hands-off approach is understandable within the context of Uncanny Valley’s branching design, with the decisions you make quietly shaping how the narrative eventually unfolds, but the variables at play are so opaque that there is no way of actually knowing what actions effect what outcome until it has already happened.
Part of me loves that uncertainty and unpredictability, because it fits so nicely within Uncanny Valley’s theme of insecurity and helplessness in the face of industry and technological innovation, but Uncanny Valley never finds a way to balance its mechanical desires with those of its narrative. Either the story plays out linearly (or with enough present information for you to knowingly guide it) and loses the element of unpredictability needed to really sell the plot, or it keeps narrative forks hidden to the player and in turn causes the plot to feel uneven and shallow by keeping so much of the story locked away on paths the player may or may not ever see.
Which is a problem inherent to any game which requires multiple replays to see fully, but it is especially bad here because the unpleasant and inscrutable nature of the game left me with little enthusiasm to venture through it again. Uncanny Valley is upfront in telling you it needs to be replayed multiple times, but it never gives a reason to want to. So much of the game consists of tiresomely meandering through empty rooms, uselessly attempting to interact with objects which may or may not change how the narrative actually unfolds. I felt as lost during my first playthrough as I did having beaten the game, as incapable of understanding the underlying forces at work within Uncanny Valley’s plot as when I was first introduced to them, and the idea of spending another few hours trying to break out of that mold is actively off-putting rather than compelling.
Uncanny Valley wants to be a game you discover slowly, that eats away at you a little more with each new piece of information discovered until the whole thing is finally laid bare in grotesque completeness. But for as much as it might pester me to see it through again the mystery hidden under its tortuous mechanics never became intriguing enough to force me to make sense of how to find it. Uncanny Valley scratches at the surface of some of the most internalized and adaptable fears of modern society, but doesn’t go deep enough to leave me more than mildly perturbed by its gloomy theatrics.

Rather than a traditional review I think I'll just tell you my first experience with the game.
I spawn miles above an airport, hurtling to the warzone below me. Everyone everywhere is wreaking havok with explosions and fire. I see tanks chasing motorcyclists who dodge and duck in between other cars and planes, turning back to pepper their pursuers with grenade launchers and machine guns. I see helicopters circle the area, hunting down the occasional man who flees to the woods and leveling the forestry to end his life. I see military planes perform spectacular strafing runs, only for them to occasionally crash into each other and fling the wreckage below, crushing anyone who hasn't gotten out of the way. I see a man on top of an ice cream truck with a rocket launcher, who shoots a plane attempting to escape the carnage only for it to crash into the ocean. I see several people spawn small planes to launch them to the ground in kamikaze fashion, only for them to jump out at the last minute so that the explosion would kill any below, and then I see the same thing done with a Boeing 747. And in the middle of it all, in a ring of fire, bullets, and the husks of several vehicles, as planes whisk by and missiles land closer and closer, I see a stripper beating a ninja to death with her grappling hook.
I see chaos.
I see anarchy.
I see beauty.
Fantastic game as long as you have a few friends to play with, Highly reccomended!!

I originally bought Doom 3 on it's release way back in 2004 (got a free Doom 3 T-shirt which I still wear!). I built my very first computer to play this game and it was the most nerve shredding gaming experience I ever had!
Doom 3 wasn't about the frenetic, relentless action of the original Doom or Doom 2. It was about creating tension and immersion, creating fear and suspense...I found it both extremely enjoyable and highly stressful!!
Visually, Doom 3 was unrivalled in 2004. The PC I built could only play it on medium to high settings. To this day, it is still a good looking game (although the polygonal heads could be smoothed off)
I simply don't understand the hatred towards this game...John Carmack himself said that this was the Doom game he had always wanted to make! I absolutely love Doom 3, the atmosphere, the tension, the panic as you get mobbed in the dark! I loved changing between the flashlight and your gun...it created fear and some extremely tense situations! Sadly this version allows you to have both the gun and flashlight!
Would I recommend this game? Without a shadow of a doubt! If you enjoy FPS's that scare you out of your pants, then this is a classic! (On a side note: I watched Doom 4 on a E3 2015 video and it looks amazing!)

Car handling is arcadey but that's okay because the driving controls actually include a "Car-Fu" button. Like, you actually have a ramming/sideswipe attack as opposed to just ramming them the old fashioned way. Totally makes up for it.
On morality, the whole balance between Triad and Cop is just...there for show and it's pathetically easy to boost one of them without consequence to the other, especially since you never actually lose Triad Points while cop points are just ever-so-abundant. But that's not really a big deal anyway since it never affects the story. Oh well.
The world itself, while not terribly lively, has a funkily charming atmosphere to it and the vendors who sell you stat-boosting stuff are kinda funny. ESPECIALLY THE PORK BUN GUY, BEST SHOP-CHARACTER EVER. Meanwhile there's lots of♥♥♥♥♥♥to collect so you can make yourself a better kung-fu cop guy. That in-turn encourages a lot of exploration, letting you sightsee all around Hong Kong while punching its residents in the face.
Story is pretty decent, asides from a couple of predictable twists there's a bit of sudden wham moment near the climax. But then after you've got the last mission beat, the final cinematic after it's all over is just...eh.
DLC quests are a blast but incredibly short. A lot of the DLC items are kinda OP. The sidequests are kinda fun though and mesh with the vanilla game sidequests.
Overall it's pretty alright and worth a playthrough.

This game has garnered a lot of hate since it was released. Some valid (limited dialogue options, no skill checks) and some not valid. This game has grown to become one of my favorites, with a dynamic world that feels like you can actually make in impact on and npcs reacting to those choices. You can craft weapons and settlements from junk laying around your character. There are deep emotional stories to almost every location on the map (if you are willing to read and look for them) or in random encounters with characters or from the remains of the skeletons from the nuclear blasts. The best part about fallout 4 is which ending you choose to go with makes a large impact on the world afterwards and how characters interact with you. There are also many real world allegories that are fun to explore both sides of: slavery, communist invasion, nuclear apocalypse, just vs unjust killing, stealing to survive and others. My favorite part about this game is that it is just enjoyable to play whether it is for a few minutes or a few hours. So my suggestion is do not listen to all the hate, this is truly an enjoyable game and to try it out for yourself.

Context: I'm an amateur noisy guy, modular black hole money thrower, elektron junkie, Ableton believer, and burgeoning old man. I know nothing that will save me once the bombs come and I make a living working with criminals.  I've never touched a video synth, but I can comfortably flex on most other types. I prefer hardware, and I can't tolerate latency.
Meat: I want this product to succeed. I feel connected to it in the same way modular first grabbed me. I want to learn why it moves the way it does. I don't understand video production, but my synth knowledge (and basic xsplit foundation) got me where I needed to be to at least spit out a video for YouTube. Chucks challenge is a puzzler for smart people who like to take thier time and think. The first maps might be easy but after that you dont get things served to you. Every single level is beatable and can be solved with what you can see, but there is no guarantee that you will be able to. All the objects and monsters are easy to figure out how they work (since they operate on a few simple rules), but that does not mean that things wont get complicated. The way I see it complaining about not being able to beat few maps is completely missing the point. You are supposed to be challenged by the maps and try several diffrent ways of solving them, sometimes coming back to them few days after and trying again. The usual in games today is people getting it extremely easy even on hard settings when it comes to puzzles and this is not what this game is about.
The bad parts about the game is the blur that comes when you zoom out, some of the design choices are questionable, the controls sometimes are a bit laggy (rarely a problem for me though, specially since so many maps are puzzles where you think not act quickly), the ui is sometimes a bid bad and perhaps worst of all the fact that the progress is saved online after each map (by the time they show you medal). Still the game is very playable and these problems does not take away the fun of solving the puzzles.
TL;DR: If you dont like being challenged by puzzles and sometimes not being able to solve them then this game is not for you. I however love the fact that the puzzles are on the level that you can beat them but its sometimes pretty damn hard and takes time. The cons are annoying, but doesnt take away the fun of the game.

If you were burned or disappointed by Aliens: Colonial Marines, then I'd highly suggest picking up a copy of this game. Aliens vs Predator is a solid, polished shooter reminiscent of the original game from 1999, and is guaranteed to thrill and surprise you.
The player experiences three different campaigns; predator, alien and marine. Each campaign has a different playing style, and I'm very impressed by the way Rebellion has managed to polish each style so efficiently.
Firstly, the marine campaign. Probably the best of the three, you use classic weapons from the Alien films and comic books such as the pulse rifle, smartgun and double barrelled shotgun. The shooting is surprisingly tight, and you'll get into a nice rhythm of blasting and reloading. The darker levels are great at creating suspense, and the xenomorph models are beautifully animated. They take you by surprise and can swarm you very quickly, which creates moments of panic that I haven't felt in a shooter for a long, long time. You also fight other enemies like Weyland Yutani androids, who are unsettling in their own way (probably those creepy voice recordings and expressionless faces). You can also experience classic movie moments like blasting the Alien Queen out of her egg sac, which is awesome to just about anyone who has seen Aliens.
Secondly, the predator campaign. As the Predator, you'll attempt to stay stealthy and pick off enemies using the range of tools at your disposal. You have a plasma caster, a spear, throwing discs and of course, the classic wrist blades. Much like the Batman: Arkham games, you'll navigate high vantage points and isolate enemies with x-ray vision until you are able to safely dispatch them. However, the game will also make you fight Aliens in close combat, which is frustrating and clunky; this consists of repeatedly mashing buttons while aliens continuously leap at you, which makes for a frustrating experience. Also, while the execution animations are quite awesome, they also take a long time to complete and make you vulnerable to damage, which is extremely annoying on harder difficulties.
Finally, the alien campaign. Playing as the alien also focuses on stealth, and you'll climb over different surfaces while attacking with your claws, teeth and tail. The wall climbing mechanics mostly work, though they can be confusing and hard to use at times. The constant movement of the alien is also quite dizzying, and is especially noticeable when traversing the inside of buildings. Whilst this campaign is still fun in its own right, the confusing wall-climbing and lack of interesting attacks means that this campaign is the least interesting of the three.
The game looks fantastic visually, but all three campaigns take place in the same location, so it can get quite repetitive due to the re-used locations. Despite this, it is fun to see where the other species has gone after completing each campaign. For example, when playing as the Predator, there is a level where you find the dead Alien Queen after the Marine segment where you kill the Queen yourself.
Overall, Aliens vs Predator is an awesome game that doesn't disappoint. The three entertaining campaigns are immensely satisfying, despite odd design choices and irritating game mechanics. 8 / 10
