Chuck's Challenge plays just like it looks: like an indie puzzle game. You move a cute alien around and guide him to the exit of each level. The game features hazards that impede your path or kill you, items that let you mitigate some of said hazards, enemies with varying behaviors, and occasionally mandatory collectables needed to open certain locked doors. The game's puzzles start off easy enough, but gradually scale higher and higher in difficulty.
Generally, puzzles come in two flavors: the "obstacle course" puzzles and the "non-threating moving blocks" puzzles. The "obstacle course" puzzles tend to be straightforward (although naturally get more bendy in their solutions in later levels) where you have to dodge enemies and navigate through hazards to reach the end. The "moving blocks" puzzles consist of small levels where nothing threatens your life but must instead move a limited amount of boxes around a tightly-packed space onto pressure switches to open the way to the exit. The game does sometimes blur the two together, but those make up the main "types" of puzzles you'll experience.
Chuck's Challenge screams "mobile game", but it's the good kind of mobile port. You'll see all the mobile staples; from the Angry-Birds style menus, the overtly colorful and cutesey (but low-budget) graphics, the 3-star time-based rating system, and how each world (basically a level pack of a set difficulty with a unique theme) unlocks only after beating a certain amount of levels before it. However, you'll find the game runs smoothly and the basic WASD movement to be acceptable. My only complaints port-wise involve how the graphics settings only allow you to switch between the Unity-engine presets ("Fastest" to "Beautiful"), and that non-movement buttons (such as manually undoing a move) require going into the game's manual to find the button for.
My primary complaints for the game involve one subjective feeling about the game's difficulty, and the poor audio balance:
+Regarding the difficulty, I found the "moving box" puzzles to require much more thinking time and figuring out than any other puzzle in the same world. I have to hand it to Chuck, those puzzles make for great brain teasers, but also could use a much gentler difficulty curve. The non-moving box puzzles before and after them required ludicrously less amount of time to solve than those of the same world, and I can only imagine them getting much worse. To add even more frustration, the game claims to offer a "Replay system" which will show a clue how to solve the puzzle. However, I found that only one level I tried it on (the last moving-box level of World 2 I believe) actually had a Replay, and the rest did not. I find this feature to be rather useless as a result.
+For some reason, the sound balance of the game is extremely off, even painful for headphone users. Enemy noises (those that play when the main character is near an enemy), as well as wearing the ice roller (item that lets you freely move on ice) play an extremely loud sound effect. Comparatively, the sound effects for collecting items, and even the main character's death noise, are very quiet. I'm not sure what happened, but the sound balance needs some work.
Overall, if you're looking for a quick and dirty puzzle game that boasts some legitimate challenge, Chuck's Challenge will fill that niche. It's cheap and regularly on sale as well.

Northgard is a solid experience that you should be keeping an eye on.
Despite being in Early Access, Northgard already has a plethora of features that instantly grasped me. The general gameplay  is a mix of strategy, town building and RTS that feels well crafted and put together in a fitting package.
The gameplay has a bit of everything involved. Some of it feels like base building in an RTS as you set up new buildings and assign workers to them. Other bits remind me of Stronghold or Banished where resource management is key for getting through tough winters or natural disasters.
Once you get your initial area sorted out you will expand into new regions. This is done by first scouting them, then having your warriors defeat the enemies that reside there. Aside from other clans, the main enemies are things like wolves, bears and Draugr. After that you settle the area and are free to collect resources from it and build there.
The game moves in real-time but isn't fast like an RTS. It moves at about the pace of a management game like Tropico. I like that you aren't rushing, especially in the early game. It allows you to establish your clan before you meet others.
The game features a basic combat system where enemies will just run at eachother if they are in the same region. It gets the job done and doesn't need to be the meat of the game. I would like to see some more features added to it in the future.
The management aspect is casual, it sort of feels like a mobile game that was built for PC, if that makes sense. That doesn't mean it's bad, it just means it gets away with feeling easier than a game like Banished.
You can trade with other clans, war against them and strive for victory with a variety of different conditions. Conquest, research and other victories are all present in the game which gives it some extra depth.
In the current state I'm a bit worried that the game won't have a ton of replayability beyond maybe five hours or so. From looking at the different factions you can play as, they don't seem to operate very differently beyond a couple bonuses unique to each of them.
The game is currently available in singleplayer and multiplayer. There is also a planned storymode which I hope will offer more variety to the gameplay to keep people interested.
Overall Northgard has potential to be a great, polished game that combines many ideas into a unique and polished package. Because it's in Early Access still you should wait until full release to see what gets added before making your purchase decision.

Fran Bow is a game that I was very excited to play seeing the original trailer pop up on my Steam discover queue. I remember wanting to play it when it went on sale and kept track of it ever since. It was to my pleasant surpise that I recieved it in the May Monthly Humble Bundle, and it was the first game I downloaded and played.
What originally got my attention, the art and psychological horror aspects, remained the fuel to finish the game until the end. However, the ride to the end is a very bumpy and often times frustrating ride, as you try to piece together what is happening in the story. I intentionally overlooked several aspects of the gameplay in order to enjoy the story, because the game interface is difficult to say the least. Often times you will be double clicking when you don't mean to, and the whole game is controlled by the mouse, so no functionality of the keyboard is utilized. But that's not all that important because you are playing Fran Bow for the art and story, and while the art and writing will leave you horrified and mesmerized at the same time, the story just doesn't go anywhere. I admittedly am not a big fan of ambiguous stories, but when the end came I sat there thinking "What happened? what was the whole game about?"
In conclusion, this game will have you interested up until the end (discounting the slog that is chapter 3) and you will be interested in finding out what is the story of Fran Bow. But the ending will not deliver you these answers. Regardless, still worth a play.

Uncanny valley is a neatly wraped blunder.
Short list of pros and cons:
Pros:
-----
- Nice graphics
- Good atmosphere
- Good background music and sounds
Cons:
------
- Single save file (overriden with every autosave) which forces you to play all over to correct a minor mistake.
- Plot is non-linear, but structured badly.
- Main plot is predictable right from the start (kinda destroys the idea of twist ending)
- Run/Exhaust intervals are more annoying than atmospheric
- Goals are mostely unclear
- Time passing mechanism seems random and is just a burden.
- Twitchy and buggy at times, not polished enough.
For a game that focuses on storytelling, the structure is far from perfect. The prospect of multiple ending is nice, but the storylines collide more often than not and leave the player confused. The first time I played it I got the extremely bad ending without understanding who are the charachters involved. That is a huge disadvantage for a plot based game. Add to that the single save file which autosaves arbitrarily and prevents you from undoing a mistake and you get a really bad experience.

First let me quickly get the negative out of the way, and its only a very small nit picking negative. the characters. oh my lord the characters. it felt like they tried to take borderlands kinda style, failed with it and created boring emo-looking characters. which is fine. i like the emo look, but on 1 character. im not usually one to complain about the graphics or art of something (or in this case, character design), but these just felt like try-hard copies of whats been done. the look is so try hard i honestly felt embarrassed in the first comic scene.
however, once you get past that, its seriously a great game. im not too far in the game, so i cant speak for humour, but there is definately room for some jokes in the game, but since its a tower defence game, ill just get to what you really wanna know. no one really cares much for story or talk in a tower defence game.
The gameplay is sweet. its smooth, and its varied. while the different classes try to force you to reply on multiplayer, it leaves enough room for you to easily solo max difficulty levels with a little skill and strategy. i use easily as a relative term as it depends on the strategy but the most important thing, is that its possible. no one ones a single player viable game that is unbeatable on your own.
Having multiple classes simply adds to this strategy. gonna let runners leak? get a perk that kills them instantly and focus on a heavy class. gonna focus on the small guys? get high dmg tower to clean up the big guys. and each class has its own respective strategy to solo, which is really just beautiful in a game like this.
Dont get me wrong, it doesnt mean its always going to be easy through all the levels, its just nice to have single player hope.
Now the perspective. The first person view changes everything. you can now change your play style accordingly. there are high hp guys that jump at you. you can bait them to buy your towers time buy baiting his jump out. however at the same time, he may jump your walls if you play incorrectly, so it adds that bit more strategy.
As you could probably tell, i love strategy in a game and this game, has had enough thought put into it to make it playable in many ways and still succeed. in a regular tower defence game, there is really only 1 option, have towers slow the enemies, maze them through the slows with high dmg/range towers hitting them the whole way through. mind numbing. the class system that initially seems to be limiting only opens you up for different strategies. its actually genius.
As a Tower Defence game, definately at least at 8. i give it a 9. as a game in general, probably alot more mediocre. but it feels wrong to mix different genres as some do. you cant compare a closed world like this where you can see the whole map from one spot to a game that you have alot more freedom in. They are completely different and should be treated as such. Definite 9.

First for a fighting game is a single player story compaign, the story is not a literal masterpiece but it is very good in engaging you to keep playing it. The second reason is the amount of content, there is campaign, challenge tower (300 challenges), multiplayer and classic arcade ladder, this is great for single player centric players that do not want to just play multiplayer. Lastly the level of violence in this game is just so laughable, it is a great decision to use the versatile Unreal Engine to create some unimaginable/creative fighting moves and especially, fatalities.
The only issues I have with the game are the menu/UI controls. I can remap the keys to whatever I like but in the menus they seem to stick with the default (G for enter and J for exit). The last issue if the quality of the pre-rendered cutscenes in the campaign, they are very low bitrate for both the video and audio. These aren't huge issues as the gameplay and content well make up for it but are issues nonetheless.
I commend NetherRealm Studios and also High Voltage for bringing a top notch PC port of the best fighting game of this generation. I cannot wait to play Injustice for the PC.

Anyone that has ever played Mortal Kombat will instantly recognize the cast of this one. The graphics are really good and the feeling is as good as ever. The combos are easy to land, all the main characters are back. Reiko and Fuujin are missing however but everyone from the original is here.
The story itself is a repeat with a twist. As usual Shao Kahn is back to try and merge the worlds and as always Raiden is opposing him. With this there's a few changes, like Jax having his real arms and we're treated to him "losing" them to regain the cyborg implants.
The story itself starts with Cage and you get to fight a couple of fights then the story continues on a different character. Other than this, Mortal Kombat is beginning to become Cyborg Combat. There's several cyborgs fighting and it's kind of a side track from the original in my opinion. All in all the story is really good and it feels 'fresh' in a way. You have some fun for a few hours or days while you plow through the early progression of nonstop levelling up, but then the negative aspects start to become more prominent.
It's very laggy. So forget getting good at combat, and forget close fights, because monsters will just teleport around when the game lags. The only solution is to grind on lower-level monsters and then level up. This means combat is just a bland mash of sitting there wailing on weak monsters until they die. That's fun a couple times only.
The loot treadmill seems fun when you're at the lower levels, but once you start getting resplendent/shadow gear, which is not that long into the game, the vast majority of loot drops are orange gear. It's useless to you, and you can't upgrade it to a  higher rarity, so the cycle becomes: go adventure for 15 minutes until your inventory fills up with oranges, then go to your loot collector and collect your oranges one by one. You can technically not pick up the orange gear, but the way the camera system works makes it very hard to target specific gear drops on the ground.
Speaking of the camera - it's bad. Most dungeon fights take place in smaller hallways, so you will often be looking at the back of your head, running into blocks all the time. The dungeon boss rooms are somewhat better because they usually have higher ceilings.
It also crashes a lot. It's also buggy. You might craft a bunch of items but they won't actually be in your inventory. If you log off and log back on, they appear. Who knows how many items you actually lose forever and don't even know about?

TL;DR: Trove can be an amazing game to play as long as you know what you’re signing up for. Recent changes have pushed this game from the casual player’s dream to more of daunting endless grind, but that doesn’t take away from the many charming features this game still has to offer. If you’re looking for a mind-numbingly simple MMO you can enjoy in a variety of ways that doesn’t require the hardcore and demanding playstyle a lot of other MMOs have to offer, you’re not going to regret your time in Trove. If you’re into games that require strategy, coordination, or team-effort; where the mobs are all punishing, the bosses are all challenging, and the effort is always worth it; you might be the wrong place.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I’m not good at reviewing things, but seeing how the new update is inviting a lot of players to the scene, I figured I’d give people my personal words of advice. I’ve been playing this game for +1.7k hours CONSECTUVIVELY, longer than most alpha and beta players have to claim for, and I don’t regret any second I’ve sank into this game. There’s something charming about how minimalistic and childish this MMO is, and if you’re the type of person to play a Multiplayer game in Single Player Mode, you’ll probably like Trove, too.
Pros:
•	The gameplay in Trove is gloriously casual and simple. You don’t have a whole hotbar of moves to have to switch back and forth from, or an exhausting amount of combinations/builds you have to pick through. All 15 of the classes in this game literally only have three moves and three builds to choose from: DPS/Hybrid/Tank. Yet in those three moves, all of the current classes differ tremendously in playstyle and utility. You’re bound to love one of them.
•	You can play this game at your own pace. There will always be someone in the crowd to grind with when you need them. You’re not constantly queuing up looking for a dependable group to raid with every three seconds, most of the grinding can be done alone, or you have an unlimited amount of chat channels/club groups to help you find who or what you’re looking for.
•	An abundant number of diverse dungeons and biomes to explore from, all with different mobs, resources, and themes. It’s adorable.
•	Probably one of the largest selections of easily acquired costumes, weapon styles, and mounts I’ve ever come across. No two characters should ever look alike in this game.
•	There’s a lot of things to do in this game beyond dungeon grinding. If you ever get tired of the grind, you can always find your refuge in fishing, building, mining, or farming.
•	Absolutely free to play. Despite what a lot of reviewers say, you’re not forced to spend a cent on this game. 99.9% of the resources/styles/mounts/costumes/etc. in this game can be bought with in-game currency through the extensive player marketplace/trade chat, and most packs that can be bought with real money can’t be bought twice, limiting how far a player can really P2W. If you’re the type of person that can’t keep your hands out of your mother’s purse when the goings get tough, don’t blame the game for your lack of patience. Seriously, this argument is so tired.
•	Building is limitless. There’s an abundant number of easily obtainable blocks with different textures and utilities in this game.  A large variety of furniture can be crafting if you’re looking for that extra something. Everyone gets their own little cornerstone to customize for free, and anyone can create a club world to build from the bottom up or invite others to build with. Even if you’re not much for building, you will learn to love doing so in Trove.
•	The Devs are listening. A lot of the big problems you see in old reviews have been fixed. There are no unrealistically long queues anymore, All-Day-Patch Day has been cancelled, All classes can be bought with in-game resources now, patron passes are literally handed out like candy on a daily basis, and the gem grind has become a lot more tolerable. They’ve even gone and made leveling classes easier. Twice. Yes, it takes them time to get around to the big issues, but the effort is there.
Neutral
•	There’s no story in this game. After you breeze through the tutorial quests, you’re left to your own vices with only the community to guide you. Good luck with those guys. If you don’t need to be spoon fed directions in an MMO, or you’re super intrigued by game lore, you’ll be okay with this. It can be alittle daunting at first, but you’ll find your way sooner or later.
•	The Community. If you’re looking for a community of players who are always there for each other, or just that ONE person in the crowd that might help you when you’re in need, you might be in the wrong MMO.  Trove has your typical free-to-play community, so don’t expect much from them. This really isn’t a big deal, as the community does not really affect your progress in the game. You can always join a room and grind with strangers, but it takes a real effort to find the friendlier faces.
•	PvP? What PvP? Do people still care about that anymore? While it can be a fun experience from time to time, I mostly see people struggling to get the required 8 people in a room just to start it. If you’re into the kind of PvP that requires a lot of strategizing, or pumps out massive rewards, you’ll be disappointed. This, too, is okay, as PvP doesn’t play a huge role in the game, either.
Cons:
•	Player advancement can get very repetitive and tedious. After mid-game, grinding usually boils down to bombing your way through dungeons to get straight to a boss, kiting it around until it’s dead, and then repeating this process for hours until you’re sick of it.  Gems, your major source of power rank, are entirely RNG-based. No two gems will have the same stats, and praise be to RNGesus if you get a reasonable set of gem before you consider hanging yourself a couple times. If you’re going the completionist route, try imaging that struggle 8 more times for 14 more classes over several different tiers. Trove in a nutshell.
•	Glorious, unadulterated lag. There is no escaping this lag, and nobody is safe from it. If someone tells you they don’t lag in this game, they’re either lying, or they’ve been lagging for so long they’re in denial about it. You might as well learn to love it.
About the Newest Update:
The latest update in that game, Eclipse, is centered around Shadow Towers and their loot. This update has been a godsend for some of us, and has introduced a lot of interesting features, such as subclasses, into the mix, but it has also put a bit of a strain on the end-game community for the simple fact that now they have to start trying again. Before this update, anybody over 20k was in the clear, as they could solo almost all the bosses. If you were lucky enough to find yourself a couple of +20k friends, you had it in the bag. Now Hard STs are actually hard, and Ultra Mode STs can take hours if you’re in the wrong group. But this can be handled the same way it always was: with time and effort. If you see anyone complaining about difficulty, please, ignore them. I assure you, the same people complaining about STs being too hard now were the same people whining about how easy they were in the first place.
In General:
Just give Trove a chance. You really have nothing to lose but time and energy. It’s an everchanging game with a lot of potential, and even if it’s not your cup of tea, it’s bound to make you smile once or twice.
If I didn’t touch anything in this review, or you have further questions, just ask. I’ll get to them as soon as possible. Thank you for the time.

I've found myself comparing Northgard to RTS games such as Age of Empires / Mythology and turn based games like Endless Legend / Civ.
It's real time gameplay, but the way you think about what to build on the different 'hexes' on a map and the pace at which you discover and build your territory out of those hexes feels a lot like a turn based game like Civ or Endless.
Compared to other RTS games, it has the added flavor of winter... Something in which you must do some amount of prep and consideration for, though the game always keeps you informed on when it's happening and what to expect.
It's fun, it has really good pacing, and it's generally a very polished experience.

I pre-ordered this game in 2015, and I had not touched it much after the initial month. My reason for not recommending this game is because I never had fun playing this game.
The settlement feature in the game was what turned me away. Scouring the Wasteland for materials to build Sanctuary had been fun for the first few hours, but it gets downright tedious to repeat that for the 10 over settlements later in the game. Being emotionally blackmailed by Preston into becoming a worker ant killed the game for me.
However, my true intention of writing this review was not to gripe about the features of the game. I understand that one man's poison is another's cup of tea. I am writing this to voice my disapproval for the pricing of the DLCs and the season pass.
I still had hopes for the game, and had wanted to purchase the season pass at sale for the full version of this game - which ironically was what I thought I would be getting having naively pre-ordered the game in 2015. Lo and behold, the season pass is only $5 cheaper than the "GOTY" version of the game. No option exists for me to bump my base game up to this full version at a more reasonable cost.
What's the rationale for this pricing strategy? Bethesda couldn't resist gouging my wallet for a final time? That suckers who pre-ordered would still be idiots with their wallet even after 2 years? What gives, Bethesda?
The lesson I learnt is that I would have been better off had I never pre-ordered.

Let me start out by saying that I had -extreme- doubts about getting this game. I'd heard so many negative things about the developers that I didn't want to go anywhere near it. I will say that the whole "devs deleting any negative comments about their game- constructive criticism or otherwise" thing bothers me deeply, but I was willing to let that go and give this game a go anyway. People make mistakes.
I've sunk plenty of hours into this game and I intend to sink many more after the 1.0 update is released. I went into this game -extremely- skeptical, and came out of it having a new favorite game. As a fan of Terraria, I was already accustom to the art style and found it even better than Terraria's, honestly. The home designing aspects and different planets artwork was seriously stunning, and I quickly found myself enamoured by it all. It feels like there's so much more to do than there was in Terraria, which scores big bonus points with me as well.
The flow of gameplay, presence of story and quests and wide variety of items of every sort really makes this game for me. The weapons are fun and interesting and the little dungeons you find while mining really helps break up the threat of 'mining syndrome' where you grow increasingly bored/tired after doing it consistantly for too long. Each little chest I find has me excited to see what waits within, and even if it's a bad batch of disappointing loot, I look forward to finding another that yields much more impressive treasure. It's all very rewarding to me, especially when I have yet to experience any recurring loot, taking the edge off of that 'highly anticipatory chest opening' sensation.
The races and NPC dialogue (and just NPC's in general) really bring life to the world. I'm infinitely fascinated with the things NPC's say to the player, especially depending on your race. My first character was a Floran, so it was colorful dialogue, to say the least. :P
All in all, no matter what I went into this game expecting (which was FAR from optimistic) I came to the decision that I really do adore this game and everything I've seen in it, so far. I would try to find some negative aspects to remark about to make this a fairly mixed review, but I don't believe I've run into anything I don't like, just yet... so I'm refraining.
Whether or not the devs of this game have made some questionable choices on forums or otherwise, it honestly comes down to the game tha they've created and whether or not it's any good. Considering that they aren't sacrificing babies or something, I'm willing to overlook all that I've seen and heard about them and say that this game is fun, worth playing, and well done. Even if it doesn't continue to hold my attention for much longer after I write this review (which I highly disagree will even happen) I know I'll have gotten my money's worth.
If you're anything like me and skeptical over what you've heard about the devs, forget about it. Focus on the game and the aspects of it that you think you will or won't enjoy and make a decision based on that alone. No matter what they've done, they've poured what feels to be their heart and soul into a game worth playing, and I think that, at the very least, warrants an attempt to play it, if nothing else.

A reasonable quality, fairy tale-inspired, juvenile horror point-and-click. The art and music, while not impressive for the genre, are nicely put together and well in line with the ''troubled child's mind'' theme. Character designs are creative, ranging from paranoid to cute and benevolent-looking, and the looping tracks are short but impactful. Fran Bow's story, which is very roughly The Faun's Labyrinth meets American McGee's Alice, works best if the mind of the player is that of a kid's while the adventure lasts (I've clocked almost 7 hours so far and there's no end in sight).
While I'm enjoying this little game, there are downsides. Having no voice acting adds nothing to the experience; it doesn't make anything creepier or more mysterious. Everything would have been much better with it (though I understand voice talent is hard for a two-person team to get). The plot gets more whimsical as one goes, but consider the last sentence of the previous paragraph. Also, some item/environment combnations are unintuitive to the point of mild annoyance, although they are done in moderation and are acceptable as a challenge. The real flaw, for me, is not being able to take screenshots without a workaround. That I can live with.
Likely only worth full price for point-and-click enthusiasts (not a big one myself). If on sale for around half the price, give or take, I'd very much recommend it as long as it's not the first game of the style you will ever play (as there are undoubtedly better ones, but they're not similar to Fran Bow). It's also not reccomended for very young children. And of course, if you need any childhood traumas sorted out... like that one time you found your mom and dad unrecognizably butchered in the living room...
...well, then it's a gamble...

Right off the bat, Uncanny Valley gets points for doing something very few horror games do. It's a game that purports to give you control over the story, letting you actions affect the outcome. If you played Home, it's the same thing that game tried to do and failed completely at. Uncanny Valley actually makes it work, and the result is an intense and engaging game that you REALLY have to meet halfway.
You're Tom, an unremarkable everyman with some remarkably terrible dreams. You take a job as the night watchman at some abandoned facility up in the mountains, trading off with some fat jerkoff named Buck on watching the empty offices and halls. Right away, the game makes good on its promise. After Buck gives you the 60-second tour, you're free to wander wherever and do whatever you want. There's the facility proper with 4 floors, a warehouse, and a secure sector to explore, there's the apartment complex and its 4 floors of rooms, and there are some smaller areas like the woods and generator building. Within these mysterious environs you will find keycards, cassette tapes, and PCs still logged into their company emails for some weird reason. There's not a huge amount of stuff to interact with, but there's a lot of ground to cover and some clever connections between all the pieces.
The catch is that you still have a job to do. You're supposed to show up to your shift on time, stay in the facility until it ends, and get back to bed before you pass out. That doesn't leave a whole lot of time to comb the whole place, so you really need to pay attention to the clues and follow up on them intelligently instead of turning the whole building upside-down. You certainly have the option of going rogue and doing whatever you want, but there are consequences for that. It's worth trying, too, because there's a surprising number of fates Tom can meet, depending on what you do.
That really turns out to be the heart of the game, how much you're willing to experiment and work to get the whole story. I bungled my first playthrough so badly that I got unceremoniously thrust right into the dark secret of the place, which I again failed to escape and got possibly the worst end I have ever seen for a protagonist. On my second attempt I managed to work out some pretty vague puzzles and escaped the whole security job portion of the game entirely, moving into a proper survival horror crawl with weapons and healing items and video tapes and more. There was an entirely different back half to the game I hadn't even seen the first time! And that's cool, very cool, but it's going to leave you cold on the game if you don't work to find that. I mean, imagine if you never found the second castle in Symphony of the Night.
The journey to uncover the game's secrets is a pretty harrowing one, as well. The creature designs and animations are on point, as are the sound cues and music. I think I got my biggest scare in recent memory from this game thanks to a particularly excellent encounter design. That care and detail unfortunately doesn't extend to the game's inventory system, which can be cumbersome to deal with, but also somewhat underused. There are numerous bugs with the interface as well, with menus and interactables not getting proper focus and having your character scoot around as you try to manipulate something else.
Polish gripes aside, the only thing you need to ask yourself before picking up Uncanny Valley is, how hard are you willing to work to enjoy it? If you only spend an hour on it running around the empty offices, you're bound to be disappointed. It's only when you dig in, make the connections, and commit the time and attention that its brilliance starts to show through. That means it's definitely not for everyone, but for my part it's worth the effort.

TL;DR - Uncanny Valley is pretty flawed, but not a horrible game.
Uncanny Valley is an adventure game with horror/action/stealth elements in which you play as Tom, who has taken a job as a security guard at a remote robotics factory which has been shut down. To no surprise, the factory holds mysteries and secrets and you investigate those mysteries even as you're learning about what drove Tom to take a job in the middle of nowhere.
This game is all over the place for me and I ~barely~ can give it a recommend. It's got some really good points and some points that I feel detract from it. Let's start with what I liked. The art-style is retro pixel art and really well done, with good animations, character designs, and backgrounds. The music is solid and adds to the atmosphere. The controls with the Xbox 360 controls are solid, though not completely intuitive (with interaction being one button and picking up/dialogue advancement being another). The events and story are done well enough to keep interest as well. There are a lot of potential endings and ways to take the story which allow for decent replayability.
Then there's the downside. First is that the devs really want you to play through the game multiple times. Fair enough. But part of the way that's enforced is to give you a cripplingly short "work day" in which to wander around the complex to pick up cassette tapes, read emails, and otherwise explore. You have 7 minutes from the time you put on your uniform until your shift is over, after which you have a couple of minutes before Tom passes out where he is. So you functionally have about 9-10 minutes to get to the complex, explore, and get back to bedroom. You'll be running everywhere, but Tom has a realistically (but frustrating) small amount of stamina. Add in puzzles that don't necessarily have really obvious solutions or interactions and it's easy to feel lost or frustrated. When the more action/stealth elements come into play, they feel very hit or miss. It doesn't always feel fair when you're sneaking around and there's a lot of "let's just change rooms until this guy disappears"
There is more good to this game than there is bad, but it feels like it could have been a much better game. Doubling the time limit would immediately make the game more fun, if not getting rid of it. There are other minor details, such as keeping your flashlight on between rooms, would have also made for a better overall experience. I still recommend the game, but only if some of the issues get fixed or the game is on sale. On a 10 point scale, I'd rate it about a 7.

Bastion might not be something to get a ton of hours out of or regularly play, but its one of the most original RPGs. The game's simple, but felt very unique and just a joy to play. Its also a nice change from having to put in 30+ hours for RPGs. While shorter games are often considered inferior, sometimes you want to play an RPG you can finish in reasonable time.
The gameplay of Bastion is a top-down isometric Action RPG with linear level-based progression. It feels comfortable and familiar. There's a handful of weapons and skills to use and the levels are really enjoyable to play through. You can also shift the difficulty to make it much harder, but more rewarding. There might not be that much replayability, but there is a new game+ and score attack mode for anyone who loves the game enough to go for highscore runs or just play it again with their same gear.
Bastion's strongest point is the story. Jesus Christ, this game has a magnificent story. Its depressing, but beautiful. Its one of those games that really can leave an impact on you. Certainly a game I won't ever forget.
Unfortunately, I don't want to say much more on it because I refuse to spoil it for anyone who hasn't played it. Just trust me on this :)
Also, the story is narrated. It really sets the mood of the game. I couldn't imagine playing the game without the narration.
The artstyle is as good as they come. This is one of those games where you want to put posters of it up on your walls. Its quite colorful and looks hand-painted. Truly beautiful and unique.
The music is also excellent. Very interesting style. It blends a lot of different types of music together and creates this heavy electronica-inspired western style music. It might not sound good from my words, but it really is a wonderful a soundtrack. This is one of the few games that I download the OST to and listen to in my normal day.
There's a few different ways to play the game when it comes to controls. It all runs very well. No issues. There's not much to say here about it. Plays wonderfully on keyboard+mouse but just as well with a gamepad.
Bastion is just a total masterpiece. If you haven't played it you need to. Its one of those must-play indie titles that people will still be talking about years from now. My review doesn't do it justice.
Go play it now!

STARDRIVE.
The little 4X that almost could..
For starters, i must voice my bias. Towards grand-stategy and 4X-Games. They have been my personal guilty pleasure for the longest time. However, even with the enjoyment i get from them. There are examples of the genre that are not exactly the best and unfortunately StarDrive falls to that category.
This is easily explained, the game is dull. Bloody dull...  In all of my 140+ Hours of playing it, i have completed it only thrice.
And every time, the end-game played out the same. Every single time, not counting the time i went all Borg with the Opteris. This is mainly due to design issues with the Tech- political- and AI-systems, they feel unfinished and in many ways they still are. The game still crashes now-and-again and some of the mods that have been made for the game only make it even more unstable. (This just might be only on my end, but its still a noteworthy issue.)
And for a game that is aesthetically very similiar to the good old Master of Orion series, the problems only make it worse. Since in its core, the game is broken and even with the patching the developer has done (and if memory serves it was just one guy.) the game is still broken.
And i'm really sad about it, since the idea is so good. A spiritual successor to Master of Orion, with better graphics, sound and all the other fluff. StarDrive tries to be that game and in some ways it has succeeded, but the technical and design issues are the things that kill the experience, not to mention the pacing.
In all, StarDrive is a decent game. Even with all of its obvious problems, it is somewhat enjoyable. But not by much. It gets dull really fast and with the pacing being off, i really doubt that you could squeeze more than few playthroughs out of it. And even the modular ship building system, can only squeeze so much fun out of it.

If you, like me, loved the Chip's Challenge games, then you will most likely enjoy this "iteration" from the same guy. However, be aware of a few things:
1) You have to be online and connected to a server to track progress - this means waiting after every level for your score to be recorded, otherwise the game won't register that you've completed a level.
2) The level design is a lot easier and a lot less varied than it was in the Chip's Challenge games - however, this could be because there is a "rewind" feature to take you back steps, at the cost of a time penalty, so if you don't mind being marked down the levels become a lot easier.
3) Some levels are lifted almost whole from Chip's Challenge games, others are just Sokoban (way too many Sokoban levels) and a couple seem to be from The Impossible Game? Only a few levels really strike a true "Chip's Challenge" chord.
So all in all, this is a decent game if picked up cheaply, and the level creation/player levels adds a lot of lifespan. It has its fair share of faults, which is surprising for a game so simplistic.

Not a bad concept as this game is quite different than traditional 4x games, but honestly this game just feels too "small" to be anything other than a bargin bin, $5 time waster.  Here's why:
1) You can discover the entire galaxy with literally your first scout ship with almost no impunity.  No need to develop a drive or anything.
2) You can seemingly spend your time waiting on research building way points that connect virtually everywhere (seemingly no drawbacks or economic penalty for doing this).
3) Economy is ENTIRELY population based.  Expanding your empire's economy relies on you NOT building any actual buildings (at least early).  Maintenance costs on buildings that are designed to increase food, defenses, or production ALL drain more out of your income than actual ships, so it's better to just colonize and send colonists and food to the planets for seemingly forever till they have enough people to grow.  Just a bizarre concept that doesn't feel rational to me, there really is no option to have a small, but robust empire. It's zerg expansion or die.
4) Conquering enemies, likewise, involves nothing more than zerg tactics (i.e. spamming smallers missle ships and troops).  All you have to do is land more troops on the planet than the enemy has and it's soon yours, you can actaully do that by flying right past their defense fleet and zerg landing while a small number of attacks ships keeps their fleet busy.  Very silly strat but works easily.
5) Diplomacy is haywire. People either love you to death regardless of your actions or they want to murder you out right.  Then they simply want to join with you or your enemy, effectively taking the diversity out of the galaxy and matching one big against another big.  Really saps the interest in the game.
6) Ship design is convoluted and seemingly pointless.  You don't know what you need to put and where and there is no manual whatsoever to figure it out.  Simply putting a power source on a ship isn't enough, you need to add wiring that connects the guns or the shields or the bridge to that power source....at the expense of things like armor.  It's like a really terrible game of minesweep to be honest and I like complexity in games, I play 4x games and Paradox games like EU, CK2, and Hearts of Iron....but this ship design leaves me baffled.
All in all, this just feels like a very incomplete game that could have been much better if things like the economy and diplomacy had been fleshed out.  The battle system is fun to an extent, but it boils down to zerg tactics.  Bring enough cheap to produce missle frigates and focus fire for the win, leave the tactics at home.
I can't recommend this game.

I do feel I have to recommend this, but only with some reservations.  First off, this is done by a small studio, and the limited budget is obvious, but I don't want to dump on a new studio that holds some amount of promise.
The game is incredibly short.  I finished it in an hour flat (the rest of playtime for cards only).  However, I have to say that I enjoyed that hour, and it kept the variety up.
The story is kept deliberately vague.  Something about an attack taking place on the people of Petersburg and the guards are absent and it's down to you to save the day.  This sets you off on a remarkably varied, albeit disjointed adventure.  In the course of the short playtime you will lure a gem-eating monster to smash up a grate, escape hordes of the crawling undead in a maze-like sewer system (one of the first sewer sections in a game to not actually be crap!), keep your eye of a spikey centipede like monstrosity which only moves while you look away as you search parts of a dismembered guard to find a key, hunt down what essentially is a headcrab with IR vision and a taser for a spooked farmer, navigate a maze which changes depending on what door you enter, answer riddles, escape electricity-laden flying fish through cramped corridors, and face off against the end boss.
There is certainly no horror to be found here so not sure why this game got that tag.  It's surreal fantasy only.
There is a well voiced creature who has more than a passing resemblance to No Face from Spirited Away, who acts as a narrator and introduces this strange world, though the dialogue is a bit odd and even more distractingly so, the subtitles stubbornly refuse to align to the dialogue constantly.
I only encountered one bug where I accidentally fell outside the play area after going through a scripted floor collapse, but a swift reload solved that.
So despite the game's brevity I think it's certainly worth it on sale.

I like the game, and would absolutely love this game for a very long time if it weren't so frustrating.
Gameplay for me is pretty fun. Story isn't terrible. Entertaining banter and taunts from enemies from time to time as you play.
Some things I really don't like:
The min specs are a joke. Running i5 3470 and 1050ti with 8G ram @1280x720. Min specs sure, but I can't even run it on lower than minimum (after tweaking ini files) without some major stutters that in some places make it unplayable.
Tried windowless bordered, nvidia cp tweaks with game vsync disabled, mods, optimizing windows, etc.
Spent many hours searching for fixes but there really aren't any. Hardware upgrade is the only thing left for me to try. I think I'm giving up until I have a modern 1500.00 system. Maybe then it will behave a bit better.
Game looks like utter garbage when running at minimum with FXAA aliasing. Given that fact, I get better visuals on older games that run much smoother!
If you want to try it, do yourself a favor and just buy the base game. At about 15.00 it's worth checking out, and can be fun for a while until you start to see how poorly it runs and end up spending most of your time researching fixes, tweaking, and testing. Skip the DLC, not worth it given the poor state of the game. Far Harbor is even worse given the fog there. I feel a bit ripped off on the dlc.
OH, and don't be deceived by videos showing 1050ti running at ultra. You aren't getting a good run through where it stutters. If you watch closely, you can see minor performance issues in some of them (pauses and very slight choppiness) that get worse in other areas or later in the game. Maybe some people have better experiences though regarding performance on lower end hardware, Just not me.

I've been playing Starbound since its Early Access days, and let me tell you that the game has seen many changes since its debut alpha/beta launch. I've lost many characters due to updates, patches, and game overhauls, but alas that has yet to stop me from enjoying the game. With the full release of Starbound, the game is more fun than ever!
Chucklefish has done a wonderful job in bringing us a space themed crafting/sandbox game. The story is good and the infinitely generated universe keeps the game fresh and appealing. Your exploration of planets will be well rewarded with a vast loot system of weapons, armors, ores and items. Each planet is unique in design and may contain settlements, dungeons, ruins, prisons, research centers, trading post or may be void of life all together. In addition to planetary life, you may also encounter enviromental hazards as well that can constantly put you in danger! Crafting, upgrading, survival, mining and randomly generated quest will form the base of your gameplay and it is a rather rewarding grind.
Overall I recommend Starbound to anyone who enjoys crafting/sandbox games and enjoys grinding for rewards! I also recommend the Starbound Sountrack as well!

At the time of writing, Beastiarium is the only game on Steam from developer/publisher Fazan. Released in December of 2016, it thus far has only a small base of gamers who have purchased it, and an even smaller community of reviewers that have taken the time to write their thoughts about this alleged horror/adventure/puzzle title.
The only background to the "story" presented in the game is available for reading on the store page. Apparently, Beastiarium takes place in underground Petersburg at the beginning of the 20th century, and it has been 100 years since monsters have taken over Earth. The takeover caused all survivors to move underground and build a new world, but alas the cities that developed also got overrun by monsters. It is up to you to find out why people are afraid to leave their homes, and if the established Guard is actually there to protect the citizens, or if their purpose is more sinister. In-game, there are only a handful of narratives, none of which amount to much from a storytelling aspect. The voice acting is good, but even the subtitles are unpolished, in that their script does not fully match what the narrator is saying at any given time.
From a gameplay perspective, Beastiarium comes across as both drab and annoying due to its simplistic and uninspired puzzles. Throughout 9 chapters, you will find yourself answering some easy riddles, luring a monster to a preset destination, figuring out the navigation of two labyrinths, finding a keypad combination, and fighting an end "boss battle". All of the puzzle elements found in this game have been done to the point of exhaustion in other titles, and given the lack of story, or any real presentation that conveys a sense of purpose, the overall experience here just feels empty and void. After a while it begins to feel like a chore to even finish the game, which is another fruitless endeavor as the ending is underwhelming and vastly disappointing.
The only things that Beastiarium has going for it are some pretty graphics and good optimization; sadly, the rest is a complete write-off. There are no horror elements, there is barely any atmosphere, and part of the store page can be misleading; it proclaims that it has "combination of plot-driven quest and action-horror" and "seamless game world with sandbox elements". There are no loading screens, so the "seamless" part is right, but the rest is simply untrue. As well, it's a massive stretch to say that the game has "charismatic characters", seeing as you will interact with 4 people for an amazingly short period of time. Needless to say, it's best to just pass on by Beastiarium, unless you can get it for about $3.00. The default $16.99 CAD price point is far too high for a game that lasts 45-60 minutes at best, and even at $6.79 CAD it feels like a complete waste.

(Contains spoilers.)
A fantastic game set within a world that fluxes from whimsical to frightening and by the end manages to walk the line in between. Fran Bow's universe overall is surprisingly well-developed and very obviously is made of the stuff of both dreams and nightmares, as well as of real world horrors like child abuse, self-harm, pedophilia, and the very real inhumane experiments performed on patients locked within mental institutions. Along with the setting, its layers of multiple realities make for a fun game mechanic that nicely complements the exploratory elements of a point-and-click.
The writers did an amazing job of portraying Fran as a realistic child - earnest, naive, curious, and above all, resilient. She looks into the eyes of creatures that would make most adults turn and run, and she smiles and says hello because she has not yet been conditioned to fear such things. This makes her the perfect person with which to explore the setting and story of Fran Bow.
Speaking of, the game's story manages to be compelling and unexpected through all five of its chapters, introducing you to twisted authority figures and unexpected allies. Fran Bow plays with your trust, both with Fran's relationships with other characters and with its major themes: What is real and what isn't? Who is good and who is evil? (The answer is often not what you would traditionally expect.)
Yet instead of leaving players to question the ambiguous sanity and morals of the protagonist, as many psychological horror pieces do, it paints a picture of a child whose brain does not work like others' and yet is still kind and pure. Unlike others in its genre, Fran Bow is never an indictment of the mentally disordered. The monsters in the story are not Fran - they are the people trying to hurt her because of what she can see. Instead, Fran is the hero, her own hero. That is an important and powerful message, one that needs to be told more often.
The most noticeable weak point of the game for me was a few rather unintuitive puzzles. I consulted some walkthroughs and occassionally found myself wondering how on Earth a player was supposed to figure out a particular solution on their own without wildly trying to combine every object in their inventory with every part of the environment. This is something a lot of point-and-click games struggle with, Fran Bow being no different. Still, it wasn't as bad as, say, some of the later Myst games.
Mechanics wise, I didn't appreciate having to guess where my game had last auto-saved. With puzzle games, it's especially important not to lose progress and risk having to solve a complex puzzle all over again. I ended up playing to the end of chapters before quitting, just to be safe.
I will say that the soundtrack was underwhelming as well. The only place where I really noticed it was in the Ultrareality reception area because the casual elevator music really sold the humor of such an odd stop along the storyline. Because of this, I did find myself wishing the game were voice-acted so I would have something interesting to listen to, but I understand that budget limitations would make that an unreasonable request.
Fran Bow's art is beautiful, with a gothic style that lends itself well to both the cute and the terrifying. I'm incredibly disappointed that my Steam screenshot function didn't seem to be working during playthrough.
Final note: The black cat in the game is pure of heart and does not die. I want to personally thank the developers for that. The good black cat fits nicely with the subversion of the crazy little girl trope, and the fact that Fran got to be with Mr. Midnight and her other friends in the end made for exactly the kind of happy ending I believe most players would wish for her.

Just finished Fran Bow, and given the glowing reviews, I have to say I am rather disappointed.
Don't get me wrong, this is by no means a bad game, but there are several points where the game lets you down. The biggest, and worst, is that the game finishes on what is basically a cliffhanger. Not a cliffhanger that leads to another game, either. You just finish the game going "Wait, that's it?". I did thoroughly enjoy the first two chapters, and I understand that the game is supposed to represent a descent into madness, but it does it only by getting stranger. No subtle hints regarding one reality or another - nothing intriguing to leave you thinking, like say, a decent thriller.
Anyway, let's get down to points:
I really do wish I could select a neutral opinion of this game. As it is, though, I'll let you do with this information what you will.

Buggy, hanged up on me every time I died on the 3rd challenge (the three spikey things in the coveted garden). So I had to restart the game, load it and try again. I've never seen a game before in which I died so often.
The UI is bad, humongously big even though I had the game configured for 4K resolution there were possible answers to each dialog that I couldn't choose, because the top one was cut-off the screen.
Second, the narrator brings nothing to the story. It doesn't add any useful information.
Third. The quests lack common sense. This is nowhere near the quality of The Vanishing of Ethan Carter yet it is shown as "similar".
Fourth. The graphics quality is deterring. Coveted garden? Was it too hard to add a sky, considering Unreal Engine already comes with plenty of skies to add?
Fifth. Who uses the D-Pad? Whenever I've got a menu I expeted to control it with the right joystick but no, they use the D-Pad of the Xbox controller.
Sixth. Accesing the objects you've got and using them is inconsistent. You get lost in the buttons.
Seventh. The choice of music for the second challenge is, to put it midly: unfitting.
I expected something based in Spirited Away, as the narrator is the weirdo of the anime and the monsters are loosely based on it. But this is far, really far from it.
I wish I read other reviews before I paid the full price for it....got up to the garden with the 2 black spikey things, ended up watching a walkthrough in Youtube after that. I didn't like it at all. An amazingly fun game with great atmosphere, a creepy story, and good puzzling.
I enjoyed every minute of this game.
Gameplay: (4/5)
This is a point and click game, with a heavy emphasis on puzzles.
The special mechanic that this game uses is the ability to move into different realities of the same room. This allows them to effectively double the map size while keeping the walking to a minimum.
The puzzles are challenging and well thought out. There are no arbitrary puzzles with convoluted solutions.
There were a few times that I had to look up a strategy guide. Not because of puzzle difficulty, but because I missed something that I was supposed to pick up, or because I just didn't think of it.
Atmosphere: (5/5)
This game is a psychological horror, meaning it's trying to make you feel creeped out and scared.
There are no cheap jump-scares here, just pure mind games.
Music: (5/5)
The music does a great job of setting the atmosphere and being in the background enough, that it's not distracting.
The music will stick with you, after you finish the game, or when you quit for the night.
Even right now, as I write this review, I have the slow piano tune playing in my head.
Story: (3/5)
The story kept me wanting to hear more, the way it's presented is amazing... But the game ended, and now I'm looking up on Google what it all meant.

*Semi-Spoilers*
I apologize to the creators for not recommending this obvious labor of love.
Fran Bow has a lot going for it and earns the (nowadays) rare distinction of being a game I actually played until the end. Which means that amidst all these hundreds of games that fail to hold my attention or engage me sufficiently to be "beaten" this one persevered only to reward me with... nothing.
No conclusion, no reveal, no explanation, no closure.
Some people enjoy this sort of thing; going online afterwards to discuss their interpretations and theories about events that unfolded. I can even agree with this and relate to it up to a point. I just can't help but feel Fran Bow took it a bit too far leaving _everything_ up to the player. Was it all a dream? Was half of it a dream? 25% dream? Is there one single "fact" in this story anchored to reality or is everything fluid and left to your imagination?
When I read a novel I like to imagine that the author had this burning desire to share their story with me; that everything they put into writing was more or less important to the story or the setting or the mood. There will be some ambiguity or some uncertainty - certain facts will be left up to your imagination and make the story better for it.
Here, you might as well just grab a cup of your favorite beverage, sit down comfortably and use these following keywords to make up your own story in your head:
Little Girl, Insane Asylum, Dead Parents, Medicine, Psychosis,
Did you do it? There you go, whatever you made up in your head can most likely fill in for what "actually" happened in Fran Bow.

I do not know how to express the delightful nasty
that is Uncanny Valley. It is a 2D Horror Survival in which you impersonate Tom, a newly hired Security Guard at some isolated facility of a mysterious society. The story itself is pretty damn interesting, but it begins to unveil only after you start making
. Yeah, choices, the game is developed with them in mind, every action you take, every thing you do, every
you make will have an effect on the story. And that's where everything start to seem beautiful again. Even if you end one storyline you may have missed a detail or something, and... you want to play again. That's the strategy this game uses to keep its longevity. Presonally I would've liked it more if there were random-generated scenarios/puzzles. However, Uncanny Valley is one of those indie games we miss to see from quite a while, definitely worth the money.
For curious ones: the name comes from a theory from a Japanese professor. To make it brief, if we give things an humanoid appearence we start to like them, but after a while if we add too many of them we fall in the "uncanny valley", then if we make them almost looking like humans, well we will like them again.

This means you will be rollbacking the entire damn match to "adjust" to the PS4 user's "netcode build" if that makes sense. Every game I play against a PS4 user is like this. Every single one. and no, it's not my internet. Or theirs. It's just Capcom being Capcom and not fixing their game.

At the same time of this I got a free rootkit on my computer. That's always a nice bonus to the anaI boning you provided me, Capcom. Thanks man.
TL;DR I love this game. I hate it too. You will aswell.

I love ARPGs. Diablo I, Diablo 2, Path of Exile.
These are the heavy-hitting ARPGs I stack everything up to.
Diablo I had atmosphere and a pacing you cannot find in any other game. The slow deliberation as you traveled through the dungeon has not been duplicate to this day.
Diablo II had a flexible skill tree that entices players to construct a build for each and every skill. I'm not sure why, but those skills had real character.
Path of Exile. My newest love has been especially revolutionary in their currency and item modding systems. The challenge of POE drew my attention. Graphically, the game is terribly bland.
The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing II
Atmostphere: This game has a great atmosphere. Turning dark and gloomy areas into interesting scene pieces without the boredom like in POE or the ADHD tones of Torchlight II. There's a story that guides you along without being overbearing.
Sound: The voice acting is nice. The banter between Helsing and Katarina is frequent and entertaining. There is some bad voice acting for other NPCs. The spell and combat sounds could use work.
Systems: While the game is not revolutionary in its currency system, it has a good amount of gold sinks. Shopping, to respecing, enchanting, item modding, gambling: these are just some of the ways to spend your gold.
Gameplay: The gameplay is pretty standard fair for ARPGs. However there is a slight targeting issue and some environmental boundaries that you might get hung up on. The maps are not procedurally generated, but they are handcrafted nicely.
Customization: There is quite a bit of customization across the character classes. They advertise over 200 spells. They all seem quite varied and to add another layer of depth, they all can be modded further by the use of the rage system. By activating one or more of the rage buttons, it modifies the ability to perform differently. Similar to the rune system from Diablo III, albeit not as grand, almost all abilities have 3 mods. They usually come in the form of an extra projectile, more damage, % life gain on kill, first second of channeling stuns all targets, etc.
Difficulty: I heard this game on max difficult was impossible. 4 hours into my second Hunter (lvl 9), I am encountering mobs that are similar to merciless difficulty mobs in Path of Exile. It is not until around this level have I fought my first REAL rare mob. These ice witches that I am fighting, all have a slow aura........ which stacks. In a two stack of these witches, my melee hunter was moving at around 20% movement speed.
The problem with having extremely difficult monsters in these type of games, is that it forces players to kite. I still find the courage to fight in melee range. But when I'm playing hardcore against 4 Path of Exile charging Brutus', I still end up running at the end of the day.
There's something for every theorycrafter. Whether you're trying to create game breaking builds or make a subpar gimmick skill work, the game is extremely fun.

To start: I used to add a much longer header to this review, but since it often made the review too long to submit, I've opted to leave it on my Backloggery page.
Gameplay: I never did play this game back when it came out for two main reasons: I didn't have an Xbox 360 and I didn't have a good enough number crunching machine to play it. As such, I never got on the hype train about this game. Four years later, I finally was able to play it. Does it still hold up compared to some newer games? To be honest... yes. Absolutely. While Bastion is classified as an Action-RPG, the truth of the matter is that this game is RPG in the sense of leveling and weapon power/perk progression. Even then, all leveling allows you to do is add another perk; of which there are many, but I found the ones that I stuck with to be somewhat obvious picks. You have space for 10 perks (which corresponds to ten levels maximum), although in your first playthrough you'll only probably end up being at level 5 by the time you beat the game. Even still, this game is definitely one of those in which you could beat it at a very low level, so if you're into low-level RPG runs, you can find something to enjoy here.
As for the action part of the game, it's pretty standard action game fare. You walk up to an enemy, beat them over the head with your +3 or -3 Heaviness stick and they die after a while. There's also rolls and ranged weapons, but you can only carry two weapons at a time. This does allow you to take two melee or two ranged weapons at once if you so desire. Weapons also have their associated "Ultimate Techniques," which consume one Black Tonic (a normal consumable), but to be quite frank, I never felt the need to even touch them. In fact, there are 11 weapons total in the game, but I only ever found myself using two of them. While this does as mentioned earlier allow you to play it pretty much any way you want to, it also means that you'll find a couple of weapons you like and use exclusively them for the rest of the game. There's no punishment either, which is both good and bad for various reasons.
When starting the game, you have two options for difficulty: normal and easy. This game also has somewhat organic difficulty selection as well, in the form of Idols which you find about midway through the game. These idols inflict various penalties and benefits, although the negative effects typically outweigh the positive. Organic difficulty is fine and all, but I felt myself kinda wanting a dedicated Hard Mode, considering that with such organic difficulty the option to "wuss out" is always there. This is merely preferential of course, so you may feel differently on the matter.
There's about 12 different types of enemies in the game, and around four of them have alternate versions of said enemy. Most enemies won't pose any kind of threat to you and fall from many presses of the Murderize the Enemies buttons. There are a few which require some fairly artful dodging, although these only start showing up toward the end of the game. None of the enemies feel cheap however, and there's always an exit even when you're being overwhelmed with 20-30 enemies at once. There's also some bosses in the game as well, but they only usually felt like champions of the standard enemies you've been fighting throughout the area. As for the levels, pretty much the only thing that separates one from the other is the art assets. If you took away the assets and left the levels as individual parts, you wouldn't be able to tell one level from another. A bit disappointing, to be honest.
A lot of Bastion, admittedly, is mindless button mashing which does once again make me really want a dedicated Hard mode. There is a New Game + option after beating the game, but I think I'll save that for sometime in the future. It's pretty short as well; the first playthrough in which I got as close to 100% completion as possible took me about six hours. I never died on an actual level; instead, if I died it was probably due to Camp Dauncy. The combat itself is very solid and really fun; I just wish the game requested more out of me. Oh well, maybe New Game+ is the much vaunted hard mode I've been looking for. 9/10.
Story: The name of the game here as far as the writing goes is "world-building." Writing characters and character arcs is comparatively easy; writing a believable world and doing so in the same manner as Bastion does is really hard. Trust me; I write fiction as a hobby. World building can be one of the hardest parts of the story, especially if you're not going for a real-life analogue. While the characters themselves aren't too terribly dramatic, allowing for their entire character arc to be written within one page of a double spaced Word document, it does allow for the focus to be on the world around them. These characters have been shaped by their world; not the other way around. This game also does a great job of systematically telling you what's going on bit by bit in a logical manner; never too blunt, but never too obscure. In fact, when you find out how the story is being delivered, the relative vagueness of the dialogue all makes sense. I'll of course not spoil it, but if you're paying attention, you may be able to figure it out before the line that tells all is dropped. Again, the content itself is relatively mediocre at best; it's the delivery mechanism which makes it all count. If you write fiction yourself, you'll be in for a great time here. I've even picked up a few storytelling techniques myself. 9/10.
Graphics: I once again point you toward the screenshots and say, "You've got eyes. You don't need me to tell you how good the game looks." The assets themselves are fantastic; reminding me of Vanillaware's style (which I absolutely love). I will say that the levels themselves do look a bit "blocky," which can be a bit of a distraction for some, but it's one of those things that you have to distance yourself from the game a few feet in order to really notice such things. One thing that surprised me is that the characters are actual 3D models. They really do look like high-fidelity sprites until you see it in motion. Very good on this front. As for the technical side of things, there really isn't much in the options menu, but the game did fullscreen to my native resolution of 1080p which I always appreciate. There were also no frame drops for me throughout, and my GPU (GTX 760) didn't even break a sweat with this one. Again, you don't need me to tell you how good this game looks. It's a good port and it keeps its art quality throughout the entire game. Good stuff. 5/5.
Sound: I'll start out with the voice acting: there's really only two big voice actors throughout the entire game (one of them doesn't even show up until the very last area), but the main voice of the game is Rucks, the narrator. I... have a bit of a weakness for voices like that. Let's just say that if I were a woman, my pants would be quite thoroughly wet. Actually, who am I kidding; men can get their pants wet from such things as well; it's just a different spot. As for the music, it plays with a lot of styles, from Middle Eastern tones to dry, dusty Western chords. It all works together quite well. This one is definitely a soundtrack you wanna pick up. The sound design is really good as well; weapons sound punchy and crisp when they need to, enemies sound really cool and distinctive, and it all just works together really well. An excellent showing on the part of the sound crew. 5/5.
Overall scores are: 9/9/5/5; cumulative score of 9.3/10. While I haven't lost my mind quite as thoroughly as some have over this game, I still do thing that this game deserves its hype. I'd recommend this one to pretty much any gamer out there. Be warned though; if you're looking for a challenge, you may be left a little disappointed by the end of it. For anyone else though, it's an easy recommendation.

Just to clarify, the amount of time it lists for me in this game on Steam is inaccurate, because I played it offline (didn't have internet connection at the time). First off, I really wanted to like this game more than I did. The part that most appealed to me based on the description was the multiple endings. On the plus side, the game does a really good job of creating a creepy, isolated atmosphere. The music is unobtrusive yet creates a nice tone. The use of sound is minimal, which makes for a bigger impression when you do hear a sudden strange voice or a sharp shift in music tone. The story itself is interesting, and I really like how pieces of the backstory are littered around haphazardly, so that you have to put some work into figuring out the chronological order of events that happened before you arrived. The thing about that is after four playthroughs, I felt I knew what the story was. I played through three more times to see if more would be revealed, but I didn't get much  more backstory. Maybe it was just me. I got about 3 different endings, but I got the same ending 5 out of the 7 times, and the other two were unsatisfying. I don't feel like I would learn more by playing more, but I think I might know a way to get a more happy ending (all my endings were dark). But as others have mentioned, after you've played through more than a few times, it gets fairly repetitive, with you having to repeat a lot of the same actions at the beginning of the game (some things you can change, but a lot of it you can't). This creates an interesting groundhog day feel which I actually liked at first, but it got a little tiresome. All in all though I enjoyed the game, and thought it was worth the 9 bucks I spent. Each playthrough generally lasted an hour or less, and I like a game that doesn't drag on. This is a nice game to play late at night if you haven't got a lot of time to spend. Worth the money for me.

If you haven't played Lone Survivor, you might be like, "Pixel horror?! Gimme a break." But I assure you, not only is this game scary in the right, not jump scares way, it can present you with true horror if you make the wrong (right?) decisions. The story unfolds slowly, and requires a high level of reading and context comprehension. If fast-paced shooters are normally your bag, this game might not be for you. If you enjoyed slower-paced, story based games like the previously mentioned Lone Survivor, Gone Home, Home, or Gods Will Be Watching I don't think you will be disappointed. As another point of reference: This game reminds me a lot of cult indie film Primer. The story is complex and presented in an unconventional way. Also like primer, repeated playing will enrich the experience. It took me about an hour and a half to get one ending, so the game isn't very long at all if you look at it as a singular experience but the way the game limits what you can do during a single day (sort of like Bully, or Persona 3/4) leaves much to find on additional plays.

The game itself is still almost as good as it was a few years ago when I played it on PS3, but the multiplayer is dead, and you can't get DLC unless you get it off Amazon and you live in America...
I'd suggest playing it if you haven't before, but if you're coming back to this game trying to re-live your good memories, please stear well clear, it will ruin them all.

Ahh, Doom, one of the first FPS games that changed gaming. The original Doom's were pretty much perfect, perfect levels, perfect enemies, perfect weapons, great games.
Now even though Doom 3 is a good game too, it kind of lacked some things that the older Doom's had. Doom was all about rushing through hell while destroying all of hell's minions, while Doom 3 was a bit different. None the less, Doom 3 somewhat offered the same experience as the older Doom's. Same enemies and weapons, but not necessarily the same level design.
I am going to compare Doom 3 to Doom 3 BFG with some pros and cons, so you will know which Doom you'd rather get.
-You get Ultimate Doom, and Doom 2, as well as a better looking Doom 3
-Doom 3 looks much better but still the same in different ways
-You get Doom Resurrection of evil, as well as the Lost mission
-There are achievements for all Doom's
-You can use the Oculus Rift on Doom 3 BFG
-Fair Price ($20)
-There isn't many settings to lower the graphics so you'll need a somewhat beefy PC
-You can now use your flashlight while using weapons at the same time which overall makes the game less scary
-The controls could be better
-Doom 3 BFG is not moddable
-It is moddable, which makes the game have lots of replay value, which there's even a Coop mod, so expect lots of playtime
-There is actually a console you can use to spawn weapons/enemies/objects
-The Controls are fantastic, you can change pretty much any key if you wanted to, unlike Doom 3 BFG
-The game is much more scarier since you can only use a flashlight and a weapon at different times
-Better price ($10)
-The original Doom 3 does not include any DLC or the older Doom's
-The game looks a little more outdated which means the graphics aren't as good
-The steam overlay is pretty awful (small resolution)
-No Achievements
Btw I also nomiated this game for 'game within a game' award. This has the coolest minigames out there :D

Untill there is a mod or option to turn off Bosses, i would not recommend getting this game.

Wow. Stardrive. So sad. Early access is a double-edged sword. On one hand, you get to watch a promising game grow into something really special. As it stands Stardrive is okay. Not great. Not good. Just okay. A real-time 4x with fully customizable ships? Sounds awesome!
