Good game, IF, you like 4x strategy games. I am a fan of this game but there could be a lot more to it seeing how old it is. However for the time, effort, and abilities of Zerosum Games it is a good game. There are ups and downs to the game. (A lot of downs)
There are a few bad things about the game though. First there are some lag issues and stability problems. The game lags a bit when a lot of action is going on in a large galaxy. Second is mods. The whole game relies on mods at this stage to keep players interested and the game has a open mod folder to simply load one into. The website even comes with a tutorial on how to mod the game. Third is you have to be very meticulous to see what is going on when and where.
The game focuses more on combat than economy or events. The game has events but none have any significance or really game changing results whether that'd be good or bad. Events have changed over the year this game has officialy been out, that means a few events were removed, others added or tweeked. Economy is good but needs more to it as well. The game has two resources, food and production. Food is used to feed your race and production is used from building structures to ships. Other than that it doesnt get any more complicated. The only tricky thing about economies is taxing and distributing resources.
Combat offers a lot to the game seeing how that is the soul focus of gameplay. Ships can be custom designed with a traditional grid pattern and using moduels to fill them in. The possibilities are practicaly endless when it comes to combat.
Dev did abandon the game unfortunatly. After the full game came out updates have become rare. The game has absolutely no purpose but sort of sandbox game letting you do as you please. The only downside to that is there is no story to the game, no story or big explanation about the mysterious "Remnant" race. All we get as far as story to any AI alien race is a short three sentence paragraph FROM the AI. And all we get for story behind the "remnant" is a short mini event quest that, when summed up, gives literaly a short two paragraph explanation on them.
The game feels very open and at times too open. There needs to be more content before this becomes a real game because at this stage it does seem like a very high quality app than a full game.

TLDR: Bethesda is a horrible game company, Game is a horrible RPG and extremely repetitive in general, don't bother buying if you don't mod it to all hell.
Honestly, there's so many things wrong with Bethesda as a game studio and publisher and general, but I'm going to stick to Fallout 4 alone.
After sinking in over 500 hours on PS4 and PC combined, and having played New Vegas just as much, I have found out a few things.
First off, this is NOT a true Fallout game, if your coming from Fallout 3 or New Vegas, you're in for a nasty shock, coming from such amazing RPG's,  FO4 has a shockingly low amount of RPG elements, and plays more like an open world shooter than anything else.
Exploring the wasteland you'll find out something really quick, every place is basically the same, same basic layouts with either boring NPC's without a personality, or equally as boring raiders.
Oh, and want to use your fancy new 144hz monitor? Well tough luck, the game is locked to 60FPS and unlocking it manually causes extreme screen tearing and anything over 60 FPS causes the game to be to become extremely unstable.
Speaking of unstable: BUGS. Bugs, bugs, bugs, what's a Bethesda game without bugs, 2 years later and it's still riddled with bugs, with Bethesda leaving a lot of them to the Modders, a lot of which have actually produced quality patches and additional gameplay, and a lot of them being even better than Bethesda work, and to be honest, most people buy Bethesda games solely for the mods, which gets me into my next point.
Motherf***ing Creation Club.
Remember when Bethesda tried payed mods with Skyrim? And there was a huge outrage by the community? Certainly they'll have learned their lesson right? NOPE. Out rolls the creation club, with expensive, poorly made mods that have much better counterparts on the Nexus, with them even charging a buck or two for a black pipboy skin, literally just a skin that turns your pipboy black and they're selling it for a couple bucks to poor suckers who can't figure out how to use mod launchers or who don't know what the nexus is.
Which Segways me into my next point, as I said before, the mods are what make a Bethesda game, and Fallout 4 is no exception, the modding community is great, from new weapons and areas, to DLC Sized Quest mods, to just straight up jokes and memes, with modding Legends from previous Fallout's and other Bethesda games like Trainwiz and Elianora, and other amazing modders like Thuggysmurf and the team behind Fusion City Rising.
Unless you are very enthusiastic about modding, and have the computer to handle them, I can't recommend this game whatsoever, if you want a good RPG with a story, get Fallout New Vegas.

A hidden gem of a puzzle game! I wish I would've known about this sooner. It took me about 10.5 hours to beat every stage (everything up to and including flummery), but there's much more fun to be had going for more medals, weekly challenges, and using the level creator.
If you like puzzle games, you'll almost certainly enjoy this game. It's very well paced and doesn't feel repetitive - each level feels like it has a unique "trick" to it and they add new items and enemies at a good rate. I found the difficulty curve to be great as well - I never really got frustrated on a stage and never felt like a stage was too long.
The levels are always just the right size - unlike chip's challenge where you would not be able to see everything you need to see sometimes (due to levels being really large), this game makes it very clear and precise while maintaining a charming visual aesthetic.
One of the things that makes this game really fun is infinite undo and rapid restarting. You don't EVER have to go through a section you've already solved if you make a mistake because you can just hit backspace. If you're trying to beat a level without undoing (like making an attempt to get a high score), you can just hit R and instantly restart if you make a mistake. And as a nice touch, the timer doesn't start counting until you make your first move.
The level design is really what makes this game stand out for me. It's brimming with creativity, polish and game design expertise, no doubt building on Chuck's experience with Chip's challenge. Levels aren't simply about pushing blocks into specific positions - they might be about dodging enemies, using switches, building bridges, etc...it does an excellent job of making every level have a unique concept/central idea/key trick, leading to a plethora of satisfying "eureka" moments as you discover them while playing around with the level.
It doesn't just stop at being a great solitary experience - you can compete for time on every stage using the online leaderboards. At this level of play, the game does become a bit more about execution and less about puzzle solving, but still maintains an aspect of puzzling as you try to figure out the most effecient path to the goal. So, regardless of whether the execution or puzzle solving appeals to you, you'll get something out of the leaderboards. With the stages that ship with the game, you can also just replay them to try to get the silver and gold medals. There's also community-created maps and a weekly puzzle (selected from the best of the community maps each week) - so each week presents a new opportunity to test your skills against other players.
On a completely different track, you can design levels and share them with the community. There's a rudimentary voting system so you can see how people like your creations. This game gives you such a variety of tools and such a solid mechanical foundation to work with that it's an excellent platform to express your game design creativity and feel good about making something fun for other people to enjoy.
Definitely give this a go if you like puzzle games. I've played a lot of puzzle games and this game ranks up there with my top 5, maybe even top 3.

The story is an artistic obscure one, but done well for the most part. It's meanings you will have to work out for yourself. Characters are mostly intriguing and the world is definitely interesting enough that you won’t want to groan and click through every piece of dialogue.
The main character is slightly whiny and demanding but it’s a 10 year old girl locked in an asylum that just wants to find her cat and go home so it works as it’s what the character should be. The character is also consistently a child as opposed to an ‘adult’ that becomes a child when the plot needs them to. Fran also develops at a believable pace as she begins to see and understand the new world she is in and information she is uncovering.
The art is beautiful, slightly creepy and interesting, music goes well with this to give a great corrupt Alice in wonderland vibe that works brilliantly for the most part.
It's game play mechanic of switching between universes or seasons provides some interesting ways to spice up the usual point and click tasks that are happening in the background,  switching between the ‘universe’ and ‘ultraverse’ will often lead to new solutions, background into what’s happening in the normal scene and new characters or important plot elements to move you along.
There’s a few standard point and click puzzles but the use of the games mechanics and story interweaving with the game leave few moments where you feel like your just going through the motions.
There are a few issues however
First of all i had to run this at 1080p rather than my native 1440p resolution causing scaling issues in full screen, i was forced to run windowed as the game also caused a few display issues, not the end of the world but it is nice for a modern game to work properly on a modern system.
Secondly, it's clunky and not at all an enjoyable experience to physically play, Fran Bow isn't the first point and click with thee issues but the genre is so mature that this is inexcusable. navigating the world feels sluggish and unresponsive, using items both in the world is unintuitive and tedious.
There's also the great problem of what do i click on, out of all the times i got stuck only a couple were me struggling, the rest were all just "lets click everything till i find the obscure piece of interactive scenery that has the answer". I'll admit I’m not great at this genre but both times i brought up a walkthrough it was to point out the thing to click on i had missed.
As great as the story is in the beginning it does start to slip away into just being weird and the ideas it portrayed in the beginning seem to mostly dissapear as the story starts feeling less and less coherent. the late game reaches a point where there's little to be made out of the plot and it ends abruptly which left me disappointed.
Finally, while there were a few mildly creative point and click puzzles there were plenty more unoriginal puzzles that weren't interesting, challenging or even helped the narrative in any real way, this is especially true for those 'mini games' between larger sections.
It's a recommendation from me, just barely. if it's on sale or in a bundle it's worth a look but at full price it's a hard sell

Floating Point is a fun and relaxing game from the maker of Gunpoint. It's a 2D game in which you shoot a grappling hook and collect the bars that are dotted around the level. The more momentum you gain, the longer the bars become and more points you earn. The levels are generated procedurally and get progressively harder with more platforms at greater height and depth. The trick is to shoot your hook in such a way that you keep up the momentum while trying to get as many bars as possible in one swing. All that without accidentally hitting a platform and loosing momentum. Definitely worth a spin. And it's free too!

It's games like this that make me wish there was an "eh" choice for "Would you recommend this game?"
I probably wouldn't purchase it again, but I'm somewhat glad I played it at the same time.
There was a lot of stuff that Fran Bow got right. The story was alright -- engaging enough. The level of creativity that it took to make a game like this was off the scale. It was very Alice in Wonderland-ish, but in a much darker way. This is the part of the game that makes me glad that I played it. I loved the artistry and imagination behind it all.
It was the gameplay that was somewhat lacking, in my mind. A lot of the puzzles were just not intuitive. You can't sit there and think to yourself, "Alright, how would this thing I just found work?" because in all likelihood, it will not end up doing anything even close to what you think it will do. I ended up doing a lot of "alright, let's try these two things together randomly" in order to get stuff to work. But then, perhaps that was intended? It IS a chaotic, crazy world that she's in, after all. Maybe that's where the lack of intuition when it comes to puzzle solving came in. Who knows.
For whatever reason, I just don't end up enjoying a game as much when I end up needing to look up solutions to puzzles, especially if I sit there and think "what the f....?" to myself after realizing what I was supposed to have done. It removes you from the immersiveness of the game, and I would have LOVED to have stayed immersed in the universe they created. So it was just a bit of a pity from that standpoint.
All in all, if you want something that will get your creative juices and imagination flowing, and don't mind having to probably look up some answers, by all means try this game.

The original Binding of Issac was a favorite of both mine, and many people who dabble in the realm of Indie games. However, will this sequel/remake live up to the standards set by it's predecessor? Let's find out, shall we?
The story revolves around a young boy named Isaac and his mother. One day, Isaac's mother heard the voice of God, telling her that Isaac is a sinful child, and that she must save him by taking everything from him that God claims is unholy or sacreligious. Being an upstanding Christian woman, Mom agrees, and takes all of Isaac's toys and locks him in his room. Afterwards, God demands a sacrifice, and Mom, now brandishing a butcher's knife, storms into Isaac's room on a quest for his blood. Isaac, however, managed to jump into the basement below and hide from his deranged mother. How will Issac get himself out of this mess? Well, play the game to find out.
You control Isaac (or many other various characters that you can unlock by playing the game) in a quest to escape the basement, and, ultimately, defeat your mother. The camera is angled in an interesting top-down perspective, akin to games such as "The Legend of Zelda" for the NES. Isaac's primary form of attack is his tears, and he is able to shoot them in all four directions. When you start a new game, a random series of basement floors are generated for you so each run can be different, which VASTLY increases the replayability of this game. Throughout the floors that you will explore, you will encounter various objects that you can pick up in treasure rooms, shops and after you defeat a boss which will either enhance Isaac's abilities naturally, or via a usable item, whether it be one use or rechargable. Like the floor layout, the items that you will find are also randomly generated, allowing for a nearly infinite amount of combinations for your character to experiment with. Isaac responds well with each stroke of a key or push of a button, and it seems like the controls work perfectly with the camera angle given to the player. If you die, it is YOUR fault. Not the camera or the enemies
The soundtrack to The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth is a collection of amazingly atmospheric tunes which perfectly capture the area in which you are in. Mind you, and this is personal preference, the original Binding of Isaac had a superior soundtrack when it came to the amount of amazingly spectacular songs, but Rebirth's soundtrack envokes a much better sense of the surroundings that you are in. Whether it be the frantic boss themes or mysterious floor themes near the end, Rebirth's soundtrack does not exactly pale in comparison to its older brother in the sound department. The sound effects are also crisper, better quality and of more variety than in the original as well.
The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth's graphical style is one that is being explored quite a lot these days: the 16-bit pixel art style. Whereas the original Binding of Isaac utilized a sort of Flash animation style, Rebirth looks like it was ripped right out of a Super Nintendo. This graphical change is a vast improvement over its predecessor, as now items look cleaner, more vibrant, and it seems to have that 16-bit charm that we are all so accustomed to. Now, just because the graphics are not as "modern" as they could be, do not be fooled, as the character, environment and monster designs range from bizarre and funny to absolutely repulsive and gutwrenching. Clearly, the artists put their heart and soul into their work on this game.
The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth offers a spectacular amount of bonus content along with the main game. There are many different challenge runs that one can partake in which only add to your gameplay experience and allow you to experience the game from entirely new angles. Since the "Afterbirth" DLC has released, there have been additional characters, challenges, and even a new mode called "Greed Mode" which functions similarly to an arena combat challenge.
Overall, there isn't really that much that I find wrong with The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth. The controls work great, the graphics fit the style of the game, and the difficulty curve is just right. However, there is one thing that could get people to be instantly turned off of the experience: the RNG. This game LIVES by a random number generator. You will have runs that are really amazing, and you will have runs that are completely botched because you simply got the wrong item at the wrong time or didn't get the item you needed at all.
The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth is, in my eyes, the quintessential rogue-like action game. Even though you will die (ESPECIALLY when you are first starting out and have no idea what many of the items even DO), you will enjoy it all the way through. However, this game is for those who are patient, want a challenge, and have a mind that is already corrupted by the worst that the internet has to offer. After playing it, hopefully you will have that "Just one more run!" attitude that I had after my first few hours.

I liked the Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing quite a bit, so I was excited for II.  The original game had its problems, but had enough atmosphere and quirky humor and story for me to enjoy it.  Where VH excelled, VH2 does not.
Pros:
1) Game's atmosphere is beautiful.  I particularly like the outside areas.  Unfortunately, very little of your gameplay experience takes place outside.
Cons:
1) They attempted to fix the lackluster skill tree from the original game.  The original lacked choices and most of the skills were useless.  They did a complete 180 and the skill tree still sucks.  Now, it is oversaturated with no coherent structure.  Certain skills unlock other skills but have no function in relation to those skills.  For example, Want to build around ice damage?  Pick one skill on the right, arbitrarily attached to some fire and lightning.  Then, try to pick a skill on the left, arbitrarily attached to other random skills.  Makes no sense.
2) Balance.  Game balance is awful.  I played the original game on the hardest difficulty [I play most ARPGs on the hardest difficulty].  VH2 seems to have mobs that are weak [on any difficulty] and mobs that do an incredible amount of dmg on any difficulty other than "casual".  Even if I built my character around heavy defensive passives/tricks ranged/casting things [which tend to do more dmg in general] hit BRUTALLY hard.  There's also the occasional 1 shot from a challenging to see ability when swamped in a pack of mobs.
Edit: I've now played through the game with a second character.  My first was a thaumaturge that really struggled with balance.  My second was the original hunter character, but built around spell-casting.  I played my second time on hard/heroic difficulties - stacked the mana shield defensive ability and some other defensives, and could face-roll pretty much anything so long as I had mana.  Again, certain skills are way more powerful than others, effectively making the oversaturated skill tree still feel problematic.
Edit Two: Played more on the thaumaturge on heroic.  Balance is really what is holding the game back.  Built my character around abilities that could do damage while moving and crit chance/crit dmg [crit chance around 32-35%, crit dmg maxed @ 450%], and high HP, made heroic pretty easy.  The problem, though, is sometimes you just get 1 shot from off-screen, even with high damage reduction.  Difficulty basically scales like this: Mobs have higher health making it take longer to kill them.  High dmg abilities do insane dmg and can result in 1 shots.  The longer a mob lives, the greater chance of a 1 shot.  Not sure how they can really fix this, but it makes build diversity fairly limited.  At a certain point you just have to be able to do damage while moving and you have to spec heavily into defense.
3) Storyline/Quests.  This is really my main qualm with the game.  The storyline of this game is really disappointing.  Maybe the storyline isn't disappointing [as it makes sense in the context of VH1], but the way it is executed is disappointing.  The questing sucks.  Very little variation, mostly based around tower defense.  The vast majority of your missions are "secure X, Y, Z points by battling through streams of enemies.  This was my least favorite type of mission in VH and it seems to be what the entirety of VH2 is built around.  If I wanted to play Tower Defense, I'd play Tower Defense.  The final boss fight, spoiler alert, is not even a fight.  You literally kill streams of enemies until his force field's HP hits 1.  He then blows up and the game ends on a pathetic attempt at a cliff hanger.  I understand the attempt at a military strategy/real-time invasion, but it simply fails to be enjoyable.
4) End Game:  It's about what you expect.  You get "random" dungeons [just reskinned areas of the main story] and tasks to complete within them.  Some of them also have interesting things that makes them substantially more difficult [Your companion won't help, can't regen life/mana, etc].  I did a few of them on heroic difficulty.  They were a challenge.  The quirky interactions don't take place between Katarina/Helsing so it's basically just the mindless challenge of slaughtering enemies with certain affixes that make the already poorly balanced gameplay more difficult.  I'm glad they added this feature.  Unfortunately, it does not do much for me because I've already done a lot of this in Path of Exile AND Path of Exile's system is better.  All in all, I think it will be fun for people who haven't already beaten the model to death in other games, but wasn't real fun for me.
5) Multiplayer:  Much like during the launch of the first game [in which it wasn't even functional], multiplayer is quite buggy.  In fact, I've only successfully joined 1 game [I've tried to join many], and the host disconnected shortly thereafter, rendering my efforts obsolete.  I've also tried hosting multiple times.  I will get a message that "x is trying to join your game", but they are never successful in doing so.  Not sure if it is a bug, a lack of stable connection, or what, but multiplayer seems quite hit or miss.
Verdict:
If you did not play the first game, don't buy this.  The first is a much more complete experience.
If you loved the first and are desperate to see where the story goes, buy this.
If you loved the first for what it was, and aren't too attached to the story, don't buy this.
The game simply lacks what made the first game worth playing - the quirky nature, originality, and great atmosphere - while not really fixing any of the detracting factors of the first game [lack of real diversity via skill tree].

Sleeping Dogs is probably one of the most average but beautiful games I have ever played. It's not a terrible game but it's not an amazing game either. You play Wei Shen, an undercover cop who infiltrates the Triads of Hong Kong and sets about destroying them from the inside.
Gameplay 9/10
I loved the gameplay here. Fighting hand to hand is so satisfying and although you can say it copies Batman, I believe the fighting mechanics here do enough to set the experience apart. Good enemy variety make the game interesting but it's really easy most of the time. Gunplay is just far too easy for my liking because the AI here is dumb. They will stay in cover and blindly shoot at you and never move up or take advantage when you're reloading for example. So I can effectively sit there and listen to them shooting at me and hitting everything in the damn room but me. Clothes and customisation for Wei was disappointing IMO. I love the cars and how they handle and there is a real difference between a class A and a class C car. The only problem here is that to access the better cars and clothes, require a certain face level for you to even buy which was one of the only things I didn't like about this game.
Graphics 9/10
The graphics are top notch here IF you have a good rig. Downloading the high res texture pack and cranking up to ultra settings really brings Honk Kong to life. The player model for Wei is highly detailed as are the ones for the NPCs and other characters. Car aesthetics are similarly detailed and you can really see every sharp contour and crease in the bodywork. No complaints here.
Story 6/10
This was what let the game down IMO. A lot of wasted potential here. Throughout the game I felt that Wei's loyalty was divided between the Sun On Yee and his role as an undercover cop. His arguments with his supervisor Raymond and the way he really bonds with the idea of being Sun On Yee and the way he embraces the role made me believe that he was slowly but surely warming to the idea of becoming a Triad. But it's dissapointment at the end. Sure there are interesting characters although not as much as I would have liked. Pretty average and cliche if i'm honest.
Overall 7/10
The graphics and gameplay combine to make Sleeping Dogs a very good experience. For the release price I wouldn't have bought it as it just didn't capture my attention enough to want to buy it. I bought it in a Steam sale for £3.74 which is incredible value for this game. Pick it up in the sale is what I would say. Alright, I'm going to try and keep this short and concise mainly because I'd rather be bludgeoned to death than be writing game reviews at 3:36 A.M.
The basic premise of the game is explained pretty well in the description and I can tell you after nearly two hours of playing it that it's pretty on point. You play as a guy named Tom who for some reason you will likely find out later (or by looking it up on youtube...) has decided to move to ♥♥♥♥ing nebraska or some♥♥♥♥♥♥ It's pretty much just "guard simulator" if you just do the objectives that are obviously given to you. However there's a point where you need to do something in the apartment building and the game is a little unclear on what it is. If you don't mind spoilers, google it. Now you can get bored like I almost did at first and try to leave via subway but uh... well you'll find out on your own.
This game rewards exploration, mostly. I mean, it rewards you exploring as much as a horror game should but you have to work past some obstacles at points. That's perfectly fine, the obstacles kind of feel like any of the enemies from the Silent Hill series. By that I mean that the things that will hurt you are always where you want to go next. You'll find plenty of background information for the game's story if you search through the zones you're almost denied access to. Trust me, you'll want to hear and see the tapes once you find them, it really gets you invested in the setting.
While we're on the subject of setting, it is so dreadful it hurts. I don't mean "terrible" or anything, I mean full of dread. Like, from the second you hop the fence it's just this constant feeling of impending death. Like something is waiting for you every time you open the elevator or that one night you'll be killed in the forest by the things you can see in the trailer. The best part is (usually) there's nothing there to even be scared of. That just makes it terrifying when something finally wants to hurt you. Usually that doesn't happen until you go somewhere you weren't meant to be which, let's face it, you will.
Honestly, the game isn't some great blockbuster. It doesn't terrify you the way that one game would
But the thing is I think it does what it had set out to do, it builds a sense of lasting dread and even if just for a little while you might be afraid of the dark again.
In summary:
Pros:
Great atmosphere, completely dreadful and creepy
Always a sense of suspense in every room
Pushing boundaries is rewarded
Not some stupid "early access" cash grab
Cons:
Unless you try to push boundaries there's no danger, you could do the same thing for hours
After messing with the generator the objectives are significantly less clear
LOTS of small bugs and glitches(luckily the devs do work on fixes as they learn of them)
Lack of waifus(or is this a pro?)
Maybe wait for it to go on sale to pick it up. However if you feel charitable you should definately pay full price to support the devs in future projects. Seriously, look up indie game development's economic forecast for employees. 95% of indie games don't bring in a profit and as a matter of fact 80% operate at a loss. It's all up to you

You wake up in a gutter and begin wandering down a dark alley only to be chased and summarily devoured by shadow-creatures. The night terrors in this game are fantastic, and can actually make you fear going to sleep, in the game and real life. I abandoned my bed for the latter part of the first half, since not making it to bed lets you bypass night terror sequences. Eventually even your daytime existence becomes terrifying as well. There is a certain point which progresses the story. What happens during the cut-scene depends on all the tiny actions you take during the game.
The game starts out with the main character Tom being shown the ins and outs of his new security job. Each night you will hunt for clues. There are tapes that you can playback and gain a bit more knowledge about the storyline, as well as computer terminals that will drop clues about where to find keys needed to access restricted areas of the building you are guarding. Should you really descend to the lower sector? You ARE the security guard, and there MIGHT be somebody down there. Or according to certain emails, something. Do you dare to unveil the mystery?
Whichever path you unknowingly decide to go down will eventually lead you to the second half of the game, this half is less about time-management and clue-finding and more about the visceral terror the game has been building towards thus far. There are some cool mechanics in this more combat-focused half, such as damage crippling your movement. However, there are some counter intuitive aspects such needing to engage the enemy in order to activate a trap. Combat is to be avoided, which means to even try this move, you need to be extremely desperate or really lucky.
Overall I found the two halves meld together quite nicely. Just when you are into the routine and having a hard time finding something new, the game throws you a curve-ball. The art and sound design are much more than I would’ve expected from the game at a glance, though the voice-acting leaves something to be desired. The story will require multiple playthroughs to piece together, since it seems to Tarantino around. You also can’t skip the first, more monotonous half, making multiple playthroughs repetitive. Uncanny Valley is a solid game for those that enjoy a good story, but it could certainly do with a bit more polish.

Chuck's Challenge 3D is the sequel to the 1989 puzzle game Chip's Challenge, made by the same developer. It is basically Chip's Challenge but with updated graphics, a few extra game elements, a level editor and user created content by putting the levels made in the editor in the Steam Workshop. If you are a fan of the original game, you really should buy it, not only because it has near infinite levels thanks to the Workshop, but also because it's dirt cheap.
For the guys who have never played Chip's Challenge before, Chuck's Challenge is a puzzle game where you control a character (Whoop) on a grid and you have to find the exit. On your way are doors, ice tiles, fire, movable blocks, pressure plates and a dozen different type of monsters. The monsters move in a predictable pattern: Bouncers bounce back and forth between obstacles, Limpy will always turn right if possible, Blue Golems reverse direction when you pull a lever etc. These few simple mechanics make a surprisingly challenging game. Don't let the aesthetics fool you: this game can be very, VERY hard.
This game is not without flaws, as of the date this review is written, there are a couple of problems. Main soruce of anger is the unresponsive menu screen and controls. There is a bit of lag between pressing the up key and going up, which takes a while to get used to. Despite that, the core gameplay is great and I recommend this game for any puzzle game fan, especially for the very low price this game is.

This game, goddamn, it took all of about the first 20 minutes of gameplay to show me why this is such an awesome game. The premise of the game is simple, bugs come in from direction A and head to point B, you have to stop them. The characters are pretty simple and cover pretty well whatever basic character you want to play be it a sniper, rifleman (Riflewoman in this case), a shotgunner, a rocketeer or a Russian chick with a crossbow. For those of you who like a challenge, there are a few Feats of stength which can be added into any game to make it harder for you in some form.

Uploaded 2 days after the Eclipse update fiasco:
As a player who started playing Trove when it first hit Beta; I've been playing for quite awhile. It's an amusing game with decent gameplay and graphics, but recent changes have made it much harder for me to recommend to anyone. For whatever reason, the devs keep adding systems that make the game more of a grind then it really needs to be.
An example are the 8 new dragons that have been added with the Eclipse update.
Now, if you've never played Trove, Dragons are mounts that can shoot projectiles that destroy what you hit while also being able to fly around. They come with different looks, and give your character stat boosts as well. The thing about these dragons is that almost all of them you have to grind for in some way, but the grinding isn't generally too bad. These new dragon's fragments (parts of the dragons you must collect to craft them) on the other hand have an extremely low drop chance by doing very specific actions.
This, mixed with a welcome but time-gated way to change/improve your classes' gem stats (Gems are items you collect to increase your characters power and stats), make this update a very mixed bag.
Another change that didn't seen to be well thought out is that Shadow Towers (Arenas where players go to fight difficult monsters for extra rewards) were vastly increased in difficulty, but mostly giving out the same or slightly reduced rewards as before.
The devs did add subclasses, which give your character tiny stat boosts along with an additional effect, as a way to further customize your character. But that seems to be the most positive addition to the game with this update.
So overall, Trove can be a fun game, but the devs keep piling on extra systems that make the game more grindy, less rewarding, and less fun. Maybe they'll finally listen to our feedback, but considering how they've practically ignored player's issues with recent updates, that seems unlikely.

Fran Bow is a labour of love --- down to every detail you can feel the creativity that went into producing this game.
It is a point-and-click, story and text- based game with some choice and several unique mini art games and puzzles that break the gameplay up to make things fun and interesting on your journey into Fran's world. A love of gamemaking, puzzles and beautiful concept art is everywhere in the landscape of Fran Bow. No screenshots are allowed in this game because so many of the visuals hold clues to the story and are unforgettable scenes you will never find in any other game.
This game defies genre, it starts off as doll-core horror in a mental asylum for children and then becomes fantastical, magical, mythology- inspired; reminiscent of some of the old Sierra adventure games like King's Quest 6, except the mythology is completely invented by Fran Bow.
The game deals with the stigma of mental illness in children and attempts to give the player the experience of a child's curious mind marred by delusions and trauma. The game itself is therapuetic for the imagination to play and it is easy to become immersed in the mythology of Fran's mind.

This game will give you nightmares; but if you perservere through the story, it will reward you in spades. It speaks true to Winston Churchill's famous quote: "If you are going through hell; keep going."
The only criticism I have is Fran's purse inventory made it a bit awkward to access items and try them at times - maybe a bar at the top to access items or a drag feature for combining items would have made it easier. But otherwise, I wish there were more games like this.
Good job Kill Monday and kudos to the artist here for beautiful storyboarding and concept art.

I was disgusted by the crazy, graphical look to it, but it is strangely addicting!
Isaac's adventures has brought him to the depths of... using his tears as a weapon, and the enemies using their own bloody ball as an opposing source of power to attempt to defeat him. Dungeon after dungeon, floor after floor, the weird lookin' enemies get more tough the lower you go; gamble with the price of choice, what should I do? Use this key on a golden chest, or unlock the door to the shop, and take the risk of purchasing an unknown item with little to no knowledge in there? THE CHOICE IS YOURS, grab over 50-100 different, unique abilities that really do not make sense when you choose them (They are marked down in some sort of encyclopedia of abilities in-game on the menu)!
Find unbearable bosses/creatures to fight against, take strange pills to either enhance or decrease your stats, deal with the devil (at a certain cost), and continually become stronger!
The best thing is... the DLC, The Binding of Isaac: Afterbirth, brings EVEN more possibility and fun to the normal, average game! Amazed of how certain actions can benefit you or almost kill you, the dungeons are the same as Minecraft worlds' generative ways... as you can use a "seed" number to play the same dungeon!
Share your seeds with your friends, play it with them together, PLUS (which was a big surprise to me), you can play Co-op with a controller, and/or plus the keyboard!
I am just going to cut to the case:
This game brought a freaky horizon to gaming, has endless amounts of achievements, interesting challenges, and SO MUCH MORE! If you are not the person to enjoy a type of shoot-to-thrill (AC/DC!), move to the next dungeon, almost similar to the first Legend of Zelda dungeons, do not get this (I am not trying to relate this to Legend of Zelda, as the two gameplays are different, well, storyline-wise)!
This game makes me so angry all the time, and I keep returning, because I know I want vengeance!

You like Diablo3? Then it's very unlikely you won't like this one. It got soul.
You even know and liked part 1? Then you'll definitely love part 2!
What a nice successor. They took everything that worked from the first part and made it even better/larger/funnier/bigger/enjoyable/etc.
On a technical basis not very much has changed but to hell with that. In times where multi-million-dollar-projects are boring and completely shallow, pearls like this stand apart.
Let me sum it up:
+ Totally acceptable story for an ARPG. It's no "Planescape: Torment" but it does its job very well
+ Loot, loot, loot. Socket it, enchant it, remodel it, change its appearance, compare it...
+ Inventory management is nice. Lots of keys to access both character's inventory fast, and a lot of space too
+ Interesting character progression, nice and many skills. Your companion is more configurable than the main character in other ARPGs
+ The companion. Not as funny as "Claptrap" but it adds to the atmosphere
+ Send your troops/captains to extra side missions. Nice idea. Some variety to the usual fighting
+ The base/lair. Everything you need (incl. respec-NPC) and some gimmicks for variety
+ Tower-defense minigames. Love it! If you're not that much into TD you could skip it though
+ fitting/nice soundtrack, decent SFX
* Except Katarina and the Protagonist the voice-overs are feeling unmotivated. But it's acceptable for that budget
* Just 3 classes. And each with two major specializing differences. Could have been some more but...
* Mobs do not vary much in each region, but just in time before it starts to get boring you're in the next area with other fitting mobs
- not found anything negative yet. Suprising!
One last word: Don't let the "cheap" price fool you. This fellow is very well on par with Diablo 3. At least single-player-wise (as I have not yet tested MP).

The Binding of Isaac is a rouge-like, dungeon exploring, heartbeat increasing, thrill of a game. You will want to proceed through as many dungeons possible to fight the final boss in the end. Compared to the original Binding of Isaac, this one is much more abundant when it comes to characters, applicable items to characters, enemies, and dungeons. As you fight through the basement of your mother's dark and twisted mind, you will encounter everything your character fears, and it is up to you on whether or not you will let this evil consume you or if you will over power it.
I really, really recommend buying this game even at full price. I don't know how else I can convince you other than saying that the replay value of this simply has no words for it. You'll definitely find yourself playing this for maybe even more than 100 hours.

There's really no way to over state this, but doom kicks♥♥♥♥♥ It's the quintessential FPS. If you haven't played it, I don't believe you. At all. Seriously, how the hell have you not played Doom? ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
So, you're on steam and you see Doom 3 BFG edition, and you think “oh hey, this could be cool. It's Doom 3 remastered with the Resurrection of Evil, Doom 1, Doom 2, and new levels for Doom 3. For 20 bucks? That sounds like a deal.
Well, it's not all good. It's better than a poke in the eye or an Assault Horizon in your steam inventory, but some of the things that were done to the BFG edition don't make any sense. Because, these days, remastering doesn't translate to updating the visuals but rather ♥♥♥♥ing everything up, there's a lot of bizarre choices made here.
First, let's address Doom and Doom 2 here. They're complete and they work, but neither have any real options for visuals and it runs at 35 FPS constant. So, drop those bad boys into GZDoom and forget about it. You'll run it at 60, have loads of options,  and even superior sound quality.
But, if you wanted those games, you'd just get those. You wanted Doom 3 in a higher fidelity. Well, it's Doom 3, so it's not terrible. But, they've really messed about with the game in some weird ways. This opening cutscene is a perfect example of what I mean. Just look at those new facial textures. This really sums up the BFG edition in a concise example. It's still Doom 3, but there are odd things going on. Design changes without rhyme or reasons like Why the ♥♥♥♥ did they change the rates of fire? Why did they ruin the chaingun? Why did they reduce the rates of fire for both the Machine gun and plasma gun? Why? Seriously, the Chaingun is terrible now? The intentional design changes make little sense, if at all. I will give them this though. They attached the flashlight to your armor. That does make a lot more sense than having to literally tote around a flashlight. It never really bothered me, but I seem to be in the minority on that one.
So, let's just begin with the actual remastering work done here. I use the term work loosely. They've really done almost nothing at all in that regard. They've changed a few textures here and there to try and make characters look better, but it really just comes off as putting lipstick on a pitbull. They haven't increased polygon counts, they've barely touched up textures, and they've ♥♥♥♥ed up the FOV. Cutscenes aren't framed as well as the used to be.
So, most prominently, a lot of weapon physics have changed. As I mentioned before, the Chaingun is all but worthless now. It has value against killing cacodemons and that's about it. The Machinegun and plasma rifle also have seen changes. Again, why? I know why. This was some attempt to “balance” things for multiplayer. Because, Doom 3 was really well known for being great in multiplayer, right? From the get go, it was a game focused on a good singleplayer experience, with multiplayer coming secondary. It's very much an old game in that regard. You know, when developers actually put effort into their products? But, you'd think that'd actually make it harder, right? Nah. They've made the game ridiculously easy, now. Check this out: I usually play on Veteran. Let's go through the first level. When you get the shotgun, 8 rounds loaded, 4 in reserve. Now, in BFG edition? 8 by 8. That doesn't seem like much, but it adds up really fast. So, by the time you encounter the first Imp in the regular edition? 8 loaded, 10 reserve. And in the BFG edition? 8 rounds chambered and friggin 41 in reserve. And, by the time you reach Marine HQ? Check your machinegun. Full load. 60 in the mag and 600 rounds reserve. Gone is the deliberate corridor crawl, desperately looking up cabinet codes to get a few more precious rounds. Now, you can just skip over that all together. Sure, both original Doom 3 and Resurrection of Evil are here and intact, but they're made bland by the new less conservative gameplay. On top of that, there's a new campaign called the lost levels. It's a little shorter than Resurrection of Evil and starts out ok. There's even some new levels here, even if they feel less inspired than the other two campaigns. But, they just decided to be ♥♥♥♥ing obnoxious. I like challenge, but for christ's sake there's more Archviles in this single campaign than the original two combined. And the ending is seriously DeviantArt levels of fan-fiction. The story isn't complex: you're helping a scientist, teleporting to hell, fighting literally the Guardian of Hell boss reused from the original, and then escaping. So, you escaped from Mars during the actual ♥♥♥♥♥torm of 2145? But, it says at the beginning of Resurrection of Evil that there was only one survivor. Not going to explain that, game? Why not? Where were you on the evening of April 5th, 2015? Were you the one that took a♥♥♥♥♥♥on my lawn? Do that again and I'll ♥♥♥♥ing kill you.
So, it's clear that BFG Edition was aimed at improving multiplayer and, frankly, that's like beating MovieBob in a footrace. This, ironically, ends up as its weakest point. Ok, so the competitive multiplayer is.. pretty much dead. But, from what I've toyed around with, it seems actually really cool. But, goddamnit, I don't want my microphone on at all times. On PC, we have other alternative Voice-over-IP programs like Teamspeak, just let us ♥♥♥♥ing turn off the ingame mic and use that. I guarantee you that the sound codec in game blows anyways. But, this is all there is to multiplayer. Given that one of the most popular mods for Doom 3 is OpenCoop, I think they might've failed to recognize something that people might want. Seriously, why the ♥♥♥♥ isn't there co-op? The Xbox version had coop, even. Why the ♥♥♥♥ doesn't the latest incarnation have it?
So, Doom 3 BFG Edition, despite its flaws, is still Doom 3. Kind of. It's $20 and that's not an awful price? Oh, wait, yes it is. You can get Doom 3 and its expansion for $13. Just get that. You're really missing nothing in the lost levels other than a fan fiction level story and a fairly forgettable campaign.
And for ♥♥♥♥'s sake, you've played the original Dooms. So, really, just skip on the BFG edition. It ♥♥♥♥♥ on lawns.

An excellent entry by Square Enix into the third-person crime genre, alongside more celebrated titles such as Grand Theft Auto and Saints Row. The game revolves around a well-written plot involving the player as an undercover Hong Kong police officer returned from America who has been tasked with infiltrating the local triads to shut them down. An fantastic cast featuring some very distinctive and memorable characters who you grow to sympathise with and love or hate regardless of their faction complements a twisting, turning, and storyline, with an explosive conclusion.
While many games which do not focus on driving have driving issues, the driving in Sleeping Dogs is quite smooth, regardless of the vehicle you may be driving, whether it be a car, van, or motorcycle. This is complemented by the damage you can do in vehicles, and also by the incredibly fun ability to enter moving enemy vehicles... provided you don't fall off, of course!
An incredibly fun open world experience based on the city of Hong Kong, the lack of air vehicles does not actually limit the game, with the ability to get to various places, even some quite high, on foot. The map and city is well-designed, and the game's ability to mix things up with extra side material such as catching criminals, hacking cameras, cracking locks, and singing karaoke only increases the game's allure.
And then, finally. The combat. Despite the ability to slow time, and move over, to and around cover while shooting is quite nice, it is in close quarters hand-to-hand combat that the game shines. With the ability to pick up various items and wield them as weapons, from cleavers to handbags to fish, you can be sure that a fistfight will turn bloody and conclude quite brutally. The visceral nature of hand-to-hand combat is furthered by the implementation of "environmental hazards" - objects or locations in the world which you can use to finish off your enemies. Incredibly enjoyable and interesting, if very violent, the close combat in this game is truly a standout feature.

The more I played Uncanny Valley the more I realized that pixel graphics are just as capable of scaring me as any FPS horror. However Uncanny Valley brings in some really fresh ideas and ways of dealing with monsters, story decisions, and death.
The story is front and center here first and foremost. Albeit the way that it is told is through observation. You read what became of the former employees of the company you now work for. You listen to audio recordings and eventually even see video logs. This all changes in the second act of the game. You become front and center and every decision you make can lead to an ending. Speaking of endings. Uncanny Valley has quite a few of them. You are free to do what you want and go where you want just about. The developer does a nice job of making sure that scenarios the player can come up with are handled. Never is this more present then in the second act. Where if you make a mistake and get caught. Its all over. Start over and do better. This is a great and bad thing. While the game does instill fear in you and makes you think and be careful. One who doesn't know what their doing is doomed to repeat the first act of the game over and over until they read a walkthrough or figure out the puzzles. The game only features one game save file and that's it.
The game features a unique combat/heath system. Where you tend to wounds and reload your gun. While the game is a Survival horror it almost plays like a point and click adventure game. Criss-crossing between these genres seamlessly and without letting you know.
Uncanny Valley has some really good ideas and executes them effectively for the most part. There is a few blemishes in the replayability and weird wonky bugs. However these are all minute and don't detract from gameplay. In all I can't wait to see what Cowardly Creations cooks up next.

Uncanny Valley is a 2D horror game where everything revolves around your choices, but will you want to play it ? In Uncanny Valley we play as Tom. Tom arrives in an isolated location to work as a night guard at a building that was shut down due to lawsuits. Once you arrive you don't feel welcomed and there's tension in the air as people around act strange and you try to find out what kind of secrets Tom's new job holds. So how is Uncanny Valley ? This is probably my favorite horror game I have played in a while. This game forces you to think fast if you want to survive. This game also doesn't rely on jump scares as there's only one sudden thing that happens that could be considered a jump scare. The game makes you feel uneasy due to the fantastic atmosphere, sound effects and music and you feel like danger lurks around every corner. The game is a simple 2D horror adventure game. You find stuff and interact with other stuff so you can progress the story but this game is very simple and it doesn't put incredibly cryptic puzzles in front of you cause a lot of the puzzles are incredibly simple and you will find the solution within seconds but there are a few exceptions. The story is amazingly put together. As soon as the game begins you begin to feel uneasy and that's why Uncanny Valley is so scary. Hell it might be one of the scariest games I've played to date. There are also multiple endings you can get with different choices you can make throughout the game. There are a few bugs like text's merging into one blob of unreadable nonsense and a few instances where the game didn't let me pick up items. Overall if you are a fan of horror games you simply need to own Uncanny Valley cause this is one of the best horror games out there. Well worth the 9 euros. I give Uncanny Valley an 8.5/10

Do not buy Stardrive. This game is an unfinished product. It is, at best, “glitchy”. It's an “early access” with no chance of being fixed. Apparently, for reasons beyond the developer, he isn't allowed to work on the engine of the game any more, or something.
This is rather sad because the game needs optimization, badly. The controls and interface of the game aren't adequate. It makes an obtuse game with a steep learning curve even more convoluted. Basic RTS controls, like finding idle workers or rally points aren't implemented. At least one technology in the science tree doesn't work as described. Ships, especially freighters, lack a good path-finding, making them delay deliveries of vital goods, but it happens to offensive fleets too. Trading technologies requires you look up, -or know the cost by heart-, of everything in the science tree or risk the ire of the IA. The planet managing screen lacks clarity and the possibility for quick changes. The ship building interface refuses to show critical information, like the rate of fire, the global ammunition consumption per second or the global energy consumption. While it can be nice to figure out this puzzle, you have to recalculate everything as soon as you improve your design with new technologies. Having to look up the wiki for vital weapon-data is also unforgivable for a game that requires such precision in its main mechanic from the player. Personalising larger ship becomes a tedious chore.
Speaking of ship building, while it is nice to modify them depending on your style, it doesn't take into account how the game works as a whole. The IA isn't a big threat later on in the game as much as it is in the beginning, and that can be circumvented as soon as you realise what variable the computer uses for it's moves: the size of your fleet. Just build a big fleet, and you've won. You don't even need to research, or spend hours personalising cruisers. In the end, it is completely pointless, because you will already be winning by the time you get to bigger spacecrafts, making their puzzle-like personalisation moot and time wasting.
Worse, this system isn't as open as it pretends to be: you cannot build viable ships if you deviate from a certain type of fighter. If you are thinking of building a huge flying fortresses which shoots at everything in all directions, think again: one ship attacks one ship. Sure, the area of effect damage might hit others too, but that's leaving it up to chance, or worse, the IA. The attacks your ships employ are always the same: charge! There is an option to turn on a “broadside” tactic but it doesn't work according to the forums.
When you get right down to it, the changes you make to your ships are quantitative, not qualitative. You decide the weapons and the defences, and how much of each, and then try to figure out the best way to power the whole thing and keep sufficient ammunition. In essence, this more open system is just more complex than the one in Endless Space, replacing the straightforwardness of it with inconvenient and pointless creation tools. Also, Endless Space has more tactics
the combat phases, with three different phases, defining tactics for each, heroes and hero abilities. In Endless Space, the ships are not just flying towards each other like a Middle Age jousting competition.
It's a shame since Stardrive sounds good on paper. A better IA and path-finding across the board would have gone a long way. An IA that changes tactics depending on difficulty, rather than giving it a boring bonus to resources to compensate for it's inadequacies, would also give a more organic and challenging experience. Being able to annexe other civilizations peacefully by building a federation is great but removes diversity from the game world, by having the player taking control over the planets and fleets of the ally, making end game seem even more without challenge when you suddenly control half the map.
Finally, on a positive note, the aesthetic of the game, the design of the races and the ships, are very pleasing and enjoyable even thought there are basically references to other media (like the Wing Commander series, the mythos of Cthulhu, the Asari from Mass Effect, etc.). The mixture of all the references kind of creates its own style. The rest of the game though needed a lot more polish.

We'll let you know if you're allowed to make them or not. You just relax and watch these overlong execution animations that we built the game around.

Aliens vs. Predator is a 1st person shooter that continues the tradition of the earlier Alein vs. Predator games. There are three campaigns, each starring a unique character. You can play as a Human Marine, Predator or Alien, and each character has their storyline and playstyle.
Having recently played some of Alien vs. Predator 2000, I knew a little of what to expect. What I was hoping for was a modernization of that game, because I found that while it may have been a worthy title in its time, it did not really stand up to the test of time in my opinion.  That is an issue with early 3D games and FPSs in general. This game delivered on that, and more so.
The first improvement to address is the tutorial. AvP 2010 gives you a short tutorial as an introduction to each character so you can become accustomed to the controls. I found myself quickly mastering the majority of controls, although walking up walls as a Xenomorph was still a bit tricky. Aiming your various weapons is easy enough, and the button placement seems to make sense.
The graphics are really fantastic for what is now a 4 year old game. This was a huge improvement from AvP 2000, and shows you just how far games have come in 10 years. Better graphics help add to the atmosphere, which can be downright scary at times as a Marine.
The voice acting and sounds are another high point. The beeps on your motion detector mixed with the gutteral sounds of your Alien attackers will begin to fill you with dread. The rave like scene of an early set piece really uses music well to add to the intensity.
With 3 campaigns, there is a lot of variety to this game not usually found in FPS games. I found that the Marine campaign played much like a Survival Horror FPS, the Alien campaign like a Stealth shooter, and the Predator campaign like an overpowered mixture of both. It really is quite an accomplishment that they could pull all of this off in one game. Being able to switch easily between campaigns after missions is a nice touch.
One thing to keep in mind is that Aliens vs. Predator is a licensed game. A lot of your enjoyment will be derived directly from that universe. If you enjoy that license, I can whole heartedly recommend AvP. It's an enjoyable FPS on its own accord, and you will love being able to play as all three species. If you are not a fan of Aliens and Predator, I'd still say this is worth a try. The concept is pretty unique, and the gameplay as the Alien is some of the most enjoyable I've experienced. You will, however, probably find that the story does not do much for you since it requires a bit of knowledge from the movies to fully enjoy.
Grade: B

I'm writing this review in December 2017 so well after the whole debacle about the Titans DLC being a cash grab and how the original owners where shafted.  I myself had bought the original version and then the Titans expansion when both were on sale.  Do i think Uber acted badly towards their fanbase and clients? Yes.  Do I think Titans is a game worth playing?  In it's current state hell yes.
I'm a huge fan of RTS games and one of my all time favourites was Total Annihilation, followed by it's spiritual successor Supreme Commander and the incredible Forged Alliance expansion.  Supreme Commander 2 was a bit of a letdown due to it's much smaller scale.  Playing this game now for the first time, I was very happy to find what felt like a Supreme Commander with new mechanics (the planetary attacks and globe maps).  I was also VERY impressed with the UI both at the menu stage and during gameplay.  The community mods are very well integrated in the game with a submenu dedicated to them and recommended mods highlighted.  The mods also automatically download any other required mods they need to operate.  And these mods really improve the game immensely.  The Legion mod adds a whole new faction to the game making it feel even more like Supreme Commander.  And there are countless other mods which improve anything from the hotkey system to the Galactic War mode to new units and maps.
So while i would rate the base game a solid 8/10 to how it stands now (Dec 2017), the mod community has elevated the game to a solid 9.5/10 in my books.  Please note that this review is just about the game as it stands now.  I'm completely ignoring the somewhat dishonest practice and prices of how this game came into being.  If those are taken into account I couldn't recommend the game.  However, if you're deciding right now whether this is the game for you and since the previous decisions regarding pricing, dlc etc. won't affect you, I can wholeheartedly recommend this game especially if you're a TA/Supreme Commander fan.

Revisiting my review now that I've completed the campaign. TLDR: buy it now.
Van Helsing II stars right where the first game ended, allowing you to continue your campaign with your existing character, or start a new one either at level 1 or 30. Unlike, say, the transition between Diablo 1 and 2, there are no changes in fundamentals; VH2's tactic is to be a bigger, better version of the first game, and at that it's wildly successful.
The gorgeous visuals of the first game are enhanced by excellent weather and atmospheric effects, plus some truly impressive spell effects that had me constantly wanting to mash the screenshot key.
The excellent soundtrack returns, plus around the same amount of new music again, joined by surprisingly good voice acting and an array of viscerally satisfying sound effects layered on top of an ambience that combine to give the game a wonderful sense of atmosphere.
(By the way, it does support multi-channel configurations, though I'm not sure if audio effects are fully positional with respect to the extra channels.)
In terms of gameplay mechanics, VH2 takes the first game and extends it; all of the features from VH1 return as-is, and are expanded by enough new skills and abilities to give the game a great deal of customisability. There are three character classes, but by the time you've customised your character with the skills you want, two players with the same class could - probably will - have radically different play styles. I think they did a pretty good job of avoiding the Diablo 3 problem where some skills are effectively mandatory, and others are basically worthless, and I think overall it has a greater degree of viable character customisation, but of course there are some skills that seem weaker or stronger than others. You can fully respec every character choice if you wish, though it comes at a price. If you want to try out a wide variety of options with the same character, prepare to save up a *lot* of gold. If you choose to start with a level 30 character, there are a few pre-made options to pick from that give some variety in character builds (or you can make up your own of course). Being a game about one specific character, you obviously don't get to play anyone else, so there's not going to be any option for a female hero - the game would need to be entirely rescripted. Of course this is so obvious that I almost didn't even bring it up, but I know that kind of thing disappoints some players so I thought I'd mention it.
I found the gameplay to be highly engaging throughout, even when I was getting my posterior handed to me (I'm just saying, that's a whole lot of ornithopters to fight while there are pools of poison all over the floor and homing incendiary bombs being launched at my face). I can't imagine anyone who liked the first game being disappointed here. I'd say that the main campaign is probably about half as long again, with some added variety in environments and fight mechanics (I can call down an artillery strike? Hmm, that has significant friendly-fire potential). Don't expect any *major* novelty there - we're still basically visiting wilderness, city, and areas in the ink - but it's not just rehashes of exactly the same zones, and some of the additions are... honestly pretty breathtaking. I love being able to look down at the city far below me. One of the things that sets the VH games apart from other ARPGs like D3 or Torchlight is that there are a lot of areas where you can see, for example, another level in the dungeon, and rather than being essentially just a complicated backdrop that tantalises but remains forever out of reach, here it's frequently another part of the level that you can get to.
I've played a lot of ARPGs since the first Diablo, and honestly I'd be pretty comfortable in saying that this is the best since Diablo 2 was released in 2000. I'd have no hesitation recommending it even at three times the price.
Original, first impressions review follows:
First, if you didn't like the first one, look elsewhere. This is basically more of the same. You can import your old character, and the game starts seemingly immediately after the ending of the first one. In fact, it's so much like an extended version of the original game that I'm a little surprised it wasn't released as an expansion. The gameplay is essentially an incremental step from VH1, with some added features and extended character progression.
That said, I'm not upset about this. I enjoyed VH1 a great deal, and this - so far at least - seems just like a further iteration, which is exactly what I was expecting. The gameplay updates may be fairly minor in the overall scheme, but they're good nonetheless (and I've only played a couple of hours - there could be more in store). Given that it costs less than an expansion pack for most big-budget games, anyone disappointed by the similarity in gameplay might do well to think of it as a standalone expansion, if that helps.
I find the game has a great visual appeal - I love the art style and the atmosphere, and the music is great (it can all be found as oggs in the install directory, and it has all the music from VH1 plus about the same amount again).
Overall I'd say this is one of the better entries in the genre for quite some time.

An excellent entry by Square Enix into the third-person crime genre, alongside more celebrated titles such as Grand Theft Auto and Saints Row. The game revolves around a well-written plot involving the player as an undercover Hong Kong police officer returned from America who has been tasked with infiltrating the local triads to shut them down. An fantastic cast featuring some very distinctive and memorable characters who you grow to sympathise with and love or hate regardless of their faction complements a twisting, turning, and storyline, with an explosive conclusion.
While many games which do not focus on driving have driving issues, the driving in Sleeping Dogs is quite smooth, regardless of the vehicle you may be driving, whether it be a car, van, or motorcycle. This is complemented by the damage you can do in vehicles, and also by the incredibly fun ability to enter moving enemy vehicles... provided you don't fall off, of course!
An incredibly fun open world experience based on the city of Hong Kong, the lack of air vehicles does not actually limit the game, with the ability to get to various places, even some quite high, on foot. The map and city is well-designed, and the game's ability to mix things up with extra side material such as catching criminals, hacking cameras, cracking locks, and singing karaoke only increases the game's allure.
And then, finally. The combat. Despite the ability to slow time, and move over, to and around cover while shooting is quite nice, it is in close quarters hand-to-hand combat that the game shines. With the ability to pick up various items and wield them as weapons, from cleavers to handbags to fish, you can be sure that a fistfight will turn bloody and conclude quite brutally. The visceral nature of hand-to-hand combat is furthered by the implementation of "environmental hazards" - objects or locations in the world which you can use to finish off your enemies. Incredibly enjoyable and interesting, if very violent, the close combat in this game is truly a standout feature.

This game is one of my favorite games of all time. Just for a moment forget the older Dooms and the new Doom, just look at this game on its own, don't compare it to the other Dooms, that's the best way to approach this game. I played the older Dooms and the new Doom and as much as I love them, I really appreciate this one as well. I played the original Doom 3 modded to hell and back and this BFG edition and I prefer this edition over the modded Doom 3. Sometimes less is more and this version just simply gives everything you need to enjoy Doom 3 at its best. All you need is a working and functioning Doom 3 with all the missions (including some extra ones) and the flashlight attached to you armor instead of holding it (for some reason there is no flashlight mod that gives light for all weapons). Also, I like how BFG edition adds so many health packs, armor and ammo all over the levels on all difficulties except nightmare. This makes the game less like a survival horror game and more action packed and that’s how I like Doom. Come on it’s Doom, not Silent Hill. So just buy this game so you can boot up a complete package and have fun, instead of fighting just to stay alive. Well unless you like that, but then you can always play nightmare mode.
PS: I completed nightmare mode.
Tips for nightmare mode:
You have the soul cube right from the start, which makes this mode possible to beat.
Quick save after every battle.
You don’t really need to get your health above 25, it just drains back to 25, so just use health stations (there are no med packs) to keep your health at 25.
I’m sorry but just get good (git gud). You need to be fast, responsive, adapt and learn which guns are best used when and how to use them. For example, the grenades are tricky to use because of their bouncing physics. But if you play long enough you can almost predict exactly where the grenades will land and explode. So once you know that, I recommend using that skill to take out the gunners that can kill you the fastest in this mode. Every other enemy has a projectile attack or runs at you, but these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s just need to shoot and you will get hit by every bullet. You must stay out of their line of sight or else you will be dead in seconds. So if you throw a grenade around the corner you can kill them without having to look at them and thus staying out their line of sight.
If you want more tips, let me know.

Sleeping Dogs is an open world, third person sandbox game. It is the same style of game as GTA is, but with quite a few differences that make it stand out on it's own, and in more ways than one, it is superior to GTA IV in a lot of gameplay elements. I started my review with the reference to Rockstar's game for one reason, this game is part of the open world genre and comparisons are almost inevitable.
Sleeping Dogs is a behemoth of a game in terms of content. The main story is engaging, with a few cliche moments, and you will feel simpathetic with the main character's trials and tribulations, and pretty much all the characters you interact with are quite memorable. The first difference between Sleeping Dogs and GTA IV is the voice acting, which is far superior on this title, making it a lot more engaging. Having a stellar cast voicing the characters is a big plus, well known actors and actresses like Tom Wilkinson, Emma Stone, Lucy Liu and Kelly Hu provide very believable and convincing voice acting.
There are 30 main missions, plus a whole lot of side quests, favours, races, gambling and more surprises to complete during the course of the game, and combined with the story related DLC's, make for one huge game to complete.
On a game of this nature, it is always incredibly hard to nail all the gameplay elements really well, but Sleeping Dogs manages to do just that. The fighting system is brilliantly simple to master, the driving is spot on and responsive, and even if you chose to explore on foot, everything is always under your control, it is almost intuitive and uncomplicated.
The game takes place in Hong Kong, which is extremely well recreated in the digital form. You can explore absolutely everything, which is basically an entire living and breathing city. Hong Kong is so well recreated that it becomes a character of it's own, worth exploring and getting lost into.
You play as Wei Chen, an undercover cop sent to infiltrate a triad in order to break it from within, but Wei has his own reasons for doing this job. The story will keep you wanting to find out more of what happens, and you can expect to not be let down by it. It is a great ride from beginning to end.
This game gets compared to GTA IV quite a bit. Having played and finished both games, Sleeping Dogs is the better game in my opinion. The fighting system is better, the driving is better, the story is miles better, and the voice acting is vastly superior. The world it takes place in, the city of Hong Kong, feels much more alive and full of life than GTA IV and it's sometimes dull world. Sleeping Dogs is a game worth playing, it is the top of the crop in free roaming, sandbox games.

When I read the reviews for this game, I was beyond excited about playing it. The art looked amazing, everyone raved about it, so I bucked up and bought it. Then I actually turned it on and started playing.

So many games have so little gameplay, or perhaps getting through the events are tedious. I admit, I expected something with pretty graphics and good music, but more along the norm with a few more twists behind it. This game though, shot beyond my expectations, which is saying something once you actually see the reviews posted for this game and take in your first pre-game impression.
The artwork and music are breathtaking, and the narrator, with his deep voice, makes this game more than worth every single penny you're putting into it, whether it was on sale or at full price. There are no random drop weapons, no cutscenes in the middle of a dungeon that take up ten minutes and make you wish there was a skip function, no. When you hear the story behind this whole world, see the characters, and interact with everything, all described and explained with the rich and gruff voice of Logan Cunningham, you're gonna love every moment. Trust me.
There's a story behind everything, from your enemies to the grey people standing in the streets. Behind every single item and piece of land that rises up and falls below, its difficult to not enjoy every moment of this game as it comes because of that.
Its also a bit ambiguous in story and plot elements, especially in the classical sense of fighting good and bad, in a beautiful way that melds perfectly with the fact that you play as a character who is trying to restore the only piece of a broken world so the survivors can truly start living and rebuilding.
