First of all I will say that this is not a bad game per se. The gameplay at its core is good and it is a fun experience. However, as it stands at the time of this opinion, the game is unfinished. It feels like an early access game rather than a AAA title. Missing modes, not well tested mechanics, the ever adition of content which should have been there from the beginning, etc.
If this is your very first fighter it is ok, since it is simple (compared to other fighting games) and it will allow you to understand the basics of th genre. The game was even designed with the philosophy of making it begginer-friendly in an effort to  bring the casual audience along. However, this very principle makes the gap between well versed players and begginers much more aparent. Players with a medium to good understanding of the neutral game will crush begginer-leveled players, possibly making them leave in frustration. While begginers leaving the game out of frustration is nothing new in fighting games, in previous iterations it tended not to matter because the game was focused and designed for the hardcore crowd anyway. In this game, however, some tiers of the ranking system feel depopulated and artificial. (At the time of this review I stand at the Gold tier, which is more or less like the first of the medium-leveled tiers).
One minor, but very annoying thing is that characters have very few colors, and even though you can unlock a some of them by playing, others have to be bought. The alternate costumes also have to be bought, but in previous iterations you could buy packs with several for 10 bucks. Here, EACH COSTUME costs 10 bucks. Its too much money if you want to have all the alternate costumes.
Overall I really do not recommend this game unless, like me, you used to play ultra but now play this game since capcom no longer supoorts USFIV and the mainstream tournament scene has refocused to this game.
EDIT: With the balance changes in Season 2 I have to sat that the game improved quite a lot. There are some debatable changes like removing the invencibility of meterless reversals, but overall I feel the game is more fun. That doesn't mean it is balanced though: It feels like the god tier characters are really OP. I still don't recommend this game because it is missing the same things it was missing in season 1. However, you might want to buy it at a reduced price just to try it out.

There is also a storyline complete with varieties of quests to follow.

When it comes to racing games, I've never been attracted to those top-heavy ultra-realistic simulators. I don't care how accurate your gear-to-tire ratio is; I just want to go fast. When I race, its definitely a preference for style over substance.
So Burnout Paradise is just the sort of thing I want out of a racer. It lets me drive fast and recklessly (there's incredible damage modeling on the cars, but it doesn't effect your driving in the slightest); there's good graphics and good music, a varied map, lots and lots of cars to unlock and a total disregard for realism.
It is not without problems; the game lacks the depth that will keep you coming back. This is the sort of game you keep on your hard-drive for a quick pick-up race every now and again rather than playing it intensely. Its motorcycle races pale in comparison to the automobile races (no surprise since it was originally DLC on the consoles). The game's hook -that you can finish a race following any route you want -rather than fixed tracks- works against it in the beginning of the game when you are completely unfamiliar with the map (a better navigation aid would have been very useful).
But still, these are all minor issues; the game is fun and follows through on its main premise: fast, care-free driving. I expect this title will lurk on my computer for a while, always ready to provide me with a needed adrenalin rush.

I really want to like this game, as I had been excitedly waiting for its release ever since I played the demo, which I loved, last year, but sadly there still seem to be a lot of bugs to work out and rough edges to polish.
For starters, it would be nice to have the option of multiple save files – the first part of the game is rather slow, and it would be nice not to have to play through it each time you make a run of the game.
I'm also not a huge fan of the sleep mechanic in its present form. While I think having the story paced over multiple days is fine, having to run back and forth between the facility and your apartment gets tedious, fast.
Also, unless I'm completely overlooking something, I think I've already discovered a bug that prevents you from achieving one of the optional objectives. There's a safe you have to open at one point that I'm pretty sure contains a key to a certain area. Based on the clues I've found, I'm 100% certain I know what the combination is *supposed* to be, but nothing happens when I input it. The story eventually still advances even if you're not able to solve this puzzle, but it's frustrating not to be rewarded if you've taken the time and effort to figure it out.
I still want to explore this game in its entirety, and I do like its overall atmosphere and premise, so I hope the developers will work out some of these bugs and rough edges in the coming weeks. Sadly, I can't quite recommend it at this point in time.

Uncanny Valley starts out in a fairly overtly clichéd way. The unease one is supposed to feel while their reality is being questioned is not there. While this gave me a sort of bad feeling in regards to the game, it swung right back at me with the real beginning, and the establishment of the real. When you walk out of the dilapidated subway train, into the even more decrepit subway station, and the reticent atmosphere grabs hold of you, that is where it all begins.
The interesting thing about a very pixelated aesthetic qua uncanny, is that it brings out the dread that comes with not bringing everything out in the open. The blank faces and vague outlines of every gestalt gives both the unfamiliar feel of the unheimliche (literally translated to un-homely) that is immanent in the appearance of the creatures themselves, but also gives room for an imaginative terror, the terror that our mind creates by filling out the blanks. This is further developed with the deliberate choice to have some scenes relatively silent, where footsteps and a zoomed out perspective creates a sort of looming threat from all directions. Since you sometimes walk behind objects (obscuring your character completely; also, if you can be behind it, something else can!), it creates in the process a sort of three-dimensional space in an otherwise visually two-dimensional space. There is a feeling of helplessness when you are in a three-dimensional environment but your mechanics are restricted two-dimensionally, this is perhaps not a novelty, but it creates an interesting play on the format itself, where dread can come from the very choice of format itself.
Mechanically, there are interesting aspects to it from the beginning that adumbrates the compromises you'll have to make, and subsequently the dreadful situations you'll have experience. While noticing that I could not run with my flashlight out, I immediately realized the dissatisfaction of running away from a threat, since it would mean plunging into complete darkness, but at the same time, the lack of speed makes the unknown's eventual bringing-into-light and attack on you so much more frightening.
Ambivalence. There is this essence of morbidity and flesh in the sense of Francis Bacon. Bodies contort in fear or in torturous spasms, you see your character wake up from a nightmare and walk hazily, with an emotionally worn down stature, all perfectly portrayed with the otherwise indistinct artstyle. I love the macabre aspects of the game, the naked blank bodies – made distinct only by minor differentiating colors in pixels – that are hanging from the ceiling, and their truly uncanny animation. What the problem is, is when the game takes a duller turn with some of the creatures, like in the first scenes of the game where the black forms chase you down and envelope you. These have no interesting quality to them, which unfortunately makes their appearance feel like they rob you of your unease that otherwise makes the experience what it is. Uncanny Valley sometimes mistake the uncanny or unfamiliar with the unknown or indistinct, which unfortunately results in a visual ennui, it results in a consternating sigh in an otherwise visually stimulating/interesting world.
Moreover, while some of the agents (enemies, hostiles, creatures, “things”, who knows...) in the game are perhaps not the most interesting, there are some absolutely amazing pixel art to be seen in Uncanny Valley. I prefer more than anything the coloration, and with it the great understanding whoever made the art must have of how crudely juxtaposed colors make a beautiful image, or how to create a more detailed or fine image from indistinct broader “strokes”. This is something you can see in the screenshots of the game in the store page and decide what you think for yourself, so me saying so is most likely pointless.
While there are hints everywhere of what is going on, on my first completion of the game, I had no idea of what was going on, what was real and what was not. You continually wake up in different places, with different jobs, outfits and characters that lead you in different directions. Nothing is established as real, and you don't know what consequences are actually consequential. This is a game that requires multiple playthroughs to get any idea of what the game is all about, both to exhaust the story-elements and the different mechanics and art designs. This is not a streamlined game, for the most part. You are blind, and that blindness has consequences. I was just trying out things when awoken in a new place, and this lead to the end of the game. I had no idea why, or if there should have been a reason or character-motivation for what I did, but instead it felt like a mechanical ending. I did something with items I had, and I got to see a horrific end cutscene, that wasn't as uncanny as it should have been since I had only met that character once (I missed out on an objective, which may have been why the ending turned out like it did) and then the end credits rolled. The consequence system, that they advertise, is one that most likely can lead to a lot of flailing about haplessly, only to be jolted back into the story in a place where you no longer have a grasp of what is going on or why things are going on. This was my biggest issue, that the pacing suffered at the hands of the consequence system. Although this is possibly due to how I played the game, since a consequence system will personalize your experience with the game to a certain degree, I still have suspicion that I might not be entirely alone in this lostness in the game.
I would probably recommend this. At this point in time, on a fairly lackluster first playthrough story-wise, I still enjoyed a lot of the elements of the game. The atmosphere and figures the game put forth were for the most part interestingly designed. Morbidity and contorted flesh was a prominent feature that I truly enjoyed. Uncanny Valley has some nice things in store, nice in a disturbing sense, whereby the core experience reaches higher levels of enjoyment than other pixel horror games, but sometimes, due to how certain consequences play out, the story falls flat. What is fortuitous herein, is that the game offers more than what is seen at first glance. But you have to work for it, it is on you to find the points of interest, and to make the story what it is. That must make me a lazy, lackluster and rather boring player. I think I'm okay with that.

The follow-up to Chip's Challenge for the Atari Lynx and Windows 3.1. You can tell it was optimized for things like iOS and Android, but this is still a worthwhile follow-up to the original tile-based puzzler.
I must mention: The menus, the characters, and the levels elements are like an oversized dollop of cottage cheese: big and chunky. Plus the navigation of menus is just odd, where you use the mouse like you would a finger on a touchscreen. But PC optimization issues aside, it's your job to solve the puzzles as Woop. And yeah, he's no Chip, but the little bugger does have charm, I'll give him that.
As for the gameplay, well, it's Chip's Challenge 2.0, and that's precisely why I threw my money at the screen in the first place. If you're not familiar with that game, it's a tile-based Sokoban-like game where you have an area filled with locked doors and hazards, and it’s your goal to collect the required items before exiting the level. For the most part, it's the same game with new puzzles and a new look. Like, you're not collecting chips here, but little glowing blue things, and the enemies look totally different. But a lot of the puzzle elements are the same, like water, fire, ice, moving floors, etc. And you still have the same types of power-ups that let you circumvent these hazards where appropriate. There are five sets of levels to complete with 25 levels each, but the first selection more or less follows the rules of the original game. When you move beyond those, the game really starts to open up into its own thing, with a slew of new enemies, hazards, and puzzle components. It never has to give you a dumb tutorial either, since the rules of upcoming levels are clearly laid out for you with an easier level earlier on. But don't let the first set of levels fool you, this game can be just as brutal as its predecessor.
Well sort of. It's a bit easier as well, with the ability to take back any number of moves at any time. This means you don't necessarily have to restart the entire level if you screw up, so no bummers here. Time keeps ticking while you do this, but it's far less rage-inducing to make a stupid mistake now. It even asks you if you want to skip a level if you suck to the point of shaming your ancestors. The levels are also far smaller than many of those in Chip's Challenge, and I assume this is because of the time and screen size constraints of the mobile version. And when you finish off or rage quit the main game, there's a fully-featured, easy-to-use level editor. You can upload your own or download other people's creations right from within the game. Oh and you can apparently get hats, because freaking hats man, why developers haven't shoehorned them into every game already is beyond me.
Personally, I find Chuck's Challenge to be a perfectly adequate successor to Chip's Challenge. It's more of the same kind of logical puzzle-solving with only a few concessions made for mobile platforms and slightly more forgiving gameplay. But even with a few iffy changes, if you enjoyed the original game or just enjoy these types of logic games, I'd give this one a look.

This game has neat graphics and an interesting story, but it is fatally flawed in many ways.  Spoilers may follow.
Mechanics
The dialogue is slow and halting due to the way the text boxes work, and the boxes can go off of the screen where you can't read them.
The inventory and item system is clunky and hard to use, and there are no tooltips to explain what the items are without clicking on them, which forces you to exit the inventory.
When you move furniture it snaps around all crazy, and can be moved through walls.
The flashlight turns off whenever you move between screens, which is absolutely pointless and annoying.  It also turns off when you run, but this is forgiveable despite the fact that it often means you are staring at a black screen when moving between areas.
Gameplay
You go in and out of dreams/hallucinations, and wake up suddenly somewhere else.  It is sudden and just does not work well as it feels contrived as a wayto make the gameplay move between set pieces.  It is not exciting or mysterious, it is just kind of pointless and annoying.
You are supposed to be doing shifts at work, except it is just always night time and the clocks never change, and there are no real mechanics related to working... you just wander around exploring until you fall asleep and are forced into a sudden set piece change.
It is not clear what you are supposed to be doing, ever... and then some people will run towards you if you are in a hallucination and then it is time to move to the next set piece.  The scripting is just awful and totally ruins the experience.  I smashed a mirror with a blue box, or something, and then put a shard in a hole in the wall.  When I did that I suddenly teleported back to aprevious room being dragged into a medical area, then the person says something threatening to me and I watch her go stand by a cabinet... after a couple minutes of her standing next to the cabinet doing nothing and me being unable to interact with her I decided to walk to the left.  Apparently this triggered what I imagine is supposed to be a chase scene, because she suddenly bolted towards me and did a wierd hip bump that apparently knocked me out.  Then suddenly I am tied to the wall of that same room and she is all ripped up for no reason and cuts my arms and legs off and I beat the game.
I feel like this could be a very creepy and interesting game, it was fun to explore the world and read people's emails, and the inclusion of voice tapes was neat except that they are very hard to listen to due to the clunky inventory system.  It almost felt creepy, but the ambience was ruined by the bad mechanics and pointless sudden set changes.
All in all I am disappointed by this game as it seems like the developers had a good idea and came close to pulling it off but just couldn't quite do it.
Try Lone Survivor for a well done version of what I think this game was trying to be.

* Unfinished product with $60 price tag.
* No Arcade Mode and lacks of single player content.
* Caters to pro and tournament gamers only. The game's release date was rushed to be out in time for the Capcom Pro Tour. Only Ryu can parry and one of the pro Ryu players is famous for his parrying skill. Coincidence? No.
* Announced three beta tests back in July 2015 to test out online infrastructure, couldn't even get things right on the very first phase. Postponed until one month later.
* After multiple beta tests, server problems occurred right on the launch day.
* Expected to sell 2 million copies, but 1,4 million copies shipped (not sold!) in May. Short by 600,000 copies or 30% is really bad, in case you are not good with business subject.
* Survival Mode for merely unlocking colors, from 10 matches up to 100 matches non-stop and must be online. Considering the game's poor server, better pray not getting disconnected on your 99th match or right on your 100th match. It's a no-brainer that no one likes the way to unlock colors. How does Capcom solve this? Capcom sells the colors. Ka-ching!
* Claimed that all gameplay-related content earnable for “free” using Fight Money (FM);
- Characters: 100,000 FM each
- Costumes (Story Mode only): 40,000 FM each
- Stages: 40,000 FM – 70,000 FM each
- All titles, profile skins, and some colors also cost FM.
- How much you get per online win? 50 FM. That's what Capcom means by “free”. Marketing.
* The developers were unable to deliver promised contents on time.
- “Trial Mode, Alex, and Shop in March”. Except Shop, eventually available almost at the end of the month, 28th and 30th March with last minute trailer for Alex. Again, marketing. As long as it's still in March, right?
- “Guile in April”. 28th April, precisely. Again, as long as it's still in April. Shop still not available.
- “Ibuki in May”. Unable to deliver on time. Announced delay until (again) last week of June after choosing to stay mum until last minute.
- The promised Shop was not available until June, which is three months late from the promised timeline.
- The rest DLC characters were available near the end of each promised month. Never earlier.
* After teasing for months, released a subpar “Cinematic Story Mode”, required to download its 7GB+ update file prior.
* More than six months after release, the game just had its system to deal with rage quit. Of course, not without problem. The system somehow penalized those that didn't rage quit. Good job.
* Showed stage transition in its first ever official Street Fighter V announcement trailer. The stage transition feature was only added after more than seven months had passed since release.
* Promised “daily challenges” mode for players to earn in-game currency, Fight Money (FM), since release. Available after more than seven months had passed and this so-called “daily” turns out to be “weekly challenges” mode.
* Versus CPU mode added after more than seven months had passed since launch.
* The update containing the anticipated stage transition, “weekly challenges”, and Versus CPU mode came with ROOTKIT by Capcom.
* Capcom released the update containing hidden ROOTKIT called “Capcom.sys”. Capcom was busted sooner than expected when the rootkit was found out by tech savvy gamers.
* As of this review posted, the game's sales figures still stuck at 1.4 million units, same as in May.
* Released a DLC stage called “Skies of Honor”. The stage caused motion sickness for some players and eventually the stage is banned from tournaments.
* Claimed “Available soon after launch”, Extra Battle Mode still not available.
* The AI in this game is basically auto-counter bot based on your button input. Less button input, less action and reaction from the bot.
* Awful netcode and server problems since launch.
* Hours and hours of server downtime for maintenance.
* Update patches in gigabytes.
* Mediocre soundtrack.
* Pricey DLCs.

Let's get this out of the way, Planetary Annihilation is a genuinely new RTS. It's also a good game.
Here is the way to get started on this game, get a buddy with voice chat and play team games. 2v2v2 etc. One of you handles econ and the other handles the military. Between the spherical map and the economy that would only be familiar to the Total Annihilation/Supreme Commander crowd, you both are going to have your hands full for quite a while. All the issues with trying to deal with multiple planets etc. goes away when you have another buddy to help you out. Supreme Commander is not big enough after you play PA. I sunk my teeth into it, and I was hooked.
This is not a game geared toward the micro players, in fact there is hardly any of it in the game. The units do not have individuality like in TA or Starcraft or even AoE, there is barely any special abilities that you would need to account for. But the thing is that when you are dealing with spherical battlefields where you can attack from basically anywhere (land, air, sea, orbit), the game is still rich with possiblity. So in other words, this isn't TA units with planets. The macro is where it shines.
I loved that 2 hour game where we were honed our invasion on the other team's planet as they kept nuking our beach head. I loved that ridiculous game where we were completely kicked out of our main planet, but managed to rebuild on another and win the game. I loved that other game where we managed to come back and build the annihilasor winning after losing everything in that massive 3v3v3. I loved that 1v1 game where we were fighting on the entire planet; the whole planet being turned into a massive battlefield for our will. And far from being the few and far between, a surprising number of matches were like this. There just isn't many other games that can give you that kind of satisfaction.
But ultimately, I just want more, more and more. I want more terrain so the world doesn't feel so lifeless. I want it to be so big that I feel like I am in a flat planet when I zoom in. I want a more complex resource/upgrade system. I want a bigger variety of structures. I want some supply and logistics rather than the simple power+metal limitation you have. I want air to be so high that it actually feels like they are flying 4+ miles up in the air. I want space battles.
It's quite unique, fun, and really is setting out to create the "next-generation RTS." But it needs to be even bigger than what it is.

Quick first line summary:  I really enjoyed this game, and would recommend it with very little hesitation.
It’s a point and click adventure game.  So you gather items from the various screens you can access and you use those items on characters or objects in the area to get access to more screens where you do more of the same.  This is pretty standard fare, so unless you have never played one before you already know how this works.  I will say that the puzzles are very logical for this sort of game, and the few times I got stuck it was entirely because of my own mistakes.
The visual look of the game is delightful.  I loved all the character art, and the locations were convincing and immersive.  If you are turned off by gore and upsetting imagery you might want to give this one a miss.  I found that the cartoony look offset the violence depicted, so it didn’t bother me, but I know I would advise my mother to stick to more light hearted stuff.  I did really like the spookiness of it all, and the odd moment where they decided to depict something particularly grotesque kept me always waiting for what would come next.
Point and click adventure games seem to be the place to go for story these days.  Fran Bow’s story kept me strung along for the entire ride.  I liked what they did with some characters, the surprises they dropped here and there.  There wasn’t really any plot twists or sudden shifts of character that just came out of the blue and left me disbelieving.  Everything could, and was, explained with context and perspective to make sense.  Having said all that, there is one aspect of the story that I would need to say is this games weakest point, and unfortunately that is the ending.  I’m not going to spoil anything specifically, but if you want to experience the game completely blind, you might as well skip the next paragraph.
For the entire game there was one massive looming adversary with infrequent hints of shadow players in the wings.  When the final chapters rolled around that adversary just disappeared and was replaced with new ones at the last minute who were just as quickly bumped off in the most contrived way possible and then the game ended.  Just like that.  After all the build-up, all the hidden hints, all the vague clues to various possible twists and various possible conclusions, and all the uncertainty about how it could possibly work out well in the end, all the loose ends are just gathered up all at once and tied into one big deus ex machina bow.
My final word on it echoes my first words.  I do highly recommend this game.  It has a few flaws, but it is an entrant in my library that I’m happy to have there.  It does make me want to check out other things this developer brings to the table.

StarDrive will provide a fix you've been craving all these years since MoO2.  Is it the complete experience you've long for? Unfortunately, no, probably not.  However, a good selection of features, and the module layout based ship creator, allow for some classic MoO style fun and enjoyment.
The original launch of the game in early access had some issues from what I've read, but StarDrive was one of those games on my "To Play" list for almost a year before finally coming around to it after the latest patch (1.15 of this writing).  The core gameplay is there, but a tech tree that's lacking much depth is probably the most glaring flaw I've experienced in my playthroughs.
This lack, thankfully, can be remedied with a mod which adds much more MoO-like tech tree into the game.  The current non-mod tech layout allows for a very balanced approach that was likely intended for multiplayer(which as of yet hasn't surfaced), with early ship designs still being marginally useful against even high tech ships late in the game.  For fans of MoO2 and it's tech singularity that often happened late game (Psilons, anyone?), this is a mixed blessing.
As mentioned earlier, the ship creator is the main feature of the game, and the one I've had the most enjoyment from.  Going in blind, you'll come up with design iteration after iteration, and love each one as much as the one before.  Every module has a certain length and width that you try and shoehorn into the various ship hulls, with each race having a specific design.  There's generally an overall "feel" for each race's ships (such as long, relatively narrow hulls that allow for greater head on armor layouts for Terrans, or a greater number of possible weaponry on Kulrathi), and even the actual shape of the ship's hull can have very drastic effect when combat comes to your fleets.
There is a slew of ease of use features in the game which makes play more friendly on the UI front.  Unfortunately, a lack of any decent game provided documentation makes some of these a complete secret until they're stumbled upon and discovered.  Definately do some searching for UI tips and tricks for this one.
The tougher AI levels allows for some challenge, but expect the game to be a fairly easy breeze until you design some better ships for the AI to utilize.  The game has some of the spark of MoO, but it's not a drop-in replacement for it.
Overall, I'm in love with StarDrive for what it is, not what it was promised or wished to be.  At it's core, it's engaging and enjoyable.  Hopefully the next offering from Zero Sum will be full spiritual successor that we long for, but this one is better than most MoO clones that pop up now and again.

I had a solid amount of time to play Uncanny Valley before it was released, being able to reach a few different endings, and I had a great time with it!  The pixel graphics are done very well and were used to create a haunting and dark place to explore.  From the music to the SFX everything was as it should be for a suspense/horror game audio-wise.  There aren't a lot of characters in this isolated place but they were fleshed out well enough for me to feel one way or another about them as you played through.
Once♥♥♥♥♥♥starts going south, as they do in horror games, things really get challenging and I found I had to get creative on the spot in order to avoid harm/death.  There is no permadeath unless it lend to the story via one of the many endings you can earn.  Dying otherwise would be seamlessly worked into the game via "waking up" from a nightmare or something along those lines.  There are various penalties for playing poorly (IE. Not being able to sprint as long) so playing carelessly is not recommended.
There is a bit of humor I enjoyed as well as some really gruesome scenes that were difficult to watch, even in pixel graphic style.
The game keeps a great pace with its "shift" mechanic where you get to explore during your night shift for work until you are too tired and have to fall asleep so you get in a mad dash to find clues while you can.  There is a helpful timer you can few by pushing T which was nice to have.
My favorite part of the game is that I didn't see the twist regarding the monster element of the game until I put the pieces together in my head and I hadn't seen this used in any other games.  A fresh take in a world of all zombie games all the time was welcome.
Long story short (too late) Uncanny Valley is a great game with solid replay value and definitely worth getting if you like suspense/horror/pixel games.

Uncanny Valley isn't that place where children eat vegetables smothered in ranch dressing and it isn't exclusive to sex sequences in David Cage games. The uncanny valley is a theory that suggests robots and CGI too lifelike (but still "off" or unrealistic in that uniquely robot/CGI way) is SUPER, SUPER CREEPS.
I subscribe to this theory, personally.
Uncanny Valley is a story as old as time: Tom, our hero, managed to score a security job at a facility tucked away in the mountains where The Shining was filmed. Over the course of the two hour game you'll explore the facility, shoot the♥♥♥♥♥♥with your coworker Buck, and unearth horrible secrets you should probably not have unearthed. It's classic survival horror down to a T, and Uncanny Valley nails the mechanics and atmosphere admirably.
Uncanny Valley revolves around the night guard job. Tom's shift lasts seven fleeting minutes, which at first seems a little punishing. Muster enough motivation, however, and you can cover a lot of ground during your rounds, checking emails and exploring offices, labs, and warehouses. During Tom's rounds he'll pick up video recordings, audio recordings, and plot progression tools. With each passing night scripted events will occur which, depending on the player's actions, will alter the events resulting in a variety of endings and fail states. I haven't seen a game with such subtle variety since Silent Hill 2 (the thematic opposite of later series entry Silent Hill 5: Back 2 tha Hood).
But is it scary?
If you watch my video you may determine that no, it is not. Which is what I thought initially! And I'm pretty easy to frighten. But you'd be wrong to think such naive thoughts. While it isn't overtly terrifying, it is... creepy. Unsettling. Sinister. It plays a lot like a Japanese horror game where you can't quite shake the feeling that you're being watched by something bigger and badder than you that's just biding its time, watching you squirm while it finishes its taxes. And I'll be honest with you: I'm a pretty jaded guy. But there were some moments in this game where I was revolted, and that's not a sensation I can say many games have made me experience.
But it isn't all starshine and puppy farts, unfortunately. Besides some weirdly written dialogue, wonky voice acting, and typos here and there there are some bugs. Manipulable objects can sometimes be pushed out of frame, and Tom will occasionally load into an area and plop down as if he were hovering. Worse still I encountered a bug where Tom's shift would end before it began which led to some Kafkaesque shenanigans where I couldn't make him sleep and he just passed out where he stood after some time (at one point I couldn't even get Buck to leave the office). I'm not sure how frequent this is, and if some of the "bugs" I encountered were just the game being spOoOoky. If you have any trepidation just wait to see what bugs are encountered at launch and hopefully the devs will patch any serious offenders.
All that aside I think Uncanny Valley is an atmospheric, enthralling horror game. Classic survival horror enthusiasts will have fun pursuing the different endings, solving puzzles, and getting out of sticky situations.

Mortal Kombat won huge amounts of praise when it was released on consoles in 2011, and it looks and plays even better on PC. The combat mechanics are deep, challenging, and inventive, and the game includes an overwhelming amount of content for solo play, including a long, engaging story mode. The combat moves fast and feels visceral- hits have impact and special moves are satisfying to pull off. As expected for Mortal Kombat, there is also an absurd amount of gore and detail to the violence. Bones break, limbs fly, and blood spews with comical excess. Rest assured, though, there's much more than shock value here. It's the most fun I've had with a fighter since Soul Calibur 2.
I fully recommend this game, with one major caveat: online play is broken. Really, really broken. Although I can find players online, I haven't been able to have a single stable match. I have no idea why High Voltage Software (the studio that ported this title to the PC) have so utterly failed to provide a coherent online experience, but bear this in mind when purchasing the title. If, like me, you're not that interested in playing online anyway, then MK is still a great choice. Aside from the online problems, this is a solid port, and I've encountered only a few minor technical issues during my playtime.
Put simply, NetherRealm Studios is currently making some of the best fighting games out there. This and the more recent release of Injustice: Gods Among Us (although I haven't had a chance to play it yet) are excellent additions to the limited selection of fighters available on PC.

This game brings back memories. The graphics and characters all look great, they move smoothly and combat seems to run at a normal pace. Its not super fast like the new Street Fighter. The fighters attacks arn't difficult to execute. A lot of them seem to share the same button patterns although they preform different attacks. This helps minimize the amount of codes needed to learn.
I like the combos also. Granted their not very long (mostly 3 hits). Some can be easily chained together with special moves (like freeze ball or scorpions chain) without needing to study the move list. For longer combos you will need to find your fighters 'pop up' attacks. Pop them into the air with a basic attack or special move then lead into a combo.
They have added a "power bar" at the bottom that fills when you take damage. The same as in Street Fighter X Tekken. or Naruto Shippuden: Ninja Revolution. Although limited It does add a slight compliment to the gameplay. It allows you to: Power up special moves (3 times per round), Break combos (2 times), and use a super special move X-ray attacks (once per round). Energy does carry to the next round.
The X-ray attack does ~33% a health bar (roughly 2 combos). They do come with an awesome cinematic scenes of you smashing your opponents bones to bits but only 1 x-ray cinematic per fighter. They can give you a good advantage but note that most x-rays can easily be blocked.

There are 5+ modes you can play but I won't go over all of them. The Story mode is fun and gives you some background info on some of the charecters incase your new. It very roughly if not at all follows Mortal Kombat's original story. The difficulty gets unconsistently hard.
Ladder is like the original arcade mode, here you face 10 opponents. All but the top 3 are randomly chosen. As with the story I feel the AI difficulty isn't very consistent here eather. They grow hard very quickly. Also if your matched against the same character your using it can be difficult to tell you and your opponent apart. Your opponents costume will be only slightly off color.
There are a lot of unlockables; You open them with coins that you get from playing the game. The only ones worth mentioning really are: extra character costumes and extra fatailites! They've also included character costumes from the original Mortal Komabats!! (MK1 to MK3) For those nostalgic players that miss those sweet threads.
Lasty and most importantly the Fatality! You won't be dissapointed here. Each fighter has a handfull of finishing moves that are each unique and all so very gorey. They go cinamaticly way beyond the super special moves (X-ray attacks) I mentioned earlier.
So in conclusion this definitely is a great game and solid 'Fighter' for anyone looking for that genre. You will want to use a controller to play this; I had no need to remap any of the default buttons. You can remap up to 4 different ingame configs for a 4-player battle if needed.

When I first purchased this game, I was very concerned when I read all the reviews. I should have known better than to purchase a game without reading the reviews. As stated by the reviews, the game was unplayable due to excessive bugs and lag when first downloaded. However, one thing that I have found very strange about this game is that the more you play it and the more you explore, the less likely bugs are to occur (kindof like the exact opposite of
). IDK if this happens on everyone's computer or if it is just a wierd quirk of mine, and I have no idea how this could happen in terms of programming, but for about the last hour of playtime (about at 10ish hrs.), I have never seen any lag or not registering clicks to the degree that I first experienced it in the game. I still have some pretty significant trouble with the game not registering my mouse clicks, but it has become at least playable, and the problem is now only a minor annoyance, unlike the total hairpulling frustration upon first download. Sometimes, due to lag, it still registers that I clicked on something that I moused over earlier, rather than what I actually have my mouse over at the time of the click. I wonder if a similar phenomenon caused the programmer(s) to think that the bugs were fixed when they were unable to reproduce reported bugs.
If you have the patience for the bugs, the game itself isn't too bad. The ability to adjust your species for tactical, RP, or mixed  gameplay allows you to play a species according to your own interpretation of how they are or what they could be. I prefer a much more strategic and magical Vulfen to the brutish, early-game swarmers version that they are set to by default (retaining their militaristic tendancies, because IMO Vulfen aren't really Vulfen if they are too peaceful, but upon player preferance this could be changed too). It does have a fairly
/
type feel, which I very much appreciate. Diplomacy is critical, and there is a high degree of intrigue involved (though taking the few abilities and technologies for intrigue that exist will make it very simple, as max rank agents can pretty much do as they please at this point, only occasionally getting discovered or even foiled but not killed). Players should keep in mind, however, that there are few guides to this game, and the videos that are out there regarding this game often do not involve enough information to really give you the feel for things. With no tutorials missions, you will likely be completely lost in the beginning, even with deep research. For this reason, I would advise setting up your first species to give you a large margin for error. Additionally, I found race customization to be very confusing initially, but once you get it, it is very straightforward.
I have come to enjoy the game in time, but I cannot bring myself to recommend this game for its current price. It is simply too high.

Oh, StarDrive. Where do I start with you? You're the most promising space-themed Strategy game I've played, and that's both good and bad. You can be challenging at times, and despite having the re-playability of a 10 year-old's view of Peace and War, terrible, the fact that you are updated once every now and then has me sitting in bed, staring at the ceiling, wondering, "What will be next?" This game has far to go before reaching the elite status, but the steps it must take are simple things to add. This game has one play mode, Sandbox, in which starting out, you have one planet and a few spaceships, and you must find a way to colonize beneficial planets on the road to galactic empire. Other alien species will be right next door, and your actions can (possibly) decide whether or not war will ensue. There is a full tech tree and a very simple, yet important management system that you, as leader, must lead. Sweet and ultimate victory will not be achieved until every species you meet is either your friend (boring) or completely eradicated to the point of extinction (yay). If you decide to be an Adolf Hitler, you can with the ability to bombard any planet's (and I mean ANY) surface with nuclear weapons and murder every last thing that resided there. Did I mention there is also a full ship constructor as well? You can create your own vision of whatever the Super Star Destroyer was in Episode VI of Star Wars during the two minutes it was on screen, and giant, flying pieces of metal with a million death rays are always fun. But this game is SOOOO repetitive! Every game you start up will have the same sequence of events happen, and no matter what you do, they always seem to take place. There's no multiplayer(Note to creator of StarDrive: Make this happen!), and even with mod support, what is in the game to be modded will take a LOT of creativity to make something out of. This game is fun, don't get me wrong, but in order for a consumer to get his/her money's worth PLEASE wait for a sale(like me). ZeroSum, you have a rough diamond here, and polishing has been done, but it is far from the Hope Diamond. 7.25/10.

I don't really understand why this game is rated as "overwhelmingly positive."
Maybe it's because I expected this game to be like a point-and-click American McGee's Alice, but I did not like this game past the first 2 chapters. The game begins pretty well, showing the disturbing point of views of children locked in a mental asylum, but quickly strays from that theme entirely and becomes a huge cluster-♥♥♥♥. I honestly think the game was TRYING to be like Alice, but the major problem it had was IT GAVE TOO MANY EXCUSES. The appeal of Alice and other completely-insane storylines is that there is no reason for why anything is happening. Why is that character missing their legs? Why is there a pig-centipede that ate a rat? Why is there a floating goat skull trying to kill you? The player shouldn't get the answers to these questions. They should just have to accept the asthetics as they are.
TLDR; If you want a disturbing game, don't get this one. If you want an acid trip, sure, try it, but don't expect much substance.
Oh, and the story is incredibly anti-climactic. I don't understand why there are raving reviews for it.

As a player of Fallout 3, Fallout New Vegas and Fallout 4, essentially one who got into the Fallout Series just as it entered the open world, rpg era, I have to admit I'm kinda having mixed feelings about this game. I'm gonna go ahead and use a full review so....
1) Graphics Overhaul
Omg the graphics are just wayyyyy better than ever before. While other mods may exist for the other Fallout series, i felt really immersed into the game simply because of how good the graphics were
2) The VATs Revamp:
Tbh stopping time was way cooler but i have to admit, they did up the FPS portion of this game a lot. Now every move I make in the game during combat carries so much more weight
3) The dialogue:
When Codsworth first said my characters name, it was in passing and on my third playthrough (I wanted to support the Railroad) and I literally had a meltdown. Beyond that, I felt that the dialogue and voice acting were vastly improved and I felt less inclined to killing kids in this one than I did in Skyrim.
1) The Campaign:
Oh my god really, saving my son was such a powerful motivator until it isn't. I felt that the ending of Fallout 4 was extremely abrupt. It was either, save the syths, kill everyone or kill the institute. There wasn't much of the in betweens and the playthrough post-ending was meh because I had to either live without my vertibirds, without having a cool safehouses around (who am i kidding, screw the rairoad) or even living without my syth army. #feelsbad
2) The AI
Beyond the repeated "who's there!"; "I'm gonna kill you"; it was honestly amusing to have a lone raider attacked a fully armed player clad in X-01 Power Armor and his T-60f Companion with nothing but a tireiron. Like...for the first 2 times. The melee combat was just meh, while i did like the ability to bash with my gun, i got to say most of the time i just double tap and swap to a super sledge.
Honestly, there is a lot of hate out there towards this game and I don't think all of it is entirely justified. However, there are serious issues that I took with the game.
1) RPG Elements:
I've lauded the FPS, I've mehhed the Campaign but I gotta say, I don't feel like this was anywhere close to an RPG game. Sure there was the whole perk thingy (not even a tree) but i felt like the whole storyline was actually rather scripted with a fixed end goal in mind. The whole thing wasn't immersive and basically felt like a stuffing full of side quests and overwhelming the player before rushing him to the ending of the campaign in literally less than a day. It was horrible really. While Fallout NV had a inferior combat system as compared to Fallout 4, at least the story made me feel involved in the conflict between Caesar and the NCR and Mr House and even the minor factions like the BoS. At least I understood their motivations and why they were fighting each other but not in Fallout 4. Sorry mate but I didn't really give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about Shaun and played SimCity with Preston. (Whats up Babe?)
2) The DLCs:
Oh my god, the DLCs were crap. Seriously, you can mod most of them and robot companions are only helpful if you want help guarding the settlements but by the time you get all 6 guard robots, you'd have time for 18 rocket turrets so...nah really.
Far Harbor was interesting honestly...I liked that concept a lot but the story was far from intriguing (although I appreciated the look into the Children of Atom's chapter) and in the end, I used it as an offshore farm and trading centre more than anything.
The Vault Tec one was cool...if not for the fact that you needed to build the whole damnned thing from scratch and they kinda just threw it in your face like hey heres a defunct Vault with all new specific items. Good luck and hey remember its JUST ANOTHER SETTLEMENT!
Nuka World was HONESTLY the one i enjoyed the most. Except for one thing, i had to kill ALL the raiders just to enjoy life as a Minuteman. Again, the false dichotomy really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off here because I personally enjoy harmony and playing in a bloody theme park (literally)
3) Creation Club:
Cash for Mods. #ea. 'nuff said.
I think overall I would recommend this game if its selling at about 12-15 dollars because its really nothing more than an Open World Shoot Em up game. Ultimately, it depends on what you want. If you want a shooter that combines survival elements, this is for you. If you want a storyline and an actual RPG that makes you go "holy♥♥♥♥♥♥what do i actually want to do" rather than "damn. which faction do i wanna sacrifice. Oh wait its the Railroad." then play Fallout New Vegas.
So overall as a game in the fallout series: Not Recommended

So . . . where to begin, where to begin. No, I don't recommend this game is the short answer.
A Wild Catgirl Appears is a (very) short, yuri VN. I suppose. One girl is a catgirl. Well, 2 are. They are female, though, so I guess that still makes it yuri, right? I mean, you play as a female human. A redhead apparently. But you're Japanese? It's unclear. And that's where the issues started for me.
The character sprites are pretty to look at, for sure. Starla and Ria especially are attractive. There aren't many expressions for them, though and it all feels a little . . . unfinished. I fell in love with this game the first time I played it. I'd been on the fence regarding buying it since I'd heard a few detractors saying it wasn't as good as GTA.
I love the GTA series, but this tops them. Why? Because not only the story is good, but also the fighting mechanic - GTA was never good at fighting, it was all about driving and shooting. Sleeping Dogs brings in the Arkham series' style of freeflow fighting (though not as good as the Arkham games, it's not far off) as well as cool things like being able to jump from one car to another to hijack vehicles, take hostages, have bullet time vault shootings and much more.
The game is 2 years old but still looks as good, if not better (at times), than Watch Dogs. It runs really well, too. I was able to run it at ultra settings the day it came out, even with the hi-res PC-only texture pack that was released. Nowadays, I can run it at 2880x1620 (and would expect to run it at 4k, if my monitor supported it).
If you've been disappointed by Watch Dogs, then give this a try - I personally find it's more fun than Watch Dogs, allows you to interact with the other people in the environment more and has a great fighting system. It doesn't have all the hacking stuff, and is more action-orientated than stealth based, but that's not always a bad thing in the open world genre.

All I can say is that "The Binding of Isaac : Rebirth/Afterbirth" is an amazing expansion on the original game. This game is a great, innovative, expansive, and endless supply of fun. I am wanting two do two separate reviews in this particular review. One on Rebirth, and one on Afterbirth.
Rebirth:
Pros
-----------------
- Tight Controls (Even for keyboard users)
- Amazing environments
- Controller compatibility
- HUNDREDS of achievements
- HUNDREDS of collectables
- Endless possibilities with the game's randomly generated floors
- Amazing, overpowered, hilarious synergies with the game's amazing item selection
- Almost horrifically replayable
- A booming community
- 20 challenges to test your skill, and ways to play
- Improved graphics from the original
- Unique, crude art-style
- One of the best soundtracks in video games I've played
- Insane challenge. (But also very fair)
Cons
-----------------
- The story isn't really well-explained. Unless interpreted, the story isn't as fleshed out as I would like.
- The gameplay is almost completely luck-related
"The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth" is a game that I have sunk many, many hours into. Over 320 hours, in fact. I bought it quite a while ago, and just got back into it after watching TearOfGrace
(Check him out, I strongly recommend it) play it, where I learned a few tricks from him. I cannot recommend this game enough. It is VERY much worth your money. Support the creator.
I will be judging "The Binding of Isaac: Afterbirth" a little differently. I will judge it on how it expanded on the already amazing "The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth." I will see what it did better, and what it may have done worse.
Afterbirth:
Pros
-----------------
- More achievements
- More (But frustrating) environments
- Tougher enemies
- More items
- New game mode (Greed mode)
- Two new characters
- New bosses
- More transformations
- Even better, crazier synergies
Cons
-----------------
-Honestly, there's not much wrong about the game I can say. The only possible flaw is that the challenge may be too much for some.
The Binding of Isaac: Afterbirth is a fantastic expansion of this already amazing game. I cannot say much new about Afterbirth without me repeating myself more than I already have.
I cannot praise these games enough. So much about them are creative, expansive, and innovative to their genres. These games are well worth the $21 I spent. Both of these games are nearly perfect.
Rebirth: 9.5/10
Afterbirth: 9/10

Obligatory header to the review: I focus on four primary areas whenever I review a game: gameplay, story, graphics, and sound/audio/general things that go into your earholes. Gameplay and Story get a rating scale from 1 to 10, and the AV stuff gets a rating from 1 to 5. My philosophy on this is that there are some instances in which a game may not necessarily have that much in the way of gameplay (take Amnesia for example), but the story/atmosphere/whatever it may be is reason enough to pick it up. Also, take the cumulative score with a grain of salt; it's just a numerical feeling about the game as a whole. That's part of why I do these subscores. Also, keep in mind that I'm not going off of school grade based rankings. A 5/10 denotes what I feel to be an average game. Likewise, 7/10 is a game that I think is pretty cool, and something that gets a 2/10 is near-abomination level. Pinning scores to an even further obfuscated rating scale is kinda senseless, but for the sake of my backloggery, I'll repeat again that 1.0-2.7 is a one-star game, 3.0-4.7 is a two-star game, 5.0-6.7, 7.0-8.7, and 9.0-10 are three, four, and five stars, respectively.
Gameplay: Truth be told, I probably shouldn't even bother writing a review for this game. If you're here and you're reading this, then you most likely already have an opinion on the game. Nevertheless, I've been told quite often that just writing for writing's sakes isn't harmful; rather, the opposite. So here I am, talking about a remarkably popular series and giving my two cents amidst the stream of million dollar bills or something i dunno thought i'd try a metaphor
Left 4 Dead is a game about zombies. Many zombies. Specifically the 28 Days Later kind of zombies that can tear it through areas. There's also quite a few of them; roughly the amount you'd expect from a Serious Sam game or another game in its ilk. I love me some Serious Sam, so this is definitely a perk. I didn't have the fortune of playing with friends, and since I'd prefer not to potentially deal with the most cretin-like of online players, I kept to single player for all six campaigns. Your partners have pretty good AI, although they do seem to get a bit confused whenever you're making your escape.
One thing that I wasn't too much of a fan of as far as the gameplay feel - although I do recognize it as a function of the game's design - is that all of the campaigns feel pretty much the same. They all have a few sections of shooting many zombies followed by holding out for "ten minutes" while some sort of rescue arrives. I put ten minutes in quotes because there have been many a time where ten minutes most certainly had not passed, but rescue still arrives. Don't get me wrong, though; the stages are still quite good and often have multiple paths that you can take through the level to get to the end, but it can get a bit repetitive at times.
One of the things that this game does in order to keep things interesting is to have certain points throughout the level where a random "special infected" can spawn; there are five special infected that can show up, with each having their own unique strategy to dealing with them. This does keep the tension at a good level, although an unfortunate spawning of a tank can kinda take you back out of it. Nevertheless, these enemies don't feel cheap, as there's always some way of dealing with them.
Again, you probably already know this, but this is certainly a game that would be a lot of fun to play with friends. The option to play as the special infected in a certain mode of multiplayer is one that again I would have liked to try, but I didn't have enough friends that owned the game for Steam. Nevertheless, even as a single player experience, I still had a lot of fun with this game. 9/10.
Story: Much like how the levels themselves are organized, the story for each individual campaign comes down to Enter Area (most commonly through breaking down of a vehicle) - Fight Zambies - Escape in New Vehicle to Soon Break Down. Obviously, the origin of the zombies and all that isn't of concern to the story. Then again, it doesn't need to be. The focus of the writing is more on the characters. It's always fun to listen in on each character's banter with the others (and about how Francis hates everything). One thing I wish they would have done for the sake of the story would be to do... something after the final campaign. It just seems weird that it just ends and puts you back at the main menu. Nevertheless, the banter is still  quite enjoyable. I still wish they had provided that closure, though. 7/10.
Graphics: Given that this is a Valve-published game, one thing that you can expect is a very well optimized game that looks quite good. This game looks quite good, even if the graphics aren't artistically timeless. I really dug the art design of the special infected; specifically the Smoker portraying the "long, shady" look that smokers are stereotyped with. The environments look quite good, even if it is a bit hard to make out what you're looking at due to how dark it can be. Also, the technical things work just fine and as well optimized as one would expect from a Valve game. It's no surprise that it runs well on my relatively high-powered graphics card at 1080p Ultra settings, but admittedly it not running on those settings on my computer would be surprising. You don't need too much stronghth (yes, that was intentional) to run this game, and I'd imagine an integrated graphics chip could run this game. Even though it may not be the nicest thing to look at in ten or so years, it still looks and works perfectly fine today. 4/5.
Sound: Most of the music in this game is very ambient, but there are a couple of actual songs in there. The ambient pieces are very good at adding to what's going on; the ghostly wailing signaling the presence of a Witch adds the right amount of tension  to make you careful, the cacophonous wails of violins signal the onslaught of common infected, and it all works quite well. Each special infected makes their own sounds, and they're all quite distinctive and useful for identifying what special infected is just around the corner. The four survivor's voice actors do a quite good job at making the characters believable. All in all the audio portion of the game is quite well put together and adds just that much more to the game. 5/5.

I am completely unqualified to review a fighting game, so this is for people who know themselves to be casuals and want to know if this game could be satisfying to a casual player.
In short, it sort of is, sort of isn't. It has a nice presentation, STELLAR sound design, and some responsive controls. I would recommend it to a couple of button-mashers who want to have a fun, mindless game to spend a few hours killing each other in. If you want to get a bit more in depth with its systems, the combos and special moves aren't hard to pull off, and they have a list you can access in the pause menu. Moves can still be strung together to juggle your opponent and knock off upwards of 50% of their health bar, but thankfully they're very hard to pull off and are not part of the "official" list provided by the game.
The story campaign is kind of neat for MK fans who played the classic trilogy, reprising most of the old environments and characters with a nice nostalgic effect. But having said that, it's overacted pulp garbage and won't satisfy anyone looking for a real story.
The other main single player mode is the challenge tower, and it's a nightmare. I punched my printer and broke it. I also almost broke my controller. I am not proud of that, but it's to illustrate the levels of frustration you might experience trying to conquer the single player mode. It only gets really tough in maybe 20 of the 300 challenges, but those difficulty spikes are insane.
And this is where my only major problem with the game comes into play: single player against the AI comes down to cheesing one move over and over again. Most bosses can be killed by staying as far away as possible and spamming a projectile. Or perhaps spamming a teleport move. Or maybe a low kick over and over again. In challenge #300, I killed Goro, Kintaro, Mileena, and Shao Kahn all in one life by spamming Shang Tsung's projectile attack over and over again, occasionally jumping to avoid a counterattack to vary things up.
Whatever the specific strategy, it's essentially useless to do anything else besides that one particular move, since the rest of your moves will likely be blocked (or arbitrarily have absolutely no effect sometimes, as is randomly the case for the bigger bosses). Those blocks are usually followed by massive combos that just wreck you. The AI has an inhuman reaction time, so most of your attacks will be blocked before they even begin, which means that if you can't follow up a rare successful attack with 4 or 5 other ones in a combo chain, you will likely lose the match. Moreover, the AI "learns" your attack patterns, which simply means that if you land an uppercut or a jump kick, the next ones will be much harder to land again, forcing you to really vary your technique throughout the match. This sounds good on paper, but for a casual....not fun.
If you are a competitive player, the game instead becomes about waiting for openings to unleash your own combo chain, which would be a more legitimate way of playing. But the game is already super fast, and quicker reflexes will take a veeeery long time to develop. And since the entire game can be cheesed with a single move, there isn't a super good reason to become a better player, at least against the AI.
If you're interested in taking the fight online, you can do so, but the multiplayer is VERY laggy (even on a strong connection) and not particularly well developed. The population is also very slim. Again, I am not an expert, but my time in the online mode wasn't particularly fun, and I understand that there are much better fighting games out there to master.
So if you approach this game with the understanding that it's mostly for local co-op, maybe a quick spin through the campaign and a few climbs up the arcade ladder, then you will enjoy yourself. Any objective-based play, i.e. achievement hunting or competitive play or that unfathomably annoying challenge tower, are probably not good reasons for purchase.

A creepy and gory game, yet, not a violent one...
Fran Bow catches the essence of old children stories from the 1800s and before, before Hollywood and Disney made them cute. Stories had meaning, they were written as educative examples for children to behave well. They werent necessarily happy stories.
Fran Bow is full of visual display of blood and gore, but never you feel like you are in world of torture-porn. You are in world turned wrong, and you want to end it. Then, you enter the rabbit hole, and game turns into modern version of Alice in Wonderland.
Great story, great atmosphere, great sound and art. I was first disappointed by the lack of voice acting, but the way the game is presented made me forgive it very quickly. Its like reading a picture book, which doesnt require voice.
Game has many chapters and is fairly long, taking 10+ hours with semi-easy puzzles, Easy enough for everyone to get through, but still require a bit of thinking most of the time. What I liked is how unpredictable the game was. You are not set into one setting for the whole game, but inside a broken mind of a child, which can really change to any direction, at any time... In the end, someone might feel like its open ended and doesnt give you any answers, but one shouldnt overthink about it. The game gives you what you need to know, and from the perspective of the protagonist, Fran Bow, everything is just the way you need to know everything.
I can see how it was influenced by excellent movies "Pan`s Labyrinth" and "The Fall", which also are surreal stories playing with the broken mind of an orphan child. Overall, Fran Bow is an A+ grade modern Adventure game. Some companies such as Daedalic and WadjetEye make great classic style adventures, but it is games like Fran Bow that really show the best of the independent game development has to offer. Fran Bow offers something that big studios would never touch, and Fran Bow does it with style.

My expectations for this game weren't great, probably because of the sheer volume of incredibly short indie games that seem to have flooded the market now. Fran Bow, however, absolutely
What I expected to be a small game with standard gameplay turned out to be incredibly engaging, and for the first time in a long time, I found myself genuinely full of curiosity about what was to come. Each chapter has a very different feel, which breaks the game up nicely and adds a bit of variation.
From the screenshots shown above it is obvious that this game was made with a great weight on the aeshetics, but the unique visual style is not a gimmick as it is in many other Indie titles, and although the visuals are beautiful, Fran Bow would hold its own as a fantastic point and click diamond even without them.
I personally love point and click games, where you collect items and use them to solve problems in the world. Fran Bow's such trials were a fair amount more challenging than I anticipated, with some of the solutions being bizarre in an almost Discworld-esque way.
As the game progresses, the tone of it all becomes more and more surreal. There were many ponts during the story I found myself questioning what was happening, but it's fun and different. The way the characters talk can still break immersion occasionally even so, as it's just not believable, unfortunately. There were a few grammatical errors I noticed, which I believe seem to be due to a poor translation to English.

Overall, still a lot of fun. Would defintely recommend.

I first played and finished this AVP on PS3 (even got Platinum trophy) and I was disappointed. At least, I was able to trade it but still, that game was very disappointing on many aspects not respected from previous AVP games. Instead of using the things that worked so good on previous AVP games, this AVP 2010 simply decided to discard many aspects that was amazing on older AVP games and shove you that lack-luster product that's more related to the pathetic AVP movies than the previous games that were closer to the Aliens, Predator 1&2 movies. A huge step backwards and I hope, IF there's another AVP in the future, that it'll be made by a competent developer studio or get back with Monolith who did it perfectly on their AVP 2. Rebellion did a sloppy job on this game.
PROS:
+The graphics are truly amazing, especially this PC version.
+Faster Alien speed than previous AVP games.
+Lance Henriksen (Bishop) and William Hope (Lt. Gorman) from ALIENS voice cast.
+Multi Player fun when played with friends.
+Trophy kills are quite cool (at first).
+Gore is well done.
+Great character/monster modelling
+No flashy orange WY uniform
+No cartoon-ish visuals in this game unlike AVP 2.
CONS:
-Uninspiring level design.
-Weak narrative and story.
-No Rich Ragdale or similar sounding soundtrack (Made AVP 1999 or AVP Classic soundtrack).
-Majority of in game sounds are used from the AVP movies instead of the original AVP games and/or original movies
-Many scripted sequences during campaign mode.
-Lack of controls in this game (no crouching, no leaning, no aiming).
-Lame contextual situations (Sequential auto-kill (Insta-Kill)) are badly implemented, makes you vulnerable during that action phase. Worse is its in effect for the MP as well.
-Multi Player mode takes very long to join a game.
-NO DEDICATED SERVERS for the PC versions. It was promised then discarded just before game launch
-Lack of MP maps (unless you fork your hard earned $ for the purchasable Map packs DLC).
-Same single player maps for all three species
-Weak A.I. (One of the badder I have ever seen in a game).
-Predator HUD is well crafted and feels refreshing BUT, the health and energy gauges are poor represented and even confusing. It was better made from AVP 1999 with the red and blue predator symbols on each side.
-Indestructible Sentry Guns (you can only power them down by smashing a nearby computer keyboard); and the sound used is poorly done, not the same used in the Aliens movie.
OVERALL:
The Multi Player... lack of dedicated servers killed the PC version. Lack of maps is a huge letdown too. It just shows you that todays gaming scene wants to milk map packs as DLC and charge you. As for the game play, not as good as it was in my early AVP gaming years. Rebellion's AVP 1999 game (since they made their first AVP on Jaguar around 1994) was the king of online game play. Required you to have skills over all races, and it was faster paced. Even the single player of AVP 1999 was better than this one. AVP 2 introduced a class system which worked rather well online. The only gripe I had with AVP 2 MP was the poor network coding, making huge amount of lag even for broadband internet.
RECOMMENDATION:
On a finishing note, even as a huge fan of this gaming franchise and even the movies and comics, this AVP is a serious stripped down AVP 1999 except much disappointing. Too stripped, way too much content removed from Rebellion's AVP 1999 and it shows badly. HOWEVER, I'd recommend this AVP game any time over "Gearbox Aliens: Colonial Marines". The gameplay is way more fun and consistant. Also, AVP looks much better than Colonial Marines... a game that came out two years AFTER AVP! Lastly, you may want to get this game for the campaign mode since the MP is quite pointless without dedicated servers and the matchmaking truly suck bad!

I usually avoid Hack & Slash games, but Bastion is special.
Instead of drowning you in endless grind, the designers kept it short & sweet. This allows story to actively drive the game all the way through, rather than merely serving as punctuation. The smooth, standout narration deserves your careful ear, as its backstory adds so much depth to the overall experience. Bastion is one of the few games which enticed me to seek out other's analysis on its themes and philosophy afterwards.
The cartoonish, hand painted world blends together to defy the sterile, methodical aesthetic many isometric games suffer. It's cute how these gorgeous tiles and assets fancifully fall into place just a few steps ahead of you, all in theme with the recollective nature of the story. The only jarring result of Bastion's isometry is you can only move in 8 directions; not granularly. However, the important thing is weapon aiming is granular.
I won't lie, there were times I found the combat frustrating, but it did improve as I levelled (and equipped) up, and by the end, I was even enjoyed it. I also appreciated the fact that you have a good old fashioned hunk o' metal shield. As in, one you have to actively face the enemy and raise to counter with. The combat is definitely more interesting for that decision.
Besides, Bastion is worth it for the music alone.

I love Sandbox games, so long as they aren't GTA, and while my favourite franchise is Saints Row, Sleeping Dogs is actually one of my favourite indiviudal titles. Perhaps I'm a sucker for Sleeping Dogs' indulgent, fully fleshed Hong Kong setting. However, it's such a joy to traverse this map, and have admittedly stale mini-games and expected mechnaics rethemed as a Kar-wai, To or Woo film.
One way, however, that Sleeping Dogs rises above its competitors, and the myraid of gang-related snaboxers beyond the setting and theme is how your character traverses the world. It was a stroke of genius to have the game open on an adrenaline-pumping, parkour-inspired chase scene. It sets the tone for the rest of the game, begging the player to rely on these skills far more than other games as they fluidly bound across the map.
It was also refreshing that the game constantly forced the player to ask which side of the line they were really on: are you more a cop or a gangster?
Loved it. Pure and simple.

I think there are some good messages and themes regarding tolerance and individuality and self expression presented here in this VN. It was nice that each character has their own route and you could pursue them all as romantic interests too, since not all VNs with yuri content allow that. I had the most difficulty uncovering Starla's route between all of them.
I think if I could suggest where improvements to the experience might be made, I would have liked to have seen a bit more resolution or at least exposition in some of the endings.
Ending spoilers and minor nitpicking ahead:
And one really minor but distracting thing, the UI sliding in from the sides of the screen over and over was just jarring. I think the timing on that either needed to be sped way up so they popped back in rather quickly, or else slowed down enough to where you'd have to wait a good 30-60 seconds even after finishing reading a longer dialog box worth of text before they appeared, that way when you are just clicking through the game text at a reasonable pace they didn't keep slowly creeping back on the screen so frequently. I eventually got accustomed to it but it was weird. Not a huge deal though.
Overall, I enjoyed the game and appreciated the messages it was presenting about open mindedness and different walks of life.

Street Fighter V: The Fighting Game that doesn't know what it wants to be.
Bottom Line:
Purchase this if you really like the mechanics of fighting games and want an "honest" take on competitive play. If you are a casual fighting game fan, I would caution to steer clear until Capcom releases an update with more casual/single-player content.
What Works:
The moment to moment gameplay in a fighting game is why hardcore enthusiasts select certain games and stick with them. SFV has one of the most satisfying meta-systems in fighting games and has been fine-tuned by pro players through months of beta testing and QA. The game has a strong emphasis on fundamental play, spacing, and smart use of normal moves.
Gameplay has been tweaked from SFIV to provide a more approachable system with the removal of many low-risk/high-reward link combos and the FOCUS attack system, however the V-Skill, V-Trigger, and V-Reversal systems create more individualized character strategy - and arguably more depth. Character trials are well designed and help to show players of any skill level how each character works and gives them ideas through the combos that the system presents to help the player to think of new ways to approach the skills they have learned. Training mode also deserve props for the amazing amount of options and recording features. Only Killer Instinct comes close to providing a training suite that is as robust as SFV.
What Doesn't Work:
SFV was made for, and still caters to the pro-player. Even 10 months post release, with 6 new characters for a total of 22, multiple new stages, and a few new game modes, there just isn't enough single player content to satisfy casual players. The individual character stories, overall story mode are FAR too easy even for the most novice player and provide very little actual gameplay. The Survival Mode has the worst difficulty spikes I've encountered in any fighting game - you can go from blowing through characters with relative ease and when you encounter a "boss" character they have the adept readability of a pro player who has been playing for years. Even the most seasoned players cannot best this mode. It's uneven and sloppy. There is no Arcade mode to sit through while waiting (AEONS) for online match play or to provide a robust single player experience. Basically, there is little reward structure built in to keep a casual player coming back for more. The only reward structure built in focuses on online ranked play.
The Presentation:
Where SFIV has a wonderful, fun presentation that focuses on the series storied history with great artwork and tons of menu options, SFV takes a more minimalist approach to menu design and presents something that would feel more at home on a smartphone or tablet. It's boring, doesn't get you excited to play the game, and has little to offer the user in interesting content.
Where the menu system fails though, the in game graphics are absolutely beautiful. If you can run this game in 4K/60, you will be treated with a visual feast of highly detailed and colorful characters that seemingly pop out of the screen. The post-process special effects really add a lot of character to an already stylized game as well. Even running in 1080p the game still shines. The background run at half the frame rate (30fps) to ensure that action between the two characters stays at a constant 60fps. While many backgrounds are great, there are a few that have colors or effects that distract from the fight. Kanzuki Beach, Airplane, and 4 Generals stages are the most notorious and have been banned from tournament play due to their distracting nature.
Overall, I'll recommend this game to any fighting game enthusiast or for any player that is looking to get into fighting games because they are interested in the mechanics only. If you are a casual player looking to relive the glory days of the 90s playing SF with your friends, I'd highly recommend Ultra Street Fighter 4 instead.
