Firstly, if you have played DOOM 3 before, really liked it and you're wondering whether it would be worth getting the BFG edition or not: Get it yesterday already, marine!  You get DOOM 3, yes, but also more of the same asskicking gameplay in two awesome mission packs (Ressurection Of Evil & Lost Mission) and, on top of that, DOOM 1 and DOOM 2 are added on just for old time's sake so you can relive where first-person shooting really began.
If you're brand new to DOOM and you're a first-person shooter kind of gamer, well, are you in for a treat! - DOOM 3 is said to be one of the best FPS games ever, developed by the people who actually popularized the genre: id Software.
The story in short:
It is 2145 and humans, under the auspices of the Union Aerospace Corporation (UAC), have established a research facility on Mars.  Employees are mostly engineers, scientists or soldiers.  Research is being done in the fields of biology, space exploration, teleportation and weapons development.  Furthermore, exciting evidence has been found of previous inhabitants: an alien civilization that was destroyed by a vicious and seemingly unstoppable enemy.  Incredible times.
However, a growing unease has filtered through UAC personnel.  Rumours are abound of strange things happening,like unexplained voices and otherworldly creatures roaming the facility, sometimes resulting in accidents or even loss of life.  In addition, the facility, under Dr. Malcolm Betruger, is running an ever-increasing tab on the corporation's resources and Earth has sent a representative to investigate.  It turns out that Betruger, through his work in teleportation, has opened a portal to another dimension and in so doing has enabled hostile creatures to come through to Mars.  In reality, these creatures are demons and the place they come from is ... hell.  They are the same malignant creatures that destroyed the ancient Martian civilization.
You play a marine, freshly imported from Earth and dumped into the chaos, on a crusade to stop the evil from invading the Mars facility and, ultimately, Earth.  You have a range of weapons to your disposal, but you will also have to gain information and access to other parts of the facility to complete your task.  You do this by collecting PDA's from personnel, dead and alive, scattered throughout the base.  Since the main portal is situated in hell itself, you will have to travel there (following in Betruger's footsteps) and retrieve a powerful artifact called the Soul Cube which can be used to defeat the enemy's mightiest warrior (as well as assist in the downfall of many other along the way) and close the portal.
The game can be divided into three large sections: 1) the Mars facility, 2) Hell and 3) the Mars facility revisited, although in the latter part the Mars base and hell ultimately becomes indistinguishable from each other.  Once in possession of the Soul Cube (you bring it back with you from hell), demon attacks become more vicious and your strategy in using the artifact to your advantage becomes key.
Slight changes have been made to the original DOOM 3 (for example, certain triggers and enemies have been taken out and some of your weapons sound a bit different), but you may not even notice it.  The biggest change maybe is how the flashlight works: it is not handheld anymore but a fixed item, so you can use it while you're actually shooting (a definite plus), like in QUAKE 4.  However, the flashlight dies after about 30 seconds and then needs to recharge (in a few seconds) before it can be used again.  Whether this is a good or bad thing probably depends on individual opinion.  Of course, the benefit would be that you don't ever need to manually turn it off, maybe saving you some seconds to concentrate on enemies.
Mission Pack 1: Ressurection Of Evil (RoE)
You play as a different marine who finds a new artifact on Mars but in the process opens another gateway to hell.  An old enemy, Malcolm Betruger, revels in the prospect of newly invading the world.  Three bosses ("hunters") are released that you will later have to defeat one by one.  You get instructions from Dr. Elizabeth McNeil to destroy the artifact, which (of course) must be done in hell.  So, once again your character travels through the complex on Mars untill you find a portal to hell.  Enough said, no more clues.
Some new weapons are introduced: a "grabber gun" and Sarge's shotgun (find the cabinet code first, though).  The grabber gun may not seem like much, but it will make life easier.  It is used to move object (like crates, boxes, drums and stones) and to catch fire balls mid-air and throw them back at enemies.  It can be used to directly kill small enemies and pick up items that are out of reach.  Sarge's double-barrelled shotgun is a valuable tool at close range, boasting more punch than the game's regular shotgun.  It fires two cartridges at once, which are replaced manually by your character in about three seconds.
A few new enemies make their appearance, including a tougher kind of imp that throws white-blue fire balls.  There also is a new large, slow-moving enemy with a powerful ranged attack, but one can easily use its lack of speed to one's advantage.  It may involve guerrilla tactics, running for cover or making sure to have some obstacle between you and your foe when you're not shooting.
Mission Pack 2: Lost Mission
You play as the only surviving member of Bravo team (remember them from the original Doom 3?) who got wiped out while on a mission - it all starts with a replay of the cut scene from the original game, showing the demise of the team by the hand of some maggots/imps (it is the same incident that damages a cooling rod in the reactor, the one that is replaced by your character in the original game).  Having survived the attack, you then roam the facility continuing the fight on your own.  You link up with a scientist, Dr. Richard Meyers, who informs you of a problem: it so happens that there still exists a working teleporter in "the other dimension" (hell) that could assist the enemy's ultimate goal: invading Earth.  So, once more into the breach you go.  You find your way to hell and reach the portal, fighting enemies large and small, until you face off with a copy of an old enemy from the original game - the Guardian (no seekers this time) - to achieve your goal.
In Lost Mission (as in RoE) you get to travel through other, quite scenic parts of hell (obviously, the place is quite expansive).  Your journey even includes a short boat trip on molten lava.
There are no new artifacts (also no Soul Cube).  Sarge's sawed-off double-barreled shotgun as well as the grabber gun from RoE make a return.
All in all, "Doom 3: BFG Edition" is one of the best FPS game bundles you can buy.  It is an extensive, zombie-shooting, demon-hunting experience that should keep you coming back for more until you've cleared out hell of all its evil, and then do it all over again.
Enjoy big time.

I don't know whether to recommend this game or not. It's a lot of fun, in that I have no doubt. Most of the players you run into from game to game can be really fun and cool people to hang out with.
But lately the game has been taking a turn for the worse. People will just randomly vote up people for roles, when there is no need (Like day 2 for example). They'll out people who's roles are important, like the Jailor or Town Protective so that the Mafia or Neutral Killings can kill them at will. Sometimes they'll get lucky and hang a random Serial Killer or Arsonist or Mafia member, but most of the time they just end up hanging an innocent townie. Not to mention people seem to fail to understand the basic Executioner plays when they pop up and just go along with the hanging anyway. Not to mention that when the town does hang you following one of these "random lynchings," they report the random person they voted up for gamethrowing.
In addition, it is hard for the devlopers of this game to crack down on external cheating (such as using Skype or Teamspeak to share information and roles with other people in a party). Now I know that the rules of the game even say that outside communication is allowed and encouraged, and I'm all for that! It makes the game more enjoyable when you play it with your friends! But the rules don't allow for players to share information "illegally" with each other without providing the means in the game as This could provide an unfair advantage to one side or the other. This type of cheating is very common in the game now, I seem to see it every 1 to 2 games. And the worst part is that they will openly admit it when they die or win!
For those reasons, I hesitate to recommend this game. If you want a game that will give you hours of fun, especially with friends (when played correctly), and something that will put your mind to the test, then this game is for you. I'd say this game is closer to being a Tony Hawk-style "stunt game" than it is to being a racing game. Sure, there are races, but there are also challenges based on doing sick flips off of broken parts of bridges as well as ones based on seeing if your car can beat up the other cars. The world that the game takes place in is also very nice; they basically mashed a bunch of cities and settings together into one city specifically designed for racing (though sometimes it's eerie how despite it being a large city, there are 0 pedestrians or otherwise any signs of life apart from empty, self-driving cars), and it works great. And despite this game being relatively old, it still looks great, and the great news is that it still works! Several other old games are unplayable now because of DRM-related issues, and this game is not one of those games (though "DLC Island" is extinct now)
This game has a few flaws though. If you're a "purist", this game might upset you since everything feels very arcade-y (for me this was a plus though). Second, some stuff like the aforementioned "DLC Island" is no longer accessible (at least as far as I know) due to DRM shenanigans, so if you're one of those people who boycotts games that suffered from DRM, this might be bad news for you, though having said that the game works fine even with DRM shooting it in the foot slightly (and hey, if you were expecting any better from EA, then... yeah). The in-game announcer DJ Atomika is also annoying, but it's not anything that would completely ruin a game IMO.
Overall, I'd say this game is a good buy. I got it in a Humble Bundle many years ago, and it has ended up becoming my all-time favorite racing game, so there's that. (also sorry in advance if this review reads weird, I was a bit tired when I wrote it)

So i'm sitting here with my plate of noodles, thinking what to say about Sleeping Dogs. Since it is one of those games that i'm two minds about. On one hand, it delivers a well crafted and realised Hong Kong cop-drama, but on the other hand, it feels like a very lackluster open-world game.
A bit of history, this game started off as a continuation to the True Crime series, but for reasons i cannot remember at this point, the development stopped. And  i think the game was saved in part by that decision. True Crime was not considered to be the best of series and if Sleeping Dogs (At time of original development True Crime:Hong Kong) it would have just fallen into obscurity with the rest, only to be remembered by the fans of the series. But does Sleeping Dogs survive on its own Or does it deserve the long sleep ?
STORY:
The story follows Wei Shen, an undercover cop sent to covertly infiltrate one of Hong Kongs famous triad gangs. And since i try my best to avoid spoilers, i will only summarize. That the story is heavily influensed by many of the famous Hong Kong cop-movies. And it is interesting enough to warrant playing through more than once.
GAMEPLAY:
Unfortunately for the game, the open-world nature really does it no favours. On the other hand it offers a very lively representation of Hong Kong and on the other it feels useless. There really is not enough content to warrant an open world, no random flippentry to perform besides some of the social challenges things and annoying the police. And that is about it. One oddity, that i believe also alienated some of the playerbase. Is the scarce amount of firearms, the game is mostly centered around melee combat and the system they used is so similiar to the Arkham-series that it feels almost like it was ripped off. But what there is, is functional enough. There are enviromental attacks that are flashy but a tad lengthy and a few other minor issues with the combat system.
The game has a great number of glitches and bugs, some are funny and some are absolutely infuriating. Most of theese bugs are centered around the freerunning system, i feel like it should have been polished a little more for the pc-version. Since  the game was designed for consoles, there are also some annoying problems with the camera. Overall, the porting could have been done much better.
SOUND DESIGN:
Like GTA, theres a decent amount of copyrighted music. Nothing to be annoyed about, but nothing to remember neither. The only funny thing is, that there is a karaoke-bar, with actual karaoke. A pattern minigame, but worth it to listen Weis voice actors vo over the song. Yes, they went there...
CONCLUSION:
Considering the problems that Sleeping Dogs, could i recoommend it ? Short answer, YES. Long answer, the game feels padded out lengthwise, several minor problems deteriorate the gameplay experince, optional activities feel like diversions, experience leveling is questionable and the rewards they give are minor to say the least. The story is the only thing that is supposed to carry the game, but does it ? Not really...
I would give this game a C+. It feels a little low, but as i have tried to explain, the only thing worth something in this game is the story it tells and really nothing else. What there is on the activities side, is forgettable and getting a 100% feels like a wasted effort.

Sigh, you most likely already know what worms is about, it's one of the most well known video game series, and it is the essential party game. For the antisocial people that live under a rock (no offence though), Worms are creatures that have a long cylindrical tube-like body and no limbs. Worms the video game series is about teams of those creatures killing other teams of those creatures in a turn based format, sometimes with usual weapons, like an Uzi, and sometimes with a CONCRETE DONKEY.
But really, it is a very simple game, that's probably the reason why it's so popular, it's incredibly easy to just pick it up and play, and 18 years and 60 million copies sold later, the worms formula has been basically perfected.
Now, the worms games have been heavily criticised for publishing new games without much new content, and I completely agree, and this game also follows the same format, it's still the old 2D, worm killing, psychopath game we all love. But it also add some new content, I know, weird right?
This game has 3D graphics, the whole terrain, items, worms and weapons are fully modeled and rendered in 3D, even though the gameplay is in 2D. Also, it adds a single player campaign, now, I usually dislike having a single player campaign just for the sake of it, but in this game I feel like it is it's highlight, the story is really quirky and funny, and the narration by the psychopathic Crypt Creeper Tara Pinkle is just wonderful and really funny, one of the best parts of the game. The game also has an extensive character and terrain editor, with steam workshop compatibility, making it really fun to customize your game. And finally, the game has extensive additions to online multiplayer, there's a Clan option, allowing you to create a team up to 8 players and face off against other clans, and ranked mode, for both player vs player and clan vs clan, a clash of clans, if you will.
This game also looks really good, the 3D models and textures are really well done, and the game looks gorgeous, the 3D graphics are a step in the right mine-filled direction. And as I previously mentioned, the game has Steam Workshop compatibility, and it allows for some really funny and creative worms, like one that says Terry Crew's lines from the insane Old Spice commercials.
Also it has a very User-friendly interface, it's easy to figure out what each weapon does, the help menu is extensive, and the game has a great controller support. Also steam achievements and cards.
Overall, this game more than just more of the same, but it still is basically more of the same, so if you don't yet own a Worms game, this is undoubtedly the one for you, but if you already own one, the only real reason to get this one is Tara's spectacular voice acting.

I really like the Visual Novel genre, which is why I can be really critical of it. And it pains me when I come across games like this that will turn people off to it before they get to any of the good stuff.
I think the dev's heart was in the right place, as it's clear that he or she has played games like this before. And while the art style is Western, there are clear anime and general Japanese influences on the setting and some of the characters. But the art is just not very good, and the writing is incredibly weak. There's nothing interesting about any of these characters and the humor falls flat every time. The best that can be said is that it does take the difficulty of a same-sex relationship somewhat seriously. The music is better off muted, especially the time-of-day transition tune which fills me with rage.
Another issue is that whatever program this was made in (I've seen it before) has an awful UI. I'm guessing it's a free or low cost VN creator. There is extremely limited functionality for the player, and it seems to miss some clicks as well when in the save and load screen. You do get achievements and five endings which is a plus if you like the game. (Note: I'm not sure what the true play time of this was due to trading card idling but it's fairly short for each run).
I'd avoid this one or at least don't get your hopes up too high for it if you get it from a bundle.

Aliens, Predators and Humans.
Review of Aliens vs Predator for PC (2010). Compared with ACM (2013).
Made by Rebellion
Released in 2010
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Spoilers ahead.
Aliens vs Predator is the latest AvP title from Rebellion. The first game was AVP (1999).
The second was developed by Monolith and realised in 2001. The first version was improved (AvP gold) and can be purchased at steam. AvP 3 was released on february 19, 2010 in Europe and features three distinct story lines. You can play as Alien, Predator or Marine. It has no connection to the AvP films other that it features three characters and some familiar organisations like Weyland - Yutani.
(tip: before you play this game, you should have seen the Alien films and/or played other Alien related games)
Story and gameplay
The story is mediocre. But it offers unique perspectives on the Alien and Predator franchises. Weyland - Yutani is the main 'villain' in this game. This game let you play as Alien, Predator or Human.
- Compared with the story off ACM, this story is not quite as good. Because it has no connection to the films. ACM is better in this regard.
The Alien is nicknamed 'Number 6' and you will try to escape the facility and return to your queen. In the end you must fight the Predator.
The Predator is nicknamed 'Dark' and you will try to obtain a weapon that the marines captured. In the end you must fight the Predalien.
The Marine is nicknamed 'Rookie' and you will try to unravel the secrets of Weyland - Yutani and fight deadly Aliens. In the end you fight with Mr. Weyland.
The Alien campaign is the shortest. Crawling against walls and objects can be a bit difficult. You have no longe range weapons. You are the weapon. You can perform fatality moves with the 'E' button just like the Predator. You see with a 'fish - eye' perspective. The Alien can crawl into vents and airducts.
The Predator campaign offers high - tech weaponary and is quite entertaining. You can perform fatality moves just like the Alien. You cannot crawl but you jump from tree to tree. You have the ability to cloak yourself. With your helmet you can view in three 'modes'.
The Marine or human campaign is the longest. It is the standard FPS genre. You have weapons and you have a flaslight to illuminate dark areas. You are the 'soft' character, compared to Alien and Predator.
- Compared with ACM, the campaigns are original and fresh. You can play different characters. AVP is better in singleplayer aspect. ACM does offer co - op campaign unlike AVP.
Artifical Intelligence
The A.I. of the game is very good. You can set your difficulty and the enemies will become tougher. If you play on the highest setting: only for die hards.
- Compared with ACM, its a tie (difficulty settings).
Multiplayer
If you play multiplayer, you will play team deathmatch. It offers the three main characters in a brutal war against each other. You can also play other modes like survival in which you fight waves of enemies. Just like other games (Left for Dead for example).
- Compared with ACM, multiplayer is quite the same. It offers less modes but you can play as more characters.
In-game bugs and screen tearing in singleplayer and multiplayer.
There are no bugs - except the Aliens themselves - in this game.
- Compared with ACM, there are no bugs or screen tearing. AVP is better.
Graphics
The graphics of this game are really good. If you compare this game to A:CM, AVP offers much more detail. With DX11 you will enjoy high end graphics. If you have a good pc you can play this game with maximum settings. Humans, Aliens and Predators look very good. Facial expressions are good. Lightning effects and environments are exceptional detailed. AVP is the best looking Alien game until now.
- The graphics of AVP are much better then ACM graphics if you focus on detail. But ACM offers an 80's setting. If you like detail go for AVP. If you like 'old school' style and resemblance to Aliens (1986), go for ACM. All in all, AVP offers superb graphics.
Sound
The sound of this game is really good. The Alien and Predator sounds are very good. But if you compare the sound of the weapons in this game with the weapons in Alien,  Predator or AVP movies, they are not the same. ACM offers better sounds.
- If you compare the sound of this game to ACM, both are quite good. Although I prefer the sound of ACM weaponary. The sounds of the Alien in AVP are very good. Sounds of both games are good.
Replayability
Replayability of the game is high because of the three distinct campaigns and the multiplayer options. It offers no co - op mode like ACM.
- Both AVP and ACM offer high replayability if you are Alien fan like me. ACM offers co - op unlike AVP and more multiplayer modes. ACM wins.
Conclusion
AVP 3 from 2010 is a game that delivers the AVP universe in a fresh setting. Because it offers unique campaigns, you will play this game again. The graphics of this game are unique. Much better then ACM graphics. They are not so good like Crysis 3 for example, but they are still very good. The story of the game is mediocre. The latest installment of the AVP series offers superb graphics and animations, a mediocre story, good sounds, three distinct playable characters and fun multiplayer modes.
AVP has better graphics then ACM, three campaigns with different characters and fun multiplayer modes. It is not movie related but it offers a decent story.
All in all, AVP is not as good as ACM. Co - op, upgradable weapons and better multiplayer modes and DLC belong to ACM.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The good
* Based on a existing franchise;
* Very good graphics;
* Three distinct stories;
* Multiplayer and survival mode are very good;
* Fresh and innovative gameplay.
The bad
* No co - op modes;
* No upgradable weapons;
* Less multiplayer modes compared to ACM.
* No canon story.
FINAL VERDICT: 7.5 out of 10.

username: Don't let your dreams be dreams
text:
This game doesn't need a review.
Guys is DooM, who doesn't know DooM?
NO...WRONG....IT NEEDS A REVIEW.....AND EVEN A LONG ONE!
Let me tell you this story (true). I was talking with this guy, you know the typical modern videogamer all about "cuda cores/memory bandwidth/fov/blablablablabla" when I asked him, informed person, what he thought of DooM.
"Oh yes pretty graphic lot of light and shadow games nice horror scenario"
And I was like "no...no no no...no no no no no...I mean DooM...the old one...the one from 1993...you know right?"
And the answer was "DooM?...the old one?....no man I don't play such old games like those with that pixel graphic without details....."
And while he was still talking I gently and slowly stood up I grabbed my chair and I've smashed it on his head so hard that today he's still spinning.....AND THIS HAPPENED FOUR YEARS AGO OKAY?
I mean seriously, if you are a true gamer you don't really care about graphic because mostly you will look for few things like:
- Gaming experience
- Entertainment
- Fun
- Gameplay innovation
- Soul
This is what you will find in the BFG edition of DooM 3...all the three DooM complete with their expansions and even the deleted levels!
Games of those days are too much linear and too much easy to understand and even to finish....but....
What other game will make you cry about looking for the "Red Card" to open the door?
DooM!
And when you will find the "Red Card" you will discover that you will even need the "Gold Card" to open the last door and you will want to cut your veins!
What game will make you turn your head side to side, upside down, on an angle, etcetc to try to understand the map?
DooM!.......................Layout of map that even Blizzard copied for Diablo!
You like action? You like shooting? You like running all over maps that looks like a labirinth looking for a key? You like plasma guns that you don't need to reload every 40 shots? You like a end boss that you will have no idea how to kill it? And at least...you like REAL big enemies?
Then DooM 1 and 2 are the games for you...but what about DooM 3?
Different but not boring or a fail at all. Where DooM 1 & 2 are more direct action, DooM 3 is a more elegant soft impact game that in some parts will drastically increase when you will be locked inside a room and something like 20 monsters will starts to spawn around you.
Where DooM 1 & 2 doesn't care about scaring you DooM 3 will focus more into trying to get you focused on the game, so focused that you will jump form your chair when something will try to hit you from a wall.
Where DooM 1 & 2 have a short text story where you will be the only one hero of the situation, DooM 3 will give you a better story and plot experience by adding even a lot of info about this and that in the game, dialogs and recordings too.
If you will find this pack on a sale...simply get it, it will entertain you for a lot of time and you will hardly get bored of it. Even because when you will finish it you will feel the need to play it again.
Overall:
Graphic 8/10
Sounds 8/10
Gameplay 8/10
Longevity 9/10
Piece of art!

Honestly never thought this game would be so great. I'm not even done the game and it's blowing me away. This game probably tops my list of point and click games I've ever played.
The music is amazing, the stories are creepy and sometimes very scary and disturbing, artwork is 11/10 in my eyes, reminds me of old Angela Anaconda and that was a decent part of my childhood as well.
The fact that this game dwellls around mental illness/disorders/murders is actually amazing, honestly what games have you played recently that almost ALWAYS makes you have different perspectives on every single character/npc you come across?
The puzzles are actually pretty simple but of course there are times everyone is a complete idiot and misses the easiest solution to things, there are times where you will be stumped, and I think that's probably one of the best parts of the game, the attention to detail and the hints you get through different conversations or Fran just making comments in her head will make you think on how you need to progress.
Might update this once I actually finish the game but for now I'm already gonna say that if a sequel is coming to Fran Bow, I WILL be buying it.

Burnout Paradise is a culmination of all things that makes Burnout great. Fast racing, great crashing and fun cars, but situated in an open world area where you can make your own way to the finish line fastest. There are multiple different types of race or challenge to compete in, ranging from stunt races, demoltion races to your standard point to point race and also the classic Burnout 'Crash' mode.
Pros:-
- Great variety in cars.
- Brilliant and large open world.
- Great variety in race type.
- Fun collectibles in the smash boards.
- Fun sense of progression.
- Fun multiplayer that includes great races or fun activities/challenges to do in the open world with friends.
- Driving feels great, even to this day
Cons:-
- Some repetitiveness not uncommon in open world games.
Note, this review was completed as a part of the 'Steam Awards.'

Can't get your puppy or grown dog to settle down to sleep at night? Does it whine all night long? Here are a few ideas about how to change this behavior—or accommodate it in your home.
Identify the Problem. Puppies may miss the noise and warmth of a litter. Dogs are creatures of habit-- a change of sleeping situation may be the problem. If something stressful to the dog has recently happened, perhaps this needs to be addressed.
For a sleepless puppy: Make sure you have the following things: a warm bean bag or mat, and a clock that makes a rhythmic ticking sound. Put these articles under a cushion or a blanket where your dog sleeps! It should work like magic. You can also put the clock next to your dog. However you could also try putting a radio on softly.
If your dog is accustomed to sleeping in a crate, kennel, or other small space he or she may have a hard time sleeping in an open room. If you prefer your dog to sleep out in the open, or you don't have a crate, it may take a few nights of whining and pacing for her to get used to the new situation. Be patient! Show her where you want her to sleep, and, if she knows the command, tell her to do a "Down" and "Stay." You may need to get out of bed to correct incorrect behavior--but it'll be worth it in the long run.
If you want your dog to sleep in a crate, but he isn't "crate trained" it may take some time to get him used to the crate. Put special treats in the back of crate before you lead him to it. Make sure that when you say "Kennel" or "bedtime" you use a positive tone of voice--going into the crate to sleep shouldn't be a punishment. If you use it as a punishment, you may find that your dog never grows accustomed to the crate as a relaxing and quiet place.
Perhaps there are other issues--a big event, a change in household set-up-- that the dog is responding to. Just remember, dogs are happiest when the same thing happens everyday in the same way. A small change to you (like moving your bedroom furniture) may seem like a big deal to the dog. He'll get used to the change with patient and consistent correction from you.
Exercise! Dogs need about 40 minutes a day of running, panting, aerobic exercise. A restless dog at night may be a dog who needs more time tiring himself out.
Food. Dogs absorb energy from their food differently than humans do--because their food is a little different. Generally, dogs get a big energy push right after eating, so if you feed your dog late at night, she may be too energetic to get to sleep. Try feeding her earlier, and be sure to let her relieve herself before bedtime.
Warnings
Be careful about the temperature of the hot item. It should be warm to the touch. A normal dog's body temperature is around 102 degrees Fahrenheit, so oppositely, don't make it too cold.

Sanctum 2 is an interesting combination of 2 game genres I like: tower defense and first-person shooter. You place pedestals that hinder enemy movement, and then turrets of varying types on top of those. Then, once the baddies start attacking, pick up your assault rifle and defend the cores along with them. It's a pretty good game with a simple objective. The tower designs are nice and futuristic, the enemies are interesting (especially bobbleheads), and overall it's just fun to play. Something that I enjoyed is that the game doesn't try to hold your hand through everything. It gives you a basic idea of "this is a tower" and "protect this core", but the finer points are up to the player to discover. And I don't mean something like up up down down left right left right B A (Google it, if you must know) where you need someone else to tell you about it, I mean through playing the game and experimenting with how everything works, you can figure it all out on your own. It's put together mostly well, but it is not without it's flaws. I find myself pretty frequently running into things on the floor, stopping me in my tracks over essentially nothing. I also have occasional difficulty with the XBox controller support. It seems to only happen in menus, but sometimes, the game does not respond to me pushing the directional buttons or analog sticks.

While this new installment of Street Fighter did not come with all the standard content that the previous games did on release day, the core gameplay itself is very solid. However, at the time of writing this, they have added quite a bit of content and continue to do so. There is a fully fledged story mode which takes a 1~2 hours to complete (provided you don't skip any cutscenes). They've added challenges/missions to help players to gain in-game currency a little faster. There are 6 more characters added to the original roster and will continue to add more over time. There new stages and also added the promised stage transitions for each stage. I don't believe there are currently any balance changes at the moment as they seem to be focused on adding content, but I'm sure they will shift that focus to balance changes once  they feel there is substantial content.
I have mixed feelings about how the game handles network play. Unlike the USF4, it uses roll back. While roll back does not greatly interrupt the input of your commands/combos, the downside is that you may see some "teleporting" if you do not have a very good connection with your opponent. If you do have a good connection with your opponent, then for the most part, it's very playable with either little to no "lag/teleporting". Technology has come a long way and has allowed games that emphasize lag-free play to play with others around the world. While it's not currently perfect, I think it's a great achievement thus far and eventually will improve over time as we discover better ways to code the networking. Don't expect to be lag-free if you're playing against someone from the other side of the world. We're just not there yet.
I only recommend this game if you are a fan of fighting games as it really does not appeal to casuals. In most cases, casuals are probably looking to play the story mode/AI and play with their friends only. That's not to say that they shouldn't purchase the game, but they probably won't appreciate/enjoy the game as much as hardcore fighting game fans would. If you like competitive gaming and want a challenge, this is probably for you as this has a high skill cap and a steep learning curve.

What do you mean, I never wrote a review for the Steam game I have the most time on by far that's not multiplayer-only?  I guess it's time to fix that.
Now, I usually write long, wordy reviews going over many details about a game, but I'm going to keep this brief.  Binding of Isaac is wild, ridiculous fun.  If you like roguelikes or retro action games or top-down shooters or faux-action RPGs at ALL, you should check this game out.  It's one of the most fun, addicting games I've EVER played, period, and is a huge cornerstone of the action-roguelike genre.
And forget about the original.  It was great for its time but Rebirth is just simply a superior version of the exact same product.  The vanilla game contains ALL the content of the original game AND all its patches and expansion plus much, MUCH more, and then Afterbirth adds onto that about the same heaping amount all over again.  Plus, Rebirth plays much more smoothly and is much less buggy, has cooler interactions between many more of the items (just about every combination you could possibly think of works as intended in often insane ways), and well.. it's just better.  Straight up.  get it, love it.
And for the squeamish?  Seriously dude, I'm the most sensitive guy I know and I usually hate body humor but Isaac is so GODDAMN GREAT it just doesn't matter.  Play it for more than 10 minutes and you'll see.  If this type of game appeals to you at all, you'll end up loving the insane, quirky art and design styles in time too.

The Binding of Isaac is not for the weak of heart. For starters the game is filled with grotesque designed areas and enemies which for some will be a surefire turnoff. Hell, you use a child's tears for combat throughout the game if that gives you any idea. It's also fairly difficult, with RNG being one of the biggest causes of difficulty, but not without challenging mechanics either. If you can get past that though, or even enjoy these factors, Isaac is a brilliant game. The RNG adds tons of replayability and difficulty, with "useless" or hard to use items being important to recognize as much as if not more than the good ones. Most everything about this game is fun to me, but only because I can get past the imagery of the game, with all sorts of malformed and malignant enemies and environments. Definitely pick up if you like rougelikes, rng, gross imagery, and/or being screwed over by tiny weak spiders after killing demons.

Realm of the Mad God is a massively multiplayer online shooter video game created by Wild Shadow Studios (acquired by Kabam in June 2012, and later sold to Deca Games in July 2016) and Spry Fox. It was in public beta from January 2010 and the browser version launched on June 20, 2011.[2] On February 20, 2012 the game was made available on the digital distribution platform Steam for Microsoft Windows and OS X.[3]
The game has been described as a "massively-multiplayer cooperative bullet hell shooter" with an 8 bit pixelated art style.[2] Players control characters who have been transported to the realm of Oryx (the titular Mad God) to become food for his many minions and abominations, which the players must dispatch. Central to the design of the game is the fact that character death is permanent. Upon death, the player's character is lost along with all carried equipment, although the player may store a number of items for safekeeping in a limited capacity vault away from danger. Different character choices in class also help make the game more diverse and help to support teamwork.
The game is free-to-play with optional in-game micro-transactions. Items which can be bought with optional transactions include in-game equipment vary from high-level equipment, pets that provide aid to the player (by attacking enemies, paralyzing enemies, healing the character, restoring the character's magic points, and acting as a decoy) increased storage space, and aesthetic features such as skins, cloths and dyes.[4]
This game client is written in Flash and can be played in-browser on the official site, on Kongregate, or it can be downloaded from the Google Chrome Web Store. Realm of the Mad God is also available on Steam.[5]

Gameplay[edit]
The game consists of players shooting projectiles from their weapons and destroying enemies to earn experience, fame, and equipment. A character moves around using the WASD keys (though other controls can be chosen) and uses the mouse to aim and clicks to shoot.[6] Contrary to usual practice in MMOs, the experience for killing monsters is awarded in full to each player present, rather than split. This, along with the possibility of teleporting to any player on the map instantly and a cooldown of 10 seconds to teleport again, makes it very easy and attractive to team up.
After a certain amount of experience has been earned, the player levels up and their attributes are raised, allowing them to fight more powerful enemies and unlock more classes. The maximum level a player can achieve is level 20. The player can then gain "fame" on their character, which eventually grants permanent stars that indicate accomplishment and may entitle one to a place on the game's leaderboards upon death. Character death is permanent, meaning that the character's items and statistics are lost.
Players begin their game sessions in the Nexus, a safe haven which can be teleported to at any time. In the Nexus, players may buy consumables using gold purchased with real-life money or they may trade with another character. Another currency is fame, gained when you die. The player enters realms (i.e. game map instances present on the server). Each of these realms are named after powerful monsters in the game(i.e. Medusa, Djinn, Cyclops, Beholder). The capacity of each realm is 85 people at once, and a full realm cannot be entered until a player in it dies or leaves. However, if many players enter a realm at the same time, it can exceed 85.
Players fight a monster in game. HUD elements such as the inventory can be seen on the right-hand side.
During gameplay, the player is directed to "quest" monsters indicated by a red marker at the edge of the game window. As they level up in the realm, they are guided from the "Lowlands" areas at the edges of the map, through the "Midlands" and "Highlands" to the more difficult "Godlands" in the center of the map. The Godlands hosts powerful monsters known as the Gods of the Realm. Completing certain quests allows "event" bosses to spawn, which can be killed to obtain higher-tier loot and open portals to the rarest dungeons.
Killing high-level monsters can grant the player permanent stat boost potions, which are rare and exist in eight variations that correspond to the major attributes(life, mana, vitality, wisdom, defense, dexterity, attack, and speed). Consuming stat potions allows the player to improve their characters stats after reaching the highest level, which can be done until the attribute is maxed out (indicated by its text turning gold). Upon death, the size of the grave left behind corresponds to the number of stats maxed. Items could previously be retrieved from graves, but this functionality was removed as it led to players luring others to their doom to loot their graves.
The 14 classes currently available are Wizard, Priest, Archer, Rogue, Warrior, Knight, Paladin, Assassin, Necromancer, Huntress, Mystic, Trickster, Ninja, and Sorcerer. Players begin with only the Wizard class unlocked and successively unlock the remaining classes as they gain experience with each class.[7] There are 8 main stats, defense, attack, speed, dexterity, vitality, wisdom, mana, and life. Each class has its own weapon, armor and ability specifications, base statistic averages and statistic caps. For example, Warriors, Knights, and Paladins have high defense and are the only ones that can use swords and heavy armor, while the Assassin, Rogue and Trickster have the highest potential movement speed and dexterity (rate of fire) statistics and can only use daggers and hide armor.
Items are classified into tiers, with higher tier items having better stats. Tiers range from T0-T12 for weapons, T1-T13 for armors, T0-T6 for rings, and T0-T6 for abilities.[8] Some items are un-tiered, giving them a special classification. These items are typically unique, with examples including limited use items, powerful weapons, armor, rings, abilities, and April Fools' Day accouterments. The best items appear in special bags, known as White bags, Purple bags, Cyan Bags, or Potion Bags. These Bags will only drop for players who have delivered a certain percentage of the monster's damage, and can only be seen and picked up by the player it dropped for. Un-tiered (UT) items are currently "Soulbound" which means it is unable to get picked up by any other player or traded to another player.
The game features guilds, each allowing for a maximum of 50 players. A guild costs the founding player 1000 fame to name and create, and has a guild hall which can be accessed by members of the guild. Upon a member's death, guild fame is earned proportionally to the amount of fame that the player earned. Guilds can buy upgrades such as larger guild halls and cosmetic features with the guild fame.[9]
Development[edit]
The game was originally created by Alex Carobus and Rob Shillingsburg, founders of Wild Shadow Studios, for TIGSource's "Assemblee Competition" in October 2009, which limited the competitors to a very small sample of art resources.[10] The developers described the aim of the game was to "shake things up by breaking as many MMO ‘rules’ as we could"[11] It was noticed and received a good response from players,[12] prompting the developers to work on a full game. The game was finally launched in a beta stage on January 10, 2010.[10]
Following the initial launch, Spry Fox joined the development team, helping bring the game to a full release out of beta on June 20, 2011.
To help fund the game's development, optional microtransactions were added to the game, drawing a mixed response from players.[13] The developers defended the microtransactions, saying "they seemed like the most convenient, customer-friendly way to pay for the game... those that passionately love the game, can spend as much as they want, helping us to grow the game over time."

As unbelieveable as it sounds, Fran Bow does a remarkable job doing exactly what Antichamber does; twisting what you see, making you question if what you are seeing is actually real or not. It's astonishing how sucked into a point & click game I've somehow become. A game where the ending raises more questions than answers, and that's not really a bad thing in this case. Currently the ending allows for much of a player's own interpretation of what actually happened. I personally feel that it was a buildup for some kind of sequel or DLC to come for the game.
Do yourself a favor. I saw the game played back when it was still in development, and it was only the first chapter and then some. Take your time exploring the game world, many things can be clicked on repeatedly for some additional info, which helps you understand the lore a bit more. I would estimate the first blind playthrough will take about 10-15 hours. Personally, I wish I had spent waaaay more time walking around in chapter three anyway because of the absolutely amazing environment.
Seriously, the chapter three area has more soul and charm than any other game location I've seen in a long time.

Can't get your puppy or grown dog to settle down to sleep at night? Does it whine all night long? Here are a few ideas about how to change this behavior—or accommodate it in your home.
Identify the Problem. Puppies may miss the noise and warmth of a litter. Dogs are creatures of habit-- a change of sleeping situation may be the problem. If something stressful to the dog has recently happened, perhaps this needs to be addressed.
For a sleepless puppy: Make sure you have the following things: a warm bean bag or mat, and a clock that makes a rhythmic ticking sound. Put these articles under a cushion or a blanket where your dog sleeps! It should work like magic. You can also put the clock next to your dog. However you could also try putting a radio on softly.
If your dog is accustomed to sleeping in a crate, kennel, or other small space he or she may have a hard time sleeping in an open room. If you prefer your dog to sleep out in the open, or you don't have a crate, it may take a few nights of whining and pacing for her to get used to the new situation. Be patient! Show her where you want her to sleep, and, if she knows the command, tell her to do a "Down" and "Stay." You may need to get out of bed to correct incorrect behavior--but it'll be worth it in the long run.
If you want your dog to sleep in a crate, but he isn't "crate trained" it may take some time to get him used to the crate. Put special treats in the back of crate before you lead him to it. Make sure that when you say "Kennel" or "bedtime" you use a positive tone of voice--going into the crate to sleep shouldn't be a punishment. If you use it as a punishment, you may find that your dog never grows accustomed to the crate as a relaxing and quiet place.
Perhaps there are other issues--a big event, a change in household set-up-- that the dog is responding to. Just remember, dogs are happiest when the same thing happens everyday in the same way. A small change to you (like moving your bedroom furniture) may seem like a big deal to the dog. He'll get used to the change with patient and consistent correction from you.
Exercise! Dogs need about 40 minutes a day of running, panting, aerobic exercise. A restless dog at night may be a dog who needs more time tiring himself out.
Food. Dogs absorb energy from their food differently than humans do--because their food is a little different. Generally, dogs get a big energy push right after eating, so if you feed your dog late at night, she may be too energetic to get to sleep. Try feeding her earlier, and be sure to let her relieve herself before bedtime.
Warnings
Be careful about the temperature of the hot item. It should be warm to the touch. A normal dog's body temperature is around 102 degrees Fahrenheit, so oppositely, don't make it too cold.

A Wild Catgirl Appears! follows the story of high schooler Ami as she is forced to join a club. While creating a game featuring a ninja catgirl, the catgirl figure (basically an Amiibo) comes to life and starts living with her. You'll be able to go down one of four romance paths in this fairly short visual novel.
A Wild Catgirl Appears! features some of the most clashing art I've ever seen. Some CG images are very clearly done by two different artists, often with parts of their "regular" model pasted onto the body of some MS Paint drawing. The internal resolution also seems to be no where near what the resolutions you can set the game at, causing a lot of pixelation in both the images and the menus.
There's not much notable about the story besides there suddenly just being catgirls. You can't scroll back through the dialogue at all either, as A Wild Catgirl Appears! lacks certain basic functions every other VN I've read has had - a backlog. There's also no way to fast forward through previously read text, meaning if you want to get all the paths, you'll have to click through it manually.
There's not much in the way to really recommend about this game. There are much better VN's out there. So save your money and just look elsewhere, even if you are into the whole catgirl thing.

I don't want to give this a thumbs down due to the fact that I did get enjoyment out of it, but I will be mentioning the problems I had with it before the things I liked, mainly so we can END on a good note. A lot of these things are issues noted in previous reviews, but I felt a lot of them seemed a tad on the aggressive side, so let me try my hand at this.
-The art is really inconsistent. The basic conversation models I like, but once you get into actual "scenes", bodies look strange and different, as if the head were cut and pasted onto someone else's work. This didn't bother me as much as it did other people, but I can certainly understand why it would be a turn off.
-The writing and story seemed... rushed. I will admit that the entire plot seems a little cliche, but that wasn't my issue. As an author, what bothered me was that the game seemed to want to rush the relationships into your face as soon as possible, with very little development of ships or the characters to serve as the meat of the romance sandwich. At face value, the characters are cute and likable, but if you go a bit deeper there's just something... lacking.
-The routes are really unclear. My first playthrough, I ended up with Ria when I was making every choice with the intent of trying to cater to Starla. It left me questioning where the route divulged, and that's not good for a visual novel. While this wouldn't be a major point if the story and choices weren't the focus of the game, they are so it impacts the experience pretty heavily.
Now, onto what I enjoyed:
- The characters, as I said, are likeable, at least at face value. We have a few of your common archetypes here, and they're all character tropes that I enjoy seeing. The shy nerd, the hyperactive goofball, the aggro tsundere, they all made for a funny experience to me. Not only that, but the art that wasn't odd-look appealed to me. I mentioned being an author, but I've also been drawing for about 10 years now, and I like the way the characters look.
- Despite the lack of character development, things in general are very quirky, in a good way. There were certain things that made me chuckle, and why the catgirl thing has been done to hell and back, that doesn't make it bad. Despite the aspects the game falls short in, it still has its own kind of charm.
Something to keep in mind is that my first dating sim of any kind was Huniepop, which is vastly different from most dating sim/visual novels. I knew what to expect with a typical one like this, but I think I may still be holding things to Huniepop standards. This is by no means a terrible game, it just feels more like someone's first attempt, a game I'd sit down to beta test for a friend rather than something that was obtained by paying money.
I think, with a proper, dedicated staff, the devs of this game could really do something amazing, and I honestly look forward to what they put out next.

Sleeping Dogs was a game I wasn't sure about at first. It looked too linear, not enough weapons or vehicles, possibly a garbage campaign. But I bought this game when it was on sale to try it anyways. Needless to say im blown away. This Game has an immense focus on fighting and hand to hand combat whichy is suprising given the GTA style free roaming. Another great thing is the wide diversity of vehicles at your expense to use. With multiple races and side missions to play in game, having different vehicles to test out and play around with sure is a blast. Manuvering the city is also a fun little challenge due to the crowded streets of Honk Kong, it makes it sometimes hard to get away fromm the cops as easily as you'd like. Another thing is the campagin. I figured it would be like GTA, or Saints row, where you're part of a gang and you go do illegal things over and over. But nope, your character is Wei Shen, and undercover cop! Thats something I really loved about this game. The Campaign was so fresh and different. And massive credit to the voice actors of the game! The interactions between Wei shen and the Honk Kong PD as well as fellow Gangs was superb! You will definetly get your moneys worth out of this game AND the DLC. If you havn't picked up Sleeping Dogs already, do your game library a solid and add it to your collection!

Note : this is the third review I'm doing on this title. the original one was ~40hrs online gameplay and I rated it positive.
We're now in 2017, second season.
The game being almost about human VS human gameplay so I'll rate this here.
Now after +100hours of online gameplay :
At short term with friends the game is fun, much more than the initial release, after the multiples patches but....it is STILL absolutlety in any way balanced, making it infuriating for network play.
Balance being critical in a game with large characters roster it is the very precise point which permit the review to rise or fall.
Unfortunately it falls, really, really down.
The game core actually lacks the presence of actuals goldens rules (main rules you'll never break no matter what).
The goldens rules should put the main game accessible and action/reaaction learnable and results understable by the players.
In this game, be prepared to be anti-aired by straight low punch, ultra being stopped by similar situation and so on...
The second flaw is that the characters roster is growing larger on a regular basis and the general character balancing doesn't evolve correctly to fix the 1st point.
Introducing more and more characters with obviously bad ideas such as:
* zoning though fireballs high firing rate
* 40% + juggle combo damages
* multiple normals being anti-air (of course one isn't enough, lets give them 2, 3 or more...)
* ...leaving more than half the roster with no tool to be useful in combat situation.
In network VS you'll find the same 5 characters over and over due to this evident lack of balancing.
It provides a really bad feeling at long term as the game seems disabled of more than half its potential (and it grows worst due to the arrival of new characters).
The whole SFV gameplay is a battle of action/reaction but it also fails hard here.
Having a human opponent at the other end doesn't helps : the gameplay gives almost no room for personnal expression and creativity : you'll always see the same strategies over and over and its boring if not frustrating.
In a regular round you tend to expect being able to read about 8 to 12 times the actions of your opponent and react accordingly ( or fail and be punished ). In SFV it is reduced far too low; expect a battle to be a 3 to 5 read at most. Multiples characters tends to do high output damage with quick stun effect behind leaving you open to much more damage. I think damage reduce is not correctly tuned here.
Too many unpunishables moves are still presents per characters may they be specials or normals. Reducing them will surely help with over-pressure symptoms and will help increase the number or read-react per round.
In the current state the game is still at the limit of fun/meh mostly due to the previous points mentionned previously.
Therefor for long term games use, I can't recommend it. At all.

Doom 3 stays faithful to the early ID formula of well-done hallway shooter.  The horror element is accomplished by continual jump scares that I learned to love.  You creep along, then all hell breaks loose as creatures teleport into a room, the doors lock, and you frantically dodge and switch weapons.  Frequent saves and deterministic spawn points are the only defense against this, but that's Doom for you, and it was fun.  I've only played hard-mode, I died a lot which made for a lot of scares, not sure if easier modes are as fun.
Update for Doom 2: tons of fun, I may have gotten more enjoyment out of this one than Doom 3.  1990's graphics, but the gameplay that often involves fighting tens of enemies at the same time is just plain arcade-style fun.
Update for difficulty: After playing Doom 3 on Veteran (Hard) difficulty, I played Doom 2 and the last Doom 3 add-on on Medium difficulty because I kinda wanted to experience their maps without saving every few minutes.  It wasn't nearly as scary, so I'd recommend at least the first Doom 3 on Hard, and then just have fun with the remaining episodes on Medium.
